Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz to traffic within seven days if certain conditions are met, as the cost of the seven-month conflict begins to weigh on both sides.
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said in New York on Thursday that mediators have submitted a plan to the White House that would pave the way for the waterway to reopen in a week and talks to restart.
He said Iran’s demands were contained in the Islamabad Memorandum signed by Trump earlier in the year, before talks broke down.
Earlier in the day, Araghchi met with UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband, the first meeting between British and Iranian ministers in a year. Miliband urged the importance of freedom of navigation, warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple held in Tehran.
US and Iranian negotiators were also exploring a possible ‘phased’ solution to the crisis, prioritising the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, per Reuters.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey discuss aid for Riyadh in New York
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly to plan a meeting to discuss aid for Riyadh in its fight with the Houthis, the Saudi Gazette reported on Friday.
The ministers were said to have reviewed ongoing preparations for a chiefs of staff meeting, which will look at their respective responsibilities under their defence pact.
And Turkey’s defence ministry said on Friday that the military chief of staff was heading to Saudi Arabia for a meeting with peers.
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have ramped up attacks on Saudi ships and infrastructure in recent weeks, seizing land on the Red Sea coast to squeeze the Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which Riyadh exports oil with the Strait of Hormuz closed.
Saudi Arabia has a joint defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey - under which an attack on one is considered an attack on all - but neither have yet offered material support.
The latest: Iran suggests Strait of Hormuz could reopen within a week
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said in New York on Thursday that his country’s mediators have submitted a plan to the White House that would pave the way for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen within a week.
“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the mediators that if certain conditions are met ... the strait will be open in seven days”, he said.
Should both sides reach an agreement, they could restart negotiations for a final deal, Araghchi added.
Reuters reportedly separately on Thursday that US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a possible ‘phased’ solution to the crisis, prioritising the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
Iran’s motivation to end the crisis is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation, officials said, noting that neither side wants to be the first to back down.
A phased agreement would involve Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix after the interim Islamabad Memorandum collapsed in July.
A central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Yemeni VP says weapons, technology should be kept from rebels' hands
Arguing that protecting the strait "is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation," Yemen’s vice president Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels' hands.
For years, the UN Security Council has imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis and an asset freeze and travel ban on their leaders and top officials.
Iran denies arming the Houthis, but smuggled Iranian weapons and parts have been seized from numerous shipments bound for Yemen, and a report by UN experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies.
Al Alimi-Bawzer contended on Thursday that the rebels wouldn't have been able to maintain their position for a dozen years without Iranian weapons, expertise and military technologies.
The Houthis claimed on Thursday to have fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia's southwestern Jazan province. A Saudi military spokesperson, Major General Turki al-Malki, said the kingdom intercepted six ballistic missiles targeting its Red Sea port of Yanbu and the southwestern city of Taif, blaming the Houthis.
His statement followed alerts by Saudi civil defence authorities, who later noted the danger had passed.
Yemen tells UN that Houthi rebels' moves on key strait threaten global economy
Yemen's internationally recognised government pressed world leaders anew on Thursday for help defeating the Houthis, saying that their new perch along one of the world's busiest waterways presents an international economic risk.
The Houthis — who have controlled Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north for over a decade — stormed down Yemen's coast this month and seized the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands.
That gives them better surveillance of ships passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, at the sea's southern end. About 12 per cent of the world's trade usually passes through the waterway.
The rebels have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping. While asserting there's no other threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, they have warned other nations not to get involved.
But the vice president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN General Assembly not to trust the Houthis' assurances and to see a bigger picture in the strife around the strait.
Russian, Iranian foreign ministers say only diplomatic solution to conflict around Iran
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov and his Iranian counterpart met on Thursday and Moscow said both agreed that only a diplomatic settlement could end tension in the Middle East sparked by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
"Current regional and international issues were discussed with emphasis on the situation around Iran," Russia's foreign ministry said in a statement after Lavrov and Iran's Abbas Araqchi met in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"It was stressed that there is no alternative to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the illegal actions of the United States and Israel."
Russian president Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian signed a strategic cooperation partnership in 2025 which provides for a deepening of bilateral ties and closer defence cooperation, but includes no mutual defence clause.
Each side has provided the other with military know-how and equipment.
Pezeshkian thanked Putin earlier this month for Moscow's position on the Iran war and said together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism".
Netanyahu praises Trump during his UNGA speech
Benjamin Netanyahu was making a short visit to the US for his UN address and, unusually, without a planned meeting with US president Donald Trump, whom he praised during his speech.
"We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice. In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump. I thank him. I thank him for his bold leadership," he said.
UN delegates walk out of Netanyahu speech
Delivering a defiant address to the United Nations on Thursday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu mounted a firm defence of Israel's regional military actions, attempting to push back against deepening global isolation ahead of upcoming domestic elections.
As he approached the podium inside the General Assembly hall, several delegations staged a walkout in protest, prompting the Israeli leader to label those departing "moral cowards."

The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?
In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”
Also Read: Google to report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities
The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?
While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.
While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds
Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.
Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?
NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.
Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.
Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?
Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.
NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Scientists sound the alarm over disappearing kelp, lobster and crayfish as marine heatwaves worsen
The shifting conditions are altering aquatic ecosystems with devastating impacts on certain European fisheries and coastal livelihoods

The intense heat that brought widespread drought and wildfires to Europe this summer extended far beyond the land.
Sea surface temperatures across the continent reached their highest levels for the summer period since dependable satellite records started in 1982, an analysis of marine data shows.
Temperature records were broken from the English Channel to the Mediterranean Sea. On 5 August, an offshore buoy anchored near Mallorca registered 33.02 degrees Celsius (91.44 degrees Fahrenheit), marking the warmest temperature ever recorded by the Spanish port authority's monitoring system.
Experts caution that marine heatwaves of this nature are growing in frequency, severity, and extent as global greenhouse gas emissions elevate air temperatures worldwide. Earth's oceans take in most of this trapped thermal energy, holding onto it far longer than land surfaces or the atmosphere.
These shifting conditions are altering aquatic ecosystems with devastating impacts on certain European fisheries and coastal livelihoods, based on scientific literature alongside testimonies from over a dozen analysts, researchers, and fishing sector figures. Marine species that long supported local communities in southern England and Spain are departing, replaced by non-native species migrating into newly warmed habitats.
"What is surprising is the speed at which this occurs," Jean-Pierre Gattuso, senior research scientist at France's National Centre for Scientific Research, said of Europe's warming seas. "Records are broken almost every day in many places."
Across the continent as a whole, European marine waters averaged 21.6 C (70.9 F) from June to August, setting a peak across 45 years of collected observations.
Among the most affected regions was the Bay of Biscay, situated along the Atlantic coast shared by France and Spain.
Reaching from Galicia’s Cape Ortegal to Pointe de Penmarch in southern Brittany, the bay—where waters are typically cool—averaged 21.4 C (70.5 F) across the summer, exceeding the 1991–2020 baseline by more than 2.4 degrees (4.4 degrees). Measurements from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reached a satellite-era high of 23.2 C (74 F) on 13 August.
Marine heatwaves are defined by researchers as periods of five or more consecutive days where water temperatures significantly exceed historical baselines. While the Bay of Biscay experienced only a few heatwave days annually during the 1980s, analysis shows it had accumulated 186 heatwave days by late August this year, representing over three-quarters of the period.
DISAPPEARING KELP, LOBSTER, CRAYFISH
The Bay of Biscay's cool waters, long prized by Spaniards seeking relief from the heat of the Mediterranean coast, were immortalized in Ernest Hemingway's 1926 novel "The Sun Also Rises." The book's protagonist recovers after weeks of dissolution on the northern beaches of San Sebastian.
"Now if you want to swim in cold water, you have to go to the westernmost portion of Galicia," in the far northwestern corner of Spain, said Jose Manuel Rico Ordas, a professor of marine ecology at the University of Oviedo in the northern Asturias region.
Galicia benefits from strong winds that push warm surface water away from the coast during the summer months, allowing cold, deep-sea water to take its place in a process known as upwelling.
Rico Ordas has been spending summers on the bay since he was a child and now studies its transformation.
Back then, there were extensive underwater forests of kelp, which provide vital food, shelter and nurseries for dozens of species that sustain the region's small-scale fisheries. But he estimates roughly 95% of the large, brown seaweed stands have disappeared, based on sampling along the rugged Asturias coast since 2010. He attributes the decline primarily to climate change.
Kelp needs cold water – typically below 20 C (68 F) – to survive. Higher temperatures were once exceptionally rare in the bay, Rico Ordas told Reuters.
"Now, it's the opposite," he said.
Fish overgrazing – in particular by dreamfish, which thrive in warmer temperatures – has added to the kelp's decline, he said.
The impacts have been stark.
"We are finding no more lobster, no more crayfish, no more sea urchins and many other species that are associated with the good status of kelp forests," Rico Ordas said.
Concerned fishermen have been teaming up with scientists and environmental activists to try to restore kelp forests by planting seedlings grown in laboratories.
Manuel Angel Reiriz Gonzalez, president of a local fishermen's guild in Galicia, recently ferried members of one such project in a boat he uses for sport fishing charters out of the port of Ribeira. The group brought a box full of small stones seeded with kelp, which they tossed into the choppy waters.
Climate change threatens a way of life that has sustained Gonzalez's community for generations, he said. His family has been diving for sea urchins and harvesting clams for more than a century. But now, he said, recurring heatwaves are hurting shellfish stocks.
The area has also seen an influx of Portuguese man o' war and trigger fish from warmer climes to the south – species that prey on local fish and crustaceans.
"We had some very bad years for clam production, but we worked on seeding them, and the species gradually adapted," Gonzalez said.
He hopes the seabed restoration efforts can do the same for kelp forests.
The disappearance of kelp could lead to the decline of sea urchins and other species fishermen depend on, he said. "At that point, as a fishing guild, we would cease to exist."
'OCTOPUS APOCALYPSE'
In other European waters, new, invasive species from the Red Sea and beyond are entering the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, displacing native populations, reshaping food chains and threatening fisheries, researchers say. In all, there are more than 1,000 non-indigenous species in the Mediterranean, according to a recent report by the Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts, based on surveys by scientists in 11 countries.
Some native species are coping with the warmer temperatures better than others.
A massive swarm of jellyfish shut down reactors at France's Gravelines nuclear power plant in August when they clogged its cooling system – for the second time in as many years. The plant in northern France is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea.
Fishermen on the south coast of England are reporting a surge in landings of common octopus. Around 2,600 metric tons were caught last year and upwards of 3,000 tons so far this year, according to figures compiled by the UK Marine Management Organisation. Before 2025, annual landings were less than 30 tons.
Octopus larvae are carried into British waters on currents from breeding grounds near the Channel Islands, Brittany and places further south, said Bryce Stewart, senior research fellow at the Plymouth-based Marine Biological Association (MBA).
Previously, many didn't survive the frigid temperatures. But since 2022, the English Channel has been under heatwave conditions for around six months out of the year on average, logging more than 900 days in all, the Reuters analysis found.
"Now they're actually breeding in UK water quite prolifically," Stewart said.
For Ian Perkes, owner of the eponymous fish merchants in the south Devon seaside town of Brixham, the octopus bloom has proved a boon.
There is a ready market in southern Europe for the once-rare species and no fishing quotas, he said. "There was one week where we had 200,000 kilos (200 tons)."
But not everyone profits from the shellfish-loving octopuses, which feed on local lobsters, brown crabs and scallops.
For members of the South Devon and Channel Shellfishermen's cooperative, 2026 has been an "octopus apocalypse," according to its executive officer, Beshlie Pool. One recent fishing trip yielded a single crab all day, she said.
The MBA estimates the octopus bloom could account for about £10 million ($13.25 million) in lost shellfish catches against about £12 million in octopus landings between January and September 2025.
But the benefits are not evenly distributed. Some shellfishermen have switched to catching octopuses, but many do not have the necessary equipment, Pool said. Four of the coop's 90-some vessels have gone out of business in the past 12 months.
The unpredictability of the changes makes it hard to adapt, Stewart added.
"Will the octopus still be here next year?" he asked. "If they've eaten all the crabs and lobsters, and the octopus die off, then what do we do?"

Each additional 100 grams consumption of ultra-processed foods daily could be associated with a 14% increased chance of cardiovascular events, according to a study.
Every 10% increase in weight per energy intake due to ultra processed foods was associated with a 16% greater risk of metabolic syndromes or diabetes, findings published in the journal Family Medicine and Community Health showed.
Researchers, including those from Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore, analysed data from 51 studies from the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Oceania, involving more than 88 lakh participants -- on average aged 23-77 -- with follow-ups ranging between 2 and 32 years.
Eating a lot of ultra processed foods was associated with higher risks of cardiovascular events (24%), cancer (12%) and obesity or overweight (23%).
Consumption of the energy-dense, high-on-sugar and salt products was also related with a higher chance of metabolic syndrome or diabetes (24%), depression and anxiety (27%), digestive diseases (31%), high blood pressure (11%) and death from any cause (18%).
Ultra processed foods are ready-to-eat or heat-and-serve products that have undergone extensive industrial processing. They are low in dietary fibre, protein, vitamins, and minerals.
“Dose-response analyses demonstrated each additional 100 (grams per day) intake was associated with 11% higher hypertension risk, 14% higher cardiovascular events risk, 4% higher cancer risk, and 3% higher all-cause mortality; each 10% increase in weight (per) energy intake was associated with a 16% higher MetS (or) diabetes risk,” the authors wrote.
Emerging evidence suggests that a combination of multiple additives may exert a ‘cocktail effect’ on human health, they said.
The team added that lab studies have shown that the extensively altered physical composition of ultra processed foods may adversely affect the gut microbiome, and promote inflammation and insulin resistance, among other things.
Several compounds that may form during food processing, such as acrylamide -- a contaminant formed in heat-treated processed foods -- and acrolein, generated during fat heating, have been associated with a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease, they said.
"Given that UPF related chronic diseases often cluster as multimorbidity, reducing consumption of UPFs (ultra processed foods) and replacing them with minimally processed alternatives may be relevant for chronic disease prevention and primary care management," the authors said. PTI

Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim too
- Published
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.
Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.
"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.
Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.
Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".
But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external
Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.
In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.
"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."
In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.
But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.
In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.
Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.
"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.
Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."
Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."
'She should pay for it'
Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.
A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.
The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.
Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.
Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.
The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.
On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.
"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.
Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."
"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.
"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."
The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.
The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want.
"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."
Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.
"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.
"These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."
Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime.
"People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says.
"Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

Two smoke shop employees have been arrested on felony drug charges following a police raid near the University of Mississippi, days after two students were found dead in separate incidents with packages of kratom found at the scenes.
Officers seized more than 500 units of kratom, THC cartridges, gummies and other suspected narcotics during a raid on Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store, roughly a mile from the Ole Miss campus.
Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, from Oxford, were booked for possession of Schedule I controlled substances with intent to distribute. Authorities noted that the store’s owner, 40-year-old Amer Alowdi, fled the country after being indicted for narcotics trafficking in 2022.
Freshman Aidan Hamilton, 18, and junior Robert Strang, 20, were both found dead Monday. Though officials have not confirmed a direct link between the shop and the fatalities, the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit previously disclosed that “packaged Kratom sold from a retail store” was discovered at both scenes.
Strang, a Phi Delta Theta fraternity member from Atlanta, Georgia, was found at an off-campus home, student newspaperThe Daily Mississippian reported. Hamilton, from Colorado, was reportedly discovered at a male dormitory on campus. Emergency services responded to a “possible OD” at a dorm on the day the bodies were discovered, according to a Lafayette County dispatch recording obtained by WMC Action 5 News.
“They do not believe the subject is breathing — trying to start CPR over the phone,” a voice said on the recording. “I believe they’re still trying to get somebody in the dorms to do, or in the building to do CPR.”
Investigators are awaiting expedited toxicology results to determine what caused the students’ deaths and what substances were involved.
The narcotics unit stated that it did “not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death.”
A representative from the American Kratom Association, an advocacy group representing the industry, told Fox News that bad actors often deceptively market illicit or chemically modified products under the guise of natural kratom. He expressed condolences to the families and the Ole Miss community while cautioning against attributing the fatalities to any specific product before official toxicology results were finalized.
“We’re not defending a product involved in these deaths because no one yet knows what that product, if any, caused them,” the representative, Mac Haddow, said.
Kratom, an opioid-like substance, is legal in parts of Mississippi but remains restricted within Lafayette County, where Ole Miss is located.
The Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit said that “Kratom has been prohibited from possession, distribution, and sale within the City of Oxford since 2019.”
The investigation is ongoing and more arrests could follow, according to officials.
“Our message is direct: if you choose to illegally sell these substances in our community, expect law enforcement to come looking for you,” investigators said Friday. “We will investigate. We will obtain warrants.
“We will seize illegal products, and we will hold those responsible accountable. This investigation does not end with these arrests. These individuals and this business are not necessarily the only people involved in the illegal distribution of these products, and they should not expect to be the last arrests made as our enforcement efforts continue.”
Police have urged the public to “avoid kratom and any other medication or substance that was not prescribed to you or obtained from a trusted, regulated source.”

Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
- Published
A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.
An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.
Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.
Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.
As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.
For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.
Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.
The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.
Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.
Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community.
By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.
The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.
In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.
When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.
They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible.
Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List.
"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool.
"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds.
"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."
Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.
But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.
For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live.
"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore.
"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."
The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.
And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.
In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.
But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise.
"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."
The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow.
Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years.
Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.
Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success.
South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.
Then came the scandals.
In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.
Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal.
It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.
South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.
Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience.
Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more.
"Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs."
The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong.
The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition.
Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted.
While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances.
Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets.
"I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy."
For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance.
"I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin.
"Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream."
Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube.
"Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um.
"It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations."
While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life.
As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd.
Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut.
As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

Taking action like this allows GoFundMe to protect donors’ generosity and our continued ability to support people who are fundraising to help others.”
The campaign was set up after Erin Howell, a local resident, spotted Johnson struggling with heavy bags.
“The other day, I looked out my door cam and saw an 81-year-old man slowly and painstakingly carrying my heavy luggage that had been lost on a recent flight up a steep flight of stairs,” Howell wrote in a GoFundMe entry. “He looked absolutely exhausted, and his steps were heavy with effort.”
After speaking with him, she learned that Johnson began working as an independent contractor delivering lost luggage to people's homes three years ago to help pay for his wife, Josephine, who is battling cancer, Howell wrote. The couple has been together for 57 years.
Howell asked Johnson why he picked such a physically demanding job, and he reportedly told her that it was the “only job that will hire me.”
“The staggering medical bills, continuous treatments, expensive prescription medications, and everyday costs of living have completely overwhelmed them,” Howell wrote of Johnson's situation. “At an age when he should be resting and spending every precious single moment by his wife's side, he is out on the road lifting heavy bags just to keep her alive and cared for.”
Howell said she started the GoFundMe to help Johnson retire without having to give up on paying for his wife's cancer treatments.
She said that all of the money raised would go toward paying for Josephine's medical bills, which would allow Johnson to stop working and focus solely on caring for his wife. She added that Johnson was unlikely to ask for help.
“He is a deeply proud, selfless, and dedicated husband who would never ask for charity himself, which is exactly why I am stepping in… to start this GoFundMe campaign,” Howell wrote. “He shouldn't have to carry this crushing financial and physical weight all by himself anymore.”
Before it was deactivated this week, the fundraiser had garnered over $281,000 in donations, according to Dallas station Fox 4.
In an interview with Fox 4, Donald and Josephine Johnson said they were extremely grateful to everyone who donated to help support them.
“I think I'm going to be able to stop working, and that's amazing,” Donald Johnson said. His wife added: “Some have made comments and they're praying for us. And it's just, it's a joyful feeling.”
It is not clear what specific “factual misrepresentations” were uncovered by GoFundMe. The Independent has sought further information.
“GoFundMe’s policies, along with those of our payment processors, require authenticity and transparency for donors, and are strictly enforced,” the company’s statement noted. “Because that standard wasn't met here, donors were protected under our GoFundMe Giving Guarantee, which guarantees a full refund in the rare case something isn't right.”

Mitsunaka came to ARK from Kawanishi in Hyogo Prefecture after his owner became ill.
Named after Minamoto no Mitsunaka, a powerful and wealthy samurai associated with the area, this Mitsunaka is a gentle soul and quite reserved.

Mitsunaka is fine with most other dogs, but being a gentle soul, he sometimes gets bullied.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Wednesday said the party stood firmly with the demand of the people of Ladakh for meaningful constitutional safeguards, including the Sixth Schedule, to protect Ladakh's land, employment, fragile environment, culture and identity.
He also demanded that the judicial probe into the deaths of four people during statehood protests must ensure accountability and bring out the truth.

In a post on X, Kharge said that a year ago, four young people were shot in Leh during the agitation for the democratic and constitutional rights of the people of Ladakh.
"On Martyrs' Day, we pay our solemn homage to them and stand in complete solidarity with their families.
"The judicial inquiry into the tragic events of September 24 must establish the full truth, ensure accountability and deliver justice without fear or favour. The people of Ladakh have waited long enough for their legitimate aspirations to be addressed," he said.
"The Congress party stands firmly with their demand for meaningful Constitutional safeguards, including the Sixth Schedule, to protect Ladakh's land, employment, fragile environment, culture and identity," the Congress chief said.
Democracy and representative institutions must be fully restored, and the people of Ladakh must have an effective voice in determining their own future, he asserted.
The people of Ladakh have been demanding statehood, which led to violent clashes last year.

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was "nearly killed" in the US-Israel strikes in February targeting his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Mojtaba was then rushed to a Tehran hospital, only to be “pulled from the rubble” again after the US and Israel bombed the medical centre, an Iranian cleric said this week.
According to the New York Post, Mohsen Heydari, a member of Iran's Assembly of Experts, made the revelation in an interview with Qatari television network Al Araby on Thursday (local time).
After obliterating Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s Tehran in February — killing the 86-year-old supreme leader and dozens of his top leaders — the US-Israel also reportedly bombed three different hospitals in Tehran at some time in the days that followed.
“Even after he [Mojtaba Khamenei] had been wounded and taken to the hospital, three hospitals in Tehran were bombed,” Heydari said, according to the New York Post.
“Mojtaba Khamenei was in the third hospital and was pulled from the rubble,” Heydari was quoted as saying.
The New York Post reported that Mojtaba Khamenei, 56, subsequently disappeared to an unknown location and has not been seen publicly or heard from since.
The New York Post also reported that speculation had continued over Mojtaba Khamenei’s condition following the earlier strikes. US intelligence reports had reportedly suggested that he was badly disfigured in the attacks.
Last month, US President Donald Trump stated that he believes Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is still alive, though he suffered severe injuries during ongoing military operations, as a mystery continues to shroud the appearance of the Iranian leader.
Speaking in an interview with US commentator Glenn Beck, Trump addressed widespread speculation regarding Khamenei's fate following months of public absence.
"I don't think he's dead," Trump told Beck. "He was very seriously wounded. The left side of his body, the arm, the leg, the whole thing. He was very seriously wounded, but I don't think he's dead."
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, said in an interview with Fox News this week that Mojtaba Khamenei was “completely” healthy.
“We met for about seven hours,” Pezeshkian told “Special Report” host Bret Baier, referring to a meeting between the two Iranian leaders last month. “We conducted talks.”
According to the news report, Heydari also spoke about the process through which Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as Iran’s new supreme leader on March 8.
He said Mojtaba Khamenei apparently did not know he had been chosen until the announcement was broadcast on Iranian state television.
The Assembly of Experts, which is mandated to choose Iran’s supreme leader, was itself reportedly targeted during the strikes.
The New York Post reported that its Qom Secretariat was bombed, killing eight people and destroying reports and recommendations concerning the selection of a new supreme leader.
Heydari said members of the Assembly subsequently wrote their votes on paper before being summoned to a secret room for the selection process. He recalled being the first member to suggest Mojtaba Khamenei’s name.
“Given the enemy’s position, we will choose and elect no one as leader and supreme guide of the Islamic Republic except Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei,” Heydari recalled saying, according to the news report.
“We obtained information that Mojtaba Khamenei was healthy and able to lead, and we determined that he met the requirements of religious qualification, justice and competence to manage the country,” he was quoted as saying.
The New York Post reported that Mojtaba Khamenei received 50 of 59 votes during the meeting, while eight members voted for Ayatollah Alireza Arafi and one member abstained.
According to the New York Post, Heydari also referred to Mojtaba Khamenei as a “man of the shadows”.
He said Mojtaba had not held a political position within the Iranian state before becoming the supreme leader, although he had reportedly served as an adviser to his father.

IRDAI Resets Insurtech’s Economics The IRDAI has proposed a radical overhaul of the insurance tech sector. The draft norms threaten to dismantle lucrative payout structures, impose commission caps and introduce tighter expense limits for insurance distributors. Can the sector adapt to this new regime? The Commission Reset: IRDAI’s consultation paper seeks to re-introduce product-level commission ceilings. Under the proposed framework, mandatory or near-mandatory products will attract nil or low commissions for IDEs (such as PB Fintech and Turtlemint’s insurtech arm), while products requiring greater selling and servicing efforts will have 15% cap. The IRDAI Eclipse: The regulator has also proposed lowering EoM limits for life and general insurers, while mandating cost audits for all IDEs above ₹100 Cr revenue. The draft norms also ban compulsory loan-insurance bundling, restrict employee incentives and introduce a three-tier distribution structure, with clawback provisions, to curb misselling. Insurtechs On The Edge: For starters, the proposed caps could threaten the high upfront commissions of aggregators, which in turn could take a toll on their user acquisition strategies. Unbundling insurance from loans could also potentially lead to revenue compression across various categories, while pushing competition toward service, technology and product discovery. Markets React Sharply: The draft norms resulted in a major sell-off. PB Fintech shares crashed 36% to ₹1,210, while Turtlemint stock tanked 20% to hit an all-time low of ₹109.1. Brokerages flagged severe margin compression. While Jefferies projected a 10-12% earnings cuts for distributors, Citi warned of 70–90% economics compression in high-margin categories like credit-linked insurance. What's Next? With stakeholder comments due by October 25, final rules may differ from current proposals. Yet the market’s reaction underscores the stakes. Platforms will have to cut acquisition spends and diversify into new areas. They will also have to rethink products and insurer partnerships. So, will lower commissions drive transparency or squeeze margins? Why banks are open today, Sunday — What customers should know
The Reserve Bank of India has approved the opening of all bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches and currency chests on September 27.
Public sector banks and regional rural banks will remain open and operate normally today as the government seeks to ensure uninterrupted services ahead of a proposed three-day nationwide strike from Wednesday.
The Ministry of Finance said the decision was taken in view of the strike called by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU), which comes immediately after the weekend holidays.
Why are banks open on Sunday?
The Reserve Bank of India has approved the opening of all bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches and currency chests on September 27. These facilities will remain fully operational, the ministry said.
The move is aimed at giving customers an additional day of services before the proposed strike begins, preventing disruptions for several days in a row.
“The welfare and convenience of bank customers remains the Government's foremost priority,” it said, while appealing to bank unions to defer the proposed strike.
The government and bank managements had on Tuesday also appealed to the unions to resolve their remaining demands through dialogue, while taking steps to ensure essential banking services continue without interruption.
Strike coincides with month-end closing
The government earlier pointed out that the proposed strike coincides with the half-yearly closing of banks on September 30.
A disruption at that time could affect several operations, including reconciliation, provisioning, treasury and market-related activities.
By keeping banks open on Sunday, authorities are effectively providing customers with an extra day of service, while also seeking to limit the impact of the proposed shutdown on banking operations.
Why are bank employees planning a strike?
The proposed September 28-30 strike follows a one-day strike held on September 11. Bank unions have primarily been seeking the implementation of a five-day banking week and withdrawal of the Performance Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.
The government said it has already decided to keep the PLI scheme in abeyance following discussions with the unions. However, the demand for a five-day workweek is still under examination.

White casts doubt on Fury-Joshua after 24 hours of chaos
- Published
Two days after the announcement British boxing had waited a decade for, Dana White - the UFC president and Zuffa Boxing chief named as one of the figures promoting Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua - was asked whether the fight would actually happen.
"I don't know," he said.
White was speaking at London's Copper Box on Saturday, where British heavyweight Johnny Fisher beat Michael Pirotton on his Zuffa Boxing debut. But for much of the media in attendance another heavyweight fight dominated the evening.
Asked whether Wednesday's scheduled Fury-Joshua news conference in London would take place, White added: "I have no idea."
On Thursday, Fury and Joshua were officially announced to meet at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, live globally on Netflix. By Friday, that certainty had unravelled.
A dispute over who is entitled to promote the event led to claims of contractual breaches, talk of possible replacement fights and another flurry of cryptic social-media posts.
Even by boxing's recent standards, the past 24 hours have been extraordinary - and not a particularly flattering look for the sport.
Why has White's involvement caused a problem?
Netflix and Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's fight announcement was striking for who it included - and who it did not. The event was presented as a collaboration involving Alalshikh's The Ring and White.
There was no mention of Matchroom's Eddie Hearn, who has promoted Joshua throughout his professional career, or Queensberry's Frank Warren, Fury's long-time promoter.
White's involvement was not entirely unexpected.
The Zuffa Boxing promoter has been saying for weeks he would be involved in Fury-Joshua.
Hearn has been equally adamant he would not. After Thursday's announcement, Hearn said Joshua's contract specifically prevented White and American sports entertainment company TKO from having a promotional role, claiming Netflix had not been made aware of that provision.
Hearn said there had been breaches of the agreement which needed to be resolved and cast doubt on whether Wednesday's news conference would go ahead.
Fury says a similar restriction originally appeared in his own contract but was removed because he wanted White involved.
Warren has taken a more pragmatic position. Speaking to BBC Sport before the latest dispute escalated, he said his understanding was White had helped secure the Netflix deal and compromises had been necessary to get the fight made.
On Saturday, White was generally non-committal on the future of the contest but much clearer in his criticism of Hearn. "The guy who is supposed to be helping the fight has been hurting the fight," White said. "He hasn't done the fight any favours."
How did it go from 'official' to rumours it could be off?
The uncertainty intensified on Friday evening.
Reports emerged that Fury-Joshua could be in jeopardy and alternative fights for 11 December were being discussed, including Ryan Garcia against the recently retired three-weight undisputed champion Terence Crawford.
Crawford appeared as surprised as anyone, publicly questioning the suggestion he could be fighting Garcia.
Then Fury intervened.
In a video posted on social media, he claimed Joshua and Hearn were "trying to pull out" and blamed the dispute largely on Hearn's objection to White.
There has been no announcement from Joshua saying he intends to withdraw.
On Instagram, Alalshikh posted pictures of himself with White and later shared a cryptic message in Arabic about somebody attempting to "stab you where you told them it hurts", although he made no explicit reference to Fury-Joshua.
Hearn, meanwhile, posted a picture with a shushing emoji and the message: "Bet against me."
For a fight negotiated so publicly for so many years, the familiar mix of claims, counter-claims and cryptic posts had returned almost immediately.
Fury-Joshua talk takes over Copper Box
Among the media in east London on Saturday, much of the conversation centred around Fury-Joshua.
Who had heard what? Was the fight genuinely in danger? Would Wednesday's news conference happen? And, with White in the building, would he provide any clarity afterwards?
Instead, his post-fight comments only underlined the uncertainty.
White has been openly critical of Hearn, while the precise nature of his own role in Fury-Joshua remains at the heart of the dispute. That distinction could prove significant when lawyers examine exactly what Joshua's contract permits.
During Saturday's US broadcast of the Zuffa Boxing card, it was suggested White was helping Alalshikh on a personal level rather than acting as a promoter. White rejected that interpretation. "I don't know where that came from," he said. "That was weird."
And White offered another tease when asked whether he would attend Wednesday's news conference if it does go ahead. "I guess I'll leave that as a surprise," he said.
So is Fury-Joshua still happening?
For now, officially, yes.
As of Saturday night, Netflix continued to list Fury against Joshua at the Principality Stadium on 11 December and said the fighters would attend Wednesday's news conference.
But the contractual disagreement remains unresolved.
The unusual position is that, little more than 48 hours after the fight was officially announced, one of the central figures in its promotion cannot say whether it will happen - or whether its first major launch event will go ahead.
There is too much money, time and work invested in Fury-Joshua for anyone involved to walk away lightly.
But if the past decade has taught boxing anything, an agreement does not necessarily mean the fight is safe. Fury-Joshua is once again waiting for another hurdle to be cleared.

Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business.
Can Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince save the web from AI?
Cloudflare’s mission to remake the business of the web for the AI age
Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it turns out things are even wilder because of AI, and Matthew and Cloudflare are right at the center of it.
Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.
AI is also upending everything inside of Cloudflare. Earlier this year, the company laid off more than a thousand people — 20 percent of the company — and then Matthew wrote an op-ed about that decision that ran in the Wall Street Journal under the headline, “How I choose which Cloudflare employees to replace with AI.” That’s pure Decoder bait in every single dimension: AI, big controversial decisions, and org charts, all in one.
And one last thing, before we get going: You can subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Matthew Prince, you’re the cofounder and CEO of Cloudflare. Welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks for having me.
I’m really excited to talk to you again. It’s been about two years since you were on the show. I was just looking back over that episode and I said something to you like, “it’s a momentous time for the internet.” And I was not even close. It’s now an even more momentous time for the internet.
You are at the forefront of rebooting how companies work with AI. That is the most Decoder bait of all time. I want to talk about bots and the internet and publishers and Google and all the things that you are in the middle of. But let’s start at the very beginning.
Cloudflare is a complicated, important company. The last time you were on the show, you said, “Cloudflare is a service that makes the internet faster and protects it from bad guys.” Is that still how you would describe what Cloudflare does?
That’s usually what I say when I’m trying to answer a question at a cocktail party and I don’t want to talk to the person any more. What I say if I’m interested in talking to the person more is that Cloudflare is trying to rebuild the internet the way it should have been built from the beginning if we knew how important it was going to be.
We run a giant network. We’re in over 350 cities worldwide, literally thousands of data centers. We have equipment running in all those places, and then we do a handful of things. If you’re trying to put an application or content online, we make sure that it’s safe. If you’re a person or an employee online, we make sure that wherever you go online is safe. We help give people the ability to write applications that can scale to an entire internet audience and run on the infrastructure that we have. That’s the fastest-growing part of our business.
We’ve recently started to think about how the business model of the internet is changing dramatically and we’re trying to help shape what that future business model of the internet looks like and make it as healthy as possible.
Can I connect the dots between the business model of the internet, how the internet should have worked, and Cloudflare trying to build the internet as it should have been?
That is different than, “Cloudflare protects from bad guys.” I will note that’s what you said to me last time, which now makes me feel like you don’t want to talk to me at the cocktail party, but that’s fine. That’s a shift. It’s just a notable shift.
The business model of the internet has dramatically changed because of AI, because of bot traffic, because of AI scrapers, the whole thing. Describe what you think the business model of the internet is right now and what it should be.
For at least the last at least 30 years, the business model of the internet has been advertising. It’s not the entire business model of the internet, but it’s really driven all of the growth of the web and built what we all enjoy today, which really is a miracle.
The company that is responsible for that more than any other is Google, which for the last 28 years has really defined that. We all think about it for search, but they really built out all of the ecosystem around advertising online. They bought DoubleClick, they built things like Google Analytics that let you actually see who was coming to your property. It really is the hero of what I call the first generation of the internet and the first generation of the web.
What’s changing though, very quickly, is who is actually using the web, or what is using the web. Last November I was at Web Summit, the big European tech event, and I was asked, “When do you think that non-human traffic — agents and all of those things — are going to pass human traffic online?” We have a lot of data because we see a huge percentage of the internet, so we pulled all of that data and looked at it and said that in the second half of 2027, automated traffic would become larger than human traffic. It felt like a big deal that we could see that for the first time in the internet’s history.
I was asked again at South by Southwest in March of this year, 2026, and we pulled the data again and it had moved up, where it was going to then be the first half of 2027. We’re like, “Wow, this is growing. This AI thing is a big deal and people are using it like crazy and it’s driving a huge amount of traffic.”
I was stunned when just a few months later in May, the team came to me and said, “You won’t believe it, but automated traffic has now passed human traffic online.” And that’s just expanding like crazy. If you extrapolate that out, with the giant caveat that I’ve gone wrong so far in every prediction that I’ve made on this, five years from now, we think that automated traffic will be 1,000 times human traffic online. Not because human traffic is going to decline, we think it’ll stay around the same, but because we’re just seeing such an explosion in all of the rest of the traffic.
The challenge of that is, if you have 1,000 times more traffic, someone’s got to pay for the infrastructure to power that. That’s going to require bandwidth, that’s going to require servers, that’s going to require a lot of things in order to make that happen.
And, the traditional model of how to pay for that, which was advertising, doesn’t work for bots. Bots don’t click on ads. The gating mechanism of physical media, which provided some scarcity, and thus some economic value that you could measure, went away and we decided information should be zero and maybe supported by advertising. Google has by and large been a great company, but Google begets Facebook, which begets TikTok, which has us in this attention economy hole, where we’re trying to get as much attention as possible. And the best way to do that is to actually stimulate, again, a deep mammalian response. That’s the media landscape that we live in today. So what could we move to? There’s a lot that can go wrong here, but if you talk to Sam [Altman] at OpenAI, or Dario [Amodei] at Anthropic, or you talk to the teams at Google, that are building the AI systems at DeepMind and others, what do they really want?
