In June 2026, three spacetech startups became the first cohort to receive funds selected under the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre’s (IN-SPACe) Technology Adoption Fund’s (TAF) ₹500 Cr scheme. Bengaluru-based Astrobase Technologies was selected along with SatSure Analytics and TakeMe2Space, and got the backing despite being just two years old at the time. For Neeraj Khandelwal and Devakumar Thammisetty, founders of Astrobase, this milestone was a vindication of their passion for space tech. Classmates at IIT Bombay, the duo’s career paths diverged soon after graduation, before converging for Astrobase. Thammisetty spent 13 years at ISRO, where he worked on cryogenic engines. He also contributed significantly to CE-20, India’s only cryogenic engine. On the other hand, Khandelwal took the entrepreneurship route, and cofounded cryptocurrency exchange CoinDCX in 2018. Khandelwal told Inc42 he had actually considered entering the space sector when he started CoinDCX in 2018. However, private companies did not have the same opening into the sector at the time. To be sure, the ‘space’ for the private sector opened up in 2020 and private companies were able to access the facilities and services of ISRO, via the establishment of IN-SPACe, which acts as a single-window regulator-facilitator. This is when Khandelwal decided to return to the idea. He said his motivation is rooted in what he sees as a gap in India’s space infrastructure. While ISRO has built significant technological capabilities, he believes the next phase requires private companies to build manufacturing, scaling and operational capabilities around space infrastructure. For Astrobase, that opportunity begins with launch vehicles and, more specifically, propulsion. The startup is currently developing a launch vehicle, with its immediate focus on building the propulsion system that will power it. In August, Astrobase unveiled its first full-flow staged combustion (FFSC) engine called Everest. An FFSC (Full-Flow Staged Combustion) engine is an advanced type of liquid rocket engine where 100% of both the fuel and the oxidiser pass through separate pre-burners before entering the main combustion chamber. This is different from conventional engines, where only a fraction of the fuel or oxidiser passes through a pre-burner to drive pumps; the rest bypasses it or gets dumped/wasted. This makes FFSC engines more efficient and ideal for reuse. With this achievement, India joined the United States, Russia and China as the fourth country to develop and build an FFSC engine. The startup’s ambition, however, goes beyond building an engine or even a launch vehicle. Khandelwal wants India to develop the capacity to send 1,000 tons of payload into space every year by 2035. Building The Propulsion Stack At the heart of Astrobase’s approach is propulsion, which Khandelwal described as the core technology in a launch vehicle. The Everest rocket engine is an 80-tonne-class, 800 kN engine designed and manufactured in Bengaluru. Khandelwal said developing the engine has involved around 20 to 30 design iterations on average. Some individual components have gone through more than 50 iterations, reflecting the complexity of developing an engine comprising hundreds of components. The company is positioning EVEREST as a key building block for an indigenous, reusable launch system. The programme is now progressing through subsystem testing, including powerhead testing, as Astrobase prepares for full-scale engine hot-fire testing. Another important part of Astrobase’s propulsion strategy is its use of methane as rocket fuel. The company has built what Khandelwal described as “India’s first methane-based engine test facility”. The facility is designed around liquefied oxygen and liquefied methane, with methane being positioned as a next-generation rocket fuel. Khandelwal pointed to several advantages of methane. Apart from being easier to operate and widely available, he said it can extend the usable life of an engine because it does not damage the engine internally to the same extent as some other fuels. According to him, a kerosene-powered engine can typically be used around 10-12 times, while methane engines can potentially be used more than 50 times. For Astrobase, the methane capability is therefore not simply about environmental considerations. The company sees it as an important part of developing reusable propulsion technology. The company’s methane test facility is located at its Ananthapur facility, which spans 22.5 acres and has received Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization (PESO) approval, according to Khandelwal. Its Bengaluru manufacturing facility spans around 44,000 square feet and is designed to produce complete rocket engines end-to-end. The company has also focused on keeping much of the development process in-house. “You cannot develop such frontier technologies if you are dependent on vendors,” Khandelwal said, explaining that rapid iterations require the entire development loop to be controlled internally. That does not mean Astrobase operates without suppliers. The company works with more than 100 vendors in India, particularly for raw materials and components that it does not manufacture itself. However, the engine is designed and manufactured in-house. While the engine remains the immediate focus, Astrobase is also developing a launch vehicle. Khandelwal said the company is targeting its first orbital flight by the end of 2028. The company expects to have a larger vehicle team in place as it moves towards that milestone. Astrobase currently has around 70 people, but Khandelwal expects the team to reach around 300 by the time of the first launch. The company is hiring across aerospace, civil, mechanical, computer and metallurgy engineering, along with scientists and technicians. The choice of Bengaluru as the company’s base is also closely tied to its talent strategy. Rather than moving its core operations closer to a launch site, Astrobase plans to build the vehicle in Bengaluru and transport it to the launch site. Khandelwal said access to talent was a major reason for this approach, particularly because building rockets requires highly experienced engineers and scientists. Targeting The Medium-Lift Gap Astrobase is developing a medium-lift launch vehicle, which Khandelwal sees as a gap in the current Indian market. To be sure, a medium-lift launch vehicle (MLV) is a rocket launch vehicle that is capable of lifting between 2,000 to 20,000 kg of payload into low Earth orbit (LEO). An MLV is between small-lift launch vehicles and heavy-lift launch vehicles. Companies like Skyroot Aerospace (the Hyderabad based startup which conducted the first successful orbital launch by a private company) and Agnikul operate in the small-lift launch vehicles space. The medium-heavy lift launch vehicle market has been growing steadily in recent years. According to the Business Research Company, the market is expected to grow from $10.39 Bn in 2025 to $11.29 Bn in 2026, at a CAGR of 8.6%. The growth is being driven by rising demand for payload delivery to low Earth orbit (LEO), expanding government and commercial space programmes, advances in rocket and ground-support technologies, and greater investments in reliable launch systems for scientific and defence missions. Besides Astrobase, Bengaluru-based EtherealX is another Indian startup working towards a medium lift vehicle; globally, Elon Musk-led SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is a popular example in this category. From a technology perspective, Khandelwal said moving from a small-lift vehicle to a medium-lift vehicle is not a straightforward extension. A larger vehicle requires new infrastructure, new ground infrastructure, and a larger propulsion system. The company is therefore building its propulsion capabilities first, before scaling up its vehicle development. Astrobase also sees the opportunity as global rather than limited to India. Khandelwal pointed to countries including South Korea, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan, Indonesia and Japan that are developing or relying increasingly on satellite infrastructure, while many of them do not have independent launch capabilities. This creates an opportunity for launch providers outside the US and China, according to Khandelwal. Astrobase has already partnered with Italian company Impulso for launches. Impulso aggregates satellites and acts as a logistics partner for satellite companies. The partnership is intended to help build India as a launch destination for satellite companies in Europe and other markets. The Ambition Beyond Propulsion For Khandelwal, however, the ultimate objective is much larger than Astrobase’s first orbital flight. With money finally flowing into the India spacetech sector, startups can plan big if they have the right foundation. According to Inc42’s data, homegrown spacetech startups have already raised $252.9 Mn so far this year, nearly double what the sector raised in 2025. The Astrobase cofounder believes India needs the capacity to send at least 1,000 tons of payload into space annually to build meaningful orbital infrastructure capable of supporting hundreds or thousands of satellites. As for Astrobase, the next course of action is to manufacture 50 Everest engines annually; this will set pace for its ambition of enabling approximately 100 tons of launch capacity per annum in Phase 1 before expansion. For now, the company is focused on the first step: completing and testing its propulsion system, scaling engine manufacturing and developing its launch vehicle. The company currently has one engine production line and plans to establish five to seven lines, with each line eventually capable of producing five to 10 engines a year. The first orbital flight is targeted for 2028. By then, Astrobase expects to have a much larger team, a functioning vehicle programme and a propulsion system that has moved from the test facility towards flight. Khandelwal sees this as the infrastructure that Astrobase is building to be instrumental to support India needs before it can build a much larger space economy. The company is reportedly in talks to raise $40-50 Mn at a valuation of $250-300 Mn, which Khandelwal declined to comment on, but it would be exactly the kind of round needed to operationalise the infrastructure that Khandelwal spoke of.

'I lost my love for swimming' - Smith comes out of retirement
- Published
Having ended a two-year exile from competitive swimming, South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith has revealed she "lost the love" for her sport before stepping away from the pool in 2024.
The 29-year-old's decision to retire straight after the Paris Games came as a surprise, given she had just won 200m breaststroke gold in the French capital to add to her 100m title from Tokyo 2020.
But after two years away, which included several months in which she did not swim at all, Smith says she is now "free from the things that made me hate swimming".
"My whole life, I was kind of a robot towards swimming," she told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"You're so zoned in, you're obsessed with something, so there isn't actually time for you to think about things outside of the pool that you potentially have a passion for.
"I think probably everyone would think that the timing [of retirement] was the worst. But I absolutely 100% believe it was the best decision at that time, and I still have so much peace about it."
Having also picked up a silver medal in both Tokyo and Paris, Smith's total of four Olympic medals for South Africa is matched only by fellow swimmer Chad le Clos, who claimed one gold and three silvers across the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Games.
But despite making history for her country, Smith says financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, also contributed to her decision to retire.
"The financial burden on any athlete is so tough," she explained.
"I relied on my parents funding me until I broke the world record at the Olympics. And then, all of a sudden, now people are interested in maybe sponsoring you.
"But the majority of sponsorships for athletes are based on performance. So then you have that pressure and expectation to always have to perform, otherwise you're not going to get paid.
"I think the financial side, and also being in a system where they're not really putting the athletes first, made it really difficult."
'The world is so overwhelming'
Smith won her first Olympic title under her maiden name Schoenmaker, before changing her surname when she married sports agent Joel Smith in 2023.
The marriage made her part of a wider South African sporting dynasty, given that her sister-in-law is Rachel Smith, who was married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi before their split.
Tatjana Smith admits her own marriage changed the way she thought about her future.
"Thinking about families as a woman, you have to time it perfectly, because if you're pregnant, it's not like you can still compete."
While children are not yet part of her journey, Smith says working out what to do next was far from easy.
"I definitely understand what athletes mean from the post-Olympic depression," said the 2023 200m breaststroke world champion, who also counts Commonwealth and African titles among her achievements.
"It was such an emptiness in my life, because my whole life revolved around swimming.
"I don't have to eat at a certain time, I don't have to sleep at a certain time, I don't have to think about travelling or not spending time with family anymore.
"The world is so overwhelming. It's like, in which direction to go?
"It was definitely the toughest season that I had to go through. I think it's probably why it's made me a stronger person."
Initially, Smith took on speaking engagements to pay the bills.
She smiles when she admits: "I hate public speaking. I hate being in front of people."
The same cannot be said of her love for competition.
Having returned to the pool in order to keep fit, she decided to have a crack at triathlon, something she describes as a "crazy idea".
"The training was so intense, and I was like, 'OK, I might as well just go back to swimming if I'm going to train this hard'," she said.
"Every time I went back to the swimming pool and I dived in, I was like, 'Yeah, this is a feeling that I really miss so much'.
"I think slowly over the year and a half, I just realised 'Wow, I really do love swimming'."
A reinvention for LA 2028
Having made her decision to come out of retirement, Smith now wants to freshen things up and "try something new".
That means a change to the 50m breaststroke, an event which has just been added to the Olympic schedule for the first time ahead of the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
"I thought, 'Why don't I try? Why don't I give myself that challenge? Reinvent myself'," said Smith.
"I always try and describe it to someone that maybe doesn't understand swimming; it's like a 400m runner and a 100m [runner]. It's two different body types, two different trainings, and that's where I'm going."
It means she has more than halved her training volume, with three sessions a week instead of eight - a change she believes will help her retain her love for her sport and live a more balanced life.
"I feel like I'm being so lazy because I used to do 12km per day and now the focus is on taking time to be as explosive as possible.
"Now I'm doing 12km over a whole week.
"I have 20 years of endurance in my pocket, but I can definitely see I don't have those fast twitch [muscle] fibres. It's a whole different way of teaching my body how to swim."
Those initial 20 years in the pool left Smith feeling burned out.
Now she says she has earned the right to do things on her terms.
"Swimming was an opportunity given to me by my parents and I believe I took it on full heartedly.
"But, for the first time, it's my decision whether I want to come back. I'm choosing swimming.
"I've achieved way more than I ever dreamed in my whole life, so I have nothing to prove."

The Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

These are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. The best party speakers are introducing the idea of raving anywhere to a whole new generation who may have missed the classic block-party boom box of the 1980s. These new speakers look like compact PA systems, and often sound just as loud, with bold and brash looks and bass-heavy profiles. They’re honestly a huge amount of fun.
The rising popularity of party speakers coincides with a broader shift toward entertaining at home rather than in bars and nightclubs, particularly among younger consumers. A July 2026 Harris Poll found that 68 percent of US Gen Z adults say going out is just too expensive, while Attest found that 64 percent now drink primarily at home, up from 42 percent a year earlier.
Where people socialize may be changing, but the need for good atmosphere certainly isn’t. Traditional Bluetooth speakers are convenient and sound great, but they struggle to bring the party. Party speakers, with their serious volume, portability, and LED lights, don’t have that problem.
For more audio guidance, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Turntables, and Best Computer Speakers.
What Is a Party Speaker?
Party speakers are large, high-output Bluetooth speakers designed for social gatherings, sitting somewhere between a conventional wireless speaker and a portable PA. Current battery-powered models range from around 100 to 800 watts of power, with most offering between 12 to 25 hours of battery life, if not more. Expect large drivers, bass-boost modes, LED lighting, handles, wheels, and even replaceable batteries to keep the party going. Microphone and instrument inputs, karaoke controls, and the ability to link multiple speakers are also common, as are partner apps that give you the chance to play DJ, curate the lighting, and alter the sound.
How I Test Party Speakers
I’ve tested party speakers indoors and out, and at background, party, and ear-bleeding volumes. Sound quality is still important, but it’s party time, so bass, vocal clarity, and minimal distortion are key, as is how well the sound can travel (especially outdoors). Karaoke testing was dutifully undertaken by a gaggle of excitable but discerning tweenagers.
As well as playing rave classics at top volume (sorry, neighbors), I’ve analyzed the various EQ and control apps, AI features, digital signal processing (DSP) modes, and the speaker's ability to pair with DJ equipment, separate sources, and musical instruments.
What Should I Look for in a Party Speaker?
Power: Party speakers range from boxes one person can comfortably carry to 60-pound-plus towers on wheels. Power varies, but I’ve tested designs from 100 to 800-plus watts. As a general rule, the more watts it can output, the louder it will be, but clever DSP means brands like JBL and Sony can often make more noise with less watts than you might think.
Battery life: Your needs will again depend on how you party, but between 12 to 25 hours is common. Remember, though, high volume and lighting can cut that number down. Soundboks, for example, quotes 40 hours at mid volume but only six to eight hours at maximum, depending on the speaker.
Connectivity: As well as Bluetooth for wireless convenience, 3.5-mm or other line inputs are useful for DJ controllers, mixers, and sources beyond your phone, while some models add RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections. Outdoor users should look for an IP rating. Replaceable batteries, wheels, sturdy handles, and physical controls become considerably more important once a speaker leaves the living room.
Can I Use a Party Speaker With DJ Decks?
Yes, provided it has a suitable wired input. DJ controllers and mixers typically have a line-out option, commonly through RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections, although a 3.5-mm aux input can also work with the right cable.
If you are mixing, use a cable where possible, as Bluetooth introduces enough latency between moving a control and hearing the result to make accurate cueing and beat-matching difficult. Some specialist DJ systems like the Aiaiai Unit-4 Wireless+ Studio Monitors use proprietary low-latency wireless connections to get around this, but ordinary Bluetooth isn’t designed for the job.
What About Karaoke?
There’s plenty of crossover between party speakers and karaoke machines, but they’re not always the same thing. Some party speakers include one or two microphone inputs, while better-equipped models add wireless mics, separate vocal volume, echo or reverb, ample controls, and even vocal removal. The $350 Soundcore Rave 3S, for example, includes two wireless microphones and real-time vocal removal.
A dedicated karaoke setup puts singing rather than music playback first, and may offer more extensive microphone controls, song management, and accessories. WIRED’s Best Karaoke Gear guide covers those options in more detail.
How Do I Connect Multiple Phones to the Same Bluetooth Speaker?
Bluetooth multipoint lets two phones stay connected simultaneously, although switching between them varies by speaker. For larger groups, Spotify Jam and Apple Music SharePlay let guests choose music from their own phones while one device stays connected to the speaker. YouTube Music also supports collaborative playlists, enabling several people to add songs in advance or during the party.
Best Overall Party Speaker
LG xboom Stage 501 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 25 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1 with multipoint, Auracast, USB-C audio, USB-A, 3.5-mm aux input, two 6.3-mm mic inputs | 
| Special Features | AI karaoke, AI lighting, app EQ and DJ effects, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 11.7 x 23.4 x 11.6 inches | 
| Weight | 25.8 pounds | 
The Stage 501 turned the open workshop next to my testing studio into something close to a daytime rave (minus the crowd and superstar DJ). Bass was deep and clean, and carried easily across the room. Even when it was so loud I couldn’t hear myself think, there was volume to spare. And best of all, it sounded good, not just loud.
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, it has twin 5.25-inch woofers and two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. There’s 160 watts available on battery and 220 watts when plugged in. The battery is replaceable and lasts up to 25 hours. At full power, with the light show on, it’s less than that, but still more than enough for me.
There are louder and larger options here, but for me, the Stage 501 strikes the ideal balance between outright party power and decent sound quality. It even manages to impress at normal indoor listening volumes, which is often the downfall of party speakers.
LG has embraced the sillier side of the genre too. The app gives you EQ, AI karaoke, synchronized lighting, and DJ effects that are a bit cringe but hard to ignore. Two built-in phone/tablet stands are genuinely useful for karaoke, and there are twin mic inputs, though microphones are sold separately.
At 25.8 pounds, the cabinet remains manageable enough for me to move around on my own, but it is still a big unit to carry and find space for. If it’s too big, the smaller xboom Stage 301 keeps much of the same styling and app functionality, just in a much smaller package.
My Favorite Party Speaker
JBL PartyBox 130 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 15 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 |

At 24.8 pounds, the JBL PartyBox 130 isn’t exactly lightweight, but its modest size hits the sweet spot for me in my city home and garden. It’s solidly built, has impressive power for the size, and can be moved without risking my fragile L5 vertebrae.
Two 5.25-inch woofers and a pair of 1-inch tweeters produce 200 watts of output, with plenty of bass and enough volume to get a decent-sized party moving. JBL’s AI Sound Boost uses DSP (clever digital wizardry) to keep distortion under control as the volume rises, while an automatic EQ adjusts the balance depending on what’s playing. Both work well, although I got better results tweaking the EQ myself in the app, and for my ears, the LG xboom Stage 501 still outperforms this speaker.
The light show on this speaker is one of the best, and the app has a collection of lighting and DJ effects that range from fun to downright silly. Big, easy-to-use physical controls on the top of the speaker also make it easy to use without reaching for my phone.
The 15-hour replaceable battery feels a little short, but a 10-minute charge gives another 80 minutes of raving. The speaker is IPX4 splash-proof and has Auracast, optical, USB-C, and aux connections, plus dual mic and guitar inputs.
Best Premium Party Speaker

| Battery Life | 40+ hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP55 |

Marshall has been bringing the party with its speakers since 1962, so its recent foray into Bluetooth party speakers isn’t much of a stretch. The brand's first release was the $1,300 Bromley 750, an enormous, hugely impressive party speaker that makes you look like a roadie.
But for most people and typical house parties, the smaller but still premium Bromley 450 is a much more manageable option. At 27.2 pounds, it’s still hefty, but it packs the punch of a small PA system.
It also looks the part, with Marshall’s signature black-and-brass finish and metal grille giving proper rock-and-roll vibes. Maybe I’m just old, but the classic design feels more authentic than the modern LED-loaded Bluetooth boxes. (The tiny reactive LEDs, however, feel a little limp compared to its rivals.)
Two 6.5-inch woofers powered by 90-watt Class D amps, plus four full-range drivers with 55 watts each and a pair of passive radiators (400 watts total power) provide plenty of volume. The 360-degree arrangement spreads sound impressively around a large room or garden, and bass is powerful without overpowering everything else. If you prefer your vocals front and center-, you may want to spend some time tweaking the EQ in the app regardless.
Connectivity is anything but retro, with Auracast, multipoint, RCA, USB-C, aux, and twin mic/instrument inputs. The physical controls are particularly nice and a joy to use. The replaceable battery lasts an impressive 40-plus hours, while IP55 protection makes this speaker genuinely usable outdoors without having to baby it.
Best Value Party Speaker

| Battery Life | Up to 12 hours |

With two wireless microphones and ingenious AI Vocal Removal that extracts the vocal track from almost any song you stream, the Rave 3S is already WIRED’s favorite karaoke speaker. But its 200-watt output, strong bass, and impressive beat-synced lighting also make it a solid party speaker.
The AI vocal removal tool is impressive, and much better than the party trick I thought it might be. It isn’t flawless— it occasionally leaves traces of vocals in a song, but it’s customizable via the Soundcore app, and more than capable of enabling enthusiastic duets with Olivia Rodrigo.
A 6.5-inch woofer and three 2.5-inch full-range drivers are loud and clear without sounding too bass-heavy, although if you’re looking for more boom with your bap, there is a BassUp mode that pushes the lower frequencies hard.
At 23.1 pounds, with a well-balanced handle, it’s fairly easy to move about, although being the size and weight of a full carry-on bag, it would benefit from wheels. My only other gripe is that the quoted 12-hour battery life doesn’t compete with the best, and it fell short of that figure in testing.
Best Party Speaker for Deejaying
Sony ULT Tower 7 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 with multipoint, RCA in, XLR in/out, USB-A, USB-C, 6.3-mm mic input |

| Weight | 50.3 pounds | 
Sony’s new ULT range of speakers stretches from the relatively manageable $450 ULT Tower 5 to the frankly ridiculous $1,200 ULT Tower Max. Sitting between them is the ULT Tower 7, with excellent sound, an ample selection of inputs, a combined 420 watts of output, and a 30-hour battery. Be warned, though, while it’s smaller than the Tower Max, it is still absolutely enormous and weighs 50.3 pounds.
Most party speakers will accept music from a DJ controller, but Sony goes further with RCA and balanced XLR inputs, plus an XLR output for expanding a wired setup. Auracast-based Party Chain can also connect up to 100 compatible speakers, so you can go head-to-head with Madison Square Garden on volume.
Inside is an 11-inch woofer, two 4.7-inch midrange drivers, and four tweeters, including a rear-facing pair that spread audio around the room. Bass is deep and effective, and at close quarters with the volume cranked, I could really feel it. It’s not quite bone-shaking at the club levels, but it’s still impressive.
The 360-degree driver configuration helps sound spread out and avoid sounding too boxed in, and while the bass is still quite directional, I really enjoyed the scale and ease with which this speaker filled the room.
If you have the budget and space, and you want to play loud all night, the Sony delivers, but I do wish it had a retractable handle. The built-in corner handles are OK-, but you need to angle it sharply at an odd angle to engage the wheels, and trust me, you don’t want to carry this speaker by hand very far.
Best Compact Party Speaker
Sony ULT Field 7 Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP67 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.2 with multipoint, 3.5-mm aux, USB-A, 6.3-mm mic/guitar input |

After testing the ULT Tower 7, JBL, and LG xboom models, Sony’s Field 7 felt positively pocket-sized. It sits at the junction between full party speaker and oversize Bluetooth speaker, and makes a great case for both. I think it’s ideal as a hi-fi replacement in a college dorm or apartment that can also escape outside.
The 13.9-pound cylindrical design is certainly different, but it’s well made, and can be used vertically or horizontally (though the vertical orientation does scream ashtray to me).
Sound is satisfyingly big for something you can easily pick up and carry. There’s plenty of depth and weight to the bass, and it kept a houseful of girls dancing in the garden without getting distorted. Just as importantly, at lower volumes, it remains controlled enough to work as an everyday speaker rather than something you only wheel out for parties.
The illuminated end rings are fun once the sun goes down, although plenty of rivals do the same trick better. More useful is the IP67 rating and excellent 30-hour battery life, which means this speaker really will survive soggy, grubby, festival style conditions.
There are also mic/guitar and aux inputs, and two levels of bass to choose from, plus a good smattering of inputs, as well as multipoint Bluetooth. It’s not designed to rattle windows, but it is a more practical size and weight without massively compromising on party volume.
Best Rugged Party Speaker
Soundboks Rider Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 35 hours at mid volume; 8 hours at full volume; swappable battery pack | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IP66 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 4.2, 3.5-mm aux | 
| Special Features | 118-dB max output, Adaptive Bass Enhancer DSP, app EQ and sound profiles, removable steel grille | 
| Dimensions | 13.8 x 9.4 x 7.9 inches | 
| Weight | 14.3 pounds | 
WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz tested the small but mighty Soundboks Rider and found a punchy, portable party speaker that swaps flashing lights and karaoke for serious volume and durability.
At 14.3 pounds it is much easier to move than most party speakers, but an 8-inch woofer and 1.2-inch tweeter still generate up to 118 dB of sound. Harry described the output as “astonishing,” especially as it stayed clear and detailed across the volume range, with bass that didn't overwhelm.
It’s also built for considerably rougher treatment than the average speaker, with a steel grille, thick plastic cabinet, and silicone ball corners. During his drop test, Rabinowitz was more worried about damaging his stairs than the speaker. IP66 dust and water resistance makes it well suited to outdoor use too.
The swappable battery lasts up to 35 hours at mid volume, or eight hours at full blast, which is up there with the best. It also charges over USB-C, which is very convenient for most people.
It's not without compromise, however. Especially given the price, Bluetooth 4.2 feels very old, and connectivity is limited to a 3.5-mm aux input. For $600, it is niche, but if your priorities are portability, durability, and huge, clean sound over party gimmicks, the Rider is difficult to ignore.

India’s higher education policy framework increasingly talks about inclusion. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) places obligations on educational institutions to promote inclusive education, while the University Grants Commission (UGC) has, over the years, developed guidelines and institutional mechanisms intended to ensure that students with disabilities (SwD) can participate in higher education on an equal basis.
Despite these measures, the dearth of remedial support makes them vulnerable to academic exclusion and widens existing educational inequalities. Limited digital access further restricts their access to online learning resources, digital libraries, academic databases, and other educational platforms, hindering participation in technology-enabled learning and limiting their ability to make full use of academic opportunities.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Most recently, the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities listed the Accessibility Guidelines and Standards for Higher Education Institutions and Universities, issued by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, on June 25, 2024. The UGC describes these guidelines as part of its effort to ensure equal participation and inclusion of persons with disabilities in higher education.
Importantly, the UGC states that every higher educational institution (HEI) is expected to develop an effective accessibility mechanism extending from the admission process through the completion of the course. The Commission issued fresh directions to universities to furnish a report along with statistical information in respect of students admitted, teaching and non-teaching recruitment, as well as fellowships/scholarships provided to PwD students through the Universities Activity Monitoring Portal (UAMP) by September 30, 2026. It calls for the need to form an Internal Committee comprising teachers, staff, students and parents to take care of the day-to-day needs of persons with disabilities.
Yet institutional attention to disability often becomes focused on admission, reservation, and physical infrastructure. The more difficult question of what happens to the student after admission receives considerably less attention.
“The national statistical architecture measures how many students with disabilities enter higher education but does not adequately measure what happens to them after they enter colleges and universities,” disability rights activist and Professor at University College of Medical Sciences, Delhi, Dr. Satendra Singh told The Hindu.
Students with disabilities may enter higher education with varying levels of exposure to accessible learning environments. Some may require additional academic assistance, remedial classes, note-taking support, assistive technologies, or additional time and flexibility to engage with coursework. A student who misses classes because of disability-related issues may not have access to a structured academic mechanism to navigate the backlogs. The result is a form of exclusion that is not visible in institutional statistics.
Supportive system needed
The RPwD Act itself points to Section 16, which requires not merely admission without discrimination, but reasonable accommodation, necessary support, and monitoring of participation, academic progress, and completion. The UGC’s own accessibility framework similarly speaks of an accessible mechanism covering the student journey from admission to completion. But the lack of adequate remedial support has a direct bearing on how students with disability perform academically.
“Majority of the HEIs do not have a rights-based understanding of reasonable accommodation. They are still stuck with ramps, braille and talking books,” Dr. Singh said.
Pointing to the 2023–24 AISHE data, he said, “Of the 4.50 crore students enrolled in HEIs, the reported 54,080 students with benchmark disabilities (SwBD) represent approximately 0.12% of total higher-education enrolment. This is about 12 SwBD per 10,000 students. The AISHE reporting does not provide a detailed disability-type categorisation. This is a significant data gap because ‘SwBD’ is an extremely heterogeneous category. A student who is blind, a deaf student who uses Indian Sign Language (ISL), a student with dyslexia, an autistic student, and a student with psychosocial disability can have completely different accessibility and academic-support requirements.”
Dr. Sanjay Kant Prasad, Director of the National Centre for Disability Studies at IGNOU and former Deputy Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, echoes his views. He said, “Higher education must recognise that the 21 categories of disabilities identified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act have diverse and often distinct educational needs. While some disabilities may require limited remedial support, students with blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, deafness, cerebral palsy, autism and learning disabilities, among others, may require specific forms of academic and assistive support.”
He stresses that inclusive education does not mean eliminating specialised support. Rather, it is about creating an accessible environment in which the same educational curriculum can be accessed by students with different needs.
“In higher education, teachers may not require specialised training for every disability, but they should at least be oriented to disability-related needs and know how to make classrooms, teaching methods and learning materials accessible. This could include tactile materials and Braille for students with visual impairments, appropriate seating and mobility support, hearing aids or visual aids for students with hearing impairments, and the use of assistive and digital technologies such as text-to-speech software,” Dr. Prasad said.
Citing IGNOU’s efforts to provide study material at students’ doorsteps, counselling through teleconferencing and facilities for submitting assignments using computers, while following government and UGC guidelines, Dr. Prasad feels students’ ability to remain in education depends on broader social and economic support, not just classroom accommodations. Housing, awareness of available services and support from disability organisations are important factors.
Progress has been made over the past several decades from exclusion towards inclusion, but implementation remains uneven, and continued awareness, teacher training, and institutional support are needed to navigate the barriers.
In schools, the structures for remediation are more readily available than in higher institutions. The multi-tiered systems of support are a comprehensive framework that help provide individualised support to students.
Under this tiered system, the first level of support is the universal support that is offered to all students to help them learn better; the second level is classroom-based strategies and only the third level involves intensive care such as remediation.
“Often, students who reach higher education come equipped with an understanding of their own needs, have developed learning strategies, and carry an arsenal of tools that have been offered to them since school. Therefore, not every SwD requires remediation; some might require accommodations and modifications. Here is where inclusive EdTech, digital access, and online learning resources come in handy,” Dr. Rajeshwari Muthukumaran, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Neurodiversity Research and Innovation at Christ (Deemed-to-be University), said. She runs a support group aimed at fostering a sense of belonging and building a community on campus with students with disabilities, and neurodiverse students.
Although SwD might already come with their specific digital tools/modified equipment, they may still need guidance and access to software and tech tools often used in their domain.
Significant resource gaps persist, including the availability of Braille-translated materials and books in accessible typefaces. These constraints make it more challenging to design and implement tailored remediation programmes.
Additionally, institutional resource limitations, including a shortage of faculty with both subject expertise and training in developing accessible curricula, pedagogical practices, and assessment methods, as well as limited spaces and opportunities for one-on-one student-faculty support, further compound the problem.
Drawing from experience, Dr. Muthukumaran said, “I have met students who often enter higher education with a mix of hope, anxiety, and anticipation, and are seeking a supportive and approachable guide/mentor/peer who can offer them a safe and understanding space and serve as a support system. While guiding them in classrooms, I often end up recommending students to mental health professionals/supportive online communities where they can exchange ideas and converse with individuals with similar experiences to help them deal with campus life overall.”
Evidently, more colleges have now started looking into strategies, establishing specialised cells and centres that further look into research and student support. “While there is a long way to go, this scattered chatter needs to grow louder, unanimously, to shape future education and move towards evidence-based inclusive practices,” Dr. Muthukumaran added.
The digital divide
Considering that higher education has become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, learning management systems (LMS), university portals, digital libraries, online journals, e-books, recorded lectures, online assignments, examination portals, email systems, and virtual classrooms are now integral to campus life. For many learners, this digital environment offers greater convenience, flexibility, and access to educational resources. But for students with disabilities, digital technologies can be either powerful enablers or, when accessibility is inadequate, can become significant barriers to participation and academic success.
A university website that cannot be navigated effectively with assistive technology can make admission and administrative processes more cumbersome. A PDF that is simply a scanned image may not be usable for a blind student. An online learning platform without appropriate keyboard navigation, captions, transcripts, or alternative texts can prevent students from participating on equal terms.
Digital exclusion can widen the educational divide even when the physical campus is accessible. This is particularly important because UGC’s own framework requires online programmes to meet accessibility standards for learners with disability. If education is delivered digitally, its accessibility must be inclusive.
The lack of adequate data makes it difficult to assess the enormity of students’ plight. “There is no AISHE, NAAC or NIRF indicator reporting the percentage of students with disabilities in higher education who have access to accessible LMS platforms, screen-reader-compatible material, captions, Indian Sign Language interpretation or accessible e-books,” Dr. Singh said.
Without such indicators, institutions may be able to report enrolment and infrastructure without demonstrating whether students with disabilities can actually access, participate in, and benefit from digital learning on an equal basis. The absence of systematic data also makes it difficult to identify gaps, assess institutional performance, or hold institutions accountable for meeting accessibility requirements.
“We need a stricter implementation protocol for higher education institutions as there is mostly a lack of awareness and enforceable rules that institutions should follow,” says Deepa Palaniappan, Disability Inclusion practitioner, highlighting the need for more discussions, training, and handholding, as well as forming national task forces and committees to track effective inclusion of students with disabilities in higher education institutions across the country.
Reality check
For Delhi University (DU) alumnus and disability rights activist Ashutosh Singhal (24), the challenges of being an undergraduate and later postgraduate student of Political Science were harrowing. ‘’I use a regular, mainstream computer with a screen reader that reads out the text and other information displayed on the screen. This means that questions appearing on the computer can be read aloud to me, enabling me to access and answer them independently,” Ashutosh said, who suffers from late-onset visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), a condition in which the vision can gradually deteriorate.
Beating the odds, he managed to use a computer to write his Political Science BA and MA exams in Hindi, which was the first instance of its kind.
“Initially, they gave me a computer that crashed. The computer instructor apparently knew that there were problems with the computer but did not inform me beforehand. A substitute computer was eventually provided, but by then considerable examination time had been lost. I was told that I would receive additional time to compensate for the lost time, but this was not implemented adequately. Since the examination authorities had to collect and pack the answer scripts at a fixed time, I was under pressure to finish and submit my answers immediately,” he added. Ashutosh was also made to sit in a computer lab during the exam where the constant noise made it difficult to detect the sounds of the screen reader, disrupting his flow of thoughts.
Ashutosh’s experience made him realise that the biggest difficulty for students with disabilities is often not the technology itself which is already available. It is about getting institutions to recognise and implement accessibility provisions consistently.
A student may have to repeatedly explain their requirements, submit applications, approach different departments, contact outside organisations, and persuade officials to make arrangements that should ideally be part of a standard accessible examination system. “For me, the computer and screen reader made it possible to access examinations independently. But the institutional process surrounding the technology created many obstacles. Accessible examination systems should be implemented proactively rather than requiring students with disabilities to repeatedly request, justify, and negotiate for accommodations each time they have an examination,” he added.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

If you’ve been outside, at the gym, or on a basketball court, there’s a good chance you’ve seen someone wearing Reeboks. The brand has had its fair share of ups and downs, but it’s riding a wave of increased interest driven by smart business moves, such as a refocus on sports and lifestyle, alongside high-profile collaborations like the Reebok G-Unit G6 50 Cent.
Founded in 1958, Reebok has changed hands and gone through multiple iterations. Most recently, in 2022, Adidas sold Reebok to Authentic Brands Group for over two billion dollars. You can use your old laptop to make a smart home hub
You don’t need a Raspberry Pi or mini PC to start experimenting with Home Assistant.
That crappy old laptop collecting dust in your closet might have another use after all. With some open-source software and a little patience, you can give it a second life as a smart home control system. It may not be the perfect hardware for the job, but it lets you get started with what you already have.
A smart home composed of devices from several different companies can make for a messy setup. Although standards like Matter and Thread are designed to smooth that out, fragmentation still hasn't been solved. So, some people prefer to build their own solution. The software that holds it together is Home Assistant, an open-source platform that acts as a local control center for different brands' smart home devices.
Home Assistant can run on a wide range of hardware, from premium gaming PCs to Raspberry Pis. But that dusty old laptop is another option. If you aren't ready to buy dedicated hardware just for Home Assistant, an otherwise retired laptop can at least give you a good trial run.
Why Home Assistant?
Home Assistant can serve as the brains of a scattered collection of smart devices. It supports integrations for many popular services, including Philips Hue, Google Nest, Ring, Sonos and Ecobee.
Fair warning: Home Assistant isn't always the most user-friendly platform. It has a bit of a learning curve, and its interface probably isn't as intuitive as you'd like. (Although you could say the same for many native smart home apps.) But if you're open to some tinkering, you might find a lot to like.
Home Assistant makes the most sense if you have a mix of smart home devices from different brands that won't otherwise work together. (If yours is already working smoothly, this probably isn't for you.) In exchange for some setup friction, the software can ease your reliance on your devices' companion apps. Some of the platform's integrations do still rely on manufacturer accounts or cloud services, but others can run locally, bypassing company servers. Part of the appeal is taking back control of at least one corner your digital life from big tech companies.
Home Assistant supports automations, scenes, scripts and other features that help those devices work together. You can set a rule that turns on your coffee maker on when you dismiss your morning alarm or one that dims the lights and locks the doors when you start a movie. (Provided you have all the requisite smart home gear.) You will need to run Home Assistant on hardware that stays on all the time, but hey, it's not like that old laptop was doing anything else, right?
Sizing up your laptop
Fortunately, Home Assistant doesn't need a powerful, or even remotely new, computer. A dated laptop that struggles with modern apps may still be perfectly capable of listening for sensor updates and toggling lights. The bigger question is whether it's something you'll be happy to leave in one place and powered on.
That rules out any laptop you take to work, travel with or shut down at night. A Home Assistant device should sit quietly in the background, keeping your smart home humming without interruption. Power it down or take it with you, and your automations lose their brains.
Storage requirements aren't particularly demanding. A solid-state drive (SSD) might make life easier than an old mechanical hard drive via faster boot times and responsiveness. But a spinning hard drive can still be fine. Home Assistant recommends an ethernet connection for stability, so setting up near your router is ideal. Wi-Fi can work, too, although it's more vulnerable to interference, dropouts and other connection hiccups.
Battery: Proceed with caution
Before you leave the laptop running around the clock, make sure its battery is in good condition — or remove it if the laptop can safely run without one. If the battery is in good shape, it can act as a built-in safeguard during brief power outages. (Although its usefulness will be limited unless your router or other networking equipment also has a backup power supply.) Either way, a swollen, leaking or otherwise damaged battery isn't something you want to roll the dice with.
A battery that doesn't hold the same charge as it used to isn't automatically a problem. But if it's swollen or damaged, stop using it and follow the laptop manufacturer's instructions for replacement or removal. And if your laptop has a removable battery and you decide to run Home Assistant without it, confirm that your model can operate normally from its power adapter alone.
Some laptops let you cap the maximum charge level, either through manufacturer software or a BIOS setting. That's probably worth using if it's available, since keeping a lithium-ion battery at 100 percent for long periods can make it degrade faster. Older laptops may not offer that option, so check which battery management features your model supports.
Using the laptop as a trial run
Although Home Assistant is Linux-based, you don't need to install the operating system or become a command-line enthusiast to get started. A relatively low-commitment way to try Home Assistant is to run it inside a virtual machine (VM). This lets you keep the laptop's existing operating system, whether it's Windows, macOS or Linux, as Home Assistant OS (HAOS) runs inside that virtual environment.
Running Home Assistant in a VM does add some overhead, so an extremely weak laptop might struggle with it. But at least the requirements are fairly modest: When run in a VM, Home Assistant currently calls for at least 2GB of RAM and two virtual CPUs.
Free options include VirtualBox (Windows, macOS, and Linux), VMware Workstation Pro (Windows and Linux) and VMware Fusion Pro (macOS). Home Assistant provides VM images and setup instructions for several popular platforms.
If you plan to dedicate the laptop to Home Assistant, installing HAOS directly is a cleaner and permanent option. It replaces the laptop's existing operating system and avoids the extra overhead of running a VM. That could be especially useful for an underpowered laptop with little horsepower to spare. (Before you do so, check that the laptop's specs meet Home Assistant's x86-64 requirements.)
Whichever option you choose, the idea is for the laptop to be essentially invisible after the initial setup. Once you do that, you can manage Home Assistant from another device (via web browser) or with the mobile app. Just change the power settings so that closing the lid doesn't put it to sleep and leave the laptop sitting near the router with its screen off. (And if you're running it through a VM, check the host operating system's sleep settings as well.)
Getting started with Home Assistant
Home Assistant isn't exactly plug-and-play. It may discover some of your devices automatically, but others will probably require manual setup. Fortunately, there's plenty of documentation to help when you get stuck.
You might find that the best approach is to start small. Get a few smart plugs, lights or one room's worth of devices up and running. Then, see if you're feeling it enough to keep going. Pick something you currently do manually (or rely on another smart home app to handle), and try automating it with Home Assistant. Or, try duplicating a scene or automation you currently use through a manufacturer app. Most of all, be prepared to exercise a little patience.
Check electricity use
Using an old laptop costs nothing upfront, but running it around the clock still uses electricity. (And older laptops may use more power than a modern Raspberry Pi or mini PC.) If you want hard data, a plug-in power meter can tell you exactly what yours is drawing.
That doesn't necessarily make the laptop a bad choice. But, again, it may make more sense as a way to test Home Assistant than as your long-term server. See how well your devices cooperate, if you can live with Home Assistant's UX "quirks" and whether the whole setup is useful enough to keep. If so, you can always move to smaller, more power-efficient hardware later.
Home Assistant's backup and restore tools make that transition easier. Backups carry over your settings and automations, so you can restore them to a new device without starting from scratch.

Thomas Tuchel: Why England head coach's critics forced to stay quiet despite Nations League loss to Spain
Sky Sports News' football correspondent Rob Dorsett assesses England's 3-2 home defeat to Spain in their Nations League opener; in his Reporter Notebook from Wembley, Dorsett explains why critics of Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel will be forced to stay quiet despite the loss
Sunday 27 September 2026 13:13, UK
The narrative before this first post-World Cup international was clear: if England lose, the pressure on Thomas Tuchel could become unbearable.
The big name on the big bucks, brought in to win the big games, could not afford to lose to Spain after the tactical disaster of the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina. The court of public opinion, and the bile of the English media, would combine to make life very difficult for the England boss.
Well, here we are, in the aftermath of a 3-2 loss to the newly-crowned world champions, where England were outclassed on numerous occasions, where the scoreline should have been much one-sided, where for long periods Spain looked far superior to the Three Lions, where after half an hour the visitors should have been four-nil up. That's surely it, then? Auf Wiedersehen, Thomas?
Nope. Strangely, despite all of that, Tuchel's critics have been forced to bite their tongues and bide their time. Why? Because England were true to their DNA, they gave it a real good go; there were a lot of positive signs, and ultimately everyone saw again just how incredibly good Spain are.
It's hard to criticise Tuchel or his players when they were narrowly beaten by a team who have repeatedly proven they are the best by a mile at what they do.
The game was decided by two collector's items at either end of the pitch - one a Marc Guehi calamity on the edge of his own box that gifted Spain the lead in the second minute. The other was a Harry Kane missed penalty because of a slippery pitch. And if England's captain had scored from 12 yards, giving his side a two-goal cushion, who knows what might have been.
The match statistics make for comforting reading for Tuchel too. Up against the tika-taka maestros, England had a very respectable 48 per cent possession, made more successful passes in the final third than Spain, had two fewer shots, had over double the amount of touches in the opponent's box and five times as many crosses.
Those stats may not pass the sniff test. They might seem at odds with what most spectators saw with their eyes, but the numbers that perhaps help us understand better show that Spain created twice as many big chances.
How do we digest all of that? In basic terms, Spain may have had the ball less than England in dangerous areas, but when they did, Luis de la Fuente's team had more quality and were more clinical. And the team that has not lost a match in two-and-a-half years didn't make costly individual errors with the ball, because that's not in their DNA.
If it is possible, the defeat has improved the national mood. Notably, there were no boos within the 88,000 Wembley crowd at full time, because for half an hour either side of half-time, England dominated the world champions and they played in a very "English" way.
All verve, pace and passion, full of attacking intent. They scored two goals in that period against a side that has only conceded goals to two teams in the last 12 months, and the home side could have scored more in that golden 30 minutes. If only they could sustain that for a full 90 minutes, eh?
Captain Harry Kane told me after the match that this is the mission, having not managed to put in a complete 90-minute performance at the World Cup, and he felt the same was true at Wembley on Saturday night.
What really matters now is how England follow up on this Spain defeat. They have three games in eight days. Three games they ought to win, with Czech Republic home and away sandwiching Croatia away. If they do win all three, it will have been a positive international break, one that very much keeps alive their hopes of making it to the Nations League quarter-finals in the spring. Remember, the top two qualify from each group in League A, and so practically it does not matter if England finish below Spain, so long as they finish above the other two nations.
But once again it is the next game that feels critical for Tuchel. You can imagine the England boss saying to his squad in the post-match debrief: "After the Spanish Inquisition, my friends, comes the test from the Czechs, mates".

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

A medical review committee determined that the physician "acted with due care." The Netherlands Public Prosecution Service will determine whether the physician acted within the bounds of the law.
Rumors that a child in the Netherlands was euthanized by medical professionals circulated online in September 2026.
People on social media and YouTube claimed the country had recently allowed physicians to terminate the life of a 2-year-old disabled child. One user posted on X, "My heart hurts for the broken world in which we live that has so abandoned its humanity."
The controversial nature of the claim and the ongoing debate over reproductive rights in the United States led many Snopes readers to reach out via email asking us to verify the story.
Euthanasie of a 2years old baby in the Netherlands: disabled now can be killed and they say it's human not to tet live disabled and kill them without even give thm the possibility to make an own informed decision when they are an adult.: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE TO THE NAZIS?!! https://t.co/Wp2eiNlW1g
— KaiTraudvetter (@traudvette8137) September 18, 2026
The claim was true.
A review committee made of four physicians, one lawyer and one ethicist, formed by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport and the Ministry of Justice and Security, described its duty in the 2025 annual report (translated from Dutch to English by DeepL):
The committee assesses whether a physician acted with due care in cases of late-term abortion or the termination of life in a newborn or a child between the ages of 1 and 12. In 2025, the Commission received three reports of late pregnancy terminations. No reports of end-of-life care for newborns were received in 2025. At the end of 2025, the Commission received its first report of end-of-life care for a child between the ages of 1 and 12. The committee meets every two months and will address this report at its first meeting of 2026.
The committee's judgment for the case in question — available to read on their website — determined the physician who administered the euthanasia "acted with due care."
According to the committee, "due care" is based on the premise that the physician must "arrive at the conviction, on the basis of prevailing medical insight, that euthanasia is the only reasonable solution to alleviate the child's hopeless and unbearable suffering."
Dutch law
According to the government of the Netherlands, "euthanasia (termination of life on request) and assisted suicide are criminal offences" with the only exception being "when the procedure is performed by a physician who has satisfied six statutory due care criteria."
The criteria say the physician must:
- be satisfied that the patient's request is voluntary and well considered.
- be satisfied that the patient's suffering is unbearable, with no prospect of improvement.
- have informed the patient about their situation and their prognosis.
- have come to the conclusion, together with the patient, that there is no reasonable alternative in the patient's situation.
- have consulted at least one other, independent physician, who must see the patient and give a written opinion on whether the due care criteria set out in (1) to (4) have been fulfilled.
- have exercised due medical care and attention in terminating the patient's life or assisting in the patient's suicide.
In October 2024, the euthanasia law was expanded to include children age 1 to 12. The case in question was the first time the expanded law was put into practice.
The government's website about termination of life for children ages 1 to 12 states:
Termination of life is only allowed if a child is terminally ill and is suffering unbearably with no prospect of improvement. This means the child is in constant, severe pain. And that there is no cure, and no reasonable alternative to relieve the child's suffering, even through palliative care.
In this situation, the doctor may decide, together with the parents, to terminate the child's life. This decision is always made in consultation with the parents and, if possible, also with the child.
While the committee found the physician to be acting within the parameters of the stated criteria, the next part of the process requires them to send the details of the case and their review to the Public Prosecution Service, which then determines whether the doctor acted within the bounds of the law.
We reached out to the office of Sophie Hermans, the minister of health, welfare and sport, who first announced the case to the Dutch Parliament in June 2026, for an update on its legal status and will update this article if we get a response.
Details of the case
According to the committee's report on the case in question, the child's condition included being born prematurely at 26 weeks, which caused sepsis.
Over the following months the child suffered extensive brain damage, cerebral visual impairment and severe epilepsy, as well as lack of verbal and cerebral visual development.
The review said that "the child had multiple, very severe disabilities, both mental and physical, and the prognosis was that the child would be dependent on support with all activities of daily living for the rest of their life."
The report continued that because the child was incapable of communicating, "the diagnosis, prognosis and treatment options were discussed extensively with the parents" who ultimately decided to ask the physician to end their child's life.
Other consulted physicians said there were proposed alternatives, such as palliative care, but "the parents were of the opinion that the proposed treatments would only prolong the child's suffering."
In the end, the procedure began "by administering increasing doses of midazolam and morphine through an IV cannula," and then "administered coma-inducing substances (propofol and thiopental), after which the child reached a state of very deep sedation, and died."

Six months ago, first lady Melania Trump walked into a White House education summit next to a faceless robot powered by artificial intelligence, which she said could one day give children personalized instruction.
