KYIV, Ukraine -- Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people overnight into Sunday, officials said, hours after Moscow rejected German calls to ease off its escalation toward NATO.
Russia’s top diplomat on Saturday brushed off what’s believed to have been the first tête-à-tête with his German counterpart since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The meeting was held during the U.N. General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders, as an intensifying aerial war between Russia and Ukraine shows no sign of slowing.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport that Berlin blamed on the Kremlin.
With front-line positions largely unchanged since last year, Moscow has hammered its neighbor with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months. Meanwhile, Kyiv’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine’s emergency service.
Another drone struck a single-story vehicle repair shop, leaving firefighters battling the blaze into early Sunday, the emergency service said.
Russian forces also struck Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country’s main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday, killing one person and injuring two others, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was dismissive after the meeting in New York, which was held at German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s request. Lavrov said that Wadephul “simply reiterated his official position condemning Russia”.
“You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not,” he said.
Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia’s leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to a German delegation official.
An overwhelming majority of U.N. member nations have repeatedly condemned Moscow’s invasion. The Kremlin describes the war a “special military operation” intended to ensure Russia’s security and the rights of Russian speakers.

A laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in the northeastern Congolese city of Bunia, the director of a local hospital and two health officials said, raising concerns about a resurgence of the disease as the country battles its worst Ebola outbreak on record.
The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday, September 24, 2026.
Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact.
Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge.
The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters.
A second woman, aged 32, has been identified as a suspected mpox case and is awaiting laboratory results, Musungufu said. She and the confirmed patient have been isolated and are being cared for by a dedicated medical team.
Investigations are underway to trace contacts and identify the source of infection, Musungufu said.
Adelard Lofungola, a health official who served as deputy incident manager for Congo's mpox response, said five suspected mpox cases in Bunia were currently under investigation.
Health officials have reported an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country over the past month, he said.
Dr. Lofungola said the Ebola outbreak's impact on Congo's health system was complicating efforts to monitor other infections.

The sell-off in insurtech stocks continued for the second straight session today as the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) proposed overhaul of insurance distribution commissions rattled investors. Shares of Policybazaar parent PB Fintech fell as much as 7.8% to touch a fresh 52-week low of ₹1,115.10 on the BSE. Meanwhile, Turtlemint shares opened at their 20% lower circuit of ₹87.30, which was also the stock’s fresh all-time low. The stocks later pared some of their losses. At 12:21 IST, PB Fintech was trading 5.12% lower at ₹1,148.10, with a market capitalisation of ₹53,128.6 Cr (about $5.5 Bn). Turtlemint was trading 18.84% lower at ₹88.55, giving the insurtech company a market capitalisation of ₹2,607.6 Cr (about $272 Mn). At the prevailing prices, PB Fintech shares have fallen about 39% across the two sessions, while Turtlemint has declined about 35% from its level before the sell-off began. The rout began yesterday after IRDAI released a consultation paper proposing product- and channel-specific commission ceilings for insurance distributors. The proposed framework would reintroduce product-level commission caps more than three years after the regulator removed such limits in April 2023 and shifted to an expenses of management (EoM) framework. Under the proposed framework, commissions for insurance distributors would vary based on the product, distribution channel and effort involved in selling and servicing a policy. Open-architecture insurance distribution entities such as Policybazaar and Turtlemint’s insurance broking arm would generally face lower caps than individual agents and other distributors. For digital insurance distributors, the proposed changes could put pressure on revenue from health, motor and life insurance, while forcing platforms to rethink customer acquisition costs and sales incentives. PB Fintech cofounder and group chairman Yashish Dahiya said during an investor call yesterday that the proposals have “almost forced” the company to consider entering insurance manufacturing, which would allow it to design, underwrite, and sell policies itself, though it would wait for greater regulatory clarity. The proposals are not final, with IRDAI inviting stakeholder comments until October 25. ‘Much Worse Than Imagined’ As PB Fintech and Turtlemint extended their sell-off, brokerages began quantifying the potential impact of IRDAI’s proposed overhaul. Bernstein described the proposed commission cuts as “much worse than imagined”, warning that they could unravel PB Fintech’s unit economics, particularly in health and motor insurance. Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating on PB Fintech but cut its price target to ₹1,540 from ₹2,050. It estimated that a 10% reduction in new business commission rates could translate into a 10%-12% decline in earnings. The brokerage also flagged the proposals as a risk for Turtlemint. Bank of America retained its ‘Neutral’ rating on PB Fintech but cut its price target to ₹1,410 from ₹1,970. It described the proposals as directionally negative for online insurance brokers, though it expects the impact on Policybazaar’s life and term insurance businesses to remain manageable. Morgan Stanley said that the net present value of PB Fintech’s health insurance business could fall 60%-70% under the proposed framework, while the impact on its life insurance business could be relatively limited. HSBC downgraded PB Fintech to ‘Hold’ and cut its price target to ₹1,150 from ₹2,100. It also slashed its FY28 and FY29 earnings per share estimates by 56% and 17%, respectively. Motilal Oswal Securities said that the proposals could reduce PB Fintech’s FY28 core online insurance revenue by 30%. Without cost reductions or additional revenue streams, this could translate into a 46% cut to its earnings estimate. Citi said distribution economics could compress by 70%-90% across several high-margin insurance categories if the proposals are implemented in their current form.

For decades, youth have been told they are the future — the changemakers, co-creators, and leaders of tomorrow.
But are we truly listening to what they have to say? Do we empower young people to be able to lead societal transformations? And most importantly, do we give them enough power to shape decisions that affect their livelihoods?
Younger generations are inheriting a world shaped by overlapping environmental, economic, and social challenges. The U.N.’s 2030 Agenda recognizes youth as “critical stakeholders” in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals — yet too often they remain limited to advisory roles or symbolic forms of participation with marginal opportunities to influence decision-making or lead meaningful and sustainable change.

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?
The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.
For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?
Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.
This distinction is important — a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.
The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.
It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?
No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.
The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.
The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.
If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.
This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?
The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.
There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?
The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.
The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.
The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

A recent episode of the Oprah Winfrey Podcast revealed a stunning new hypothesis in cancer research. It had nothing to do with artificial intelligence (A.I.) or a new drug’s mechanism. Instead, it was about chronic inflammation.
Winfrey’s guest was Siddhartha Mukherjee, cancer researcher, oncologist and author of the Pulitzer-winning book The Emperor of All Maladies. Partway through their conversation, when she asked about the future of cancer treatment, he said, “There are thousands of dormant cancer cells sitting in your body. Then something happens — I call it the sleeping beauty kiss — that wakes them up. We are realising that that one something is chronic inflammation... It really switches around how we think about cancer... If we could test that one particular kind of inflammation, we would have a bio-marker for future cancers that could even be preventive.”
In the longevity era, inflammation is one of the most studied biological phenomena. And increasingly, scientists are discovering evidence that chronic low-level inflammation, or extended activity of immune cells when there’s no immediate threat, is often the cause of disorders, from diabetes and cancer to autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s.
Just last week, new research published in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology showed that chronic inflammation increases the risk of heart attack and stroke by 43%. Scientists from MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences and Imperial College London found that inflammation caused silent structural damage to the heart (thickened walls, smaller chambers and poorer filling) years before symptoms appeared.
Is it any wonder then that inflammation is on everybody’s minds these days? No matter where you look, someone is telling you how to reduce it: from self-help guides to influencers on Instagram breaking down inflammatory foods, inflammation belly, and inflammation face in under three minutes.
Turmeric is hyped as a miracle cure, others swear by elimination diets. Then there’s parasite detoxes, ice baths, celery juice resets and monotrophic cleanses (where you eat only one food item). The more scientists link inflammation to diseases, the more the wellness industry cashes in by marketing anti-inflammatory products. But take them with a dollop of salt. Often, the advice is fed to us by A.I.-generated doctors, healers and wellness influencers.
Acute and chronic: not the same thing
For most of history, doctors and the public focused on what they could see and feel: red, puffy skin around a wound, pain, fever. “I remember reading an article a few years back about how people with stressful jobs have inflammation, which could lead to illnesses as they age. And I recall closing my eyes and doing a mental body check and noting that ‘no, nothing was swollen or achy, so I’m not inflamed’. I was naive and uninformed,” says Kajal S. (name changed), a media professional in her 40s, explaining how she didn’t know the difference between acute and chronic inflammation.
One evening, a couple of years later, the knuckles in her left hand swelled up, and within a few days she was handed a diagnosis of palindromic rheumatism, a rare type of inflammatory arthritis characterised by sudden, recurring flare-ups and severe joint pain. Her doctor talked her through how consistent stress, bad sleep patterns, and gut issues — and the chronic inflammation it caused (that is devoid of swelling or aches) — played the lead role in her condition.
So, what’s the difference between acute and chronic inflammation? The former occurs when the body rallies to defend itself against invading microbes or to heal damaged tissue. Capillaries dilate and grow more porous, enabling white blood cells to flood the damaged site. The region swells, which can put pressure on surrounding nerves, causing pain. Chronic inflammation, however, is often silent and occurs when the immune system is over-stimulated all the time. As researchers are discovering, factors such as poor diet, air pollution, lack of sleep and stress can have a more significant impact on it than previously understood.
“In modern life, inflammation has five faces: ultra-processed food, sleep debt, a disturbed gut, a sedentary body, and the one I speak of most — the red mind or a state of constant stimulation.”Arpit BansalOncology surgeon and chief scientific chair at the Longevity Summit India held last month in Mumbai
Over time, in many cases, our immunity can also get so active that it starts attacking our own cells, which is what autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriasis, vasculitis, Hashimoto’s disease and others are. Inflammation can also fuel chronic diseases (without autoimmunity), like Alzheimer’s and endometriosis.
“Persistent inflammation can contribute to changes in blood vessels and metabolism and is involved in several chronic diseases. The brain is also connected to these processes,” says Dr. Vinaya Bhandari, consultant neurology and neuromuscular disorder specialist from Mumbai’s Jaslok Hospital and Research Centre. “Inflammatory signals from the body can interact with the brain and its blood vessels... and continual activation is increasingly recognised as one component of neurological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases [Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s].”
Less inflammation doesn’t mean “healthier”
It is easy to see why inflammation is such a perfect social media concept: it is invisible, frightening, scientifically legitimate, associated with many diseases, simple to attach to symptoms, as well as food and products. (Ironically, emerging research shows higher levels of inflammation associated with using social media over face-to-face interaction.)
But detecting chronic inflammation isn’t as easy as going to your physician and asking how your immune system is doing. While tests such as C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) can help identify markers of inflammation, for some people such tests just come back negative.
To complicate things further, not all inflammation have dire results. “Often, a person doesn’t know they have chronic low-grade inflammation because it is not always behind heart disease or endometriosis, or cancer,” says Dr. Suganya Venkat, a Coimbatore-based gynaecologist. “Chronic inflammation can manifest as brain fog or fatigue or lethargy that just won’t go away.”
Fringe wellness to mainstream culture
Somewhere between a turmeric shot, a cold plunge and a bowl of berries, inflammation has stopped being an immune response. It has become an explanation for why we are tired, puffy, anxious, ageing, gaining weight, breaking out and not feeling okay. Just the month of September has seen hundreds of guides on how to lower your inflammation naturally or how to reset your circadian rhythm to improve inflammation. And forums such as Reddit, with their believers, sceptics and the longevity crowd, are bandying around new terms such as ‘inflammaging’ (to describe the low-grade inflammation that occurs with ageing).
But the future of inflammation is not on the world wide web. It is in labs and clinics around the world where scientists are tracking inflammation in patients over time, trying to understand what normal looks like and when it can become dangerous.
The cancer-chronic inflammation link is something Indian oncologists have begun to consider. “Chronic inflammation can create a biological environment that promotes malignant transformation,” explains Dr. Aditya Vidushi, medical oncologist at Faridabad’s M|O|C Cancer Care & Research Centre. “A clear example is H. pylori, a stomach bacterium that triggers long-term irritation, a major driver of gastric cancer. Obesity-related low-grade inflammation is linked to higher risks of colorectal, breast, pancreatic, and liver cancers.”
And the body of science is building. Senthilkumar Rajagopal, associate professor at REVA University in Bengaluru, who has led several research papers on inflammation, says, “South Asian populations may have a distinctive susceptibility to chronic low-grade inflammation arising from the interaction of genes, visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, environmental exposures and lifestyle factors.” The central insight emerging from his work is that targeting molecular interfaces between neuron signalling and inflammatory pathways may offer new strategies.
Maintaining the balance
Experts agree that combining medicine and better lifestyle habits can best prevent flare-ups. But what they prescribe can vary widely, and occasionally be controversial. U.S.-based Mark Hyman, considered the pioneer of Functional Medicine, emphasises in his books that inflammation is the common pathway for all chronic diseases. His recommended solution is an anti-inflammatory diet: omitting sugar, caffeine, beans, dairy, gluten, and processed foods, as well as taking a variety of supplements, including probiotics, fish oil, Vitamins C and D, and curcumin, a key molecule in turmeric. Meanwhile, in his book The End of Illness, American oncologist David Agus prescribes, among other things, not wearing high heels because they inflame the feet and that inflammation could possibly affect vital organs.
The healing journey of Goa-based graphic designer Antima Nahar, 48, diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) when she was 35, has taken her to doctors, nutritionists and Ayurvedic retreats. Nahar got the transformative diagnosis after a fall during a monsoon trek on the outskirts of Mumbai. Her doctors told her she would live with pain if she did not take steroids and painkillers all her life. “It started with my toes and fingers, and then became a sharp, pounding pain that kept shifting through different joints in my body. At one point, I couldn’t squeeze a toothpaste tube, couldn’t open jars or bottles, couldn’t hold a phone for long,” Nahar says.
After years of naturopathic and Ayurvedic treatments, she found a balance with lowered doses of allopathic treatment combined with naturopathy and lifestyle modifications. “The last decade has been about knowing my body. Flare-ups can be because of food, weather changes, dancing, anything. I started recording everything, thinking through everything I did.” Nahar also began making illustrations about her RA journey and is now writing a graphic novel about self-discovery through pain.
Interestingly, chronic inflammatory conditions often manifest differently in men and women. Several studies in the past decade reveal that nearly 70% of all autoimmune disease patients in India are women. In men, it can manifest more as heart disease. Indian men face a cardiovascular death rate (349 per 100,000) that is significantly higher than that of men in Western nations, according to the National Noncommunicable Disease Monitoring Survey (NNMS).
Women take note
Kochi resident Jai Krishnan Sambasivan, 62, says he wouldn’t be able to function well if it were not for steroids. At 42, he was running his own business in Alappuzha, Kerala, when he developed a high fever that lasted months without a diagnosis. Admitted in hospital for over a month, he says he “fit into the category of patients who was clinically well [all tests came back negative], but not well”. What finally led to a diagnosis of vasculitis were two high inflammatory markers: hs-CRP and ESR.
Vasculitis is an autoimmune disease that inflames blood vessels, often leading to blockage of capillaries and eventually causing cardiac failure. He has managed to control the disease with Prednesol, a steroid drug, and lifestyle modifications. “But what keeps me alive is not medicine, it is breath control,” he believes. “I can say I have mastered it. I have learnt to be fearless.”
What you eat matters
Food plays a major role in managing/ preventing inflammation. According to Delhi-based nutritionist Shonali Sabherwal, a seasonal, pesticide-free, freshly-cooked plant diet is most effective in reducing chronic inflammation. “You need to question staples: the atta that you are using, is it a hybrid variety? Do we know what we are really stocking in our kitchens?”
Sabherwal’s approach, commonly used around the world for conditions such as allergies, autoimmune diseases and other chronic conditions, aligns with Ayurvedic prescriptions for excess agni (fire/ inflammation in the body). Dr. Nitin Kochar, a Mumbai-based Ayurvedic practitioner who specialises in cancer and inflammation, says that “depending on the specific dosha [vata, pitta or kapha, the Ayurvedic way of categorising the human body’s biochemistry], I prescribe fasting, specific plant foods and spices like ginger, cumin, giloy to weaken the fire”.
How do you treat it?
One of the frustrations of treating inflammation is that treatments are so imprecise. Dr. Shreevidya, medical director–preventive health, Apollo Hospitals, says chronic inflammation is usually identified not because someone felt it, but because it surfaced during a preventive health assessment. “Two drivers deserve more attention. One is chronic hidden infection, especially gum disease [untreated periodontitis keeps the whole system inflamed]. The other is air pollution. Long-term exposure to fine particulate matter is consistently associated with higher inflammation,” she says.
Dr. Divya Gopal, additional director of internal medicine at Mumbai’s Sir H.N. Reliance Foundation Hospital, says people should start with lifestyle changes. “Pain relievers like ibuprofen and naproxen reduce inflammation, but taking them long-term brings risks,” says Gopal. “For serious cases, I prescribe newer medications that block inflammation pathways.”
What to check
As research into inflammation intensifies, new methods are being discovered. Earlier this year, researchers at University College London uncovered a key mechanism that can help the body switch off inflammation and prevent harmful immune cells from building up. Elsewhere, several clinical studies have shown that, independent of weight loss and diabetes, GLP-1 receptor agonists such as Ozempic and Mounjaro can significantly reduce systemic inflammation markers such as CRP and TNF-alpha. There’s also talk about non-invasive continuous inflammation monitors, much like glucose monitors.
Science may be on the threshold of cures for several diseases that inflammation drives, but it is important to remember the nuance of it all: inflammation is part of our maintenance and repair system. Without inflammation, we can’t heal. The challenge is to master the balance between the healing short spells and the stubborn, prolonged simmer that has profound implications for our health.
The Mumbai-based writer and journalist is behind @the_slow_fix on Instagram.

Since 2024, Microsoft has tried to sell “Copilot+ PC.” The marketing initiative was aimed at making it easy for people to know which Windows systems were approved to run AI-accelerated workloads locally.
But Copilot+ PC branding is nowhere to be found on the new Surface PCs Microsoft announced this week.
Speaking with Windows Central, Brett Ostrum, corporate VP of Surface, said that the new Surface computers “are not called Copilot+ PCs” despite meeting the label’s requirements.
“They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there,” he said.
Copilot+ PCs require 16GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and an integrated neural processing unit (NPU) with performance rated at 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS) or better.
The Surface Pro 12-inch (2nd Edition) and Surface Laptop 13-inch (2nd Edition), coming out on October 13, both run Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus processors and have a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated at 80 TOPS.
“[T]he purpose for Copilot+ PCs was to be able to deliver [NPU] experience,” Kedar Kondap, SVP of compute at Qualcomm, told Windows Central. “So, it was to define a certain category of devices with a certain bar and metric, like, for example, a 45 TOPS NPU. … So from that perspective, it’s more offering the same experiences, probably without just using [Copilot+ PC] terminology now.”
AI PCs are old news
Copilot+ PCs are “a class of AI PCs and laptops” that represent “the fastest, most intelligent Windows PCs ever,” according to a Microsoft marketing page that was up as recently as May, per Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. That Copilot+ PCs landing page, however, now redirects to a page for “performance PCs” that still names “Copilot+ PCs” but features the label far less prominently.

Humanoid robots are getting even creepier (this one can cry on command)
As robots learn to fake feelings, the line between comfort and creepy keeps shrinking.
Humanoid robots have come a long way from clunky and monotone machines. Today's models can hold conversations, dance (well, sort-of) and even mimic human facial expressions with unsettling accuracy. The latest addition to this continuously growing list is the Yansyn-X2, a robot that made headlines for something no consumer device has done before: crying on command.
Yes, you read that right. Footage from the 2026 Inclusion Conference in Shanghai shows a demonstrator asking the robot, "Can you shed tears for me?" and then, a few seconds later, a single tear rolls down its face. It's a striking moment from a technological standpoint, but also one that sparks a lot of unease.
This isn't just a novelty stunt. There's a serious engineering effort behind those tear ducts as the research into affective computing amps up in the robotics industry. If you haven't heard of affective computing, you should know it's about teaching machines to recognize, interpret and respond to human emotions. The goal isn't to fool anyone into thinking a robot genuinely feels sadness, but rather to make human-robot interactions feel more natural. Still, watching a machine well up with tears sits in the middle of uncanny valley territory — an utterly uncomfortable space where something looks almost human, but not quite.
The crying robot: engineering emotion
The Yansyn-X2 was developed by Yanxi Technology, a Chinese robotics firm based in Ningbo. According to the company, the robot relies on a three-layer technical architecture to pull off its emotional display. First, an AI algorithm analyzes conversational context and tone to determine when an emotional response is appropriate. Then, when the system detects sad or empathetic language, it signals bionic components beneath the robot's medical-grade silicone face (now that's a weird phrase to write), shifting its features into a sad expression. Lastly, a separate microfluidic system dispenses "tears" at the corner of the eyes.
The current version is a static model rather than a walking robot, although it can turn its head, track people and gesture with its arms. Plans are for future versions to use bionic muscles instead of servo motors for smoother and more varied facial changes. Is this actually useful, or just for show? A study published back in 2023 in Frontiers states that researchers found that robots displaying facial expressions matching the emotional tone of a conversation were rated more likable, trustworthy and human-like than robots showing no expression or mismatched ones. Basically, the industry is looking to build more emotionally responsive machines to ease people into working alongside robots in various settings.
The fast-growing robotics landscape
Yansyn-X2 isn't a one-off robot that's making our skin crawl. It's part of a broader wave of humanoid development happening across several fronts. At CES 2026, robotics companies showed off a ton of machines aimed at different goals. LG's CLOiD (slowly) folds and sorts your laundry. WIRobotics' Allex is handy for holding objects of up to 6.6 lbs while also creating recognizable hand gestures. SwitchBot's Onero H1 won our best robot in show award because it did what we really want robots to do — loaded the washing machine — because that's what we really want AI and robots to do instead of writing and painting in our place.
Other robots over the past year have achieved impressive feats. At Beijing's second annual World Humanoid Robot Games, the Tiangong Ultra robot ran the 100-meter dash in 9.39 seconds, which beats Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human record. Japan Airlines began testing an android baggage handler at Haneda Airport in May, seeking to offset the country's shrinking workforce. 1X's $20,000 NEO home robot promises to learn household chores, although it still needs human teleoperators watching through its cameras in the beginning.
The broader picture shows an industry working hard to increase speed, dexterity, utility and emotional believability. Robots that can spring, fold towels and now cry are inching closer to blending into daily life. While some features are definitely something we'd (maybe) welcome in our lives, others are deeply unsettling.

The Congress moved the Calcutta high court on September 23 over apparent discrepancies in the candidature of BJP’s Nandigram candidate for the upcoming bypolls, Hasirani Rath. In her election affidavit, Rath mentioned her age as ’60+’, but she also claimed she passed her Class X board examination in 1965.
Hasirani is the mother of the slain aide of Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, Chandranath Rath.
According to the petition submitted by the Congress on September 23, if Rath’s age as stated on the front page of her affidavit is factually correct, she would have been born in 1965-66. Yet, on Page 10 in the same affidavit, Rath states that she passed the Secondary/Madhyamik examination in 1965 — meaning she would have completed Class X in the year she was born, or even before her birth. Alt News has seen the petition.
Rath’s affidavit says she passed Class X from ‘Chowkhali Ganga Pada Milan Kanya Vidyapith’ (HS) in 1965.
It is also worth noting that the school is actually named Chowkhali Ganga Padma Milan Kanya Vidyapith and has been incorrectly mentioned in the affidavit as ‘Ganga Pada’.
Speaking to Alt News, West Bengal Pradesh Congress spokesperson Ajitesh Pandey said, “It is the duty of the returning officer to scrutinise the documents of the candidates. And there was a glaring error on the face of it. But they just let it go. When it came to our knowledge, we raised a complaint, and we approached the court, requesting the court to order the returning officer to call a verification and enquiry in respect of her educational qualification and her degrees, especially her Class X pass certificate.”
“In the case of Minakshi Natarajan, there was a similar error, which led to the cancellation of her candidature. But the objection was raised during the scrutiny. In the case of Nandigram, we did not object during the scrutiny because, of course, we were not given Hasirani Rath’s nomination papers, which were later uploaded on the ECI website. We will challenge her candidature through an election petition if she succeeds in retaining her nomination. But for now, our prayer before the court is that there should be an enquiry into her educational background,” said Pandey.
The petition filed by Congress states that The BJP candidate “is asking the electorate, the Returning Officer and this Hon’ble Court to believe that she appeared for and cleared a Class X board examination either before she was born, or… while she was an infant of about one year of age. No explanation consistent with ordinary human biology, or with the ordinary age at which children in West Bengal sit for the Class X examination (ordinarily 15-16 years), can reconcile the two declarations.”
Pandey, along with Congress leader and senior advocate Riju Ghoshal, represented the party in the high court. The petition was mentioned before a single-judge bench of Justice Krishna Rao.
The court allowed the petition to be filed, and it is likely to be heard on Thursday.
All Eyes on Nandigram
Byelections in Nandigram and Rejinagar will be held on October 6, with results scheduled on on October 9. The Nandigram bypoll was necessitated after Suvendu Adhikari vacated the seat retaining Bhabanipur. Adhikari had contested from both the seats in the 2026 assembly elections, and won both. The Rejinagar seat was relinquished by Aam Janata Unnayan Party leader Humayun Kabir.
The Nandigram contest took an unexpected turn when the candidate of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress faction, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her nomination on September 18. Banerjee then decided to support Congress candidate Milan Pradhan.
However, within hours of Banerjee announcing her support for Pradhan, he was arrested in connection with old cases related to the 2007 Nandigram violence. Congress and the TMC questioned the timing of the arrest, while the BJP said the police action was based on pending cases and involved no political intervention.
The BJP candidate filed her nomination on September 15. Her son, Chandranath Rath, a former aide of Suvendu Adhikari, was shot dead on May 6, two days after BJP won the elections in Bengal. He was shot point-blank by bike-borne assailants in the Madhyamgram area of North 24 Parganas district. CBI has filed a chargesheet against 11 accused in the case. Hasirani has herself been active in local politics for years and has served in panchayat bodies since 1998.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Quick Answer
Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and TripWaffle can turn flight, hotel, train, and other confirmation emails into organized travel plans. They differ in AI planning, maps, collaboration, trip tracking, alerts, and pricing, so the best choice depends on how you travel.
While traveling is something we all look forward to, the preparation behind it is sometimes quite grueling. Especially when you are doing everything by yourself. You book a flight on one site, a hotel on another, and a rental car through a different source, maybe through a referral link sent to you on WhatsApp. Traveling isn’t just about downloading the right apps before you board the flight. It is also about having all your important info at your disposal.
Just to know whether your hotel booking said 2 PM or 12 PM, you have to dig through your inbox. This is such a universal travel headache that an entire category of apps has been developed just to fix this. This list contains 4 AI travel planner apps that can convert your forwarded emails into a clean, day-by-day plan — flights, hotels, activities all lined up in order.
Table of Contents
Best AI Travel Planners
I went over the internet and actually dug through four of the more talked-about names in this space — Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and the newer, scrappier TripWaffle. These apps were put to the test to see what they are genuinely good at, where they fall short, and which one deserves a spot on your phone before your next trip. Let us go through them one by one.
Wanderlog: The one that does almost everything, and does most of it well
For me, Wanderlog has become the default travel planner app, and for good reason. The email trick works two ways here. You can either forward your flight and hotel confirmations email to a special address Wanderlog gives you, or you can just link your Gmail account and let it quietly scan your inbox for bookings automatically on its own. The details show up straight in your itinerary, and it eliminates typing in flight numbers and copying and pasting confirmation codes.
However, there is one thing that makes Wanderlog stand out from a plain inbox-scanner. After your bookings are in, Wanderlog does not just leave them sitting there as a list. It pins everything onto an actual map. You can drag your stops, reorder your day, and there is a route optimizer that can rearrange your stops to save you driving time. Wanderlog also works like a shared Google Doc. Add your travel companions by email, and everyone will have access to edit the same trip at the same time, see live changes, and more. For a group trip, this is a great thing to have.
Community members also contribute travel guides right inside the app, so you have all the interesting information about a new city you have landed. Speaking of the cons, some users have reported that once a trip is created, there is sometimes no way to edit locations cleanly, forcing them to delete and redo it. Then there is the paywall issue, where features such as offline access and automatic Gmail scanning are locked behind the Pro subscription.
Download Wanderlog: Android | iOS
Stippl: The AI-first planner that tries to be your whole travel toolkit
Stippl leans hard into AI to get there. You just need to tell it what kind of trip you want (relaxed, adventurous, culture-heavy, offbeat) and it generates out a full day-by-day itinerary for your destination in under two minutes. If you already have a rough plan and just need a day filled in, you can use Stippl for that too. Simply tap a single day, and it will generate activities, restaurants, and transport suggestions just for that slot.
For emails, it works the same familiar way. You just need to forward your booking emails, and Stippl will pick up flights, hotels, trains, and restaurant reservations and feed them to your trip automatically. Everything also gets synced to the calendar, so your itinerary shows up right alongside your regular meetings and reminders. Stippl sets itself apart from the other three by the fact that it leans into being a memory-keeper as well as a travel planner.
There is a scratch map feature that adds every country you have already visited. It gives the feel of a passport stamp collection you can show off. It can also stitch your trip photos into an automatic travel reel or photobook once you are back home, no editing required from your end. You can also purchase an eSIM from the app. Coming to the con, the AI-powered itinerary generation and offline mode sit behind a paywall. Some users have reported having run into crashes, slow email imports, and the odd date or flight not saving correctly, especially with overnight flights or long layovers. Do keep that in mind.
Download: iOS
Polarsteps: Built for tracking your journey, now sneaking in planning too
Polarsteps is a bit different than the other three apps on this list. It did not start as a booking organizer at all but as a way to automatically track where you have already been and turn it into a beautiful, shareable map, eliminating manual check-in anywhere. You just have to carry your phone, and the app quietly traces your route in the background using WiFi and mobile data with constant GPS pings. That said, Polarsteps is also slowly gaining proper trip-planning tools, and the confirmation-email feature is now part of it. You can forward your hotel or flight booking to the app, and it pulls out the address and other details automatically.
Polarsteps has also introduced an AI-powered itinerary builder. There is also the ability to manually add flights by looking them up by airline and flight number, though you cannot book through the app. Since tracking is Polarsteps’ specialty, once your trip ends, it can turn the whole route into a digital travel book that you can order and keep.
Speaking of the shortcomings, compared to Wanderlog or Stippl, Polarsteps’ booking-import feature is newer and less complete. Polarsteps traditionally allows just one person to add content per trip. This means that if you are planning a group trip, Polarsteps, as a travel planner, won’t be a good option. It is meant for solo travelers and backpackers, who care as much about documenting the journey as planning it.
TripWaffle: The newcomer that’s focused on one job
TripWaffle may be the least-known name here, but that is one of the reasons why it makes it to this list. It’s built by a small, independent team (led by a single developer, Guy King, based in Australia). Instead of trying to be a do-everything travel app, it does one thing and focuses on, which is turning forwarded confirmation emails into a clean itinerary.
The setup is about as simple as it gets. You sign up and send your booking confirmations to it from providers. Using AI, TripWaffle reads the email, pulls out the dates, times, confirmation numbers, and addresses, and puts everything into a day-by-day timeline with time zones and connecting flights already planned out.
TripWaffle earns its keep in the details that it can keep. You get live flight tracking with real position updates, alerts about delays, gate changes, and a “flight reliability score,” which tells you how a specific flight number has historically performed. You receive a pre-trip checklist email covering visa requirements, weather, and packing suggestions just a day before your departure. TripWaffle is completely free with no ads, no Pro tier, and no upsell, which is something none of the apps in this list provide. You do not get crowd-sourced attraction guides or any AI-generated itineraries from scratch.
So which one should you actually download?
Honestly, it depends on what kind of traveler you are. I travel a lot, and most of my stay is outside my home country. I would suggest you try multiple apps and then decide on the one that you want to keep. For me, the above apps do the job, and you should definitely check them out and see if they fit your bill or not. Before you purchase a subscription to any of the paid apps, do go through the free version thoroughly and see if that is what you are looking for or not.

'Serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts': Jaishankar hits out at Pakistan PM Sharif at UNGA
Without naming him, Jaishankar said Pakistan PM Sharif had invoked arguments to “normalise terrorism” and “claim immunity” from its consequences.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday slammed Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for “misrepresenting facts” at the United Nations General Assembly, calling Islamabad a “serial practitioner of terrorism.”
Without naming him, the external affairs minister said Sharif had invoked arguments to “normalise terrorism” and “claim immunity” from its consequences, while asserting India's right to self-defence.
Sharif, during his address, spoke about the four-day military confrontation between India and Pakistan in May 2025, claiming that Islamabad exercised its “inherent right of self-defence” under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter during the confrontation, and praising Pakistan's armed forces for their response.
Also Read | 'Pakistan's duplicity will neither benefit it nor the world': India slams Shehbaz Sharif's UN speech
Responding to this, Jaishankar said, “Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this assembly. Arguments were invoked to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences. That will not stand. Our right to defend ourselves will be exercised.”
"Friendship and goodwill cannot coexist with terrorism. It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend his ways," the external affairs minister added.
Also Read | 'Countries far from conflicts being penalised': Jaishankar invokes PM Modi's remark at UNGA
Following the Pahalgam terror attack in April, 2025, which led to the deaths of 26 civilians, India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7 last year, wherein it struck terror bases located in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. The military escalation ended with a ceasefire which took effect on May 10.
Deep Dive
In his address, the Pakistan PM had also credited United States President Donald Trump, claiming his “timely intervention” had come at a decisive moment.
“His timely intervention came at a decisive juncture when two nuclear-armed neighbors stood at the brink of an all-out war. And, who knows, Mr. President, the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump not stepped in at this critical moment with clarity of thought and action. Mr President, we must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches that precipice ever again,” Sharif said.
To be sure, New Delhi has consistently maintained that the May 2025 ceasefire between India and Pakistan was reached through direct communication between the two sides, with no role played by any third party.
India exercised Right of Reply after Pakistan PM's address
After Sharif's remarks at the UN, India exercised its Right of Reply, describing Pakistan as a “puppet regime”.
First Secretary in India's Permanent Mission to the UN Petal Gahlot strongly rejected Pakistan's remarks on India and Jammu and Kashmir, while also taking aim at Islamabad's record on terrorism, democratic rights and treatment of minorities.
“At the heart of the issue is the long-standing practice of cross-border terrorism by Pakistan. We demonstrated last year that terrorists will have nowhere to run and nowhere to hide. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised and continued. Terrorism by Pakistan will have consequences,” Gahlot said.
"We are confident that this Assembly will recognise Pakistan and its policies for what they really are, not what its representative mendaciously projects it to be. Reiterating falsehoods year after year does not make them true. Pakistan's terrorism, deceit and duplicity will neither benefit it nor the world," Petal Gahlot told the Assembly.

Apple hit with a $5.7 billion verdict for alleged patent infringement
Apple is reportedly looking to appeal the jury verdict.
Apple is currently on the hook for a record-breaking patent infringement case, after a federal jury decided that the iPhone maker has to pay more than $5.7 billion to Taction, a San Diego-based company that produces audio and gaming peripherals with haptic feedback. If the decision holds, it would be one of the largest patent infringement case payouts in the US, topping an ongoing case involving Intel for $3 billion.
Taction filed the lawsuit back in 2021, alleging that Apple's Taptic Engine found in its various iPhone and Apple Watch models infringed on two of its patents related to haptic feedback. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2023 by a federal judge in San Diego, but later brought back into the courts following a decision by the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit a couple of years later. The latest jury verdict from Friday said that Apple unintentionally infringed on two of Taction's patents. According to Bloomberg Law, Apple didn't agree with the jury's decision nor the damages and would appeal the verdict.
Before the Taction lawsuit, Apple was previously hit with another patent infringement lawsuit from Immersion. The company filed a complaint against Apple, also accusing it of patent violations with haptic tech found in iPhones, Apple Watches and MacBooks, but eventually settled for an undisclosed amount. More notably, Apple is in the midst of another patent infringement battle surrounding its Apple Watch and a feature that tracks blood-oxygen levels. In November, another federal jury ruled that Apple has to pay $634 million for violation patents from Masimo, but the tech giant is similarly planning to appeal this jury verdict.

From turgid to thrusting - mixed start for new Scotland
- Published
For 45 turgid minutes in Slovenia, some in the Tartan Army might have reimagined the Steve Clarke years as a time of plenty, the halcyon era of ambitious football when Scotland were an all-electric thrill-fest.
The opening half of the Sebastien Pocognoli regime was, as expected, disjointed.
It was also, rather unexpectedly, devoid of anything remotely related to what Pocognoli laid out as his non-negotiables - front-foot pressing, high intensity, speed of thought and mind, goal threat.
They had no shot on target and lost so many aerial duels that you stopped counting beyond the half-hour mark. They took 38 minutes to touch the ball in Slovenia's penalty area.
It wasn't like they were under major pressure - the hosts are a pretty toothless side - but neither were they accurate or energetic. Everybody who preached patience in the new era gulped hard. This was not good. We didn't expect champagne, but this was stale beer.
And then it changed, not so completely that Scotland roared and won the game, but they certainly cleared their throats as an attacking force.
McBurnie and co show promise without poise
From being impotent, they became thrusting. That second half was as big a 0-0 rout as you're likely to see. Frustrating, but encouraging at the same time.
It will be agonising for Oli McBurnie that he's still without an international goal - he said he wouldn't sleep after failing to convert a one-on-one with Jan Oblak - but his second-half performance was full of good things; efforts on goal, link-up play, presence and danger.
Robbie Ure hit a post, Kieron Bowie had a terrific chance, but missed. The three strikers drew a blank, but as far as 0-0s go, it offered hope that more productive days may lay ahead with these guys.
There are two ways of looking at the draw. All 10 starting outfield players had a shot on goal, the first time that's happened since June 2022, against Armenia.
Scotland had 17 shots, their most attempts in a competitive game in more than 14 years. The flipside is that they have now failed to score in three tournament games in a row for the first time in almost 22 years.
After the break, Pocognoli dropped McBurnie a little deeper, in a pocket just behind Robbie Ure and then Bowie when he came on. He got Billy Gilmour to sit lower in midfield, where he had time to dictate, which he absolutely did. Gilmour tied it all together in the second half.
Pocognoli called it "two games in one game" and he was right. The subtle shift in McBurnie's and Gilmour's positioning brought Scotland alive.
It was an impressive watch; ambition, relentlessness, belief. No cherry on top but enough there to leave most folk happy about day one and motivated ahead of day two, against Switzerland on Tuesday night at Hampden.
McBurnie, not so much the prodigal son but now the forgiven one, had that big chance six minutes into the new half - the one he would have dreamed about. He created it for himself, winning possession and getting into a wonderful position right in front of an isolated Oblak.
He could have dinked it as the goalkeeper committed himself, he could have slid it home to Oblak's left or through his legs. Instead, he went for the flourish, trying to take it round the Slovenian and marking his return to the side after 2,005 days in the wilderness with a first goal on his 17th appearance.
Oblak won the duel. Painful, for sure, but a prelude to a stirring second half from the striker and his new-old team-mates. McBurnie played a slick one-two with the increasingly dominant Gilmour, who had his shot saved. Oblak was by a million miles Slovenia's best player.
McBurnie had a header fly over, Aaron Hickey had a header just wide, Bowie came on and had an immediate impact. He had three chances in eight minutes - a tame shot, a clipped attempt and then the big one - played in by Gilmour but pulled wide. In that moment, he joined McBurnie and Ure (after hitting a post late in the first half) in the torture chamber.
In the midst of all of that, McBurnie powered a header on goal, but Oblak was equal to it. That was Scotland's ninth consecutive crack without reply. They were utterly dominant but achingly goalless. So much encouraging stuff and yet just one point to show for it when it really should have been three.
Pocognoli demonstrates tactical acumen
Pocognoli said he was heartened by that second half. Scotland fans should be buoyed by the new head coach recognising the problems in his team and then fixing them.
With such a small track record to feed off, the subject of his tactical acumen was always going to be an interesting one - the ownership of the second 45 minutes showed that he's no slouch in identifying and changing the things that need to be changed.
Going with McBurnie and Ure up front was something of a surprise, but it sent a signal out that Scotland are here to go on the offensive rather than just defend their way to decent outcomes.
That didn't materialise in the first half, but it clicked in the second. It's a touch surreal that, at the end of another game when Scotland failed to score, there is a lot to be hopeful about in the men who are there to supply the goals.
McBurnie, Ure and Bowie are an exciting trio. When others are fit, there's Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland, Tommy Conway and Ross Stewart. Young James Wilson will have his moment at some point. New blood has joined the old guard and things should be better when everything settles down.
For Pocognoli, the next test is the biggest one. Switzerland, ranked 14th in the world, are missing some serious operators, but they are brilliantly coached by Murat Yakin and they're settled and formidable.
Their whole is greater than the sum of their parts. This will be a fascinating examination of Pocognoli's prowess. Win on Tuesday night and it's lift-off time.

England embrace the chaos - but control also needed to win big prizes
- Published
Thomas Tuchel talked about England having to "embrace the chaos" as they embarked on recovery from the crushing disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.
As England took those first steps on the road to rehabilitation against reigning world and European champions Spain in the Nations League at Wembley, head coach Tuchel learned the brutal lesson that chaos without control is a loser's strategy at elite level.
Spain do control, not chaos. And this is why they are serial winners and England remain a nearly team without a major men's success since the 1966 World Cup.
England delivered moments to admire in the 3-2 defeat, even embracing those chaotic spells in an enthralling encounter, but ultimately they came up short once more against this summer's World Cup winners, who are now unbeaten in 39 games.
Once Tuchel's England stopped playing themselves into trouble by mimicking Spain's passing style without having anywhere near the quality of their opponents and followed their own "DNA", to use the buzz-phrase of the moment, they actually threatened with power and pace.
Quite how England reached the 36th minute only one goal down was a mystery to everyone inside Wembley, Marc Guehi's inexplicable turn into trouble gifting Lamine Yamal an opener inside two minutes.
Ferran Torres saw a goal ruled out for offside, was denied by a fine stop by England goalkeeper James Trafford, then rolled an effort wide of the post when clean through.
England took advantage of those reprieves to somehow be ahead by the break, through star performer Anthony Gordon's composed finish and Harry Kane's deflected header.
Kane's penalty miss just after the break was a turning point, hitting the bar after slipping and touching the ball twice, before England once again paid the price for errors.
Nico O'Reilly coughed up possession in the build-up to Alex Baena's equaliser before another substitute in Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winner in the Euro 2024 final against England in Berlin, settled matters after 74 minutes.
If it was a bad night for Manchester City defensive duo Guehi and O'Reilly, it was not much better for Jarell Quansah, who was given the nod ahead of the recalled Trent Alexander-Arnold. He was uncertain throughout and does not look a natural right-back - perhaps because he is not a natural right-back.
Of course, it could have been different had Kane scored his penalty. He did not and it was not.
Kane said: "On another day we could have won." This was not another day and England did not win.
England's bolder approach after a shaky opening 25 minutes offered up the prospect of a landmark victory, but shambolic defending saw Guehi and O'Reilly present gifts Spain were happy to accept.
As against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta, England led by a Gordon goal and lost, but at least here they went down swinging and not by going into cowering retreat.
It was a small mercy appreciated by the home support, but the gulf in class when it mattered was still evident as Spain's smooth, unhurried style cut a sharp contrast to England's often frantic efforts.
Tuchel's defence looked horribly vulnerable and easy to slice through, although keeper Trafford – given two games before first-choice Jordan Pickford returns – was blameless and will have created a good impression as he tries to create greater competition in that department.
They have now shipped 13 goals in their last six matches in all competitions, after conceding only seven in their first 17 games under Tuchel.
Ironically, it was two players now plying their trade in Spain, Gordon at Barcelona and Jude Bellingham at Real Madrid, who were England's standout performers.
Gordon was in electrifying form, while Bellingham was relentless in driving England forward, even in a losing cause.
As for the chaos, Tuchel begged to differ.
He told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm not sure there was a lot of chaos. We had an incredible amount of high-ball recoveries in the opponent's half. I think 15 more than Spain. Overall, I think 15 in total in the first half. That only goes against a team like Spain if we play man to man, so we were very brave."
Tuchel added: "The defending and the deep block were excellent, except for the third goal where we got cut open through the middle. This normally should not happen.
"Offensively, I think we played in a clear structure. We tried to switch sides a lot. We tried to put the full-backs up to make the difference and they did. A lot of good stuff but unfortunately not the result."
On the gap between the sides, Tuchel said: "We saw no gap except for the technical execution. In the last 20 metres, they were superior than us."
Tuchel's comments are questionable here, ignoring the fact that if Spain's own technical execution was better they could easily have been four goals up before England scored, but he was correct to point out the improvement after Gordon drew them level.
England captain Kane said: "I spoke before that we reached good levels at the World Cup but didn't quite put a full 90 minutes together. It was probably similar again here. We had a couple of good moments though, that period was as good as we've played in a long, long time and that's the standard we know we can reach.
"We're playing against the world champions, the European champions, and we went toe-to-toe. On another day for sure we'd have won that game."
England certainly embrace the chaos, as Tuchel suggested, but chaos alone does not claim big prizes and never has.
At least this is a lesson Tuchel did not have to wait too long to learn after the World Cup.
