Why we won't know how visible the iPhone Duo's crease is for a long time
Apple's nano-texture screen might not hide the crease forever.
Apple's first foldable phone is coming soon, and it caused quite a stir upon its announcement earlier this month. That's no surprise, since everyone was waiting to see how the iPhone Duo would address the competition's shortcomings. It's still early to tell, given that it won't hit stores until next month and all we've had so far are a few brief hands-on experiences.
But one of the most anticipated features is the new nano-texture display, which promises to make the crease on the screen much less visible. In fact, it does seem to be much less noticeable — but it will be a long time before we know for sure.
The biggest trade-off with foldable phones: The crease
Historically, foldable phones have had an unpleasant flaw: the crease. And it all comes down to physics. With today's technology, it's nearly impossible to have a flexible display that folds without leaving any crease marks. Companies have gotten much better at this, and the creases have become less noticeable even though they're still there.
Apple took a clever approach to make the crease less visible. The iPhone Duo's screen has a matte coating on top, which significantly reduces light reflection. Some people who have seen the iPhone Duo in person say the crease is barely noticeable. Others say it's still visible and that it's only a matter of time before it gets worse.
Our own hands-on report found the crease is "easier to feel with your finger than observe with your eyes." But does that mean Apple has finally solved the crease problem once and for all with the iPhone Duo? Not really.
The biggest problem here is cumulative damage. Take the Galaxy Z Fold 8 as an example. Samsung ships its foldable phones unfolded in the box, and when you look at them for the first time, the screen looks super flat. But as you start folding and unfolding it, the crease definitely becomes more noticeable. Now imagine folding that screen thousands of times over the course of months or years. It's not hard to find photos of foldable phones with damaged screens online.
Only time will tell if Apple got it right
Multiple Apple executives have publicly stated how proud they are of the iPhone Duo and how they believe the device will be much more durable than the competition. But we won't know for sure how the iPhone Duo's nano-textured screen will perform until the phone reaches a mass of consumers. Not only that, but it will likely take some time before we have any idea of how future-proof it is. That will certainly be something many YouTubers will put to the test in their extreme durability experiments.
So yes, the crease on the iPhone Duo's screen was barely visible during the hands-on sessions at the Apple event. But even the most thorough hands-on impression is really just a snapshot of a crease that hasn't had time to develop yet. The reviews that will roll in soon, ours included, can only speak to what the iPhone Duo looks like fresh out of the box. That might be different after using the device for a few months.
Still, you have to give Apple credit here. The fact that the company created a screen that already makes the crease look much less noticeable in the first few days is certainly promising. It's also something we should expect to see the competition rushing to catch up on soon.

Tens of millions of people are located in the storm's path

More than 70,000 utility customers have been left without electricity across the northeastern U.S. on Saturday as a nor’easter takes aim at the coast, bringing dangerous conditions throughout the weekend.
Meteorologists warned that gale winds might down trees while heavy rain threatens to leave roadways underwater.
With tens of millions of people located in the storm's path, powerful winds and torrential rain are already lashing the region as residents prepare for further impacts. According to the National Weather Service, severe coastal flooding is anticipated, particularly along New Jersey and Delaware shorelines.
"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the weather service said Saturday. "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water with rippling surface waves swept through streets, flooding a number of homes. Roughly 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where roads were also submerging, Mayor Mike Mangan stated he anticipated "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." Voluntary evacuations had been declared earlier for low-lying sections.
The weather prompted concert cancellations alongside dozens of grounded flights at airports in Boston, Nantucket, and Martha’s Vineyard across Friday and Saturday. Several airlines agreed to waive change or cancellation fees on various East Coast flights through the weekend.
New Jersey communities prepare for major flooding
Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.
“It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.”
Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.
Damaging winds threaten coastal New England
Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
“It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said.
Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.
Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
Storm disrupts concerts, baseball and flights
Air travel was also being disrupted, with Boston particularly hard hit. Flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 39 cancellations at Boston Logan International Airport between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. Saturday, compared with 22 at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport. Another 12 flights were delayed at Logan.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.
The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.
In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.
For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is “part of life,” said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.
“It’s a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point,” he said. “This is not out of the realm of ordinary.”
Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.
“We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend,” said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.
She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.
The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.
The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.
The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.
Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising
The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.
The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.
Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.
“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.
“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.
“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.
“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.
Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.
A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

South Africa reels from spate of mass shootings that killed 38 people in a week
Johannesburg — A spate of mass shootings in three major South African cities killed nearly 40 people this week, with such incidents increasingly common in a country already known for its high crime rates.
On Saturday night, South African police said at least 10 people were killed at a shisanyama — a common kind of local restaurant selling barbecued meat — near Cape Town, while eleven others were injured.
The same night, near the commercial capital Johannesburg, 17 people were killed when a group of men with AK-47s burst into a township tavern where people were drinking.
The perpetrators "allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident," police said in a statement.
Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
Earlier in the week, another mass shooting occurred in the coastal city of Durban. Police said 11 people, including a pregnant woman, were killed on Tuesday by multiple gunmen in an attack on a house party.
A motive for that crime was also unclear, but several people at the house were known to authorities as part of investigations into criminal activity.
Illegal guns are common in South Africa, where mass shooting events are usually linked to gangs and organized crime, sometimes surrounding activities involving illegal gold miners known as "zama-zamas."
In June, in another mass shooting, 12 people were killed when gunmen stormed an informal settlement in Johannesburg, where people live in tin shacks without access to running water and electricity. That shooting was blamed on turf wars between zama-zamas.
At the scene, NPR saw pools of blood under a snooker table in a makeshift bar roped off with police tape and traumatized residents described their fear when they heard the gunshots.
"I hid under my bed," said Angela Mopayi, 54, at the time, "I couldn't breathe, I couldn't do anything, I thought I was dying."
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, averaging 60 a day. But even so, the number of mass shootings has become a national crisis.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development," and deployed the army in some of the worst-affected areas.
President Trump has also been vocal about crime in South Africa since returning to office, but he has focused on the murders of white people on farms. While these do occur, official statistics show the vast majority of victims of crime are poor Black people.
And they are often also women. This month South Africans have been protesting amid a spate of brutal femicides in Johannesburg. On Saturday a tenth woman's body was discovered, despite police promises to crack down on gender-based violence.
South Africans head to the polls in November for local elections in which crime is expected to be a key issue.

Earlier this month, Pokémon card content creator Natalie Roush posted a video to her YouTube and Instagram pages that enraged the larger collection community. In the now-deleted video, Roush shows off two premium boxes of cards that had not yet been officially released, and implores viewers not to be mad. But they were; other creators claimed that cards Roush had purchased were stolen from the manufacturer and mocked her for trying to sell them at exorbitant prices. The Roush situation was a high-profile example of the way Pokémon card collecting culture has been upended by the influencer economy and people trying to profit off the hobby. Though Roush has been relatively quiet in the days since the blowup, Pokémon collectors have been up in arms over a different — but very much related — problem.
Pokémon card resellers have turned collecting into an online blood sport
The franchise’s renewed popularity with resellers is being driven by a culture fixated on hustling.
When the Pokémon Trading Card Game’s long-awaited 30th Celebration set finally released last week, collectors across the country lined up outside of stores in hopes of getting their hands on some shiny pieces of cardboard. The anniversary set has unusually strong pull rates — the rate at which you’re likely to find rare “chase” cards in a given set — giving more fans the cards they’ve always dreamed of, and potentially upsetting the aftermarket Poké-conomy. Some diehard Poké-fans even camped out overnight because a resurgence in popularity has made the cards much more difficult to find and buy in person. But another group of Pokémon card hunters was able to secure the highly sought-after set without having to travel to physical retailers or navigate the online Pokémon Center.
Those people — resellers who often use automated bots to buy dozens of boxes of cards as soon as they’re available for preorder online — might not have had any intention of collecting the 30th Celebration set for themselves. But they have been trying to offload their spoils at marked-up prices to fans who haven’t had a chance to buy cards for themselves. Most retailers can’t keep cards on shelves, but there are plenty of videos online of resellers showing off piles of product they were able to obtain either by placing orders with bots or using inventory checking programs that alert them when brick-and-mortar stores receive stock. It’s also easy to find footage of resellers getting into altercations over cards, and in one recent instance, a 72-year-old man was arrested and charged with a first-degree misdemeanor for tracking a Pokémon delivery worker’s location with a device secretly planted in her car.
Though flipping trading cards is nothing new, the Pokémon reselling economy has gotten much bigger in recent years as people have taken note of how durable the franchise’s popularity is. Many resellers like BotterBoyNova started off with other kinds of valuable merchandise before realizing that Pokémon products can be sold for far beyond the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, or MSRP. When I spoke with Nova recently, he told me that — like many millennials — he’s been a Pokémon fan since the mid-’90s. Nova was originally a content creator whose videos were mostly focused on reselling sneakers, but seeing how easy it was to profit from reselling Pokémon products convinced him that he needed to get in on the action.
“Resellers in what’s described as the ‘Sneaker Twitter’ space are tapped in with practically every category of collectible that can resell for a profit,” Nova explained to me via Discord. “It’s not a situation where I’m singling out the Pokémon card market. It just so happens that it’s highly profitable and difficult to purchase for MSRP, and those are the conditions that our community specializes in.”
Rather than operating independently, Nova works with Polar Chefs — a “cook group” community that sells monthly subscriptions to a variety of reseller tools and services. Subscriptions range from $660 per year to $75 per month, and they come with access to Polar Chefs’ private Discord server, restock alerts, and a selection of bots that can be used to buy cards. These bots make it easy for people to create multiple accounts on retailers’ websites that are attached to virtual credit cards, while the buyer’s IP address is spoofed with proxies. Technically, this kind of process isn’t illegal — at least not yet; Congress outlawed concert ticket-focused bots in 2016 and lawmakers have proposed doing the same for retail bots. But it does violate most retailers’ terms of service, which is why some resellers’ orders are canceled.
Retail bots aren’t illegal, but they do violate most retailers’ terms of service.
Using Polar Chefs’ tools, Nova has been able to purchase massive amounts of Pokémon cards at MSRP from various retailers without being blocked by websites’ anti-bot security measures. Nova described his process of securing cards with bots as being “almost completely hands free,” and explained that the real work doesn’t begin until he has to sort and sell his inventory to a couple of bulk buyers.
“During most weeks, I spend less than 3-5 hours a week on the reselling side of things (setting up bots, buying inventory, selling and fulfilling inventory),” Nova said, noting that he’s commonly asleep while pre-programmed bots make purchases for him. “I wait for notifications to come in from Polar Chefs which inform me of releases, bot adjustments I need to make, etc.”
Though it is difficult to pinpoint exactly when Pokémon reselling really exploded in the past few years, the rise of groups like Polar Chefs feels reflective of the way that the creator economy evolved during the covid-19 pandemic. Resellers like Nova are influencers whose videos are designed to sell people on the idea that they could also be making money by flipping cards at scale. And monetized cook groups are prime examples of how online hustle culture has become more focused on the sale of how-to guides and courses for practices that can be seen as morally suspect.
There’s an argument to be made that the scarcity created by resellers is part of what has driven the popularity of platforms like Whatnot — an online marketplace where people can pay for things like sealed Pokémon products, which are then opened on livestreams by the seller before they’re sent to the buyer. Many Whatnot streamers present themselves as entrepreneurs who are providing their audiences with a helpful service while also entertaining them. But the platform has been accused of operating more like an illegal gambling operation, and there is an entire ecosystem of creators whose content documents Whatnot streamers scamming their customers.
But with the 30th Celebration packs flooding the market with rare cards, the scammers could be out of luck. Over the past week, X and Reddit have been inundated with screenshots from unnamed Discord servers where people claiming to be resellers appear to be melting down over not being able to sell their overpriced cards. One of the more widely circulated images features a person insisting that resellers are “the people that actually ensure [The Pokémon Company] makes money,” while complaining that “there’s literally no value in these sets because everyone can pull the rare bullshit.” In another, a reseller says they are filing a class action lawsuit against The Pokémon Company “for independent vendors who suffered severe financial asset devaluation due to artificial market saturation.”
The absurdity of these posts suggests that they might have been written by people making fun of actual resellers, as does the fact that while searching Discord I found some posts that use the exact same wording. Those posters might have just been looking for attention, but the state of the larger reselling economy does seem to be having a negative impact on Pokémon cards’ availability.
Even though The Pokémon Company is printing more cards than ever, almost everything about the modern aftermarket economy has made it harder for ordinary people — especially children — to participate in the hobby. Nova told me that he thinks casual collectors who just want to pull cool cards for themselves are completely justified in feeling that resellers are making Pokémon less accessible. He also believes that collectors whose interest in the cards is “incentivized by monetary gain” are hypocrites for taking issue with resellers. Aside from actually playing with them, the real fun of Pokémon cards is in the hunt and delight when you’re able to find a pack that shocks you with its contents. It’s an experience everyone’s supposed to be able to enjoy, but it’s being ruined by hustlers.

Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
- Published
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.
Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.
The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".
"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Andy Burnham brings good vibes to Labour’s annual conference but tough choices are coming
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been in office for two months, and his party seems content for now
LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been in the job for two months, and so far his party isn’t demanding his head. These days, that’s an accomplishment.
The governing Labour Party opens its annual conference beside the River Mersey in Liverpool on Sunday, with Burnham pledging to turn the page on a decade of economic and political turmoil that has made him the U.K.’s seventh prime minister since its 2016 vote to leave the European Union.
He says his message in a keynote speech on Tuesday will be: “It’s time for Britain to have hope again.”
“We’ve had a decade since Brexit and it’s been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that,” Burnham said as he arrived in Liverpool on Saturday.
His message is aimed at both the British public and a center-left party that is hopeful but nervous — ready to embrace his promise of better times, but worried about economic damage rippling out from conflict in the Middle East.
University of Manchester political science professor Rob Ford said Burnham’s difficult task is to win over “a skeptical electorate" eager for change, "while at the same time doing that within the constraints of a very difficult economic and fiscal situation.”
In short: “How do you serve people a bowl of cold porridge and convince them it’s a pepperoni pizza?”
Britain’s main political parties all hold conferences in September and October, combinations of pep rally, social gathering and policy forum that set the political tone and agenda for the year ahead.
Last year’s Labour gathering was gloomy, as members despaired about Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s deep unpopularity, little more than a year after winning power in a landslide, and the seemingly unstoppable rise of the anti-immigration opposition party Reform UK.
Burnham, then the popular mayor of Greater Manchester, was followed around Liverpool by journalists as speculation grew that he would challenge Starmer.
Events came to a head months later when a panicky party forced Starmer’s resignation and his replacement by Burnham as party leader and prime minister in July.
Now, Labour is seeing a “Burnham bounce” driven by the new leader’s upbeat talk and modest moves to put money in voters’ pocketbooks by cutting tax on electricity bills and capping bus fares.
Meanwhile, Reform is facing parliamentary and police investigations over its finances – though it also recently received a whopping 72 million pounds ($95 million) from two cryptocurrency billionaires.
Burnham has already set out some priorities, including handing more power to local leaders in order to generate "good growth in every post code.” He says he’ll reform Britain’s privatized utilities, especially the expensive, leaky and polluting water network.
While the party is relatively united behind Burnham, he faces a divisive decision about whether to approve new oil drilling in the North Sea – opposed by environmentalists but backed by trade unions – and pushback over plans agreed under Starmer to make it harder for immigrants to settle permanently in Britain.
The next general election does not have to be called until 2029, but Labour’s revival has sparked talk of a snap election – something Burnham denies he’s considering.
“All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead,” Burnham told broadcaster ITV on Friday.
But no matter how upbeat Burnham is, economic pain is coming.
Burnham must explain to party members and voters how he will deal with economic turbulence from the on-off U.S.-Iran war, which has severely restricted the movement of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.
Treasury chief John Healey is set to deliver the Burnham government’s first budget on Oct. 28, with rising energy prices tightening a cost-of-living squeeze. Like other countries, Britain also needs to find money to increase defense spending to counter threats from Russia.
That means tax rises or spending cuts – or both – could be on the cards.
One thing that might bring an economic boost is to ease some of the trade barriers erected by Brexit. Burnham has pledged closer ties with the European Union, but it’s unclear how close.
Under Starmer, Labour was elected in 2024 on a promise not to seek to rejoin the bloc or enter its single market for goods, services and employment. Many Labour members would like to break that pledge, including former Prime Minister Tony Blair, who said last week that the U.K. and EU should start negotiations “where everything is on the table.”
Burnham has said that’s a discussion for another time. Meanwhile, progress toward closer ties has been slow.
An EU-U.K. reset summit initially penciled in for July has slipped to November at the earliest because the two sides are wrangling over the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules, which the U.K. says will hurt British producers.
Ford said that unlike Starmer, who quickly squandered the public’s goodwill, Burnham has held onto his reputation “as an optimist and an effective communicator.” But he said Burnham's “really stern test” is yet to come.
“The bills are still going to land on the doormat,” Ford said. “He’s going to have to be the prime minister who can sell the average voter on, ‘Yes, that is indeed a bowl of cold porridge in front of you, but it will get better.’”

Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
- Published
An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.
University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.
The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.
"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".
It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.
Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.

For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
- Published
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.
Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.
"There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".
She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.
Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.
Proof of a warming planet
The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".
A spiritual anchor
At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.
The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".
"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."
According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.
Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.
"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."
For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.
The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.
Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.
Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.
The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.
"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."
As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.
Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.
From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."
Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.
"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.
Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.
"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

How to properly clean your laptop fan
Start with the vents before you reach for a screwdriver.
Your laptop fan has probably spent its entire life working inside a cramped chassis, so dust eventually gets an invite. Let too much of it build up around the vents, fan or heat sink and airflow can be hampered. Over time, restricted cooling can result in thermal throttling, which is when the processor reduces its performance to keep temperatures under control.
Fortunately, cleaning a laptop fan doesn't necessarily involve disassembling the laptop. For routine maintenance, turn the laptop off, unplug it and use short bursts of electronics-safe compressed air through the vents. Lenovo recommends cleaning a laptop fan every three to six months, depending on the environment.
When dust is packed deeper inside, it makes sense to open the laptop. But be aware of what you are getting yourself into. Depending on the machine, removing the bottom cover may expose the fan or start an unexpectedly intimate tour of several thousand dollars' worth of electronics.
Try cleaning the fan without opening your laptop first
Start simple. You may be able to remove most of the loose dust without even touching a screwdriver.
- Turn off the laptop and disconnect all cables and peripherals. If it has an external battery that can be easily removed, take it out as well.
- Find the intake and exhaust vents. Look for vents at the base, sides and around the display hinge. Some laptops hide their exhausts near the hinge, so don't assume that every grille you need will be staring back at you.
- Clean away any loose dust around the vents. For accessible areas, use a lint-free cloth or ESD-safe brush. Do not poke tools deep into the grille.
- Use short bursts of compressed air. Keep the can upright and leave some distance between the nozzle and vent. Excessive air pressure from, say, an air compressor can damage fan blades, though there isn't one universal nozzle distance for every laptop.
- Do not keep blasting the fan continuously. Forcing the fan to spin rapidly isn't a good idea. Use short bursts instead.
If canned air isn't your preferred method, an ESD-safe brush, non-static cloth or hand-powered bulb blower are other options. And drop the WD-40. Standard WD-40 Multi-Use Product is designed to lubricate, displace moisture and protect against corrosion. That's a completely different issue.
Opening the laptop can turn this into a much bigger job
If airflow still appears to be blocked, or you see dust built up inside, removing the bottom panel provides better access. This is also where generic instructions stop being particularly helpful.
On some laptops, the fan is visible and can be removed independently. Others have two fans paired with a shared heat sink or vapor chamber, and if one fan is clean but the other fan, heat sink or exhaust fins are still clogged, cleaning one fan will do little. The fan blades aren't always the only problem either. Dust can build up where air is forced between the closely spaced heat-sink fins.
Before going too deep, check the service manual for your specific model. For instance, Dell's Alienware m16 R2 has separate left and right fan connections, and removing the entire cooling assembly requires taking out six regular screws and loosening six captive heat-sink screws. Dell warns that the procedure is intended for authorized service technicians only.
Some machines take it a step further. The Alienware m16 R1 requires removing the SSDs, wireless card, top heat sink, small fan, rear I/O cover and battery, then following nine system-board removal steps before you can access the fan and heat-sink assembly. The cooling assembly itself is held by eight captive screws. Dell also cautions against cleaning its Element 31 thermal material with an alcohol wipe because it can dissolve the grease into conductive metal particles and could cause an electrical short.
That's the line worth respecting. If the fan requires lifting the heat sink or vapor chamber off the CPU or GPU, you're moving from dusting to a job that might involve thermal paste, pads or other interface material.

A video circulating on social media claims to show massive flames and thick black smoke following an airstrike on an airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (here, here, here). Even a few mainstream media outlets reported these visuals with the same claim (here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows an airstrike on Riyadh Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Fact: This video is not from Riyadh. It shows a fire caused by a drone strike at the Sadovod market in Moscow, Russia, in June 2026. While there were reports of a Houthi attack on Riyadh airport in September 2026, the viral video is unrelated to that incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
We conducted a reverse image search of the viral video and found the same visuals in multiple videos published on 18 June 2026 (here, here & here). These reports confirm that the footage is from Moscow, Russia, and shows a fire at the Sadovod market following a drone attack.
According to news reports (here & here), the Sadovod market in Moscow was engulfed in flames and smoke following a drone strike on 18 June 2026. We also checked the location using Google Street View, and the surroundings seen in the viral video match the Sadovod market in Moscow, confirming that the footage is from Moscow.
However, several international news outlets (here & here) reported that the Houthis claimed to have targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh on 19 September 2026. On the same day, a fire broke out at a fuel storage depot near King Khalid International Airport, with large flames and thick black smoke visible from the area.
To sum up, an old Russian video is being shared as visuals showing an airstrike on Riyadh Airport.

Routers are rarely placed in an ideal spot. Whether they're tucked into a closet or stuffed under your bed, the location is likely less-than-optimal for spreading reliable and fast internet across your entire house. Mesh routers promise to extend Wi-Fi coverage by enabling you to place a second or third node wherever you need, and they appear as a unified Wi-Fi network. Your devices will automatically connect to the nearest option for the best speeds.
Whether you want to fix dead zones, stop the buffering in the back bedroom, or get decent Wi-Fi in the backyard, a mesh Wi-Fi system could be the answer. The Netgear Orbi 770 Series is the best mesh Wi-Fi system for most people, but I have many alternatives to suit different homes and internet connections.

If you're excited to upgrade to the latest Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, the Netgear Orbi 770 Series may be the best way to do so. This is the perfect mesh for the average family home. It is a tri-band system, and by default, there is one network name (SSID) for the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, and it supports multi-link operation (MLO). MLO is a new Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows devices to connect on multiple bands simultaneously. While a single SSID simplifies things, MLO can cause problems for legacy devices because Wi-Fi 7 has more stringent security requirements (WPA2 or higher). Something like an iPhone 5 won’t be able to connect, though you could potentially use a guest or IoT network.
Wi-Fi 7 also enables wider channels (up to 320 MHz from the current high of 160 MHz) and a handful of other improvements. The Orbi 770 offers more than enough bandwidth for multiple people in the household to be streaming and gaming simultaneously. There's potential for stable, low-latency, multi-gigabit speeds if you have Wi-Fi 7 devices connected to the main router, but I occasionally encountered a touch of lag with the satellites. If you can run Ethernet cables for wired backhaul, you can eliminate that.
The Orbi app is straightforward and shows connected clients, enabling you to check your internet speed and tweak a few other settings. You get 30-day trials of Netgear’s Smart Parental Controls and Armor security software (powered by Bitdefender), which gets you phishing and malware protection, as well as device and network scanning. As mesh Wi-Fi systems grow in popularity, you have more options than ever to choose from. While the following options didn't quite make our top picks, several only narrowly missed the cut and are still worth considering.
Asus ZenWifi BD5 Outdoor for $180: While I listed the cheaper TP-Link Deco BE25 as my top outdoor pick, you should always choose a node that is compatible with your existing mesh system. In my thick-walled Victorian home, this resulted in terrible performance for anything connected to a satellite node. Even after extensive tinkering with the Orbi 370, I struggled to get more than 15 Mbps from a node despite having a 1 Gbps internet connection. Netgear Orbi 870 (3-Pack) for $1,300: This tri-band mesh from Netgear is a step up on the 770 Series above, adding a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN port and doubling the bandwidth on the 5- and 6-GHz bands. My experience with the 870 Series was flawless. The setup was straightforward, performance was top-notch on every band and at various distances, and this mesh system was near the top of the table in all my tests. The only reason the 870 doesn’t appear above is that the 770 is likely enough for most folks, but if your internet connection is faster than 2.5 Gbps, this is what I recommend.
Asus ZenWiFi BT8 (3-Pack) for $850: Based on its mostly stellar speed and range, the tri-band BT8 is a Wi-Fi 7 mesh worth considering. Sadly, the highs were hamstrung by inconsistent performance and perplexing intermittent lag, which made testing the BT8 a frustrating roller-coaster experience. A step down from the BT10 but still more than fast enough for most homes with 2.5-Gbps or slower internet connections, the BT8 was a breeze to install, offered impressive speeds across all three bands, and delivered excellent range. Consider the subscription-free parental controls and security software, and the BT8 looks like a real contender. While the release firmware was poor, this system is now consistently stable, and Asus has started to offer tempting discounts.
TP-Link Deco BE85 (2-Pack) for $800: The Deco BE85 was TP-Link's first Wi-Fi 7 mesh. As the flagship, it offers unrivaled performance, with double the bandwidth of the more affordable BE63 listed above. Each router boasts four auto-sensing WAN/LAN Ethernet ports, two 10-Gbps ports (one is an SFP combo), two 2.5-Gbps ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Netgear Orbi 970 (2-Pack) for $1,500: There’s no denying that the tri-band Wi-Fi 7 Netgear Orbi 970 is an impressive quad-band mesh. You can get similar performance for less, and full parental controls now require a separate subscription from the security software. Ultimately, this system is only worth considering if you have a large home, a multi-gig connection, and a generous budget.
