Mesh Wi-Fi Systems: Your Questions, Answered
What Is a Mesh Wi-Fi System?
A mesh Wi-Fi system consists of a main router that connects to your modem and one or more satellite nodes placed throughout your home. The entire system broadcasts a single network name (SSID) and password, automatically handing your devices off to whichever node provides the strongest signal as you move from room to room. It's a fantastic choice for those who have multiple stories in their home that they need to reliably cover.
What Should I Consider When Shopping for a Mesh System?
Here are a few points to keep in mind when you are buying a new mesh Wi-Fi system.
Wi-Fi standards: Many devices support Wi-Fi 7 now. Many of the best laptops and phones do, and it’s only growing more common (the iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 range support it). All the models I recommend as main picks support at least Wi-Fi 6, and they are backward compatible with older Wi-Fi standards. If you have a lot of new devices, consider Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7. While the first Wi-Fi 8 mesh systems will land later this year, the official certification is still a couple of years away. Our router shopping guide goes into more depth.
Internet speeds: There are many ways to upgrade your Wi-Fi, but your internet speed is limited by your internet service provider (ISP). If the maximum speed of data coming to your modem is 100 Mbps, that’s the fastest possible connection that any router can provide.
Bands: The top speed that router manufacturers claim on the box is all of the bands added together, which is disingenuous since you usually only connect to one band at a time. MLO is a feature in Wi-Fi 7 that enables you connect on multiple bands simultaneously but you will still never achieve the top speeds that manufacturers state.
Coverage: While it’s good to have an idea of a router’s coverage and speed, understand that your mileage may vary. The construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ proximity and Wi-Fi networks, the devices you have with wireless connectivity, and the position of routers and nodes in your home are just some of the factors that can impact the performance of your Wi-Fi.
Backhaul: Backhaul channels are reserved for one mesh router or node to talk to another. It’s common for mesh routers to have a dedicated backhaul channel, enabling the main router to provide speeds as close to your full internet speed as possible to any node. This is also important for local network speed and may impact the performance of network-attached storage (NAS) systems, remote console play, and how quickly you can copy a file from one wireless device on your network to another.
QoS: Quality of Service allows you to prioritize the Wi-Fi connection for specific activities and their related apps or for specific devices. You can use it to ensure gaming, streaming, or video calls take precedence, which can be very handy in any household with limited bandwidth.
Ports: Ports and cables can help establish more stable connections. They may be essential if you have smart home hubs for lights and security cameras or network-attached storage that needs to plug into your main router. But they can also be useful on nodes to plug in streaming devices or game consoles and get the full benefit of any dedicated backhaul channel speeds your chosen system might offer.
Mesh vs. router: Although mesh systems are tempting, many homes will be better served by a single, well-placed Wi-Fi router. Check out the Best Wi-Fi Routers for options. Some of the routers I tested in the modern two-floor 1,600-square-foot home I used to live in performed just as well or better than mesh systems, but the old Victorian house I live in now, although not much bigger, has very thick walls and really needs a mesh.
Security: Most routers come with optional subscriptions for security, parental controls, and sometimes other extras like VPN service. You don't need these subscriptions, but they can be handy and provide peace of mind. Just make sure you factor in the cost or opt for a system from a manufacturer like Asus, which offers them for free.
Wait for sales: Mesh systems tend to be very expensive when first released and are often buggy. By waiting a few months, you can expect deep discounts (50 percent is not unusual) and firmware updates that ensure more stable performance.
What Are the Benefits of a Mesh System?
Easy setup is part of the appeal of mesh Wi-Fi systems, and they generally have a companion app that should guide you through the process. Mesh systems are designed to automatically manage your network, deciding on the correct bands and Wi-Fi channels for different devices to ensure a speedy and stable connection.
Mobile apps generally make it easy to check on connected devices and tweak basic settings when needed. They often offer parental controls, network security, guest network, and device or activity prioritization features, but sometimes these require a paid subscription. Mesh systems are also expandable, so you can add more nodes should you need to. Many mesh manufacturers, such as Eero, enable you to mix and match mesh systems from different ranges.
What Are the Disadvantages of a Mesh System?
The main downside to mesh systems is price, as they're generally more expensive than single routers. You may find speeds from nodes are significantly reduced compared to the main router if you rely on wireless backhaul. Mesh systems are not suitable for every home and can often be outperformed by a good, well-placed single router. Each node also requires a good spot within range of the main router with an outlet. I break this down further in mesh system vs. Wi-Fi router.
Is Mesh Router Location Important?
Poor placement of nodes is the main mistake people make with a mesh system. Nodes must be within range of the main router and need a strong signal. Think of a mesh system as the Wi-Fi backbone of your home, and avoid placing nodes at the extremities. It’s also crucial not to place nodes next to potential obstructions (metal, furniture, mirrors) or hide them away in cabinets. You also may want to avoid potential interference from other electronics like microwaves, baby monitors, and TVs. While people often place nodes too far away from the main router, placing them too close together can also reduce their effectiveness. Ideally, nodes should be anywhere between 30 and 50 feet from the router, or no more than two rooms away.
Are Mesh Systems Better Than Wi-Fi Extenders?
Mesh systems are superior to even the best Wi-Fi extenders for most folks seeking whole home coverage. Wi-Fi extenders take the Wi-Fi signal from your router and use the same frequency band to repeat the signal. You can expect slower speeds (50 percent of your main router speed is the maximum, but it’s usually much lower), higher latency, and smart home issues. They also tend to plug directly into outlets, making it tough to position them well. Cheap extenders don’t work well, and good ones are so expensive that you are better served by upgrading your router or buying a mesh system. The one case where it may be worth buying an extender is when you have a single trouble spot in your home.
Should I Choose a Wi-Fi 6 or a Wi-Fi 7 Mesh?
While Wi-Fi 6 is enough for most homes for now, Wi-Fi 7 brings improvements in bandwidth and speed, among other things, though you can expect coverage to be similar. Most Wi-Fi 7 mesh systems are still more expensive. There are some cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 systems, but they miss out on the 6-GHz band, simply offering the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands we are used to. Unless you are connecting your mesh routers with Ethernet cables to create a wired backhaul, a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 system will likely perform worse than a similarly priced tri-band Wi-Fi 6 mesh (with two 5-GHz bands and one 2.4 GHz) in most homes, because it has to use the available bands for wireless backhaul (traffic between the router and nodes). If you want to try the 6-GHz band, Wi-Fi 6E mesh systems offer a more affordable way to do so.
All that said, if you have a very busy household with a lot of devices or want something that'll last for a few years and don’t mind paying for it, a tri- or quad-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh is the way to go. If you currently have issues with latency or bandwidth, or you simply want the latest features, such as MLO enabling devices to connect on multiple bands, Wi-Fi 7 is worthwhile.
Is Wired or Wireless Backhaul Better?
As I explained above, backhaul channels allow your main router to send traffic back and forth to your nodes. For the best stability, security, and speed, you should definitely run Ethernet cables between your router and mesh nodes. Many folks can't or don't want to run cables, and mesh systems can establish a wireless backhaul for this reason.
If you can't run cables, it's worth considering a mesh system that has a dedicated band for wireless backhaul, or perhaps a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 system capable of using MLO for wireless backhaul, for best performance. I recommend avoiding dual-band mesh systems if you plan to go with wireless backhaul, because they'll have to use the same single 5-GHz band for node and connected device traffic.
Can I Add Mesh Wi-Fi to an Existing Router?
You can add a mesh system to your existing standalone router, but it’s not always the best idea. Ideally, you will have a separate modem that you can plug your mesh directly into, and you can remove your old router. If you have a combined router and modem supplied by your Internet Service Provider (ISP), you may need to plug your mesh system into that, but you should set your ISP’s router into bridge mode. Ensure you check compatibility, as some mesh systems have limitations when used this way.
Some manufacturers also offer single routers that have mesh support, so you can add mesh systems or additional routers to create a mesh. These are usually proprietary, such as AiMesh from Asus, so you can only mix routers from that manufacturer. There is an open standard called EasyMesh, but only TP-Link offers wide support across its range. If you decide to mix and match, it’s best to pick devices that support the same Wi-Fi standard with broadly similar specs.
What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers?
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved.
The way the ban is described, it applies to every new mesh system, because there are currently no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US. But companies can apply for exemptions.
All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US to learn more.
What About Firmware and Security Updates?
While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”
What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers and mesh systems folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates.
Should I Buy a Mesh Router Now?
If you live in the US and need a router or a mesh, you should buy one. Asus, Netgear, Eero, and a few others have been granted Conditional Approval already. All the other major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including TP-Link and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, though whether they will is impossible to say for sure. An FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.”
The problem with waiting is that prices are likely to go up. I've already seen some price creep on systems from TP-Link, Netgear, and Eero, though this could also be due to the AI-driven RAM shortage.
How I Test Mesh Routers
To test the best Wi-Fi mesh systems, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the mesh works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare.
I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home, including files from devices connected to the main router to devices connected to nodes. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test, and I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers.
How I Select Mesh Routers to be Reviewed
I try to test as many mesh releases as possible and have put more than 40 systems through their paces. (A handful of those have since been discontinued, but most are reviewed on this page.) It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship systems, I also strive to find more affordable systems and identify models that will suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance.
We are brand agnostic, so we will test systems from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. The manufacturers or their PR companies provide all the mesh systems we test. We do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. I would love to test one of Ubiquiti’s mesh systems but have been unable to secure one so far.
Most products are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer-term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.

McLaren’s reigning world champion Lando Norris called for Alpine racer Franco Colapinto to be given a one-race ban for triggering a crash that took him out of Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
The Argentine locked up under braking as the field raced toward the first corner after a safety car restart.
Tyre smoking, he ploughed into teammate Pierre Gasly, who in turn collected Norris’ McLaren.
The collision sidelined both Gasly and Norris on the spot.
“If you cause a crash on a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban,” said Norris after chalking up his first retirement from a race since the Monaco Grand Prix in early June.
“It is just careless from people. It costs a lot of money, all my parts are in the bin now and people should get banned.
“It is not driving that deserves to be in Formula One,” he added.
Colapinto initially continued before pulling into the pits to retire. He was given a 10-second time penalty but as he was already out that will now be converted into a five-place grid penalty at the next race in Malaysia on Oct. 4.
The crash also cost Alpine crucial points, with Gasly and Colapinto both racing in the top 10 when the crash happened.
“I don’t think I really have words,” said Gasly. “I’m obviously very disappointed for all the guys.”
Colapinto was all apologies.
“Sorry to all of them,” he said.
“It shouldn’t happen and it was locking up and completely out of control so not a lot I could do,” the Argentine added.
Race winner George Russell had some sympathy for the 23-year-old, saying a ban would have been too harsh a step.
“I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless,” said the Mercedes driver.
Second-placed Max Verstappen agreed: “Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, I think, yeah, a race ban probably is a bit much.”

Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.
The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.
“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.
He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”
His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned in Animals Asia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.
Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”
Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”
Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.
Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”
He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”
He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”
Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”
Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”
Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

USA's new breakout star? Sullivan living up to Premier League promise
- Published
With a little over a year to go before he can officially join Manchester City, United States wonderkid Cavan Sullivan has taken his next step towards the big time.
At 16 years and 363 days, the Philadelphia Union midfielder became the fourth youngest player to play for the USA - starting Saturday's 4-1 friendly win over Peru.
Ever since City moved to secure the future signing of a then 14-year-old Sullivan back in 2024, there has been plenty of intrigue around his progress, and hype to go with it.
It led to a level of expectation rarely seen around a young American player - reinforcing the sense that he might be the real deal.
Manchester City saw something in him and were willing to wait for that potential to be realised at senior level. His MLS team, Philadelphia Union, have also shown patience as they gradually introduced him to senior football.
His first run of regular starts for Union came as the 2026 MLS season resumed post-World Cup, and that first international call-up soon followed.
There is one complication, though - the ongoing news around his future club. He made his international debut the day after City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching. The club are expected to appeal.
Matching Messi
His performances, goals, and assists since the World Cup put him up there with the MLS's top individual stars, including Lionel Messi, Antoine Griezmann and Luis Suarez.
Few players beyond those mentioned can match Sullivan's goal contribution rate in MLS since the World Cup, and there is a strong argument to say the youngster has been the best player in the league during that time.
The numbers speak for themselves.
They speak of a player who has performed a key role in his team's rise up the league table in the past few months, and of one who has the output in front of goal to go with the minutes on the pitch.
The facts need no extra hype or sensational Messi comparisons. Sullivan has seven goals and five assists in MLS this season. Six of those goals and four of those assists have come during August and September.
Sullivan has scored six goals in the past six games, and has been named in the league's Team of the Matchday a total of seven times, including for the past three consecutive matchdays.
Is he the breakout soccer star that the United States have long been desperate for? He is about to become a big part of that conversation.
Hope of the States
As the expectation rises, there has to be caution when discussing a player who only turns 17 this month.
"It's well known that Americans are drawn to stars in sports, and as the World Cup showed, that applies to soccer too," Jonathan Tannenwald, chief soccer correspondent for the Philadelphia Inquirer, told the BBC.
"So it's no surprise that the country hopes for a star in men's soccer to match the many it has had in women's soccer.
"I'm not going to say today that Cavan Sullivan is going to be that player. It's too early to know for certain, and I've seen plenty of names not make the grade.
"Freddy Adu is among the infamous, but there are others, such as Gedion Zelalem at Arsenal. Christian Pulisic has come closest, but isn't really there and had a worse World Cup than hoped for. Gio Reyna has never measured up to his talent.
"What I will say about Sullivan is he has the work ethic to go with the talent. As his current manager at the Philadelphia Union, Ryan Richter, said recently, external: 'His outstanding quality is the mentality that he has, and the way that he approaches every game and every day, and that's what pushes him to get better and better.'"
Union turnaround
Sullivan's full-time introduction to the Philadelphia Union team has coincided with a turnaround in their season, led by interim coach Richter, who took over before this post-World Cup run-in.
They are unbeaten in 11 games, winning nine. This is in stark contrast to the beginning of the season when they only won one game in 15. Sullivan has played a key part in this improvement.
During this time, Sullivan has been playing in a right-sided attacking midfield role, but with the freedom to drift as a central number 10 might and cut inside on his stronger left foot.
He has a good all-round game, and also has good strength relative to his age. He is not quite at the level an emerging Wayne Rooney was as a teenager at Everton, but his physicality that means he can more than hold his own in a robust league such as MLS.
Next steps
Rather than struggle with the weight of expectation, his performances have improved as the spotlight on him has brightened.
It appears he is already outgrowing the North American league, but it might be wise to allow him to play at this level, in his hometown, with his family around him (his brother Quinn, 22, also plays for the Union) for a little while longer, regardless of the other options open to him pre-City.
"I find him to be handling the pressure of everything pretty well," added Tannenwald.
"Talk with him for long enough, and you'll know he's still a teenager, still finding his way with some things as any teen would.
"Yes, he can come across as cocky, but he's well grounded, not just by Richter, but by having his oldest brother there in the locker room with him.
"Away from the stadium, Sullivan has a strong family at home. Both of his parents, Brendan and Heike, played soccer, and grandfather Larry went from a player in the 1960s to one of the most famous coaches in the Philadelphia region.
"They all keep Cavan grounded too, even as they know he is the best of all of them."

There was a moment in the second half of the Asian Games kabaddi gold medal match against Iran when Aslam Inamdar made a daring raid deep into the Iranian half.
His teammate Pawan Sehrawat groaned inwardly as he did so. The Indian lead was narrow. Iran was still in the contest. It was a risk that could have gone badly wrong.
“It was a bad decision,” Sehrawat would say later.
But Inamdar made the dash count, securing two touches and emerging unscathed. The two points brought India closer to victory.
“It was a wrong move, but ant bhala toh sab bhala (if the end is good, it’s all worth it),” Inamdar said after the match.
He grinned when he recalled the sequence later. It had been a tough decision to make. Wasn’t he worried when he made that move? What would have happened if it had gone wrong?
“ Bhai, I’ve gone through things you wouldn’t even imagine. This is nothing,” he said.
That, in many ways, is the story of Aslam Inamdar.
There was a time when, as a 14-year-old, he travelled across Maharashtra in search of kabaddi tournaments without even having enough money for a train ticket. He slept under train seats, survived on stale vada pav or whatever food was available at tournaments. He sometimes stuffed leftover food which often spoiled into his bag to eat later.
“If there was work to be done, I did it. I’ve cleaned toilets. I’ve sold juice and made tea. I’ve worked in fields. If there was a kabaddi tournament to play, I found a way to get there,” he said.
On Sunday, in Nagoya, Inamdar stood on the mat as India beat Iran to win the Asian Games men’s kabaddi gold.
It is his second Asian Games gold medal.
The distance between those two versions of Inamdar is difficult even for him to comprehend.
“It still feels like a dream to me,” he said. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.”
The medals are the latest chapter in a journey that began in Takli Bhan in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar district, where Inamdar grew up as one of five children.
His father died when he was young, leaving his mother to raise the family. She worked in other people’s homes, doing household chores and washing utensils, to keep the family going. Later, his elder brother Waseem joined the police force and took responsibility for the family, including helping arrange the marriages of their two sisters.
Money was scarce. Inamdar remembers growing up in a house without proper flooring or a proper roof. There were times when even food was difficult to come by.
So he learnt early that work meant survival.
At around 11 or 12, he collected discarded bottles and sold them to scrap dealers to buy food. Later, he worked at tea stalls and juice bars, washed tea utensils, cleaned washrooms and worked in farm fields. Sometimes he admits he stole.
“It was just to fill my stomach. I faced many hard situations without letting them break me,” he says.
Through all of it, there was one constan: kabaddi.

His elder brother Waseem was a well-known player across several districts, while senior player Rahul Bhor also inspired him. Inamdar wanted to establish his own identity.
“No matter how long I worked during the day or night, I always went to the ground to practise,” he said.
Kabaddi was a sport he could afford. It required little equipment, and the village ground was enough. For a boy with very little money, it offered something priceless: a chance.
By the time he was 14 or 15, Inamdar was travelling alone to tournaments in the 50kg and 55kg categories. He earned between Rs 200 and Rs 500 a match.
The money was small, but it mattered. It bought him meals when he might otherwise have gone hungry. More importantly, it kept him moving from one tournament to the next.
The path was neither smooth nor uninterrupted.

In 2014, while India competed at the Asian Games, Inamdar was at home nursing a fractured leg and watching kabaddi on television. His life at the time seemed a world away from an international career.
“I was just watching kabaddi on TV,” he said. “But I believe God’s plans are always better. My hard work never stopped.”
He kept working.
Eventually, the Pro Kabaddi League changed the scale of his life.
In his first season, he earned Rs 8 lakh.
For someone who had once struggled to put food on the table, the money was almost incomprehensible.
“Eight lakh felt like eight crore to me,” he said.
He did not forget where he had come from. With his first major earnings, he bought a gold necklace for his mother.
Kabaddi had given him something that had once seemed almost impossible: financial security, recognition and a career. He went on to captain Puneri Paltan and establish himself as one of India’s leading players.
Then came the international medals.
Inamdar won his first Asian Games gold in Hangzhou. Four years later, in Nagoya, he has another.
And once again, the final was against Iran — the one opponent that has consistently pushed India hardest at the Asian Games.
“Iran is generally the main challenging opponent for us in the Asian Games,” Inamdar said. “They have a strong defence and very experienced players like Fazel, who played in his fifth Asian Games.”
For Inamdar, beating such a formidable opponent made the gold even more meaningful.

“A tough challenge makes winning the gold medal feel even more rewarding,” he said.
But the significance of the medal for Inamdar lies beyond the result on the scoreboard.
It is the culmination of a journey that began when he was a boy travelling across Maharashtra for a few hundred rupees, when he collected scrap bottles for food and worked whatever jobs he could find before heading to the kabaddi ground.
Today, he tries to pass that experience on to younger players.
At his training ground in Thane, he speaks to juniors, particularly those from underprivileged backgrounds, about his own journey. He wants them to understand that difficult circumstances do not have to determine where they end up.
“I want young, underprivileged players to dream big and aim to achieve even more than I have,” he said. “I want them to know that whatever happens, they shouldn’t stop working hard. They shouldn’t stop believing,” he says.

- The claim that Danish officials played "Send in the Clowns" when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived at the signing of a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement is unproven.
- The rumor stems from footage circulating online that social media users claimed showed Rubio entering the signing ceremony on Sept. 22, 2026, as Judy Collins' song "Send in the Clowns" played in the background.
- Two separate live streams of the event both showed that Collins' song did play while Rubio entered the signing ceremony with Greenland and Denmark's Ministers of Foreign Affairs. All three men were in frame while parts of the song that specifically mentioned clowns played.
- Therefore, the choice of "Send in the Clowns" was likely coincidental or accidental. If one delegation had chosen the song to mock another, it did not have the intended effect.
- A spokesperson for the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs said via email that "Denmark was not involved in selecting the music for the signing ceremony."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We asked the White House whether its officials chose the pre-ceremony music and await a reply. In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A claim (archived) circulated online in September 2026 that Danish officials played the song "Send in the Clowns" when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived at the signing of a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement.
The claim circulated after U.S. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the deal, which sought to end months of diplomatic squabble over Greenland, in New York City on Sept. 22, 2026.
For example, one Threads user wrote, "Listen, I'm not gonna say it's perfection, but the Danish delegation having 'Send in the Clowns' playing on the playlist as Marco Rubio entered to sign Denmark/Greenland stuff is very, very well played."
Other social media users shared the claim on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), and Bluesky (archived). Some of those users posted a video that they claimed showed Rubio entering the room as "Send in the Clowns" played, suggesting Danish officials sought to embarrass or insult him. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim.
Two separate live streams of the Sept. 22 signing event, which used two separate camera angles, showed that "Send in the Clowns" did play around the time Rubio and Greenland and Denmark's Ministers of Foreign Affairs Múte B. Egede and Lars Løkke Rasmussen entered the conference room where the ceremony was held.
A spokesperson for the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs said via email on Sept. 22, 2026, "Denmark was not involved in selecting the music for the signing ceremony." Snopes asked the White House whether its officials chose the pre-conference music and await a reply.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
What the streams showed
According to a livestream (archived) of the Sept. 22 signing event shared by MAGNO News, which said it provided "professionally licensed video content from accredited media providers," "Send in the Clowns" played as attendees at the signing ceremony were finding their seats.
The song started at time code 9:59 in the stream. Rubio, Egede and Rasmussen entered the room around time code 10:59 as Collins sang, "Isn't it bliss? Don't you approve? One who keeps tearing around, One who can't move. Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns."
At time code 11:18, the camera panned to Rasmussen as Collins sang, "There ought to be clowns."
Later, at time code 12:22, Collins sang, "But where are the clowns? Send in the clowns. Don't bother, they're here," as the camera panned to Rubio and Rasmussen.
Finally, at time code 13:24, Collins sang, "But where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns. Well, maybe next year," as the camera focused on Rubio and Rasmussen.
Another livestream (archived) uploaded to YouTube by British newspaper The Guardian also included Collins' music.
"Send in the Clowns" started at time code 5:14 on the Guardian's stream. Egede and Rubio entered the frame at time code 6:24 as Collins sang "Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns."
The song ended at time code 9:10, followed by the announcement and arrival of Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen at time code 9:46.
Given the above, the choice of "Send in the Clowns" was likely coincidental or accidental. Officials for all three countries signing the deal were in frame while parts of the song that directly mentioned clowns played, meaning that if one delegation had chosen the song to mock another, it did not have the intended effect.
Additionally, Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen entered the stage right after the song. Again, if one delegation had sought to call the head of another other a clown through Collins' song, that did not have the intended effect because the heads of all three delegations appeared together.
Greenland deal averts diplomatic crisis
Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen's deal for Greenland followed months of threats by Trump to seize the Arctic island. Trump's wish to gain control of Greenland, which is an autonomous territory of Denmark, threatened the integrity of NATO in January 2026 when his administration refused to rule out using military force.
Both Denmark and the U.S. are NATO members. The alliance has an article that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.
Negotiations for a new deal related to U.S. involvement in the island's affairs began in January and concluded with the signing in September.
According to the Associated Press, the deal allows the U.S. to expand its military presence on Greenland, but affirms the island's status as an autonomous territory of Denmark as well as Greenland's right to self-determination.
It also notes that non-NATO countries cannot open military installations on the island.
The Danish parliament will consider the deal, which can only come into force if that parliament approves it.
For further reading, Snopes has previously covered a number of rumors about Greenland.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata Airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple.
Fact: The video shows an angry mob vandalising the house of Mustafa Pramanik, an accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna, Bangladesh, in September 2026. It has no connection to the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport. While the mosque is set to be relocated due to airport security and runway expansion plans, there are no credible reports of it being vandalised. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we searched Google using relevant keywords and found (here, here) that the 136-year-old Bankra Masjid, also known as Gauripur Jama Masjid, is located within the premises of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport in Kolkata, about 165 metres from its secondary runway. It was built in the 1890s. In July 2026, prayers were suspended, and authorities supported relocating the mosque, citing airport security and runway expansion plans. The mosque will be moved, as stated by West Bengal Chief Minister Subhendu Adhikari. However, at the time of writing this article, we could not find any credible reports of the mosque being vandalised.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to several Bangladeshi news reports (here, here, and here) from September 2026 featuring the same visuals as the viral video. According to these reports, an angry mob attacked and vandalised the house of Mustafa Pramanik, who was accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna Sadar Upazila. The incident took place in the Kulunia area. Pabna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md. Tariqul Islam said that the schoolgirl’s body, wrapped in a sack, was recovered from a pond seven days after she went missing. Local grocer Md. Mostafa Pramanik, 55, and his tenant, Md. Yasin Ali, were arrested in connection with the incident and sent to jail by a court.
To sum up, an unrelated video from Bangladesh is being shared as visuals of the demolition of a 136-year-old mosque near Kolkata Airport.

(Bloomberg) -- New Yorkers can expect rain and high winds through Monday as a powerful nor’easter that caused moderate flooding in Manhattan’s Battery continues to pound the area, knocking out power to thousands and grounding hundreds of flights.
New York and the Northeast face another day of heavy rain and coastal flooding even as the storm starts to weaken and move off into the Atlantic Ocean, said Bob Oravec, a senior branch forecaster at the US Weather Prediction Center.
“The next 24 hours are going to be the worst of what is left of the storm, and after that the effects should be diminishing,” Oravec said.
Quick answers to key questions
The nor’easter has knocked out power to over 100,000 homes and businesses in the Northeast, with significant outages reported in areas like Long Island, New York City, and parts of New Jersey.
Coastal flooding is primarily due to the storm's strong winds pushing ocean water inland, exacerbated by high tides and a full moon that heightens water levels along the coast.
The storm has led to the cancellation of at least 253 flights, particularly from Boston's Logan International Airport, and is causing delays across major airports in the region, including New York.
Residents are advised to avoid driving through flooded roads, stay indoors if possible, and prepare for potential power outages and falling trees due to high winds.
While conditions are expected to gradually improve after the storm, some lingering rain and gusty winds may persist into Monday, especially in coastal and flood-prone areas.
The storm caused chaos for some air travellers but its worst impacts were coastal flooding and power outages. More than 100,000 homes and businesses were without power Sunday morning from Massachusetts to Virginia, PowerOutage.com said. Long Island was among the harder hit areas with more than 24,000 customers still without electricity in Suffolk and Nassau Counties.
Moderate flooding was reported at Little Neck Bay at Kings Point on Long Island. That will likely continue through Monday, the National Weather Service said. Moderate flooding was also seen Saturday night at the Battery, on the southern tip of Manhattan, but only minor flooding is expected during Sunday’s high tide. Sandy Hook, New Jersey, reported major flooding during high tide on Saturday, while minor flooding is expected in Boston Harbor later on Sunday.
New York City has spent one-third of the year facing flood threats, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a BlueSky post on Saturday. He said he called on city agencies, department heads and leaders to come up with a way of protecting the city’s neighborhoods.
Oravec said the storm took a bit of an “atypical” track in that it moved west for a time, pushing more ocean water into New York and New Jersey. The system should start pulling out of the area throughout the day.
In addition to the power outages and flooding, 253 flights, mainly from Boston’s Logan International Airport, were canceled early Sunday, FlightAware said.
The storm flooded some coastal and back bay roads in New Jersey, making them impassable for a time. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill said in a social media post on Saturday that conditions had temporarily eased in parts of the state but were expected to worsen again later in the day.

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western China early on Sunday for their new homes in Atlanta, Georgia, as part of an agreement between the Chinese and US governments.
While in Washington DC for a three-day summit with Donald Trump, Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would arrive in Atlanta in the coming days. The loan of the pandas to the Atlanta zoo was one of the few concrete outcomes to come out of Xi’s state visit with the US president, which saw expressions of goodwill between the leaders, but no fixes to any of the longstanding differences between the two countries.
Atlanta said farewell to its last pandas in 2024, leaving the zoo without the bears. The new agreement was announced back in April, but without any dates.
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the two adult pandas that will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and were kept at the Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding. Ping Ping, the male, has dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, the female, has a forehead that protrudes a bit, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
China has long used the pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.
Xi had said the loan program was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.

Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.
Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.
The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.
In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan
The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.
This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.
The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.
The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.
G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate. If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

Your old GPU could be worth more than you think
If the RAMaggedon's good for anything, it's turning your old GPU into a potential goldmine.
Whether it's from excessive use, sheer age or an upgrade that outclasses it, there are plenty of reasons that you may switch from one GPU to another. If you end up with an extra GPU lying around, there's a lot you can do with it — including keeping it as a back-up or re-using it to build something new. However, even a well-worn GPU can be worth a nice pile of cash on the aftermarket.
Finding an affordable GPU during the great RAMaggeddon of 2026 is no easy task, with the AI gold rush sending prices into the stratosphere. While this has been generally problematic for would-be PC builders everywhere, it has at least provided a great window for selling any old GPU you might have. Even a long-dead GPU can find new life scrapped for parts, and one with a decent life ahead of it can sell for some good money.
How much a used GPU could be worth in 2026
First, it's important to look at the prices you can expect. For instance, NVIDIA's RTX 50-series cards have shot up as much as 39 percent, and a further 30 percent hike isn't out of the cards — not to mention AMD's price hikes of as much as 10 percent. This demand comes not only from big LLM companies, but from individuals creating their own local AI setups, which means the most valuable cards you could be selling are those with a lot of VRAM (as this is what LLM's use to temporarily store data when generating or training). Most users in the AI vein will be looking for 12 to 16 GB, but bigger teams will be looking for as much as 48 GB — and there is no shortage of start-ups.
Therefore, the AI boom that sent GPU prices soaring is also what determines how much you can sell your GPU for — as a used model with a lot of VRAM is still worth a lot for AI and gaming. Moreover, many older GPUs (such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090) are even more valuable as they pack in more VRAM than many newer models. It's pretty reasonable, then, to expect a used card with plenty of VRAM (in good condition) to retain at least 40 to 60 percent of its value.
Where to sell a used GPU
Then comes actually selling a used GPU. Peer-to-peer sites like eBay or Facebook Marketplace require the most effort (you'll have to create a listing, take photos, answer questions, handle shipping and hope to even be spotted in the first place), but also yield the most reward; looking at recent Sold listings on eBay, models like the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti and the EVGA GeForce RTX 3080 not only sell at 40 to 60 percent of their original price, but can sell for higher than their original MSRP. Even busted-up GPUs can sell for a good price here, if you can catch the right buyer's eye.
That's still a lot of hassle, though, so trade-ins and over-the-counter deals can still make decent options. Going to your local PC repair shop or using Newegg's GPU trade-in program can offer great convenience, as these companies will, in most cases, turn around a quick offer and take care of the shipping process. However, that convenience comes at the expense of your payout, so you're liable to make far less in trades like this. If you have a used GPU that's still got decent shine to it, definitely play the long game by selling it yourself. On the other hand, if you've got a worn model with scarce VRAM, a quick and easy trade-in probably won't hurt.

Why Democratic Senate hopes are rising
With Republicans on the back foot, Democrats are eying an expanded Senate map.
We’re officially inside 40 days until the 2026 midterms — and Republicans are feeling the pressure.
Nearly every poll seems to bring more bad news for GOP candidates, even in what would normally be comfortably red seats. And one of the clearest signs of how the party is feeling is how they’re talking — or not talking — about President Donald Trump and his record.
As my colleague Andrew Prokop reported, some Republicans are slowly, tentatively starting to edge away from Trump and his least popular policies, including the Iran war and mass deportations.
In Florida, Rep. María Elvira Salazar — who won with more than 60 percent of the vote in 2024 — released an ad addressing Trump directly and criticizing his immigration enforcement efforts for having “gone too far.” Two Republican incumbents in Iowa, which has been hard-hit by soaring diesel prices, voted in favor of a resolution to end the Iran war.
Whether any of those gestures toward moderation will matter is another question, especially after almost a decade of unquestioning Republican fealty toward Trump. But they’re reflective of an environment that, even by usual midterm standards (when the president’s party almost always loses ground), is looking increasingly dire for the GOP.
The battle for the Senate
As things look worse for the GOP, Democrats are starting to eye an expanded Senate map and a very real chance of reclaiming the upper chamber, which once looked like an uphill battle.
Over the last two months, according to election forecasters like the Cook Political Report, more Senate races have slid into the tossup column or otherwise moved left.
Among them are the open Senate seats in Iowa and Texas — currently Republican-held — which Cook now considers tossups. Kansas, where incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is on the ballot, has shifted from likely to lean Republican. And even South Carolina has drifted out of the solid Republican column, though it’s still an extremely long shot for Democrats. (The New Hampshire Senate race, where Democrats are defending an open seat currently held by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, has also shifted into the tossup column, from leaning Democratic.)
Texas, in particular, would be a prize for Democrats; polls have consistently shown Democratic state Rep. James Talarico leading against Republican Ken Paxton, Texas’s scandal-plagued attorney general who defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in a primary.
And Kansas has emerged as a surprise pickup possibility, with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, giving Marshall a tough race. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Marshall, a doctor, sued hundreds of patients for medical debts, sometimes resulting in their arrest; one of those patients has since appeared in a Hamilton campaign ad.
One link for later
➨ We should be partying more. Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast talks with a party historian about our long — think medieval — history of having fun together, how it’s manifested over time, and why it’s so important societally and culturally, above and beyond purely being a good time.
Before you go…

Body of 10th woman found in South Africa as killings investigation continues
South African police say another woman’s body has been found near Johannesburg, bringing the number of victims in a series of killings under investigation to 10
JOHANNESBURG -- South African police said Saturday that another woman’s body had been found near Johannesburg, bringing to 10 the number of victims in a series of killings under investigation.
Police began investigating after the bodies of three women were found in July and August within about 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) of one another in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
The discovery of six bodies in Ekurhuleni over 10 days earlier this month raised fears that a serial killer or killers were responsible.
Two women were arrested and charged last week with murder in relation to the ninth body, discovered on Sept. 17. The victim had been stabbed and had her throat cut, police said. Police did not link the two women charged to any of the other killings.
Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC on Saturday that investigators believed the ninth killing was an isolated case but could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.
Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found conclusive evidence that the same person or people were responsible.
All nine of the bodies discovered before Saturday were those of women in their 20s or 30s, according to police. Several were naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads. Officers from the Investigative Psychology Unit, which specializes in complex or serial violent crimes, are part of the investigation.
Police released limited details about the 10th body, which was found early Saturday, and did not immediately identify the victim.
“We can only confirm the discovery of the body,” the South African Police Service said in a statement. “Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene.”
South Africa has high rates of violent crime and violence against women. The killings in Ekurhuleni have sparked a national outcry over women's safety.

“Because of You Ka Kui,” a documentary on the late Beyond frontman Wong Ka Kui, will open the sixth Odyssey Film Festival in the U.K., with NGO U.K.-China Film Collab also picking up the Hong Kong film for local distribution.
Discussions began in March at FilMart in Hong Kong, which U.K.-China Film Collab attended with the U.K. Film Pavilion. The NGO deployed a similar approach last year with Robin Lee’s Hong Kong documentary “Four Trails,” which opened Odyssey and then played more widely in cinemas in 2025.
The film, from Hong Kong director Rosa Pang, revisits Wong, the singer-songwriter who drove Beyond creatively and whose songs shaped a generation of Cantonese-speaking listeners in Hong Kong and further afield. The producers are Yip Sai Wing, one of Beyond’s founding members, and Leslie Chan, the manager who is credited with finding the group.
Popular on Variety
The film is built around interviews with people who knew Wong both personally and through work. These sit alongside rare concert recordings, never-before-shown archive material from his early years and footage that has not been released until now. It follows Wong from his first brushes with music through the rise of Beyond and his growth as a songwriter and performer, looking at his approach to music, his character and his ideals. Pang and Leslie Chan described it as a dedication to “a legend, an ordinary person, through memories of those who truly knew him. The film seeks to rediscover the real Wong Ka Kui.”
Wong died in an accident in Japan in 1993, at age 31. The band’s songs have kept finding new listeners since.
There is also a U.K. link. The film’s interview with Beyond founding member William Tang was shot in London.
After an earlier theatrical run in Asia, “Because of You Ka Kui” will have its U.K. premiere as Odyssey’s opening film. The festival will run Sept. 28–Oct. 10 at a number of cinemas as well as online. Each edition is built around a different theme, and this year’s is #Fashion.
“Beyond did not simply follow the fashion of their generation, in many ways, they helped create it, like Oasis for the U.K.,” said Hiu Man Chan, Odyssey’s artistic director and founder of U.K.-China Film Collab. “Their music, image, attitude and style became part of the cultural memory of Hong Kong and influenced generations across Asia. Fashion is not only about what an era wears; it is also about how a generation chooses to see and express itself. That makes ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ a very meaningful film to launch this year’s Odyssey.”
Hiu Man Chan said the opening pick reflected the festival’s aim to treat fashion as more than clothing and catwalks, and to explore how film, music, visual identity and pop culture feed into one another. Bringing the film to the U.K. was “my true honor,” Hiu Man Chan added.
The selection also stretches the fashion theme to cover youth culture and music. Beyond’s sound and look, which mixed international rock influences with a Hong Kong that was changing fast through the 1980s and early 1990s, became bound up with a generation of young fans. Yip has called the documentary a rare chance to find the “ordinary person” behind the bandleader and icon.
Malaysian company Abnormal Studios launched “Because of You Ka Kui” internationally at FilMart in March, as the lead title of its new international sales arm.
“‘Because of You Ka Kui’ is not about nostalgia. The honesty of Wong Ka Kui as a person – in what he thought, felt and believed – continues to resonate today,” Pang said.
Leslie Chan said that after hearing all the interviews, “I really felt that I came to know Ka Kui all over again.”
Odyssey’s sixth edition will program older films alongside new ones. The festival’s opening and some of its program have backing from the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London.

- Following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 24, 2026, social media users shared a clip purportedly showing him saying "America deserved 9/11" as he shook his finger in the air.
- The clip was authentic, meaning it wasn't generated with artificial intelligence or digitally altered.
- A longer video of Netanyahu's speech, however, showed he was not expressing his personal belief but rather quoting the left-leaning influencer Hasan Piker. Piker truly made that statement during a live stream in 2019.
After Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 24, 2026, a rumor spread that during his speech, he said the U.S. deserved the 9/11 attacks.
Several users on X made the claim (archived), expressing disbelief using a supposed video clip of the speech of Netanyahu saying "America deserved 9/11" as he shook his finger in the air.
While the clip was authentic, meaning not generated with artificial intelligence or digitally altered, it omits critical context from Netanyahu's full remarks. He was not expressing his personal belief when he said those words. A longer video showed he was quoting Hasan Piker, a left-leaning influencer, who did say "America deserved 9/11" during a livestream in 2019. We've left this claim unrated to account for those nuances.
At the 27:10 mark in the video, Netanyahu addressed New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, saying Mamdani was antisemitic and he and Piker were friends. As he did so, he quoted Piker (emphasis ours):
So to all those that are spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: Shame on you. Shame on you for distorting the facts. Shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor. Shame on you for spitting in the face of truth.
Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York. They talk to me. They tell me, "This isn't the city we remember. It changed so quickly."
Now it's no wonder. You praise criminals convicted of supporting Hamas. You count as friends people like Hasan Piker, who said "America deserved 9/11. America deserved 9/11." Some friends you have.
You invite into your home a Palestinian journalist who filmed Hamas terrorists beating and torturing Israeli hostages, and later admitted that he refused to publish the videos in order to protect, you guessed it, the terrorists. Your wife liked a post praising the Oct. 7 massacre. She liked another post saying Tel Aviv shouldn't exist.
It is true that Piker said these words in August 2019 while live-streaming on Twitch:
"America deserved 9/11, dude," he said. "F*** it. I'm saying it."
For further reading, this is not the first time Snopes has investigated claims attributing this quote to someone other than Piker. In August 2026, we found U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, hadn't expressed the belief that the U.S. deserved 9/11.
