What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?
For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.
For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.
Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?
Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.
Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.
There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.
There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.
Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.
Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.
From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.
But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.
A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.
Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.
You can read all five of their days here.

Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
- Published
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.
Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.
The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.
He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.
A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.
The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.
Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".
He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.
Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.
For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.
Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel
If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.
Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.
The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy
On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.
This brings up a settings panel. You can choose between Full screen and Partial screen for your recording, and there are three options for audio: None, Media (whatever your phone is playing), and Media and mic (whatever your phone is playing plus the microphone input). There’s also a toggle switch for showing taps and touches on screen.
When you’re good to go, tap Start recording. You get a short countdown, and then the recording begins—up in the corner of the screen you’ll see a widget overlay for adding annotations or a selfie camera overlay, and for pausing or stopping the recording. When you tap the stop button, the video is saved in Samsung Gallery and (if you’ve got it installed) Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on an iPhone
For iOS, the screen recorder is launched by swiping down from the top right corner of the display, then tapping the screen recorder button (it’s a circle with another circle outside it). If the icon has been removed from the Control Center somehow, tap the + (plus) button in the top left corner to add it back.
You can either tap the record button once to start the countdown and launch the recording, or press and hold the record button to choose a different app for the recording besides the default Photos option—so you can use this to broadcast your recording to Facebook or WhatsApp for example.
Pressing and holding on the record button also lets you choose whether or not to include the iPhone mic audio. (The iPhone’s native output audio is always included.) To stop the recording, tap the recording indicator at the top of the screen, then the red stop button. You’ll find your saved video stored in the Photos app.
Third-Party Screen Recording Apps
It’s worth noting that iOS restricts what third-party apps can do in terms of screen recordings, for security and privacy reasons. Most apps in this category in the Apple App Store simply tap into the iPhone’s own recording capabilities, though Record It! is worth a look if you want to add commentaries and selfie cam reactions—you just need to add these after the main recording. Clips over three minutes require the $6 Pro purchase.
On Android, there are fewer limits on what apps can do. AZ Recorder has been a popular choice for years, giving you one-tap recording options, a choice of video quality settings, and some basic editing options included as well. To remove the ads in the app and the watermarks on your exported videos, you can pay $4.49 a month for the Pro version.
Mobizen Screen Recorder is another of the leading screen recorders on Android, and comes with a similar set of features as AZ Recorder: A widget overlay for instantly starting recordings, editing tools, and a few options for video quality (both resolution and refresh rate). Again, payment is required to remove the ads and watermarks—that will set you back $3.35 a month.

How powerful of a power bank do you need to safely charge a laptop?
Don’t let the big mAh number fool you. The better comparison is watt-hours.
While most good power banks can theoretically extend your laptop's runtime by providing a small amount of charge, a proper laptop power bank will store enough energy and charge faster than the battery drains. Two values explain the experience you'll have: watt-hours (Wh) for capacity and watts (W) for output. Power banks provide their capacities in milliamp-hours (mAh), but for a proper measure of capacity across devices (especially for a higher-drain device like a laptop), you need to multiply this value by the voltage to get the true amount of energy stored in watt-hours.
Most power banks store energy in lithium-ion cells at about 3.7 volts (V). Watts are equal to volts times amperes, and you must divide the mAh count by 1,000 since 1,000 mAh is one amp. So for example, a 10,000 mAh bank stores roughly 37Wh (3.7V x 10Ah) before conversion loss. Doubling the mAh doubles the Wh as long as voltage stays consistent, so a 20,000 mAh bank is about 74Wh.
Next, you need to know the Wh rating of your laptop's battery, which you should be able to find on the manufacturer's website. Without a wattmeter, it's difficult to know how much power your laptop uses on average, so we can estimate it by dividing the Wh capacity by how many hours the battery lasts. For example, a 70Wh battery that runs for 5 hours is averaging 14W of power usage. Of course, the instantaneous power usage differs based on what you're doing (scrolling a PDF uses far less energy than rendering video).
Using modern MacBooks as an illustration, their batteries are rated from ~37Wh (MacBook Neo) up to 100Wh (16-inch MacBook Pro). That means charging your MacBook with a 10,000 mAh (37Wh) bank won't even provide a full top-up in most cases. And the capacity doesn't tell you how fast the charging happens.
Understanding what your power bank is capable of
Before you calculate how long a power bank should run your laptop for, you also must take into account that the charging process isn't perfectly efficient. For fast charging standards like USB Power Delivery, the bank has to increase its voltage to push enough power (watts) to charge your laptop quickly enough that it doesn't drain. Some energy is lost in this changeover, as well as generally from heat. 20 percent efficiency loss is a general rule for normal charging, but around 30 percent (or even higher) is more realistic when fast charging.
With all these values, you can finally estimate how much additional time a power bank will run your laptop for. Say you connect a 20,000 mAh 45W USB-C bank to the theoretical laptop mentioned above. Subtracting 30 percent for the overhead, that 74Wh power bank has an effective capacity of ~52Wh. With a laptop averaging 14W, the power bank would extend its runtime by around 3.7 hours. If the laptop ever needs to draw more than the 45W the bank can provide, it will draw power from its internal battery alongside it — the bank is thus supplementing the internal battery to extend its life.
The important point is that you can't assume a power bank's capacity is the same as its output. A portable 50,000 mAh battery is great, but that capacity doesn't tell you how much power it pushes. A large-capacity bank rated at 15W will only slow the laptop's power drain, or it could be rejected entirely. For laptop banks, the label to look for is "USB-C PD." In simple language, this means the bank and laptop negotiate a higher charging level than an ordinary USB port.
Always check the bank's per-port output too, because the total output number can be deceptive. For instance, if the bank description says "100W total," it may not be capable of this full output on any given port, or it may deliver less than 100W when you're charging a phone and a laptop at the same time.
For most people, a 20,000 mAh/74Wh bank is a reasonable emergency or partial-charge option, while a 27,000 mAh/100Wh is closer to the sweet spot. In the US, 100Wh is also the limit for power banks allowed on a plane without approval. if you need suggestions, our favorite laptop power banks span all needs.
Why can't my power bank charge my laptop?
Similarly to plugging your laptop into your car's USB port, a weak power bank might be providing power to your laptop, but not as fast as the laptop's battery is draining under use. There are a few other possibilities. Check whether your laptop supports charging through USB-C. Some USB-C ports handle data, video or other accessories, but can't run a charger. If there's no indication on the ports themselves, check the manual if you still have it or look at the product specs online.
Next, check whether the bank supports USB-C Power Delivery at a high enough per-port wattage. A basic 15W USB-C output can charge a phone, but won't make a dent in a laptop drawing 65W+. If the bank's output is below the laptop's needs, the computer will either reject it or only charge under light use after warning you of a "slow charge."
Lastly, check the cable, as not every USB-C cable is rated to carry high-wattage power. A standard USB-C cable generally supports up to 3 amps, while higher-power 100W and Extended Power Range connections will require a 5-amp-rated cable. USB PD 3.1 can provide up to 240W, but only when the laptop, bank and cable all support the needed power level.
As long as the hardware is compliant, your USB-C PD devices will negotiate a compatible voltage and current. Avoid anything that's damaged or ancient cables you hauled out of a cardboard box — those aren't going to handle today's power needs.

Shooting leaves 4 dead in Caribbean nation known for luxury tourism, police say
A manhunt is underway in St. Vincent and the Grenadines after a shooting left four people dead
PORT-OF-SPAIN, Trinidad -- A manhunt was underway Saturday after a shooting that left four people dead in the small Caribbean island nation of St. Vincent and the Grenadines, where authorities have struggled to contain gang violence.
The Royal St. Vincent and the Grenadines Police Force said late Friday that officers responded to reports of gunfire in Green Hill, a district located just outside of the capital city of Kingstown.
“Two bodies were met lying on the public road, the body of a female was discovered in a vehicle that was parked on the public road, and on an adjacent piece of land another body was discovered,” acting Police Commissioner Trevor Bailey said at a news conference Saturday.
Bailey said the corpses had what appeared to be gunshot wounds.
Four people were also injured in the shooting, with two of them still hospitalized.
There were no immediate arrests and police said they were still trying to determine the motive for the crime. Police said they registered another killing on Saturday, and were investigating whether it is linked to Friday night’s shooting.
St. Clair Leacock, the minister of national security, condemned the “unfortunate” and “unnecessary” shootings, while speaking on NBC Radio, a local news outlet Saturday. He said that while St. Vincent and the Grenadines remains a peaceful country, gang violence has plagued many communities.
According to police, 37 murders have been recorded this year in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, a country with a population of 110,000. The former British colony is made up of 32 islands and cays in the eastern Caribbean and has long relied on tourism as its main source of income.
The small archipelago is known for its volcanic landscapes, untouched coral reefs and white sand beaches that have made it a popular yachting destination. It is also home to several private islands that cater to the rich and famous.
“These homicides create a serious nightmare for us,” Leacock said.

Helicopter crash near Canadian city of Montreal leaves 4 dead, police say
Police say a helicopter has crashed southeast of the Canadian city of Montreal, killing all four people on board
MONTREAL, Quebec -- A helicopter crashed Saturday southeast of the Canadian city of Montreal, killing all four people on board, police said.
Audrey-Anne Bilodeau, a spokesperson for Sûreté du Québec provincial police, said the helicopter reportedly experienced difficulties before crashing around 2:30 p.m. in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, which is roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) southeast of Montreal.
Firefighters managed to extinguish the blaze within an hour of the crash, but the four occupants were pronounced dead at the scene, Bilodeau said.
The provincial police have not yet identified the victims or the cause of the crash.
The spokesperson said the helicopter seems to have been a private aircraft.
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada has sent investigators to the crash site.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.

Contract manufacturing company Aequs’ board has approved a fund raise of up to ₹650 Cr via a preferential issue of warrants to the promoter group, Mellwood Trustee Services Pvt Ltd. In a filing with the exchanges yesterday (September 25), the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.8 Cr warrants at an issue price of ₹231.55 per warrant. Of the total issue size, ₹325 Cr will be payable upfront upon allotment of the warrants, representing 50% of the issue size, and twice the regulatory minimum. The balance will be payable upon exercise of the warrants. The promoter issued an investment commitment letter dated September 25, 2026 to the company, confirming its intention to subscribe to the warrants for cash consideration. On full conversion of the warrants, the aggregate holding of the promoter and promoter group will increase to 60.73% from 59.09%. The issue is subject to the shareholders and regulatory approval. The company will seek shareholder approval via an EGM on October 22 (Thursday). The company plans to use the fresh capital to expand capacity across its aerospace and consumer businesses, including the development of its Hosur facility, investments in subsidiaries and joint ventures, and other general corporate purposes. "The equity will also provide the base against which the Company raises its term borrowings for the expansion. The board has assessed the Company’s current equity requirement through FY28 and has decided to meet it through this issue. A broader capital raise will be considered as and when required by the company’s growth plans," the company said. Founded in 2006 by Aravind Melligeri, Aequs provides manufacturing services to enterprises. It initially started with catering to the aerospace industry and later diversified its offerings to other sectors such as toys and consumer durable goods and products. It counts the likes of Airbus, Boeing and Collins Aerospace among its clients. Aequs is investing in building an aerospace engine component ecosystem in India. Its Hosur facility is expected to be operational next year, with shipments likely to begin by 2028. Brokerage Nuvama Institutional Equities initiated coverage on the aerospace contract manufacturer with a ‘Buy’ rating and a 12-month target price of ₹444, implying an upside of over 90% from July 6 closing price. The brokerage said Aequs’ $889 Mn order book provides strong revenue visibility, and projected a 42% revenue CAGR and an 84% EBITDA CAGR between FY26 and FY29. On the financial front, Aequs reported a net loss of ₹53.2 Cr in Q1 FY27, against a net profit of ₹3.6 Cr in the last year quarter. Operating revenue for the June quarter jumped 55% YoY to ₹395.6 Cr. The fresh fundraise comes almost a year after Aequs raised fresh capital via its initial public offering (IPO) in December 2025. The company's public offering comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹670 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.03 Cr shares. Amicus Capital, the Dempo family trusts, and individual shareholders Ravindra Mariwala and Raman Subramanian, alongside promoter entities Aequs Manufacturing Investments and Melligeri Private Family Foundation, offloaded shares via the OFS. Since listing, the company’s shares have more than doubled from the IPO price of ₹124. Shares of Aequs ended Friday’s trading session 1.38% higher at ₹246.20.

iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: What's new?
The iPhone 18 Pro isn't a world-changing upgrade, but it has a few cool improvements to offer.
Despite their higher prices, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't revolutionary upgrades. On one hand, they add enough new features and improvements to be named the "standard setter" by our iPhone 18 Pro review. But this year's batch is more akin to an incremental "S" iPhone than a major redesign. That gets clearer when you compare them with last year's iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.
Fortunately, most of the changes in this year's Pro-series phones are identical on the standard and Max models. They have the same camera hardware, so you don't need to buy the bigger phone just to get the better camera. But the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max also gets a bigger battery life boost, along with a (less fortunate) weight increase. So while most categories are a wash between the two sizes, the larger model does have different pros and cons.
Design
For the 2026 models, Apple stuck with the aluminum unibody design it introduced (or rather, reintroduced) with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The dimensions are also unchanged: the Pro stays at 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 inches, while the Pro Max stands pat at 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 inches.
But weight is another story. The iPhone 18 Pro is 2.4 percent heavier than the iPhone 17 Pro (7.44 vs. 7.27 ounces). The iPhone 18 Pro Max's increase is more dramatic: it's about 6.9 percent heavier than its predecessor (8.78 vs. 8.22 ounces). For the larger model especially, that's a difference you may feel in hand. The question is whether the newer model's battery gains make it worth the trade-off.
Both phone lineups still have Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, Ceramic Shield on the back and IP68 water resistance. Perhaps to make up for the lack of eye-popping upgrades elsewhere, Apple added new color options. The iPhone 18 Pro series trades in last year's Cosmic Orange, Deep Blue and Silver for Black, Silver, Glacier and Burgundy. (That Burgundy finish will be this year's "Look, I got the new iPhone" color.)
Display
The core display specs are unchanged. The standard Pro retains its 6.3-inch OLED display, while the Pro Max uses a 6.9-inch OLED panel. Both 460 PPI displays support variable refresh rates up to 120Hz, always-on functionality and outdoor brightness up to 3,000 nits. It's thus the same as you've come to expect: the Pro is easier to carry and use with one hand, while the Pro Max gives you more screen real estate.
The one notable change is the smaller Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro series. Apple pulled this off with a region of brighter pixels that lets just enough infrared light through for Face ID to work beneath the display. This allows for a smaller black cutout. The Dynamic Island also now supports up to three ongoing Live Activities at once, compared to two on the iPhone 17 Pro.
Cameras
The most significant change in the iPhone 18 Pro series is the revamped 48-megapixel main camera. But it isn't that megapixel count that's the upgrade; those are unchanged across the board.
The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max use a fixed f/1.78 aperture. But the new main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max can switch between f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0. This means the phone can adjust how much light enters the camera system. In practice, a narrower aperture keeps more of the scene in focus, while a wider one can collect more light and create greater focal contrast between the subject and the background.
The devices can make those choices automatically, which is likely what most people will opt for. But anyone who wants more control over depth of field can manually adjust the aperture. Apple also added new manual controls for shutter speed and white balance, along with an on-screen histogram. For at least some photographers, the "Pro" branding may feel more authentic this year.
Otherwise, both iPhone 18 Pro models have the same three-camera setup and photographic capabilities. Aside from the main camera, they include a 48-megapixel Ultra Wide camera and a 48-megapixel 4x Telephoto camera. Their listed resolution, focal length and aperture specs are unchanged from last year's models.
Video gets an upgrade, too. Rear-camera Cinematic mode now records in up to 4K at 60 frames per second, compared with 4K/30 fps on the iPhone 17 Pro series. (The new model's front camera remains limited to 4K/30 in Cinematic mode.) The phones can also apply cinematic-style background effects after recording — though in our testing, the results were hit-or-miss. Expect the best results with relatively still, clearly separated subjects.
Another new feature, Apple Reference Image, can save sensor-signed RAW data alongside the normally processed photograph, giving you a version to compare against edits. An obvious purpose is verifying that a photo was untouched by AI (or regular old editing). But the downside is having to shoot in a special mode; the feature won't activate automatically with normal shots. It thus makes the most sense for professional photographers, journalists and others whose work depends on image integrity.
Meanwhile, Photographic Styles 3 adds texture and grain controls. Fortunately, Apple keeps the effects restrained, so they don't look overly processed or artificial. Texture edit adds Glow, Soft Skin or Film effects (the latter includes an additional Grain slider). The iPhone 17 Pro series doesn't support any of these options, although it's hard to imagine many people upgrading for their sake.
Chip
Both iPhone 18 Pro models use the A20 Pro chip, replacing the A19 Pro from last year's models. The new chip is built on a 2-nanometer process (compared to the 3-nanometer process of the A19 Pro) and offers 50 percent more memory bandwidth than its predecessor, according to Apple. That should help with data-intensive tasks like games, camera processing and on-device AI.
The A20 Pro sticks with a six-core CPU, but it now includes integrated Neural Accelerators. Meanwhile, the GPU moves from six cores to seven, with Apple claiming up to 40 percent faster graphics performance over the A19 Pro. The new chip's Dual 16-core Neural Engine has 32 total cores, and Apple claims it doubles AI processing power. The A20 Pro's strengths should show more in longer, heavier workloads.
Apple also updated the internal cooling system for the new silicon, attaching the A20 Pro directly to a next-gen vapor chamber. Much of Apple's marketing focuses on the sustained performance of the A20 Pro chip; this new layout, which also places the silicon die side-by-side with the memory, likely plays a central part in that. Our experience with the phone found only one instance when the iPhone 18 Pro became hot: during intensive camera testing. (It cooled quickly afterward.)
Battery and charging
For the eSIM-only models sold in the US and several other countries, the standard iPhone 18 Pro is rated for up to 36 hours of video playback, compared with 33 hours for the iPhone 17 Pro. Streamed video jumps from 30 hours in last year's model to 33 in the new one. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a more dramatic improvement: up to 45 hours of video playback vs. 39 hours on the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Streamed video goes from 35 to 40 hours.
For the new models, Apple's specs introduced a new "typical use" battery life rating. It says the iPhone 18 Pro can last up to 24 hours, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max can reach 30 hours. The company didn't provide those estimates for the iPhone 17 Pro series.
With almost everything else being equal, this is where the iPhone 18 Pro Max makes its strongest case. Compared to the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple's video-playback rating is 25 percent higher, its streamed-video rating is about 21 percent higher, and its typical-use rating is 25 percent higher for the larger phone. If you also enjoy the bigger screen and can live with the size trade-offs, it's the way to go.
To charge those improved batteries, Apple says both iPhone 18 Pro models can reach a 50 percent charge in about 15 minutes with the right wall adapter (60 watts or higher with Adjustable Voltage Supply). That's an improvement over the iPhone 17 Pro models, which can reach 50 percent in about 20 minutes with a compatible 40-watt or higher adapter. MagSafe and Qi2 charging are the same on both generations: 25 watts.
All told, iPhone 17 Pro owners should probably stick with their current device. Those with an older iPhone might find it worth upgrading if the increased price is within their budget.

Lando Norris criticised the standard of some Formula 1 drivers after Franco Colapinto triggered a chain-reaction crash at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Saturday, forcing the defending champion to retire.
The incident occurred at the opening corner shortly after a safety car restart. Colapinto locked up and hit Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly, whose car was then forced into Norris’ McLaren and sent it into the barriers. Racing Bulls teammates Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were also involved, with Lindblad’s car spinning Lawson.
“I just got taken out,” Norris told broadcaster Sky Sports. “There’s just some drivers that shouldn’t be in Formula 1, to be honest.”
ALSO READ: Williams boss James Vowles hails Jamie Chadwick as F1 inspiration for women
Colapinto accepted responsibility for the crash, describing it as a “big mistake” and offering “big sorry to both of them,” referring to Gasly and Norris.
The retirement leaves Norris 116 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli. His title defence has suffered further setbacks after Antonelli’s victories in Italy and Spain in recent weeks.
Colapinto was handed a 10-second penalty for causing the collision. As he failed to finish the race, the sanction could reportedly be converted into a grid penalty for next week’s race in Malaysia, which was branded as the Bahrain Grand Prix in the report.
Race winner George Russell and runner-up Max Verstappen did not believe Colapinto’s error warranted a race ban.
“I think safety-car restarts, cold tires, a very small mistake can have big consequences. From what I saw today, that’s what it looked like,” Russell said. “I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless. I think it was unfortunate.”
ALSO READ: George Russell wins Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Alpine executive Flavio Briatore also apologised to Norris and McLaren after a disastrous outing for the team. He described Colapinto’s error as “a very poor move for a driver of his experience.”
“I want to take time to reflect on it and consider what course of action should be taken, so we can learn from it and avoid such a situation in future,” Briatore said.
The controversy adds to the scrutiny surrounding Colapinto, whose supporters have repeatedly faced criticism for directing online abuse at fellow drivers and race officials.

Getting my Canadian permanent residency should have felt like a win. But I've lost a lot along the way
Many of my friends who also applied for PR have left
This First Person is the experience of Areena Shrestha, who lives in Vancouver. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
I was 18 when I moved to Canada as a Nepalese international student, carrying two suitcases and a simple dream: to study, build a career and eventually call this country home. However, I didn't fully understand when I first arrived how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be.
While I studied psychology and international relations at the University of British Columbia, I interned at the Canadian Cancer Society and worked as a research assistant in a lab. I said yes to opportunities, built connections and slowly started to feel like I belonged here.
By the time I graduated four years later, my path felt clear. I wanted to work in the non-profit sector and give back to the same kind of communities that had supported me. So I began building a career in social services, supporting vulnerable communities as a program assistant, crisis responder and youth worker.
Today, I work as a case manager at a rent bank, helping people facing housing insecurity access financial support to avoid eviction. My job focuses on helping others find stability during times of a crisis.
Yet while I help others find stability, my own future in Canada has often felt uncertain.
For years, my future in Canada depended on my immigration status and the ticking clock of my work permit. I applied for permanent residency in December 2023. I would check my application status late at night, calculate points for Canada's comprehensive ranking system, and refresh the draw page for permanent residents over and over again. I thought about moving to a rural area just to increase points, hoping something would change.
As time passed, that uncertainty started to take a toll, especially six months before my permit was due to expire.
My closest friends — the same people I had grown up with and went to UBC with — began to leave. One by one, they packed up their lives and returned to countries they hadn't planned on going back to. They told me it wasn't worth sacrificing their mental health for a system that felt so unpredictable. Before one can even apply for permanent residency, you have to get an invitation to apply (ITA).
One of my friends even received an ITA for permanent residency — something we had all been working toward. But their application was rejected over a small mistake: uploading the wrong document.
Just like that, years of building a life here came to an end as they had to leave Canada within a 60-day period. Watching that happen made everything feel even more sad.
As my own work permit expiration date got closer, the anxiety became harder to ignore. I would wake up in the middle of the night with panic attacks, overwhelmed by the thought of losing everything I had built. Every phone call with my parents ended in tears — not just from stress, but from a growing sense of hopelessness.
I felt I had done everything "right." I had paid international tuition fees, built a career in the non-profit sector and was contributing to my community. And still, it felt like it might not be enough. I was not enough for Canada.
Going back to Nepal didn't feel like an option. My dad's job took him to work in many different countries which meant my parents no longer lived in Nepal. I realized how disconnected I had become since I grew up speaking Nepali, but couldn't read or write it.
Canada was the only place that felt like home. Yet I wasn't sure if I would be allowed to stay.
Out of desperation, I started relearning French — not out of passion, but because it felt like one of the only ways to increase my chances of getting an ITA.
Then everything changed.
After two years and eight months, I received my permanent residency approval through the health-care and social services occupations draw, which is a specific, express entry draw for individuals who are currently working in those fields. On March 22, 2026, my PR card finally arrived.
I expected to feel overwhelming joy. Instead, what I first felt was something quieter: Relief.
Relief that I could finally breathe without checking immigration updates. Relief that my life here was no longer temporary.
But the feeling is complicated.
Because while I stayed, many of the people who were part of my journey did not.
The friends who once made Canada feel like home are now scattered across different countries. The support system I built over the years is no longer here in the same way. And now I find myself starting over again, like when I was 18 and new to Canada: building new friendships, considering moving to a new city, trying to reshape what "home" looks like.
When I think back to the 18-year-old version of me who had just arrived in Canada, I realize she believed that if she worked hard enough, everything would fall into place.
In many ways, it did.
But what I didn't expect was how much waiting, uncertainty and quiet fear would come with it. I am grateful to be here. But I also carry the weight of everything it took to stay. And sometimes, that feeling doesn't disappear overnight.
When I voiced my concerns on TikTok, my videos went viral with more than 900,000 views. I realized that my story is not unique. Across Canada, immigrants like myself are navigating the same uncertainty while continuing to contribute to the country's workforce and communities.

Dating startup Rivet has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100.6 Cr) in seed funding from Peak XV Partners, Shine Capital, and Blume Ventures to build and scale its community-driven matchmaking platform. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to develop its product, expand distribution, and scale across the US. It announced its nationwide US launch yesterday. Besides US, Rivet has an office in Delhi NCR, with its engineering and machine learning teams largely based in India. Founded in 2025 by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor and Rajat Sahni, who previously served as CEO of CarDekho’s used-car business, Rivet offers a dating platform built around community recommendations. The startup calls its model “social matching”. Users can join as “matchers” to assess potential pairs and recommend introductions they think would work. These recommendations contribute to a social matching score for each potential pair. Pairs with high scores are introduced to each other, after which both individuals independently decide whether to connect and begin a conversation. People who are not looking to date can also join solely as matchers. The startup describes its model as a “give-to-get” approach, allowing users to help others find connections while receiving recommendations for themselves. The startup also counts former Tinder and OkCupid CEO Elie Seidman among its early investors. Seidman advised and mentored Kapoor during Rivet’s development. The startup competes with dating and matchmaking platforms such as Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, The League, and Wingman. Its community-driven approach makes participation by people willing to recommend matches an important part of its expansion, alongside attracting singles seeking connections. Rivet’s pitch centres on addressing the frustration of browsing profiles without finding a connection. Kapoor argued that while dating apps expanded the pool of potential partners, they also made the experience feel transactional and isolating. The startup is betting that recommendations from other people can help surface potential matches that users might otherwise dismiss on swipe-based apps.

William Lawrence is a Democrat running to represent Michigan’s Lansing-area Seventh Congressional District with a campaign that largely focuses on data centers and affordability. It’s not an unusual story in 2026 — but not long ago, Lawrence was cutting his teeth in progressive politics as a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, primarily focused on organizing around the climate crisis.
Why Democrats stopped talking about climate
A Sunrise Movement co-founder is running for Congress. He’s talking more about data centers than climate.
His arc, from progressive activist to politician, is emblematic of a bigger trend, as a wave of millennial progressives in midterm races across the country try to lean into issues that have broader, more immediate appeal with voters.
But that arc also raises big questions about the left’s changing priorities. In a recent interview for Vox’s podcast and video series America, Actually, host Astead Herndon spoke with Lawrence about his past activism and how he has pivoted. “It can sometimes feel like…folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved,” Herndon told Lawrence.
According to Lawrence, “that’s the reality of the time. It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage.” Still, Lawrence said, that earlier organizing shapes how he sees different challenges today.
The two also discussed whether opposition to data centers and AI has wide, regular-voter appeal in places like Michigan and how Lawrence went from hopeless and disengaged to regaining a sense of agency through organizing.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
You started in Sunrise and were at the forefront of a young progressive movement that was aligned at that time — in 2018, 2019, and I think still — with progressive members of Congress like Rashida Tlaib or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
I remember reporting about Sunrise at the time. The goal was to elect a Bernie Sanders, but the other goal was to have the party largely embrace things like a Green New Deal. How would you grade the efforts of the climate movement of that time, looking back?
I think we did some things very well.
We put climate jobs and justice at the top of the agenda for the incoming Biden administration. I think the Bernie-Biden task force is an often overlooked but very important chapter of that whole story, where Bernie and Biden both understood they had to bring their people to the table.
And that’s how Build Back Better got negotiated. We fought hard for Build Back Better, and ultimately came up two votes shy in the United States Senate.
Do you see that as a success or a failure of the climate movement?
I think Build Back Better was a success in coming to the table and negotiating, from the Green New Deal to Build Back Better, and then what we ended up with was the Inflation Reduction Act after it passed the final filter, which was Sen. Joe Manchin and Sen. Kyrsten Sinema. At the time, now, how I felt about it was, this is historic. This is the largest investment in green jobs and infrastructure in United States history. I know how hard it was to get here. I’m tremendously proud of the work that I did and so many others did.
Just in my district alone, we’ve delivered $26 billion in investment for manufacturing and sustainability because of the Inflation Reduction Act. But at the time, we knew that this is maybe 5 percent or 10 percent of what we need in scope. And now we’re experiencing the consequences of that.
Obviously, we still have a very volatile economy. We still lack energy security because we now have closed the Strait of Hormuz. We’re still too dependent on a global oil market, and we could use many more investments in solar and other kinds of renewable energy than we have now.
And ultimately, it wasn’t enough for the Biden-Harris administration to be able to win reelection, because people didn’t feel it enough in their pocketbooks.
Why do you think Democrats are talking less about climate?
I think it’s the intensity of the crises that we face. It feels like we’re falling through midair, after the end of all of the constitutional protections, the rule of law, and the economic security that people had previously enjoyed.
There are a lot of very acute and urgent crises, and I think that that has bumped climate, which is a super massive but also somewhat slow-moving crisis, a little bit lower on the priority list just in terms of what comes up for people on the Hill.
You went back to Michigan to focus on housing and advocacy. Did that make you think a little differently about the national work you were doing?
I think it’s fair to say that when I was younger, I got very focused on this climate issue, and I was very focused on it because it is this existential crisis we all face.
But it was after the pandemic that I wanted to bring my work closer to home. I wanted to do the work of putting down roots in the place that had raised me and make my life there. And in seeking to organize there, it was clear that we needed an in to organize that was more immediate.
“I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.”
More immediate than the Green New Deal.
Than the Green New Deal or than the looming climate crisis. People know that that’s an issue, but they’re like, “I’ve gotta pay rent at the end of the month.” And as an organizer, I believe that you have to listen to people, you have to hear what’s going on for them, and then work on issues that have the potential to bring people together.
Housing is one of those issues. Whether you’re in the city of Lansing, whether you’re in small towns, urban, rural, suburban, young or old, everybody can agree that the rent is too damn high and it’s too hard to buy a home anymore.
Were you surprised Trump won the state in 2024?
No.
Why not?
Because I saw it all unfold. We hoped to deliver more through the Biden-Harris administration than we ultimately did through Build Back Better. We didn’t deliver as much to relieve the economic anxiety that people were feeling. And then I do believe that the war and the genocide in Gaza and our blank check to allow that to happen with our money and our tax dollars destroyed the Democratic coalition that had been assembled from 2017 through 2020 for the purpose of beating Trump.
I just saw that unfolding over the course of the whole year, just like a slow-motion train wreck.
I want to ask locally, what do you think is most important in this race: housing, data centers, or pushing back against Donald Trump?
If I had to choose, I’d say data centers because that’s where people in the district are finding some common ground across the spectrum — in fighting back against the concentrated power in Silicon Valley, which has been fully enabled by [incumbent Rep.] Tom Barrett and Donald Trump.
So you’re saying that’s the issue that allows you to create cross-ideological coalitions?
Yeah.
Our last question is, just thinking through the scope of your career and the kind of progressive work: It can sometimes feel like folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved, right?
Like, we still have a climate crisis. The rent is still too high. All of these things are still happening. How am I to trust that AI is the crisis of our time when I’ve heard so many crises of our time?
Some have called it a polycrisis — overlapping crises.
That’s the reality of the time. It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage. I don’t think it serves us to lie about that. I mean, here’s the reality, folks.
Everything is up in the air. Does it feel like you’re falling through midair? It’s because we are. All the old protections, all the old agreements have been chopped up. So we have got to come together. This is what I believe in more than anything, if there is a through line…I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.
That’s what I learned as an organizer, and that’s what gave me hope actually, at a time when I was doomer-ing in my younger years. And I told you, I wanted to just drop out of society and all that. It was seeing that regular people have come together before, and they’ve won a better future for their kids and grandkids, that gave me a path to follow in.
It does feel like a powerless time, I have to tell you. And a lot of this AI revolution, to your point about control or about agency. We’ve talked to so many people who just think that these things are happening to them, rather than feeling that they are participating in the changes afoot.
But you’re telling a kinda hopeful story.
I’m a hopeful guy. I was angry too, even when I got into this race. I was angry especially about the wars. But then in campaigning, I’ve met so many people across the district, old friends, new friends, and they give me a lot of hope because you just see the way that people are already performing miracles on a daily basis.

Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
China touts multilateralism and growing soft power even as Beijing gives greater weight to its relationship with Washington
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.
“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has addressed the annual General Assembly gathering once in person, in 2015 for the 70th anniversary. He appeared by video in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic but missed the 80th anniversary last year when Premier Li Qiang spoke. In other years, China has generally been represented by other senior officials, including Han and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cautioned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of painkillers and antibiotics, citing the associated risk of chronic kidney disease and renal impairment.
In a circular dated September 21, 2026, the regulator said non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs Rules, 1945, and are required to be sold and distributed on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner.
The CDSCO said most NSAIDs are included in Schedule H of the Drugs Rules and cannot be sold at retail without a prescription. Most antibiotics are included in Schedule H1 and carry warnings that they should not be taken except in accordance with medical advice and should not be sold without a prescription.
The circular directed stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, hospitals, and State drug control authorities, to ensure that such medicines are used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration.
‘Don’t self-medicate’
The regulator advised the public not to self-medicate with antibiotics or use them for conditions where they are not clinically indicated, including most uncomplicated viral infections. It also said antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional should be taken strictly as advised and should neither be shared nor used from leftover medicines.
People with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment have been advised to inform their healthcare professionals before taking NSAIDs. The CDSCO also urged people to seek medical advice if pain, fever, or other symptoms persist or recur instead of repeatedly taking painkillers or antibiotics on their own.
Advise for medical professionals
For healthcare professionals, the regulator recommended considering a patient’s age, comorbidities, other medicines and risk factors before prescribing these drugs. It said the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration should be considered when prescribing NSAIDs, particularly for those at increased risk of renal impairment.
Doctors have also been advised to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles while prescribing antibiotics and to avoid unnecessary combination therapy, inappropriate drug selection, incorrect dosing, and unnecessarily prolonged treatment.
Pharmacists and retailers have been directed to strictly comply with statutory requirements governing Schedule H and H1 drugs and not facilitate self-medication.
The CDSCO has also asked hospitals and healthcare institutions to strengthen systems for rational prescribing, prescription review, antimicrobial stewardship, and patient counselling. State and Union Territory drug control authorities have been asked to create awareness about the risks and regulatory requirements.

What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.
#WATCH | Imphal, Manipur | C Vikram Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, says, “It is a sad moment. Let us see what God has for us. It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity. We want justice. An atmosphere should be created in the capitals of India… pic.twitter.com/QmHjnTkk3W
— ANI (@ANI) September 9, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

Manchester City finds itself in choppy waters after it was found guilty of all but one of the 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.
The outcome of an independent hearing that began more than two years ago could send shock waves through English football. The legacy of City’s trophy-laden era is on the line over accusations that it had been built on financial impropriety.
But Manchester City’s chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak reassured the fans in a letter to the fans on Saturday, maintaining that the verdict has not altered anything at the club.
“The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began,” he wrote in a letter published on the club website.
Al Mubarak joined Manchester City as chairman of the board of directors of the club, with the club enjoying its most decorated spell since, including eight Premier League titles and one UEFA Champions League trophy.
RELATED | Rodri confident of Manchester City innocence despite reported charges
“While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our Club. We will not give them that opportunity,” Al Mubarak added.
The Premier League charged City – under League’s Rule W.82.1 – with several financial breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. With the club found guilty of most of the charges, there can be several consequences, which could range from point deductions to, worse, relegation.
City further said in its statement: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.”
“The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence,” the club added.
