Baljinder Singh, a resident of Sujanpur in Punjab’s Pathankot district, has reportedly been sentenced to death by a court in Saudi Arabia in connection with a drug trafficking case. Singh has reportedly been imprisoned in Saudi Arabia for around three years. His family members have appealed to both the Punjab government and the central government to intervene and provide assistance. They have sought help to understand the legal proceedings and explore possible avenues for relief. The case has drawn attention in Punjab, with the family seeking government support to pursue available legal and diplomatic options to help Singh (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence.
Fact: The video has been digitally altered to depict Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and speaking about Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. The original footage is from a 2015 event at the University of Edinburgh, where Khan spoke about life lessons. AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports confirming that actor Shah Rukh Khan criticised or reprimanded Saudi Arabia over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Had such a statement been made, it would likely have received significant media coverage; however, no such reports were found.
We also reviewed Shah Rukh Khan’s official social media handles (here, here, and here). Still, we found no reference to the case or any statement regarding Baljinder Singh’s death sentence that could substantiate the claim.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on the University of Edinburgh’s YouTube channel on 16 October 2015. The background in the original video matches that seen in the viral clip, confirming that both videos are from the same event. In the video, Shah Rukh Khan speaks about various life lessons. At the event, the University of Edinburgh awarded him an honorary doctorate, and he spoke about lessons he learned through his film roles. Combining humour with introspection, Khan discussed the importance of embracing one’s unique identity, facing fears, and maintaining self-confidence in the face of challenges. He also shared anecdotes from his film career and explained how different characters had helped him view life from new perspectives. However, he made no mention of Baljinder Singh or his death sentence in the video.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the viral video has been digitally altered, with the original footage paired with fabricated audio to falsely depict actor Shah Rukh Khan making statements he never made.
To sum up, this viral video of Shah Rukh Khan reprimanding Saudi Arabia over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence is AI-manipulated.

Pope Leo XIV is a lifelong Chicago White Sox fan but also knows better than to wade too deep into sporting rivalries

Could divine intervention from Pope Leo XIV have played a role in the Chicago White Sox’s unexpected postseason return?
“No comment,” the pontiff replied with a beaming smile when a reporter on his plane to France asked whether the surprise sprung Thursday by the long-suffering team was miraculous, and “Do you have anything to do with that?"
However, the Chicago-born and raised White Sox supporter left no doubt about his excitement, adding: "Great things happen in Chicago."
His diplomatic stance reflects prior lessons learned about how appearing to favor one sports team over another can cause unintended friction.
In June, he declared that "the pope is for all teams" before upsetting soccer fans in Barcelona by acknowledging his personal affinity for Real Madrid, placing himself amid one of football's fiercest club rivalries. Real Madrid published video of the moment, which prompted social media comments suggesting the club was "the team of God."
Exercising similar caution, the pontiff also revealed his passion for college basketball during the flight. Replying to a question, Leo predicted that "the voice of the people of God" would be rallying behind Villanova University—where he pursued mathematics in the 1970s—when his alma mater meets Notre Dame in a men’s and women’s season-opening doubleheader in Rome on Nov. 1.
"They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side," Leo said.
The Catholic institutions are marketing the event as a celebration of their mutual mission and heritage. Decades prior to becoming the first pope from the United States, Robert Prevost graduated in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from the Augustinian school located near Philadelphia.
The 71-year-old pontiff's passion for sports includes tennis as well.
"I consider myself quite the amateur tennis player," he acknowledged during a 2023 interview with the Augustinian Order, though the newly made cardinal noted that his church obligations afforded him little court time.
As pontiff, Leo routinely spends Mondays and Tuesdays at the papal residence in Castel Gandolfo, located in the hills near Rome, playing tennis with his secretary, Monsignor Edgard Iván Rimaycuna Inga, along with swimming and horseback riding.
During a Vatican audience last year with top-ranked tennis player Jannik Sinner, he turned down Sinner's suggestion to hit a brief volley.
Surveying the surrounding antiques, the pope said, "Better not."

One dead as nor’easter hammers East Coast with more flooding and wind
New York Governor Kathy Hochul warned ‘Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life’

The East Coast is bracing for more rain Sunday as a deadly nor’easter storm continues to wreak havoc on the region for a third day.
The storm remained just south of Long Island and east of northern New Jersey on Sunday morning and was expected to loop around the area for another 24 hours, said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected Sunday from northern New Jersey through New York City and Long Island into southern New England. The storm was gradually weakening, Oravec said, but the threat of tidal flooding would linger through high-tide cycles Sunday morning and again in the evening.
“The most impactful parts of the storm are likely going to be the high winds and the tidal flooding,” Oravec said.
A municipal worker for the New York City Housing Authority was killed in Brooklyn when a tree collapsed amid fierce gusts and heavy downpours. Across New England and the mid-Atlantic, emergency personnel worked to clear fallen timber and restore electricity after blackouts affected approximately 100,000 households and businesses.
Tens of millions of residents throughout the region remained under severe weather threats into Sunday, with significant coastal inundation expected. The Federal Emergency Management Agency confirmed that regional response coordination hubs were operating at an "enhanced posture," while specialized assistance teams were on standby in New England to manage potential widespread utility failures.
Peak tidal surges were expected to hit shorelines north of Atlantic City, New Jersey, from Saturday evening into Sunday, threatening widespread inundation of roadways in bayfront and coastal neighborhoods, the National Weather Service said.
"Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
Residents in parts of New York and New Jersey navigated submerged roads by kayak, while adventurous surfers targeted unusually large ocean swells. In Sea Bright, New Jersey, first responders extracted a woman and her dog after their vehicle became trapped in floodwaters, ABC7 reported.
Rising waters submerge roads and businesses
Inside the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, Kenny Formica monitored security cameras from his home, watching floodwaters seep into the marina he owns. Water breaching the building is an exceptional event, Formica explained, noting the last occurrence was during Hurricane Sandy in 2012, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.
Prior to the storm's arrival, marina staff fastened dock lines, relocated loose gear out of harm’s way, and staged company trucks and forklifts on the highest ground available.
Upon waking, Formica found messages from boat owners reporting displaced vessels and watercraft. A customer forwarded video footage captured around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot (7.6-meter) boat after it had blown off its lift.
Farther south, in Norfolk, Virginia, Ellie Hodge observed from her front porch as driving traffic generated wakes along flooded streets. The coastal city saw isolated flooding all week because of the nor’easter.
"We've seen cars get stuck on the road, going up the sidewalks," Hodge said. "It's been pretty bad this time around."
Travel disruptions and canceled events
Travel itineraries across the region were upended. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
Along the North Carolina coast, a flooding-related highway closure on Hatteras Island disrupted Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad’s wedding plans. The Virginia couple made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported. A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music.
With the primary roadway shut down and local ferry service also out of service, boat travel through bad weather remained the only option, said Drew Pearson, emergency management director for North Carolina’s Dare County. The island has a year-round population of about 5,000 that swells much higher in warm weather, he said.
The North Carolina Department of Transportation said it would soon begin emergency ferry service between Hatteras Island and the mainland.
"To folks on Hatteras, you are not on an island all alone," Gov. Josh Stein said on social media. "North Carolina and county emergency responders are working hard to keep you safe and reconnected as quickly as possible."
Authorities urge vigilance
Nor’easters are not unusual as New England moves into the fall season, but "this might be a little earlier than average for a big storm," said Oravec, of the National Weather Service.
The storm’s slow movement could worsen beach erosion by subjecting the coast to a prolonged period of strong winds and waves, he said.
Hochul said coastal flooding was the biggest threat, but heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet (6 meters) were also expected.
On Long Island, ferry owner Stephanie Sherman paused operations between Patchogue and the barrier island of Fire Island.
"It’s been a pretty wild storm," Sherman said. "But nothing that we haven’t experienced in the past. These happen every so often."

Srinagar, Sep 22: Minister for Food, Civil Supplies & Consumer Affairs (FS&CA), Information Technology (IT), Youth Services & Sports, and Science & Technology, Satish Sharma, on Tuesday said that 221 out of 355 Gram Panchayats (GPs) in Jammu and Kashmir have either existing or constructed playfields under the One Panchayat-One Playfield initiative.
The Minister, as per an official statement, was replying to a question raised by MLA G A Mir regarding implementation of the 'One Panchayat-One Playfield' initiative, particularly with reference to Dooru Constituency and the status of sports infrastructure and proposed playfields there.
Quoting information received from the Rural Development Department, Satish Sharma said that 221 out of 355 Gram Panchayats covered under the initiative have playfields, either already existing or newly constructed.
Giving details of Dooru Constituency, the Minister informed the House that 37 out of 66 Gram Panchayats have playfields. He said the Youth Services & Sports Department has taken up two playfield projects in Dooru Constituency during the past three years. The Playfield at Larkipora near ADV Road Bathuno, taken up during 2024-25 at a cost of Rs 48.55 lakh, has achieved 90 per cent completion, added. He apprised that another Playfield at Shangren has been taken up as a new work during 2026-27 at an estimated cost of Rs 80 lakh.
Satish Sharma further informed that 26 playfield sites have been approved under AAP 2026-27 as part of VB-G RAM-G by the Rural Development Department, Anantnag, where suitable government land has been made available by the Revenue Department. He said that development of playfields by the Youth Services & Sports Department is undertaken after following all requisite formalities, including availability of encumbrance-free land, transfer of land and availability of funds.
He said that sports infrastructure in Dooru Constituency is being progressively improved and upgraded through the J&K Sports Council and Directorate of Youth Services & Sports.
The Minister informed that four major sports facilities are being developed or maintained in the constituency including Sports Stadium, Dooru, equipped with a change-room-cum-pavilion, cricket competition pitch, net practice pitch, chain-link fencing, main gate and dugouts. Besides, playfield at Verinag is presently under development with a change-room-cum-pavilion, cricket competition pitch, net practice pitch, chain-link fencing, main gate, dugouts and mechanical roller. The playfield at QammarShahbaad, Block Verinag, is being maintained by the J&K Sports Council while the playfield at BhahiBachoo Hiller, is being developed with cricket competition pitch, net practice pitch and chain-link fencing, he told the House.
The Minister informed that a DPR amounting Rs 1,035.98 lakh has been prepared for upgradation of Sports Stadium Dooru and is presently under consideration by the Department. The proposed works included pavilion building with change rooms, seating tiers with canopy, cricket competition pitches, net practice pitches, dugouts, synthetic volleyball court, mechanical roller and floodlights, he added.
Regarding proposals for development of playfields at Sayen/Sagam, Sadiwara, Chowgund, Qammar, Dudwangan, Akingam, Hiller Kokernag and other identified locations, Satish Sharma said the sites are under consideration for land transfer and development. He informed that the process for transfer of land to the Youth Services & Sports Department is underway with the Revenue Department while in the case of Sadiwara and Hiller Kokernag, the land-transfer process is yet to be initiated.
The Minister said that once the land preparation and transfer processes are finalised, the department would consider the required development works, subject to availability of funds, land and feasibility. He also informed that a DPR amounting Rs 150 lakh has been prepared for development of the SayenSagam playfield, envisaging ground expansion through cutting and filling, protection works, seating tiers, cricket competition pitches, net practice pitches and a synthetic volleyball court.

Srinagar, Sep 22: Deputy Commissioner (DC) Srinagar, AkshayLabroo, Tuesday attended the Grand Finale of the District Administration’s Under-19 Football Rolling Trophy-2026 at the Rugby Field, Poloview, as apart of the District Administration’s commitment to creating better opportunities for youth to excel in different sporting and art disciplines.
The event, as per an official statement, was organised by the District Youth Services & Sports Office in collaboration with the District Administration Srinagar, with the aim of promoting sports and encouraging greater participation of youth in sporting activities.
Speaking on the occasion, the Deputy Commissioner, who was the Chief Guest, underlined the efforts of the District Youth Services & Sports Office and the District Administration for providing young sportspersons with opportunities to showcase their talent and develop a competitive spirit.
The DC said that the District Administration Srinagar has initiated the Rolling Trophy Championship across the District to nurture the talent of youth by organising drawing, painting and singing competitions, seminars and debates, besides football, cricket and other sport competitions, thereby providing young people with a platform to showcase and develop their abilities.
The DC urged the youth, particularly the participating athletes, to take maximum part in sporting events and desist from involvement in any kind of drug-related activity. He emphasised the importance of sports in fostering discipline, brotherhood, teamwork, leadership and a healthy lifestyle among youth.
The DC congratulated all the teams and participating players for their performances and encouraged young athletes to pursue sports with dedication and discipline. He also appreciated the Officials, Coaches and organisers for their contribution towards the successful conduct of the tournament.
On the occasion, the Deputy Commissioner also administered an oath to the participating athletes under the NashaMukt Jammu and Kashmir Abhiyan, urging them to contribute towards building a drug-free society.
As many as 400 athletes from different schools of the district participated in the Football Rolling Trophy-2026. The final match was played between Government Boys Higher Secondary School, Jawahar Nagar, and Sri Pratap Model Higher Secondary School. The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Naomi Watts waited a long time to become a star.
“It was a grind. That 10 years before I met David, I became so locked up and I felt worthless. My agent pulled me aside and she said: ‘We need to have a heart to heart. Honey, you are too intense. You are freaking people out.’ I went: ‘Yeah, no shit.’ I was desperate! I was behind on my rent; I was getting evicted. I didn’t know what to bring to this room,” she recalled at Zurich Film Festival.
“They told me I wasn’t funny last week, so now I am trying to be funny. They told me I wasn’t sexy – I’m trying to be sexy. You reshape yourself and try to read the tone of what is needed. That’s how it went and I couldn’t be myself anymore. I was either an extreme version of myself or a diluted version of myself. It took a genius like David Lynch to see beyond all that weirdness I built up, undo it and get to the real me.”
Popular on Variety
The resilience she built up from moving a lot as a kid was helpful, however.
“You also have to know why you love it. Are you in it for the right reasons? My goal wasn’t just to be famous. I loved disappearing into these characters. I really cared and continued to investigate. I still do. There’s always more to learn.”
Watts received the Golden Eye Award at Zurich Film Festival. During the ceremony, she also recalled these difficult first years of trying to become a successful actress, “which had a lot of dry spells.”
“And then, mercifully, I met David Lynch in my late 20s and he changed my career.”
“Mulholland Drive” is widely considered as her breakout.
“That film gave me the most incredible role that affected people. To this day they still watch it. It’s still on these ‘bests’ lists. I’m just very, very proud to be a part of that film.”
During the masterclass at the fest, Watts said she was also encouraged by Nicole Kidman.
“She said: ‘All it takes is one thing, one thing could change everything. That didn’t make sense to me for a very long time. Until David Lynch, and then it became very real.”
Right after “Mulholland Drive,” she starred in horror classic “The Ring.”
“I tried to say ‘no.’ There’s no certainty to anything you do, ever,” she said.
“My agents were excited about this. I said: ‘Wait. I just got this critical acclaim, so I want to instantly go into a Hollywood blockbuster-y movie?!’ I fought with my agent at the time. I didn’t know it was going to be a massive hit! I woke up the horror genre, in a way. It was a lucky, lucky break.”
Watts also earned raves for “21 Grams” – “Extraordinary things can happen when you get tired and irritable from doing things too much,” she said, recalling that intense shoot.
“If there’s any theme in my work, it’s grief. It’s why I do what I do: I’m trying to figure out the meaning of my life. Another one is identity. I love the story [that asks]: ‘Who are you?’ That also comes from my moving around as a kid. I was always on the outskirts of the group, trying to find my way in.”
Watts’ recent role, in Ben Shirinian’s “The Housewife,” addresses that too. In the film, set in the 1960s, she plays a seemingly perfect housewife – but one who hides a terrible post-war past.
“I never played a character like this, even though I look for flawed women and I’m not afraid of unlikeable. But this was extreme,” she said.
She said: “I knew what I was stepping into. I knew it was going to be a daunting, haunting understanding. A character like that comes to you at night, in your dreams.”
Ending the masterclass, Watts admitted it took her a while to stop focusing on other people’s opinions.
“Vulnerability is a superpower. It has taken me a long time to know that, and own that. I wish I’d learn earlier on to be more myself and [care] less about pleasing people. Some people are born with that level of confidence – I was never that person.”
“I still have a lot of self-doubt, but I don’t pretend it’s not a real thing. I try to see it as a gift. It’s more effective than just bullshitting your way through it all.”
Being open about her hardships, as well as menopause, proved to be liberating, she said.
“Menopause became a huge topic of conversation, because I went through it early on in my life and had no clue what was happening with my body. Once I talked about it with my partner, who is now my husband [actor Billy Crudup], and he was supportive, I went: ‘How about I just own the story?’ I’m in on the joke, although it’s not actually a joke. Why do we just suffer, instead of getting some normalcy? Just own it.”
She recalled her first conversation about it with Crudup.
“I was crying in the bathroom, trying to scratch off my estrogen patch. I told him what was going on, so nervous, and I thought: ‘He’s not gonna want to be with me anymore!’ He said: ‘Hold on. It’s great that you are taking care of yourself. Why are you ashamed?’ It was so sweet… And sexy. I felt safer than I ever felt.”
She ended up founding Stripes Beauty, a brand designed for women navigating perimenopause and menopause.
“Men have to be curious and compassionate. And our job, ladies, is to share the story.”

Free speech and media advocacy groups urged a judge to block a California settlement with Paramount Skydance that would let the company finalize its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Twelve states led by California sued to block the deal in July and were able to delay it when US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín ruled that Paramount combining with Warner Bros. would likely reduce competition substantially and violate antitrust laws. Despite that initial victory, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a settlement with Paramount earlier this week and the other states involved in the lawsuit signed on to the deal.
Martínez-Olguín must decide whether to approve the settlement. A coalition of free speech and media advocacy groups told the judge in a filing yesterday that the deal will give residents of the states that sued Paramount “virtually nothing.” The filing was submitted by the Committee for the First Amendment, Free Press, Freedom of the Press Foundation, Future Film Coalition, and International Documentary Association.
Bonta “publicly criticized the very behavioral remedies that the parties now ask the Court to approve,” the filing said. That’s a reference to Bonta saying that proposed merger conditions such as Paramount’s pledge to release 30 movies a year are “typically not enforceable in the way that we like,” and “not particularly good at solving the problem.”
The groups said the lawsuit filed by states two months ago alleged that “the tie-up would ‘extinguish competition’ between the two and raise prices, reduce output, lower quality, and lessen choice… But whatever the reasons for the States’ about-face, neither time nor circumstance changes the fact that this merger lessens competition.”
The League of United Latin American Citizens raised similar concerns in its own court filing. The states alleged that the “merger would permanently eliminate competition between Defendants over the films and television programming Americans can watch,” but the settlement “leaves that loss of independent decision-making largely intact,” the filing said.

A new European soccer league for amputee players kicked off in Romania’s capital
A new European soccer league for amputee players has kicked off in Romania’s capital
BUCHAREST, Romania -- A new European soccer league kicked off in Romania’s capital this week, giving amputee players from countries lacking domestic leagues an opportunity to compete on an international stage.
The European Amputee Football Federation, or EAFF, inaugurated the new Conference League in Bucharest. The games were held Thursday and Friday, and the final concluded on Friday when Maccabi Haifa FC of Israel was crowned the winner after beating Scotland’s Ayr United 4-0.
The victory meant a lot to Ben Binyamin of the team from Israel. Back in 2023, the Israeli player had his right leg blown off during the Hamas attack on the Tribe of Nova music festival, which left him fearing he would never play soccer again.
“I am very happy that we won this tournament, we won without conceding a single goal,” he told The Associated Press. “Football itself for us is our physiotherapy, our life, and our second family. It helps us in life. It gives us strength.”
Four teams participated in the tournament: FCSB of host nation Romania, Maccabi Haifa FC of Israel, Ayr United of Scotland and Panathinaikos AC PwD of Greece.
“We are very satisfied, very happy to bring pride to the country,” Binyamin added.
Inspired by the European club competition model in able-bodied soccer, the EAFF described the new league as a “historic milestone” that represents “another important step in the development of European amputee football.”
“The Conference League creates an international opportunity for clubs from countries where domestic amputee football leagues are not yet established,” it says on its website.
Played in a seven-versus-seven format, on 60-meter (196-foot) by 40-meter (131-foot) fields, amputee soccer is a game for amputees and people living with limb defects. Players have one leg and a pair of crutches, while goalkeepers have both legs but one hand or arm.
Established in 2015, the EAFF aims to help people with amputations or limb defects gain access to amputee soccer throughout Europe. The World Amputee Football Federation was established in 2002 and a World Cup is held every four years.
The new league hopes to attract more spectators to amputee soccer and gives teams opportunities to build international relationships. The EAFF also organizes a Nations League, Champions League, Europa League, and holds other initiatives like women’s and junior camps.
Iain Matthew, manager of the Scottish team, told the AP that while his team’s 0-4 loss to Maccabi Haifa was disappointing, the league itself offered valuable experience for his players.
“The competition is great for smaller nations … to get European football experience,” he said. “I think we could have played better, we could have defended better, but you’ve got to praise your players for what they’ve done over the week.”

- Minecraft World at Chessington World of Adventures will get the world's first official Minecraft Hotel in 2027.
- The experience will also feature Escape the Nether, Minecraft's first themed rollercoaster.

The Minecraft Live event in September showcased how the game is going to become a full-blown vacation destination. Mojang Studios and Merlin Entertainments revealed the world’s first official Minecraft Hotel, set to become a part of Minecraft World at Chessington World of Adventures Resort in south-west London in 2027.
The Minecraft Hotel is designed to extend the adventure beyond the park gates, giving fans a chance to stay inside the block-inspired world. And yes, there’s a dizzying rollercoaster ride in the adventure park!
The Hotel will keep the game’s blocky aesthetic intact, along with Minecraft-inspired experiences. So, guests can expect encounters with the familiar Minecraft mobs, a Deep Sea Diner, and rooms designed to continue the fantasy world even after leaving the park.

The entrance of the Hotel is shown to have the famous Baby Zombie Chicken Jockey alongside rails, Minecarts, Steve with a pickaxe, and more.
The concept art for a Deep Sea Diner is seen to have Mossy Stone pillars with kelp stalks hanging from the ceiling, while the walls display the Minecraft Ocean Monuments. The rooms of the Minecraft Hotel are shown with redstone lamps, wooden chests, alongside Creeper and TNT-themed cushions.
The announcement for the Minecraft Hotel came alongside other major reveals, including the DLCs planned for the ARPG sequel. Putin appears to be eyeing NATO. The question is, will he actually attack?
European countries on high alert amid mounting signs of danger from Moscow
European military experts are tracking urgent danger signs that suggest Vladimir Putin may be preparing for a direct escalation against the NATO alliance.
What analysts are split over is whether the Russian president is merely weighing his options or has already decided to pull the trigger.
"What's pretty clear from public intelligence briefings by … a number of heads of state and defence secretaries across different member states is that Russia is planning [some] sort of aggression, probably with multiple potential forms," said Justin Bronk, senior research fellow for airpower and technology at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based military think-tank.
"That doesn't mean they've decided to do it — but it does mean it's probably under active planning and therefore the risk of it has risen significantly."
Moscow is "cooking up something big this year," warned Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski during a panel discussion as part of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, without elaborating.
The concerns have been fuelled by a threat assessment from Denmark's government that this week raised the prospect of a Russian missile attack on NATO infrastructure used to support Ukraine. The report said such an attack could happen within weeks.
A wave of incidents over the last month have put governments and security services on high alert.
Germany's government has directly blamed Putin for an attempted drone strike on Leipzig's airport that appeared to target aircraft carrying supplies to Kyiv.
A Russian drone then attacked a Ukrainian passenger train on the border with Poland, a NATO ally, just as it unloaded a carriage full of European VIPs, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson. Russia confirmed the strike but denied it was trying to assassinate European diplomats.
Meanwhile, Polish authorities stated they strongly suspect Kremlin agents were behind an arson attack earlier this week on a satellite communications ground station serving as a critical link with Ukraine's armed forces.
Going forward, analysts suggest Moscow's goals are highly calculated.
"The Russians aren't going to do something that they think leads to a long, difficult war. That's not their objective," said Bronk.
"The objective would be to do something small enough that it still definitively violates NATO territory to test the alliance visibly, but keep it small enough that it becomes very difficult to get the political will to respond directly and militarily kick them out."
Putin has denied all allegations of aggression and instead framed Russia as the victim of warmongering by the Western military alliance as he has for much of 27 years at the top of Russia's power pyramid.
"NATO is swelling up and expanding," he told a Kremlin meeting on Sept. 18, claiming European leaders are "simply trying to salvage their sagging ratings, and cover up mistakes" with accusations of Russian aggression.
Putin has repeatedly justified his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine as self-defence, falsely claiming that NATO was building up troops and weapons there in preparation for invading Russia.
'Rat in the corner'
Now, after four and half years of full-scale war, Russia is believed to have suffered as many as 1.4 million people killed or wounded and its economy is under severe strain.
One senior Estonian commander on Friday likened Putin to a "rat in the corner," suggesting that because the war is going badly he may see aggression against Ukraine's European allies as a the best means to break Western support.
On Friday, the Russian state media outlet RIA Novosti gave the theory added credibility with a story headlined: "Russia is facing another short SVO" or special military operation as Russia continues to call its war against Ukraine.
"It will be short," it said, and raised the possibility of missile strikes against Lithuania, another NATO member.
The article — which was taken down a short time after it was posted — also suggested that using nuclear weapons was not out of the question. Dimitri Medvedev, a former Russian president and prime minister, has frequently made similar threats against NATO which are widely viewed by analysts as a scare tactic.
RIA Novosti later added a sort of correction claiming the article was removed because "it did not align with the editorial team's views," or the "state policy of the Russian federation."
Eerie similarities
The situation shares eerie similarities with the weeks leading up to Putin's invasion of Ukraine.
Back then, Putin and other Kremlin officials vigorously denied any intent to invade and blamed NATO for escalation, even as Russian troops on the border with Ukraine swelled and diplomacy to try to calm the crisis continued.
Western and Russian authors who later studied Putin's road to war concluded he and a tiny circle of hard-line security advisers, fuelled by grievances against the West, froze out the broader Kremlin establishment and made the fateful decision to plunge the country into war.
Their belief that Ukraine would quickly capitulate turned out to be one of greatest blunders in modern political history.
But other facts on the ground look vastly different than in 2022.
Countering Sikorski's warnings of "something big" on the horizon, one of Estonia's top military figures claimed his country is seeing no evidence of Russian troops massing along NATO's eastern flank.
"We have no signs indicating that Russia currently intends to militarily attack any NATO ally," wrote Tarmo Miilits, the top official at Estonia's Interior Ministry.
And Britain's The Times newspaper quoted other top European security officials saying that there is "no new intelligence to suggest a Russian attack is coming."
During his visit to the UN in New York this week, Finland's President Alexander Stubb urged leaders and analysts to stop using "alarmist language," claiming the speculation about an expanded war is exactly what the Kremlin spin doctors want.
Any NATO member can invoke Article 5 — the alliance's foundational principle that an attack against one member is considered an attack against all — but this raises the crucial question of what constitutes "an attack"? And can the alliance be counted on to respond?
Latvia's president told Britain's Channel 4 this week that he absolutely believed the U.S. and the other 30 member states would come to his country's aid if Russia moves against it, but he acknowledged there is disagreement over how that might be defined.
"The real trouble starts when you have to define when Article 5 starts in this situation," said Edgars Rinkēvičs.
"Hybrid attacks could result in Article 5 but this is where we need to work together."
Article 5 has been invoked only once in the alliance's 77-year history — by the U.S. in the wake of the 9/11 attack.

The U.K. chose not to, even after Russia's blatant 2018 assassination attempt on former spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia, which left traces of a deadly military-grade nerve agent around the town of Salisbury.
Turkey came close on several occasions during the Syrian civil war after its border communities were struck by artillery shells, but emergency consultations ultimately avoided testing the alliance's collective military mechanism.
U.S. President Donald Trump's long-term commitment to the alliance remains a source of contention and right-wing populist parties are testing continental solidarity across Europe, raising the possibility that NATO's deterrence could be fatally undermined and the alliance neutered if Article 5 is invoked and member states fail to respond. In this environment, Putin may decide the occasion is ripe to gamble once again.

Terming it a "broad daylight dacoity" against patients, the Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) expressed shock over the overpricing of essential cancermedicines, noting that one drug carried an MRP of ₹27,000 despite being supplied to retailers for ₹2,700.
"It is very surprising that the authorities who are supposed to take action on this are silent," a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said.
The observations came when the Supreme Court was hearing two petitions that raised drug-related issues, including that of ensuring strict price control over medicines.
The court termed it "absolutely shocking" that the printed MRP of an essential cancer drug was ₹27,000 when the price to retailer (PTR) was ₹2,700.
"The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what it is? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment," the Bench said.
"This is absolute rampage and carnage. This is broad daylight dacoity with patients," it said.
The Bench questioned how the patients could be cheated like this.
One of the petitioners told the Bench that his plea also raised the issue concerning the prescription of generic medicines by registered medical practitioners. He said fixing MRP of medicines was of critical importance.
Additional Solicitor General K.M. Nataraj, appearing for the Centre in one of the pleas, said the government was not treating it as an adversarial litigation.
The Bench observed that price fixation was a major issue.
It posted the matter for further hearing on September 29, 2026.
Price control
One of the petitions sought a direction to authorities to make drug formulations more cost-effective by preventing alleged unethical overpricing of essential medicines by pharma companies and retailers.
It also sought directions to ensure strict price control under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to prevent violations of the price-fixing mechanism in the drug supply chain and disproportionate profit-making by retailers through unfair trade practices.
The other plea has sought disciplinary action against medical practitioners for not prescribing generic medicines to patients.

WASHINGTON — A key Senate committee on Thursday approved the nomination of top federal health official Chris Klomp to be deputy secretary of health and human services, clearing the way for him to be confirmed by the full Senate.
Klomp is currently senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He was advanced by the Senate Finance committee in an 15-12 vote. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) joined all Republicans in supporting Klomp.
He will now go to the full Senate for a final vote.
The committee voted 14-13 to advance Ge Bai’s nomination to be HHS assistant secretary for planning and evaluation.
Klomp spent two days last week testifying before Finance and the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committees, where lawmakers highlighted the power Klomp wields at HHS and questioned how he might use that power. Klomp has already helped broker drug pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies, aided in high-profile hires, and acted as a liaison between HHS and the White House.
During his confirmation hearings, Democrats joined by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who chairs the health committee, repeatedly called on Klomp to push back on his boss, Kennedy, and even President Trump, if he continued to undermine vaccine policy. Cassidy, in particular, pressed Klomp to address the CDC’s refusal to report certain measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania.
“People are dying. The American people should know that,” he said. Cassidy had previously threatened to withhold health care nominations if HHS continued its aggressive vaccine overhaul, but Klomp’s nomination was squarely in the hands of the Finance committee, which Cassidy sits on but does not chair.
Klomp, in his statements to the committees last week, acknowledged the outsized role he would play in influencing HHS.
“Part of my responsibility is to enable the smooth operations of the department. I’m responsible for personnel, among other things,” Klomp told Finance last week. “My job is to make sure that we have everything.”
Klomp joined the Trump administration to oversee the Medicare program, before taking on additional duties at HHS. He also advised the first Trump administration on health care matters. Klomp is a health care entrepreneur, and was previously the CEO of health IT company Collective Medical.

Rishikesh rafting halted indefinitely as Ganga water level rises: Officials
Rafting resumed in the Ganga on September 23 following the annual monsoonal break that began on July 1
River rafting operations in the Ganga River in Rishikesh have been halted indefinitely following continuous rainfall over the past two days. Authorities decided to resume activities only after the weather improves and the river recedes to a safer level.
According to tourism officials, rafting and related adventure activities in the Ganga at Muni-ki-Reti have been prohibited until further orders. The water level was recorded at 339.50 metres on Sunday. Meanwhile, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and Jal Police personnel made announcements at Ganga ghats and riverbed areas, cautioning people against going near the river.
“As it is currently raining across the Garhwal division and in view of Meteorological department advisories, river rafting has been halted with immediate effect until further directives are issued. Rafting will resume only after an assessment of weather conditions, the monsoonal forecast, the Ganga’s water level and the weather forecast for next week. All river rafting operators, the rafting association and stakeholders have been directed to strictly adhere to the order,” said Tehri Garhwal district tourism and adventure officer Sobat Singh Rana.
Police officers in the Lakshman Jhula, Muni-ki-Reti and Tapovan areas have also appealed to residents, pilgrims and tourists to exercise caution and avoid going near Ganga ghats, riverbeds and picnic spots, citing the high water level and increased risk of slips and falls.
“All rafting operators are complying with the administration’s directive prohibiting rafting and related adventure activities. Safety of all stakeholders is the prime concern,” said rafting association president Dharmendra Negi.
Rafting resumed in the Ganga on September 23 following the annual monsoonal break that began on July 1. The fresh suspension, within days of the resumption, has disappointed rafting operators.
“After a two-month monsoonal break, rafting resumed with religious rituals and prayers to Ganga. The buzz had returned to Muni-ki-Reti and Rishikesh, but the sudden rainy spell has led to the cancellation of dozens of bookings. Many people have left their resorts and hotels as the weather forecast for the next two days also predicts rain and cloudy conditions,” said Sohan Singh Negi, a lodge operator in Tapovan, about 10 km from Rishikesh.
Rafting operates at various points along the Ganga, including Kaudiyala, Marine Drive, Shivpuri, Brahmapuri and Clubhouse track towards Lakshman Jhula, across Tehri Garhwal, Pauri Garhwal and Dehradun districts. The rafting stretches range from five kilometers (km) to 30km.

Bihar is reportedly seeking to rebuild its mineral economy after decades of being left with little of the mineral wealth that remained with Jharkhand following the states’ bifurcation in 2000. Geological investigations conducted between 2021 and 2024 have identified mineral resources estimated at more than ₹21,000 crore across Rohtas, Jamui, Gaya and Jehanabad, reported The Indian Express. The discoveries could potentially generate more than ₹5,000 crore in annual mining revenue once the identified resources are converted into operational mines, according to state officials. That would be significantly higher than Bihar’s current record mining collection of ₹3,592 crore, which comes predominantly from minor minerals such as sand and stone. However, the transition from geological discoveries to commercial production remains a major challenge. The state is targeting mineral extraction across different projects between 2026 and 2031, with exploration, auctions, clearances and mining leases still to be completed. Rohtas accounts for a major share of the identified resources. Geological surveys have found around 130.11 million tonnes of glauconite across the Pipradih-Bhurwa and Chutia-Nauhatta blocks, with an estimated value of ₹14,048 crore. Glauconite can serve as a source of potassium for fertilisers, a potentially significant resource for India given its dependence on imports for potash fertilisers. The Bhora-Kathra block in Rohtas has also been identified with 33-39.68 million tonnes of high-grade limestone, valued at about ₹1,761.42 crore. The mineral is widely used in cement manufacturing and for producing quicklime. Rohtas is also home to the Amjhor pyrite deposits, which account for nearly 95% of India's known pyrite resources. Pyrites are used in sulfuric acid production and other industrial chemical processes. Jamui has emerged as another important mineral zone, particularly for magnetite and gold. The Majos block contains an estimated 48.40 million tonnes of magnetite, with an assessed value ranging from ₹3,817.60 crore to ₹6,000 crore. The Bhanta block has another 6.49 million tonnes, valued at around ₹511.91 crore. Magnetite is primarily used as iron ore in steelmaking and other metallurgical applications. The Sono area has also attracted attention for its gold-bearing resources. Exploration has identified 222.88 million tonnes of ore containing an estimated 37.6 tonnes of gold metal. The Sono resource is classified as a remaining resource rather than a reserve. Preliminary exploration has been carried out, with trial production targeted for 2027-28. Exploration in Gaya and Jehanabad has identified vanadium-bearing magnetite, ilmenite, rare earth elements and lithium-bearing pegmatites. These minerals have applications across strategic industries. Vanadium is used in high-strength steel and energy-storage technologies, while ilmenite is a source of titanium dioxide. Lithium and rare earth elements are important for technologies including electric-vehicle batteries, wind turbines and defence equipment. The discoveries could therefore expand Bihar’s mineral ambitions beyond traditional mining and into minerals considered strategically important for emerging industries. The ₹21,000 crore estimate is based on geological assessments that consider factors such as extraction, beneficiation and logistics. The Geological Survey of India generally progresses exploration through four stages — G4 reconnaissance, G3 preliminary exploration, G2 general exploration and G1 detailed exploration. Bihar has been aligning its legal and administrative framework with mineral-rich states such as Odisha and Jharkhand to move identified blocks towards commercial extraction under the amended Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act. The Ministry of Mines has also introduced reimbursable private-agency models through the National Mineral Exploration Trust to reduce investment risks during the early exploration phase. Under the proposed administrative roadmap, mining plans are expected to be submitted within six months, environmental clearances targeted within 18 months and lease execution completed within 12 months. The state's timeline includes advanced G2 and G1 drilling under composite licences during 2026-27, trial production from the Sono gold resource in 2027-28 and broader commercial mineral extraction between 2026 and 2031. The eighth tranche of critical mineral auctions was also launched in Patna in August 2026, adding another step towards bringing Bihar’s newly identified mineral resources into the commercial mining pipeline. The scale of the discoveries does not automatically translate into state revenue. Early auction rounds for some glauconite and nickel blocks had to be cancelled because of limited participation, with prospective miners hesitant to make large bids based on preliminary exploration data, the report noted. Technology and investment are additional hurdles. Extracting agricultural-grade potash from hard-rock glauconite and recovering vanadium from magnetite require capital-intensive processing technologies, some of which are still developing domestically. Land acquisition could pose another challenge. Although several mineral blocks are located outside forest areas, land ownership in agricultural regions is often fragmented among numerous private owners. Securing surface rights could therefore add to project timelines, alongside mandatory environmental approvals and Pollution Control Board clearances. Illegal mining is another concern as the state moves towards commercialisation. I don’t think I’m going to hurt anyone’s feelings by pointing out that Decap doesn’t have the name recognition of Kendrick Lamar, Olivia Rodrigo, or Charli XCX. But his fingerprints are all over tracks from them, as well as many other artists, including Freddie Gibbs, Bad Bunny, Mac Miller, BTS, and even Ludwig Göransson’s score for Oppenheimer.

Decap is the man behind the drums behind your favorite song
Producer and sound designer Decap’s ‘Drums That Knock’ are all over some of the biggest hits of the last 10 years.
Nicholas Piantedosi, better known as Decap, is a record producer, but perhaps more importantly, he’s the man behind Drums That Knock, a series of sample packs that have found their way onto countless records across genres. The line is so successful that, after debuting in 2016, it’s now on its 11th installment. Kenneth Blume, formerly known as Kenny Beats, the producer behind hits from Denzel Curry, Vince Staples, Rico Nasty, Idles, and FKA Twigs, said that Decap “changed a million lives with a single snare.”
Unsurprisingly for a man so obsessed with low-end, he’s got a real beef to pick with phone speakers. And even with all the modern tools at his disposal in his digital audio workstation of choice, Ableton Live, he still can’t give up his trusty Boss SP-202 Dr. Sample from 1998.
What is your most indispensable tool?
Ableton Live. It’s how I get my ideas out.
Which is the most underappreciated?
The clipper. A soft clipper can give your drums that warm analog sound, or it can make them hit super hard. It’s the tool that changed my music.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
The speaker. I wish I could hear a fat 808 on my phone. A raw 808 with no processing is basically inaudible on a phone speaker. So many people listen to music all day on their phone without ever truly feeling the low end. If I can make my drums knock on a phone anyway, I’m doing something right.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
My Boss SP-202 sampler. It’s the first sampler I ever had, back in junior high when I first started making beats. I chopped my first samples on it, and it was the start of everything I’m doing now.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Gatekeeping over gear. This idea that you’re not a real producer unless you use hardware, or unless you use this DAW or that one. It’s not true. If you’ve got a computer, you already have everything you need. The dopest producer might be a kid in North Africa with Skullcandy headphones. The only thing I care about is if you’re dope or not.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
My honest answer is nothing. I’m happy making the music I make, because it’s meaningful to me and it’s my expression. I don’t need to make anyone else’s.
What creation are you most proud of?
Creating a hard-hitting sound that I love and watching it make its way across genres.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
From my dad. No matter what, make a decision and put a stake in the ground. But remember what a stake is. You can always pull it up and move it.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I meditate. It aligns my mind and my body, and when those two are lined up I can focus way more clearly. If the mind isn’t right, everything will always be a little off.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
The 3M technique: make it, mix it down, move on. It doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s about staying in the action of creation, because that’s where the magic happens.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Really good food. Living in Los Angeles, there’s no shortage of incredible restaurants, and I love going out for a nice dinner.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
“This all started with not wanting a real job”

On July 15, Raj Rani, 52, an ASHA worker in Yamunagar, Haryana had just completed her tasks for the day when she felt a throbbing pain in her left arm and in the middle of her chin. Since this pain had persisted for a few days, she went to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in Vyaspur to get an electrocardiogram (ECG) done.
The Additional Senior Medical Officer at the centre, Gunjeet Singh, saw the results of the ECG, gave her a dose of drugs including blood thinners and clotbusters, called a ‘loading dose’, and asked her to rush to the district hospital at Ambala Cantonment, two hours away, for further treatment.
Raj Rani had single-vessel disease, with a major coronary artery blocked. “At the district hospital, they scheduled my angioplasty the next day and I got one stent in my heart,” said Raj Rani. “I told my doctors to give me good treatment so I could resume my work as an ASHA. They reassured me that I would be able to do my duties, because I was lucky: I came in time,” she said.
Had this happened even two months ago, Raj Rani would not have received the diagnosis that would have led to quick treatment. Even though the Vyaspur CHC had an ECG machine, there was no technician to conduct it and while the medical officers could interpret the results, they were not very confident.
What changed
On May 29 this year, the Haryana government tied up with Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech startup, as part of Public-Private Partnership (PPP), to set up a tele-ECG network called Spandan One. Each medical centre in Haryana received a tele-ECG device that connects to smartphone and tablets, can be operated by frontline workers and gives a clinician-reviewed result in less than three minutes.
To date, nearly 600 government health facilities including primary health centres (PHCs), CHCs, sub-divisional hospitals and district hospitals have been equipped by a tele-ECG device along with training in using it. As of September 17, 33,854 ECG tests were conducted; 9,287 ECGs were abnormal and 1,342 critical cases were detected according to the Spandan dashboard.
In the remote Ranjitpur PHC in Yamunagar district, there is a steady increase in the footfall of patients due to the tele-ECG service available. “This is a new building we started using just six months ago; there is no fixed nurse or staff or even furniture,” said Varun Singh, medical officer who has been running the centre with staff on deputation and through borrowed furniture from other centres. “Ever since we got the tele-ECG, people have been coming to the centre asking for it,” he said.
One recent morning, Ram Saran, 75, come to the PHC with his son Mangaram to get his reports examined by Dr. Singh. Mr. Saran had been experiencing a feeling of his heart racing and breathlessness for many months. He had gotten an ECG and blood tests for ₹1200 at a private hospital at Vyaspur but wanted confirmation from the government doctor. The nursing officer at the PHC put the electrodes on Mr. Saran and an ECG graph formed in the tablet in her hands, with a message that the report was being analysed. Two and half minutes later, the report was ready to be downloaded. Mr. Saran had an ‘abnormal ECG’ and he was asked to consult a cardiologist and a copy of the report was sent to his mobile phone.
Dr. Singh then consulted with Mr. Saran and his son and told them to visit the hospital at Ambala Cant. at the earliest. “Before this initiative, I would not be able to interpret ECGs with this level of sophistication. The patient would need to visit a cardiologist available two hours away and wait a long time in the OPD for the diagnosis,” said Dr. Singh. For patients who are diagnosed with critical ECGs, an alarm goes off in the tablet to draw the attention of the healthcare worker and a prescription is generated so that patients receive life-saving medicines while the referral to a higher centre is being made.
“We never thought that we would get results within a few minutes of doing the ECG. This tele-ECG service is available in all centres in Yamunagar and is available in even other remote locations in the districts. This is a very welcome step,” said Shama Parveen, senior medical officer, Yamunagar CHC.
Primary care matters
Even though PHCs are the first point of contact of medical care for rural patients, they often do not have the necessary equipment or manpower to diagnose and treat heart ailments. A 2024 pre-print that assessed the availability of cardiac care in Vadodara district in Gujarat found only 44.11% of the surveyed PHCs had functional ECGs and employed them where indicated. In most cases patients were simply referred to higher centres for treatment. The time lost due to travel between centres can prove to be fatal for patients.
The impact of Haryana’s initiative has been incredible, said Kuldeep Singh, former Director General, Health Services (DGHS), Haryana who spearheaded the partnership. ECGs and early treatment for heart attacks is now available in rural centres that had earlier not registered a single heart attack due to lack of diagnosis. “We are already witnessing a 20% reduction in deaths in the emergency departments of district hospitals because patients are being stabilised before rushing here,” he said, adding that these are early assessments and more data is still being collected.
After primary care
Once the patient is stabilised with a loading dose, they are sent to higher centres such as district hospitals with Catherisation Labs where angiographies and angioplasties are performed. “Given the geography of Haryana, most patients reach the higher centre within one hour of the diagnosis, saving lives and heart muscles,” said Dr. Singh.
The Haryana government is also in a PPP with private providers to equip and run cath labs in four locations in the State–Panchkula, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ambala Cant. and is planning to soon expand to more locations.
As part of the agreement with the Haryana government, Sunfox Technologies provides equipment, training and on-going support for its tele-ECG system apart from maintaining a live dashboard monitoring cases. “Through the dashboard, we have real-time patient information which has given us rich insights–for example we now know that patients between 30-49 years have a higher incidence of cardiac issues than those over 50 years,” said Rajat Jain, CEO of the startup. Data has also shown that the incidence of critical ECGs among women in the age group of 30-49 is as much as men and greater than men in the age group of 70+, dispelling the belief that men have a greater risk for heart disease than women. “These kinds of insights are very important for policymakers but were never accessible before,” he said.
Challenges in the process
While the project is picking up steam in Haryana, there are some teething issues – many of the centres have to conduct repeat ECGs to get accurate ECG readings if they were not conducted properly the first time. A bump in the road was that the State’s nursing union had issued a diktat stating that nurses should not be conducting the ECGs as the post of ECG technicians has remained vacant in most health centres. The DGHS, however, later issued a letter stating that healthcare workers cannot deny conducting life-saving diagnosis and would face disciplinary action if they failed to do so. There is also the question of what happens when the partnership between the government and Sunfox Technologies ends: would the pathway to diagnosis and treatment change or would it have improved by then?
Looking ahead
Making ECGs available at PHCs is a great start but we need to do much more to improve the public health system as a whole to respond well to non-communicable diseases and their complications, said Chetanya Malik, a doctor who practices in Surguja, a remote district in Chattisgarh for the non-profit Sangwari. In Chhattisgarh, an ECG facility is only available at the district hospital, revealing the vastness of the need and the unevenness of primary care provided within the country. Dr. Malik also noted the need for patients to be given support in finding transport and for referrals to higher centres to be seamless to help solve the problem of cardiac emergencies.
India’s public health systems have, for decades now, remained focused on infectious diseases and maternal and child health — both still important, but the time has come to also realign the systems to care for non-communicable diseases. Heart disease alone is estimated to account for nearly 27% of all deaths in India. The need is enormous, and the technology is available. It is time all States implement such programmes, pointed out Dr. Kuldeep Singh.

Bengaluru man kills wife, dumps body in vacant plot; civic workers find it days later
A senior police officer said inquiries at the mall helped investigators establish woman's identity and trace her address.
A 32-year-old man from Odisha allegedly kept his wife’s body inside their Bengaluru home for three days after killing her during an argument over finances, before wrapping it in a bedsheet and dumping it at a vacant plot, police said on Saturday.
The accused, Sagar Chandra Rawat, was arrested more than three weeks after the highly decomposed body of his wife, Anusuya, was found at a vacant plot in MS Nagar near Sampigehalli, police said, according to news agency PTI.
According to police, Sagar and Anusuya had an argument over finances on August 11. Sagar allegedly assaulted and strangled his wife during the argument, resulting in her death due to suffocation.
He allegedly left her body inside their house for about three days. He then wrapped it in a bedsheet, tied it with a rope and carried it out of the house around midnight, police said.
Fearing that he would be caught, Sagar allegedly dumped the body at the vacant site before returning home.
He then collected his belongings, locked the house and began staying on the premises of the small hotel in Yelahanka where the couple worked, police said.

How was the body found?
The body was discovered on September 2 by workers cleaning the vacant plot following the Greater Bengaluru Authority's (GBA) directive to property owners to maintain their premises. The workers alerted the authorities, police said.
As the body was highly decomposed, police and local residents performed the last rites soon after the post-mortem.
With the body beyond recognition, establishing the woman's identity proved difficult. Police, however, found a mall tag on her clothing that led them to the billing details for the garment. A Ganesha pendant and technical analysis subsequently helped corroborate her identity as Anusuya, police said.
A senior police officer said inquiries at the mall helped investigators establish Anusuya's identity and trace her address.

When police reached her house in MS Nagar, they found it locked. Local inquiries revealed that Anusuya and Sagar worked at a small hotel in Yelahanka and had been living there, police said.
Police said Sagar had come to Bengaluru about five years ago and married Anusuya around two years ago.
He was subsequently taken into custody and, during interrogation, allegedly confessed to the killing after investigators confronted him with discrepancies in his statement.

Plans for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua’s long-awaited heavyweight clash were in doubt on Saturday after promoter Dana White said he was unsure whether the fight would go ahead.
Fury and Joshua were announced on Thursday as opponents for a December 11 showdown at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, a contest billed as one of the biggest fights in British boxing history.
However, Fury said in a video posted on social media late on Friday that the fight was in jeopardy because Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, were trying to withdraw from the all-British heavyweight showdown between the former world champions.
Hearn’s promotional company, Matchroom Boxing, did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent on Saturday.
White, the UFC president and head of Zuffa Boxing, told reporters in London on Saturday that he did not know whether the bout would proceed as planned.
Asked about a scheduled press conference in the coming days, White said he was also uncertain whether it would take place.
Hearn has said he and Joshua had insisted on the bout being staged in Britain, while the promoters had proposed holding it in New York’s Madison Square Garden.
The dispute over promotional rights has also sparked claims of contractual breaches and talk of replacement opponents.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Wish you looked at your phone less? Then you’ve probably heard of Brick, a $59 device that claims to help you block distractions. You tap your phone against the Brick when you want to avoid distractions—the bundled software stops you from opening whichever apps you’ve decided you need to stop doomscrolling.
The idea is to add a physical barrier between you and apps like Instagram—if you want to scroll, you need to physically get up, find the Brick, and tap it. It’s a good idea, and implemented in a way that makes it easy to get started. But what if you don’t want to buy a chunk of plastic?
Good news: the Brick is basically just an NFC chip, not that different from the one in your credit card or passport. You can buy a blank NFC chip for a dollar. Even better, free applications can use these chips to block distractions, exactly like the Brick. Or, if you prefer, these apps also support QR codes, meaning all you need is a printer. Here are two free distraction-blocking apps—complete with physical barriers—for iPhone or Android.
Best for iPhones: Foqos
The oddly named Foqos is a free, open source app for iOS by Canadian developer Ali Waseem. Many open source apps lack polish, but not this one—it’s easy to configure the necessary permissions, set up a profile, and start blocking distractions.
While creating a new profile, you first choose which physical object you want to use to start and stop your blocking sessions. The two most popular options are NFC tags (there’s a handy link to buy some in the app) or a QR code. But you can also block using a daily schedule, if you prefer, or by scanning any barcode. The barcode option is nice because you don’t need to buy or print anything—scan the code on your favorite book, beverage, or anything else you keep around the house.
Foqos can block you from managing apps while a profile is running. This means you can’t just delete Foqos to get around a block you set up, which is exactly what someone fighting against their own urges needs. You can allow a limited number of breaks, if you want.
I’ve been using this to break my Reddit habit and can report that it works. I keep a printed QR code inside a cabinet, far from the couch where I tend to scroll. It creates just enough friction that I can finish reading a book instead. The application has an excellent privacy policy—no data leaves your device.
Best for Android: Switchly
Foqos is sadly iOS-exclusive, and I couldn’t find an Android equivalent that’s quite as polished. But Switchly, by Vienna-based developer Saltyy, stands out as one of the more feature-complete apps I tested. You will need to spend some time fiddling to get it set up, granted, but once you do, you’ll find it every bit as flexible as Foqos.
To get started, open the app, which you can install from Google Play. A wizard will guide you through the relevant permissions, then talk you through setting up your first profile. You will need to read everything carefully, because it’s a little bit tough to navigate the first time. You can block apps and URLs. You can use an NFC chip or a QR code to trigger locking and unlocking. You can also block based on a schedule; Premium users can trigger when connected to a particular Wi-Fi network, or when a certain Bluetooth device is nearby.
If you’d rather not block Instagram entirely, but never want to see a Reel again, good news: there’s support for blocking particular features inside certain apps. The feature is labeled as experimental, but worked well in my testing.
There’s a lot of flexibility, but Android’s open nature means how well it works depends in part on your phone model. The developer acknowledges this. Also, you don’t need the Premium version—the free tier offers plenty of features for most people.
Another application Android users should check out is Lock. This app is more polished than Switchly, but only supports NFC chips. Give it a try if Switchly doesn’t quite work the way you like.
Distractions don’t just live on your phone. We’ve written about how to block websites on your computer, with multiple free options. But let’s face it: the phone is the ultimate distraction machine. Learn to control your impulses there.
