A powerful nor’easter has knocked out power to thousands of homes and businesses in the US Northeast, grounding hundreds of flights and prompting state leaders to declare emergencies. Two weekend concerts by pop star Ed Sheeran at Gillette Stadium outside Boston were canceled as a precaution.
High winds battered the coast from Delaware to Massachusetts Saturday, and conditions were expected to get worse in New York City as the day wears on, said Bob Oravec, a senior forecaster with the US Weather Prediction Center.
Storm surges are expected to raise ocean levels by three feet along the New Jersey and New York coast, and even higher across New England. Saturday night’s full moon will make things worse by raising tides even higher.
“The worst effects of it are tonight into Sunday morning, anywhere from southern New England west across Long Island toward New York City,” Oravec said. “The coastal flooding will be the biggest flooding impact for this.”
State of Emergency
New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared an emergency in New York City and the surrounding areas on Friday as the storm developed, and New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill did the same for her state. From Massachusetts to Maryland, 101,674 homes and businesses were without power as of 1:15 p.m., with areas in Queens, Long Island and along the New Jersey coast among the hardest-hit, according to Poweroutage.com. Trees are especially vulnerable as they still have their leaves, which could lead to falling branches that down more power lines.
Meanwhile, workers in New York City were preparing for uprooted trees and clogged catch basins in anticipation of flooding, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. The rainfall forecast for the city doubled to an estimated six inches Saturday, causing coastal flooding and knocking out power to about 22,000 customers, Hochul said in a news conference Saturday morning.
“We expect this weather pattern to continue and even intensify over the next day,” Hochul said. “This could, and it already has been, bringing down trees and power lines and cause power outages.”
The Global Citizen Festival in New York’s Central Park and the All Things Go NYC music and culture festival were also called off.
Affected transit
In New Jersey, the storm flooded some coastal and back bay roads, making them impassable, and officials urged residents not to drive through them. Sherrill said in a social media post Saturday that conditions had temporarily eased in parts of the state but were expected to worsen again later in the day.
Across the US, 425 flights were canceled, mostly from Boston’s Logan International Airport and other Massachusetts fields, FlightAware said. At least 15 flights were also canceled from New York’s LaGuardia Airport. Ground stops and delays were likely in Newark, Philadelphia, Washington, and at John F. Kennedy International Airport as well, the Federal Aviation Administration said on its website.
New Jersey Transit suspended its River Line light rail service along the Delaware between Florence and Cass Street stations south of Trenton. The Long Island Rail Road suspended service to its Long Beach Branch due to flooding Saturday. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority has suspended most of its commuter ferries in Boston Harbor and the surrounding area.
National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings and watches, including for New York City, where it said tides may come in up to three feet higher than normal at the Battery, at the southern end of Manhattan, and waves as high as 12 feet may crash into the shoreline in Brooklyn and Queens through Sunday. From the coast in New England through the New Jersey coast, wind gusts may reach 60 miles per hour.
Oravec said the storm will remain intense in New York and New England through Sunday but will have weakened by Monday morning when commuters face a return to the office.

క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలోని రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై జరిగిన వైమానిక దాడికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో రియాద్కు చెందినది కాదు. ఇది రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జూన్ 2026లో డ్రోన్ దాడి వల్ల జరిగిన అగ్నిప్రమాదానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై హౌతీలు దాడి చేసినట్లు వార్తలు వస్తున్నప్పటికీ, వైరల్ వీడియో దానికి సంబంధించినది కాదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 జూన్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోకు చెందినది. మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్పై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడి కారణంగా వ్యాపించిన మంటలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతోంది.
వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 18 జూన్ 2026న మాస్కోపై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడిలో సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో మంటలు, పొగ వ్యాపించాయి. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న ప్రదేశాన్ని గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, అది మాస్కోలో ఉన్నట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
అయితే, 19 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న రియాద్లోని కింగ్ ఖలీద్ అంతర్జాతీయ విమానాశ్రయంలోని ఇంధన డిపోపై తాము దాడి చేసినట్లు హౌతీలు పేర్కొన్నారంటూ పలు అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వెల్లడించాయి.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జరిగిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

Beyond pay, work-life balance, and scheduling, there are other basic challenges affecting the US submarine workforce, including how workers get to the job, a Navy official overseeing workforce concerns shared.
The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office says it, along with its federal and state partners, has observed success in addressing region-specific problems, like transportation, that can be make-or-break for attracting new workers. Regional teams have been critical in examining the particular workforce needs around submarine construction and repair yards.
Erica Logan, the office's director of workforce, told Business Insider earlier this year that her team looks at local factors, including education, demographics, unemployment, and cost of living. Transportation is also part of the assessment.
"What does the transportation system look like? Is it a very rural area where there may not be transportation?" Logan said. "How would we get folks there? What could we do to help a supplier that lives in an area like that?"
The office, she said, has supported several transportation pilots with bus systems to make it easier for submarine workers to get to and from work. These programs have prompted further questions about free bus passes and van pools.
"I think we've done a lot in that area using this regional approach to really just get a good understanding of what that region has," Logan said.
The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office is working on rebuilding the network of suppliers, builders, and manufacturers that construct Navy submarines. As part of the broader efforts to fix decades-old shipbuilding problems in the US, the office has focused on attracting and retaining workers, as well as addressing everything from pay and work-life balance to problems unique to individual communities.
In one example provided by the office, General Dynamics Electric Boat partnered with the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority to provide direct service to the Quonset Point shipyard. Ridership has more than doubled year over year, the office said, and it came at no cost to the Navy.
In another, the Hampton Roads Workforce Council provides workers with gas cards and bus passes to help them get to work. Since September 2023, the Hampton Roads Maritime Training System program within the council has provided nearly $200,000 in transportation assistance, funded through grants, donations, and the Virginia state government.
Housing is also a challenge. The office hasn't funded permanent housing or related subsidies for shipyard or supplier workers. Instead, its efforts involve state and local engagement to expand affordable housing, as well as partnerships with specific yards or vendors.
Some initiatives specifically support trainees. For instance, the Accelerated Training in Defense Manufacturing program in Danville, Virginia, offers students housing during their 16-week training. The program quickly trains candidates in manufacturing skills and trades to create a sustained flow of workers for jobs in naval shipbuilding and the submarine industrial base.
Addressing these issues, along with competitive pay and benefits, is key to recruiting and retaining the workers that the Navy needs to meet its shipbuilding goals. Over the next 10 years, the service estimates it'll need to hire 250,000 skilled workers to account for the expected attrition and retirement in the workforce.

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.

A delegation of the Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF), led by its president Mohammad Yaseen Khan, on Tuesday called on newly appointed Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar Singh and discussed issues concerning the trade community across the Valley.
The delegation congratulated Singh on assuming charge as IGP Kashmir and expressed hope that his experience and leadership would further strengthen police-public coordination.
The meeting focused on traffic management, parking, policing, movement of commercial vehicles and timely resolution of traders’ grievances at the district level.
Representatives of various district trade bodies apprised the IGP of local issues affecting traders and business establishments and stressed the need for regular coordination between the police and the trading community.
The IGP gave a patient hearing to the delegation and, according to KTMF, issued on-the-spot directions on several issues. He also directed the concerned district SSPs to examine and address the grievances raised by traders from their respective areas.
KTMF senior member Javaid Ahmad Zargar, representing the Jamia Masjid and Downtown Srinagar area, raised the long-pending demand for a fire station near Jamia Masjid, citing the congestion in the area and the need for an effective emergency response mechanism.
Zargar also highlighted the shortage of adequate parking facilities in Downtown Srinagar, saying traffic and parking difficulties continue to affect traders, residents and visitors.
KTMF president Mohammad Yaseen Khan described the interaction as constructive and appreciated the IGP’s prompt response to the issues raised by the delegation.
He said traders were important stakeholders in maintaining a peaceful and orderly commercial environment and stressed that regular interaction between police and trade bodies could help resolve genuine issues before they escalate.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said.
The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.
In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as a shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.
The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.
No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.
South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.
Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.
“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a spokesperson, Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.
“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”
Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama joint at around 1.46am on Saturday night and starting shooting at customers.
“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained ... Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”
In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.
South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of 10 women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, the majority in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country and has piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.
Associated Press in Cape Town contributed to this report

A court in Shopian on Tuesday sentenced a man to life imprisonment for the murder of a person in 2019, observing that the case did not fall within the “rarest of rare” category warranting the death penalty.
Principal Sessions Judge Shopian Mehmood Ahmed Chowdhary awarded life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Bilal Ahmad Seh, who was convicted under Section 302 of the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
The court said the convict had been in custody since his arrest on April 21, 2019, and had spent nearly seven years in custody during the trial.
The case, registered as FIR No. 19/2019 at Police Station Zainapora, initially involved charges under Sections 302, 307, 147, 148, 506, 109, 341 and 34 of the RPC.
While deciding the quantum of sentence, the court considered the mitigating and aggravating circumstances and referred to the Supreme Court’s guidelines on awarding the death penalty.
The court noted that the case was based on four eyewitnesses as well as circumstantial evidence. It also took into account that the convict was a first-time offender, was a farmer by profession and had been supporting his family.
The court observed that there were no aggravating circumstances of such an exceptional nature as to warrant capital punishment.
“Life imprisonment is the appropriate punishment to be awarded to the convict for commission of murder of the deceased,” the court said.
The court also noted that other accused named in the case, including the convict’s brother and two sisters, had been acquitted, while proceedings against another accused had abated following his death. A juvenile accused in the case is facing separate proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board, according to the case record.
Since the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the court directed that the case file and judgment be submitted to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh for confirmation of the sentence as required under law.
The convict was directed to be sent to Special Jail Pulwama to undergo the sentence. The court also informed him of his right to appeal against the judgment and sentence before the High Court within 15 days.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Haptics tech company Taction sued Apple in 2021, alleging it infringed two of its patents. Now a federal jury in San Diego has awarded Taction over $5.7 billion in damages. According to CNBC, “The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input.”
Apple hit with $5.7 billion in damages over haptic patents
Apple’s Taptic Engine was found to infringe on two of Taction’s patents.
Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine in its Apple Watches and iPhones used technology that it had developed without a proper license, and the jury agreed. It found that Apple had infringed on two claims in one patent and one in the other. However, the jury did not find that Apple willfully infringed. Taction had accused Apple of reverse-engineering the tech from two Kannon gaming headsets.
Apple has said that it intends to appeal the decision. We’ve reached out for additional comment and will update the story if and when we hear back.

The ministry of road transport and highways (MoRTH) has introduced a new Model Concession Agreement (MCA) on 18 September for highway projects awarded under the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM), replacing the framework used for earlier projects.
The new MCA covers the entire project cycle, from conditions precedent and right-of-way to construction payments, operation and maintenance, termination and dispute resolution. It also introduces more granular milestones and monitoring mechanisms.
Mint explains what has changed, and what does it mean for developers, lenders and the government.
Why a new HAM agreement?
Under the HAM model, the concessionaire finances and builds the road and is subsequently paid through a combination of construction-stage payments and annuities. The new MCA explicitly covers design, financing, construction, operation and maintenance obligations.
The new agreement introduces more granular milestones and monitoring mechanisms. Most importantly, payments are now explicitly linked to independently certified physical progress.
For developers, this means a clearer framework for converting construction work into receivables, while the government gets a more direct mechanism to link payments to work completed on the ground.
How will developers get paid?
The most consequential change is the payment mechanism.
The new MCA provides for 40% of the bid project cost to be paid by government agencies during construction in 10 instalments of 4% each, against physical-progress milestones ranging from 5% to 90%.
The independent engineer has to certify achievement of each milestone, after which the authority is required to make the payment within 15 days.
The remaining project cost is to be paid through 30 biannual instalments beginning 180 days after the commercial operation date.
The agreement also provides for inflation adjustment through a 70:30 WPI-CPI formula, allowing the bid project cost to be adjusted for changes in the price index between bidding and invoicing.
For developers, this provides greater visibility on when construction expenditure can be converted into receivables. It also means, however, that payment is more directly dependent on measurable and certifiable physical progress.
Does it make construction financing easier?
The new MCA includes a significant liquidity-support mechanism. The authority can provide a mobilization advance of up to 10% of the total project cost, in two instalments, against a bank guarantee.
The MCA also introduces an incentive linked to newer construction technology. If a concessionaire purchases and registers qualifying alternative-fuel construction equipment—electric, hydrogen or biofuel machinery—or specified automated intelligent construction machinery within the prescribed period, the interest rate on the corresponding portion of the advance is reduced by 50%.
At the same time, developers bidding more than 10% below the estimated bid project cost will have to provide additional performance security equivalent to 10% of the difference.
Who bears the risk when projects are delayed?
The new agreement creates clearer consequences for both sides.
The authority must provide key conditions precedent, including right of way, relevant environmental permissions, forest and wildlife clearances and appointment of the independent engineer.
If the authority delays these conditions, it has to pay damages at 0.1% of the performance security for each day of delay, subject to the prescribed ceiling. Conversely, the concessionaire faces damages of 0.2% of performance security a day for delays attributable to it.
The MCA also provides a structured termination-payment mechanism. In the event of concessionaire default, the payment increases with the physical-progress milestone achieved, rather than being treated as a simple recovery of expenditure.
For example, termination after the 20% milestone provides for 50% of debt due or 3% of bid project cost, whichever is lower. The corresponding percentages rise progressively at later milestones.
This makes the point at which a project fails particularly important for lenders and developers, since the termination payment is linked to the project's physical progress.
What changes in construction monitoring and road safety?
The new MCA places greater emphasis on continuous verification rather than monitoring only at the end of construction.
Physical progress is to be measured using predefined weightages for individual construction activities. The agreement also requires monthly progress reporting, inspections, testing, video recording and technical audits.
Road safety receives a separate layer of oversight. The authority is required to appoint a safety consultant, including for a safety audit of completed construction works before COD.
The independent engineer is also to be changed every three years, potentially reducing the risk of one monitoring agency remaining associated with a project throughout its life.
What does this mean for highway construction?
The immediate effect is likely to be a more milestone-driven HAM construction regime.
Developers get a clearer payment calendar, inflation protection and access to mobilization funding. At the same time, the government gets stronger safeguards against low-ball bidding, delays and poor-quality construction.
The new MCA also extends the contract beyond simply building the road. Its maintenance framework requires creation of an asset-management system covering an inventory of road assets, their condition, maintenance needs, costs and a real-time database.
That could gradually shift HAM projects towards a more data-driven lifecycle approach, with the quality of the road during its operating period becoming as important as its construction.

New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

So, I initially found out about the burnerverse in February 2025, a few months, about nine months, before Maddie went viral. And I found out about it because I saw this young woman's name trending on X, and her name was Mary Kate Cornett. And I was really curious. I was like, who is this person? This is happening years after Elon Musk has purchased the platform formerly known as Twitter. He famously got rid of much of the trust and safety team. The content policies have been relaxed from what they used to be. And so, how responsive was the platform in getting the content to go away?
Ej Dickson: Well, I mean, the platform didn't respond to me when I asked for comment, and I had a lot of questions for them. I mean, I don't think that this would've happened were it not for Elon Musk acquiring X and dismantling the regulations because X's algorithm amplifies divisive or inflammatory content in such a way that it doesn't really matter what's trending. It's just going to be broadcast nationwide. And it's like a game of whack-a-mole. You can file a take-down request, and apparently the Kowalskis said that X was pretty responsive in terms of actually getting the videos down individually once they filed the request because they're legally required to do that because of the Take It Down Act. But, if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead. That's just the way the internet works.
Zoë Schiffer: As things stand now, has anyone specifically been held accountable for what happened to Maddie?
Ej Dickson: So, the men are being charged with sexual cyberharassment which is a misdemeanor that is punishable by up to one year in prison and an $1,000 fine. I believe one of them is ... The police department is alleging that he'd financially profited off of her humiliation. When I reached out to Theta Chi, their fraternity, they said that they were on interim suspension and completely disavowed their activities and said, "This is not what Theta Chi is about." I don't know if that was prompted by my reaching out or if that had already been underway prior. I don't want to speculate, but I had said that she will see them posting from parties and stuff.
Zoë Schiffer: And where does this leave Maddie?
Ej Dickson: She's traumatized. I mean, can you imagine the worst moment of your life goes viral when you're 19 years old, and you don't even remember it? She doesn't think she'll be able to date and find love. She thinks this is going to follow her wherever she goes for the rest of her life. And the first time I met her, she wasn't even particularly emotional about it. It was just fact for her. And I was just sitting there. I'm a parent. It broke my heart. And that's the thing that really haunted me after reporting this and what really stuck with me when I spoke to her best friend who's quoted in the article. They stole her youth. They stole her girlhood. They stole her optimism and her sense of hope and belief that she could do something great with her life. Because that's what college is all about, right? You're kind of on the precipice of all of that. And that just seems like the most egregious theft of all.
Zoë Schiffer: Her experience also isn't an isolated incident, right? How far-reaching is this? How many people has this happened to?
Ej Dickson: So, there are degrees of it. All told, I was able to identify about a little less than a dozen women across the country who had been doxed in this fashion and on this scale. They were all young women in their late teens, early 20s, college students or recently graduated from college, conventionally attractive, and they had all been subject to some sort of salacious rumor or had nonconsensual videos or images of them circulating and were perceived to have transgressed the boundaries of sexual norms, I guess, in some way was kind of the unifying criteria. But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale to teenage girls whose photos were posted on college's incoming students' Instagram pages. They were taking their photos and posting them and making fun of their bodies and the way they looked and posting their full names. Girls who weren't even in college yet, incoming freshmen, they were doxing on a much smaller scale. And they do that pretty regularly. Or, they'll take photos of somebody's dating profile, some girl's dating profile or a message, and they'll post it, and they'll release her name and make fun of her. So, it happens all the time. I think that it's really the scale that differs, but the exposure aspect of it happens all the time.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, I'm curious how she felt. Like you said, you talked to her after the article came out. Obviously, it's this decision that I think a lot of sources face where it's like, do you not speak out and hope that the story kind of goes away? Or, do you take the chance and try and take back a little of the narrative?
Ej Dickson: That was really difficult. That was something I was really concerned about because I thought that there was a possibility that it could renew the harassment against her. And we had a number of conversations about that. And I think she understood and understands the impact that her story has and that she has an opportunity to speak for other women who have been through this and to sort of ensure that shame switches sides, that she doesn't need to be ashamed of what happened to her. I think she was a little overwhelmed, but she's a very strong person.
Maddie Kowalski: I'd like to end this with something really important. Although I don't have control over what happened to me, I can control what I do moving forward, and I want to move forward with healing.
Zoë Schiffer: Here's Maddie again. We thought she should close out the story in her own words.
Maddie Kowalski: These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life, but I'm still here, and that's something that I'm really learning to be proud of. I'm taking steps to rebuild myself, to feel safe again, and to understand that what happened to me doesn't define me. And I know that this is a long path. I've unfortunately also realized that there are so many women and girls as well as men who go through things like this in silence, feeling alone or ashamed or afraid to speak. And if sharing my story can help even one person feel seen or teach one person why consent and decency matter, then it's worth it.
Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered
- Published
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.
Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.
BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on all almost of the charges.
We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.
But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?
What are the 115 charges?
In February 2023, City were charged and referred to an independent commission over alleged breaches that were said to have taken place between 2009 and 2018.
The charges - relating to Premier League financial rules - are:
- 54 x failure to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 14 x failure to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 5 x failure to comply with Uefa's rules including financial fair play (FFP) 2013-14 to 2017-18.
- 7 x breaching Premier League profit and sustainability (PSR) rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18.
- 35 x failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations from December 2018 to Feb 2023.
City have always denied wrongdoing and BBC Sport has been told they would appeal were they found guilty.
But what does that actually mean?
German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked documents, including emails purportedly sent between top City executives (some of whom remain at the City Football Group), across several seasons following the club's Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
It alleged these showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from state-owned airline Etihad and state-controlled telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from their holding company (Sheik Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group, or ADUG) as sponsorship income by channelling the funds through the companies' accounts.
This, it was alleged, was a means of meeting FFP rules introduced by Uefa in 2011 - and PSR brought in by the Premier League in 2012 - limiting clubs' permitted losses.
There then followed further allegations of misreporting financial information centred on documents that claimed to show secret 'off-the-books' payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
It is also alleged the club gave players more money than was officially going through the accounts so recorded spending was less than it actually was.
City, who have always maintained ADUG is a private fund rather than an arm of the state, refused to comment on any of Der Spiegel's revelations, saying the leaked emails were obtained illegally, and they were an "attempt to damage the club's reputation".
City - along with the companies involved - strongly denied breaking any financial rules. But that did not stop both Uefa and the Premier League launching investigations as a result.
What has been the timeline of the case?
November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules.
March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings.
May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process.
November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible.
February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine.
July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas.
July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches.
April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims.
February 2023: The Premier League charges City with 115 financial breaches.
September 2024: The start of a 10-week hearing between the Premier League and City on the 115 charges.
February 2025: City manager Pep Guardiola says the club expect to learn the verdict "within one month". Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season.
September 2026: Reports emerge that a verdict has been reached, with sources telling the BBC that City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges.
What punishment could Man City face?
It was never expected the verdict would come complete with the sanctions.
We now face a waiting game for even that verdict to officially be made public by the independent panel.
We don't know who was on the panel that heard and ruled on the case, and that will only come once a written judgment is released.
All options are open to the disciplinary commission:
- Points deduction (immediate or suspended).
- Financial penalties (immediate or suspended).
- Removal from the Premier League.
Being removed from the Premier League would mean City lose their membership and are demoted to a lower division from the end of the season.
That could also happen through a points penalty so severe they would effectively be relegated.
What has been said?
The Premier League declined to comment on the case when approached on Friday.
City issued a statement that showed frustration news of the verdict had leaked.
It read: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.
"As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
Will there be an appeal? How long would one take?
An appeal from City is expected to be a formality.
City's legal team is being led by Lord Pannick KC, who is reported to charge £5,000 an hour for his services. He helped City overturn their two-year European ban in 2020.
However, considering we are already eight years into this process - and two years beyond the start of the hearing itself - it is impossible to speculate when this could come to an end.
Until now, the case has been watertight, with no media leaks from any of the parties involved.
This is just the latest chapter.
However, while the commission's judgement can be directly appealed against, it is not possible for City to take it to Cas.
What titles did City win and who was affected?
City won the Premier League three times during the period in question.
That includes their first in the Premier League era in 2011-12, plus 2013-14 and 2017-18.
They won the FA Cup in 2011, and the EFL Cup three times - 2013-14, 2015-16 and 2017-18.
Since their 2008 takeover by ADUG, City have won eight league titles, and multiple cups including the Champions League as part of a Treble in 2023.
If the commission choses to hand City's titles to other clubs, this is who could benefit:
Premier League
2011-12: Manchester United
2013-14: Liverpool
2017-18: Manchester United
FA Cup
2010-11: Stoke City
EFL Cup
2013-14: Sunderland
2015-16: Liverpool
2017-18: Arsenal
Could affected clubs claim compensation from City?
Earlier this year, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m over the impact of a breach of the Premier League's financial rules.
The case - heard by a Premier League commission - relates to the 2021-22 season, when Everton were found to have broken PSR regulations over a three-year period.
Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
The Clarets were awarded £26m in damages and a further £9m in interest.
Clubs who had their league positions impacted by City's offences could potentially claim a loss of chance to win potential honours.
These would need to be individually heard by an independent commission.
How much has the case cost?
This specific case was six years in the making, so legal fees on both sides were estimated at tens of millions of pounds before the hearing even started.
Whichever side 'wins' can be expected to make a claim for costs.
For context, the Premier League wanted Everton to pay the full £4.9m legal costs of their first PSR six-point deduction case.
However, an appeal board ruled Everton should pay £1.7m and the Premier League cover the remaining £3.2m legal fees.
Any costs being paid by the Premier League at the end of the City case would have to be spread across the 20 clubs which make up the league.
Have there been other cases involving Premier League teams?
Comparisons have been drawn to the cases brought by the Premier League against Nottingham Forest and Everton respectively over breaches of PSR.
During the 2023-24 season, both clubs were docked points for making more losses than they were permitted to for the three-year period from the 2020-21 to 2022-23 seasons.
Those cases were of a single charge, were easier to decipher and involved significantly less evidence.
Everton were twice deducted points. For the first charge, they were docked six points - reduced from 10 points on appeal. The second offence led to them being handed a two-point penalty.
Forest, meanwhile, lost four points.
However, these relate purely to PSR.
Why are the Man City and Chelsea cases different?
Chelsea have faced 74 charges of rule breaches, but these were quite different and primarily focused on transfers that happened between the 2010-11 and 2015-16 seasons, including deals for Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o and Willian.
The Premier League fined Chelsea £10m and handed out a suspended transfer ban after admitting making £47m in secret payments.
Importantly, Chelsea reached a settlement with the Premier League in relation to historical regulatory matters that were self-reported.
This has not been the case with City, who have always denied wrongdoing.
The Blues were also fined by Uefa and the Football Association.

‘I love women,’ Trump said. ‘I think they're great. But what a ridiculous statement that is’

President Donald Trump told a female reporter to be “quiet” in his latest tense exchange with the press, then separately dismissed the idea that women govern better than men as “ridiculous.”
The 80-year-old president made the remarks Saturday while speaking with reporters outside the White House before departing for a college football game in Tennessee.
A female journalist asked Trump whether he wanted only outlets that “support” him included in the White House press pool after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House last week. A federal judge blocked that decision Thursday but Trump barred CNN from Air Force One Saturday and replaced the outlet with LindellTV.
“No, no,” Trump responded. “I want real news, not fake news like you. Listen, I want real news. I love an open free press. What I don’t like is the fake press.”
Trump went on to claim that CNN and MS NOW had low ratings. When the same reporter, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner, followed up by asking: “Do you not want tough questions?” Trump cut her off.
“Wait wait, quiet,” Trump said, raising his index finger. “What I don't like is fake news. And they’re fake news.”
Trump has long had a combative relationship with the press, accusing reporters of biased and unfair coverage. He has also directed personal insults at journalists and suggesting that some should face punishment.
His attacks have often been aimed at female reporters. In June, he lashed out at CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins, saying she had “hatred in her eyes” and that “I never see a smile.” He had earlier called Collins “stupid and nasty” after she questioned him about the White House ballroom.
Last November, Trump told a female Bloomberg journalist, “Quiet, piggy,” when she tried to ask about Jeffrey Epstein. The White House responded to that remark by saying Trump is “very frank and honest with everyone.”
Trump was also asked Saturday morning about comments former President Barack Obama made this week about women in government.
“If you put women in charge of every government for like two years and then just kind of saw alright how are things going, I have a strong belief that things would — they wouldn’t be perfect — but they’d be better,” Obama had said Monday.
“It's ridiculous,” Trump opined. “I love women. I think they're great. But what a ridiculous statement that is.”
Trump also addressed a number of other issues. He said the United States would not put “brakes” on artificial intelligence development, which he again described as “super intelligence.”
He separately urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to “make a deal” to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and claimed that the U.S. has “total control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
- Published
Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.
The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.
Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".
It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.
In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.
Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.
In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.
In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.
"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."
Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".
Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".
Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".
The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.
A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.
Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.
Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.
Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.
Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.
The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".
The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

Sweden and Finland have scrambled fighter jets to intercept Russian military aircraft over the Gulf of Finland, in their first such joint operation.
The Russian aircraft was flying in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, an area on high alert as Russia’s war with Ukraine spills into Europe in the form of gas pipeline outages, drone sightings and airspace violations.
Ulf Kristersson, Sweden’s prime minister, said the Thursday operation showed how the so-called Quick Reaction Alert cooperation could defend the nordic countries’ airspace.
"It is a concrete expression of the readiness and trust we have built together – and an expression of the strength in the Nordic, Nordic-Baltic, and broader NATO cooperation in our part of the world," Kristersson he wrote on X.
It comes as Denmark’s intelligence has warned that there is “a low but growing risk” that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several Nato countries that border it.
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
Recap: Ukraine WILL receive Patriot licences, says Zelensky
Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that Donald Trump had at last agreed to issue Ukraine with the licences to produce vital Patriot interceptor missiles in house, reducing reliance on foreign imports and allowing the country to defend against Russian aerial attacks.
“There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses,” the Ukrainian president said.
“At our meeting, President Trump stressed that he had made his final decision: Ukraine will receive licenses to produce Patriot missiles.”
100,000 homes without internet following Russian strikes on data centres, says Ukraine
Ukraine has accused Russia of ramping up strikes on its data centres and telecommunications facilities, causing massive disruption to internet access across the capital.
Some 100,000 homes in Kyiv and the surrounding areas were hit by temporary internet outages following strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry said.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Wednesday the attacks on the data centres endangered people's lives.
"Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives," he wrote on X.
Russia's Defence Ministry, in a post on Telegram, said its forces had launched strikes on a number of data centres and logistics and warehouse sites it said were being used for the benefit of the Ukrainian military.
Finland asks Musk to expand Starlink coverage for Ukraine
Finnish president Alexander Stubb said he has asked Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage into Russian territory, arguing that it could help Ukraine locate Russian ballistic missile launchers.
Starlink has been a key part of Ukraine’s battlefield communications since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 and is also used to support drone operations, but its coverage does not extend over Russia.
Ukraine faces a shortage of air defences against ballistic missiles and believes access to Starlink over Russian territory could improve its ability to identify launch sites.
Nato says it is prepared for sabotage and drone incidents
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has reassured member states that the alliance has plans to respond to drone and sabotage incidents, following a Danish warning that Russia could intensify hybrid operations across Europe.
The concerns were heightened by a fire at a Starlink facility in Poland, which Polish officials said was deliberate, although they have not identified those responsible.
Rutte said Nato was prepared for such threats, as European governments increasingly focus on protecting critical infrastructure from cyberattacks, sabotage and other forms of disruption.
Moscow has denied involvement in sabotage incidents attributed to Russia.
Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept Russian military aircraft
Swedish and Finnish fighter jets were scrambled on Thursday to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft flying in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, the Finnish Air Force said on Friday.
The operation was carried out as part of a joint Swedish-Finnish framework for monitoring and protecting the two countries’ airspace, the Finnish Air Force said in a statement.
The fighter jets tracked and identified a group of Russian aircraft, including a transport plane and several fighter jets, it added.
Zelensky broke confidentiality with North Korea POWs disclosure, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung says
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung accused Ukraine of breaking a confidentiality agreement by publicly revealing that two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia had been sent to South Korea.
Zelensky announced the transfer during his UN speech, saying Ukraine had handed over the two POWs to South Korea after consultations.
Lee wrote on X: “I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing.
“The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula,” he said.
His comments came as opposition parties in South Korea questioned Lee for hiding arrival of North Korean troops in South Korea after it was first revealed by Zelensky.
Lee said those who “harm someone's life, national interest, or security for their own petty gain are called murderers or traitors”.
“Criticising valid and justified confidentiality measures is wrong,” he said.
Russian strikes kill eight across Ukraine
Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed eight people on Thursday, including six people at a vegetable storage facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region, according to Ukrainian officials.
Two people were killed in Kyiv, where strikes damaged residential buildings, a maternity hospital, a post office, warehouses and dozens of cars.
Ukraine’s air force said the overnight barrage involved 282 drones as well as an unspecified number of hypersonic and ballistic missiles, authorities said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine needed more ballistic interceptors to protect civilians, while claiming Kyiv had reached an agreement for a new package of missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
Europe's crackdown sharply reduces number of shadow fleet ships, report says
Western efforts to crack down on Russia’s shadow fleet have sharply reduced the number of vessels sailing under false flags, according to a 25 September report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
The number of such vessels fell from a peak of 101 in October 2025 to 45 by the end of June 2026, as European countries stepped up enforcement and traditional open ship registries tightened oversight, The Kyiv Independent reported.
The crackdown has pushed many vessels towards Russia’s own registry: the number of ships registered under the Russian flag rose 36 per cent to 382 between January 2025 and June 2026, with 87 per cent of the newly registered vessels already under sanctions, CREA said.

In the latest battle over access to medicines, an Indonesian court recently struck down a provision in a law that allowed so-called patent evergreening, a tactic used by drugmakers to file additional patents containing minor tweaks to existing medicines and, ultimately, forestall competition.
The decision, patient advocates say, sends an important message to other countries to challenge the industry practice.
The Constitutional Court ruled that a two-year-old amendment to a law, which had removed a prohibition on evergreening, was unconstitutional after deciding the original restriction is needed to balance the rights of patent holders with the broader public interest, particularly public health. The case had been brought by several patients and advocacy groups.

The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe said on Sunday, September 27, 2026, days after the revelation that a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked the country's health-system database.
The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the U.S.
OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have been sent written requests to appear at the inquiry, which is to hold public hearings in the capital Canberra on Thursday, said a spokesperson for Senator Sarah Hanson-Young of the Australian Greens party, who chairs the probe.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside business hours.
The OpenAI agent's incursion on one of the country's most used government agencies may prompt Albanese's Labor government to toughen AI-specific laws it is readying for next year, adding pressure to Australia-US relations already tested by Canberra's ban on social media for teens, tech policy experts say.
The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on Australian communities, industries, water and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.
"There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites," Hanson-Young said in a statement. Altman and Amodei "must front up, face the Senate's questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like", she said.
Albanese, who revealed the June breach of Medicare on Thursday, called it "unacceptable", saying he had voiced "extreme concern" to Altman.
OpenAI says it only learned of the breach — one of at least four of Australian government websites — in August. It says the incident was not intentional and did not compromise any private information.

A Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly directed to stop wearing a keffiyeh at a Sydney government school because it was a symbol that “may cause discord” has lodged a racial discrimination case in the federal court against the state of New South Wales.
Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School – an inner-city selective government school – alleges the then acting principal told him in 2024 that the keffiyeh was seen as a symbol of conflict. He alleges the state’s conduct is unlawful for breaching the Racial Discrimination Act.
El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh – a traditional scarf linked to the struggle for a Palestinian state for decades – at school in January 2024, three months after Hamas’ 7 October attacks and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza.
His statement of claim, filed in the federal court last month, alleges Geoffrey Denyer, the then acting school principal, met with him on 15 May 2024 and said words to the effect of “I have been directed to direct you to remove this item of clothing”, indicating to El-Haj’s keiffeyh.
Denyer also said words to the effect of the direction had come “from above, possibly from the minister” and that action would be taken if El-Haj did not comply, the statement of claim alleges.
In an email sent the same day, after El-Haj requested the issue be laid out in writing, Denyer outlined the terms of the direction he had received.
“Consistent with the Department’s Controversial Issues and Code of Conduct policies, the staff member in question should be given clear advice, from you, that this item of clothing should not be worn at school, nor in the performance of any duties in connection with his employment. That advice should be complied with immediately,” the email said.
“It is understandable that, in such times as these, feelings and emotions are strong. However, our schools need to remain free of symbols which stir these emotions, and which may cause discord.”
El-Haj alleges that in a further conversation with Denyer he said words to the effect of “any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict”.
In August 2024, El-Haj met with Maria Serafim, a NSW Department of Education official, who detailed six anonymous concerns, including that he had worn a symbol of “partisan conflict” by wearing the keffiyeh, the statement of claim alleges.
An internal complaint El-Haj made about the direction did not lead to its withdrawal. The careers advisor appealed the decision about the complaint to the secretary of the NSW Department of Education, Murat Dizdar.
Responding to this, Dizdar upheld the school’s decision. In a letter to El-Haj in February 2025, he recognised the keffiyeh “is a garment of cultural significance for the Palestinian community” but said the department did not want to compromise the “safety, wellbeing and security in all our school communities”.
“Unfortunately, our schools are not immune to external events, such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the tragic loss of innocent lives,” he said.
“Regrettably, within our school communities, some individuals and groups may seek to politicise global conflicts or others may form that perception, and as such we always remain politically neutral in public schools when such events can impact on operations.
“It is with this context that the senior officers and the school advised you to not wear the keffiyeh to school.”
El-Haj took leave from his employment from May 2024 until the end of the year and resigned from Sydney Girls High School in March 2025.
El-Haj alleges the state of NSW has engaged in unlawful conduct under section 9(1) of the Racial Discrimination Act.
The state of NSW is yet to file its defence in the federal court.
The matter is due to be next heard for a case management hearing on 3 November, federal court records show.
A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education said it was “committed to maintaining neutral and apolitical school environments, in line with its policies.”
Guardian Australia understands the department is not able to make further comments while the matter is before court.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday lauded the rhino conservation efforts in the country and said the Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, and understanding population dynamics of the endangered species.
On the occasion of World Rhino Day, Modi said the country celebrates the magnificent greater one-horned rhinoceros and lauds all those at the forefront of its protection.
