అమెరికాలో ఒక మహిళ నాలుగు కుక్కపిల్లలకు జన్మనిచ్చిందంటూ ప్రముఖ హిందీ వార్తాపత్రిక దైనిక్ జాగరణ్ పేరుతో ఉన్న ఒక న్యూస్ పేపర్ క్లిప్పింగ్ (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అమెరికాలో ఒక మహిళ నాలుగు కుక్కపిల్లలకు జన్మనిచ్చిందంటూ దైనిక్ జాగరణ్ పేరుతో ఉన్న వార్తా కథనం.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది AIతో సృష్టించిన ఒక నకిలీ కథనం. దైనిక్ జాగరణ్ కానీ, మరే ఇతర విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా సంస్థలు కానీ ఇటువంటి వార్తను ఎక్కడా ప్రచురించలేదు. జీవశాస్త్రపరంగా, ఒక మహిళ కుక్కలకు జన్మనివ్వడం అసాధ్యం. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా ఈ విషయాన్ని నిర్ధారించడానికి దైనిక్ జాగరణ్ ఈ-పేపర్, వెబ్సైట్లను పరిశీలించగా, వారు ఈ వార్తను ప్రచురించినట్లు ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు లభించలేదు. అంతేకాకుండా, ఇటువంటి ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఎక్కడా ఇతర విశ్వసనీయ కథనాలు కూడా లభించలేదు.
ఇక, ఈ వైరల్ క్లిప్పింగ్ OpenAIకి చెందిన AI (కృత్రిమ మేధ) సాధనాలను ఉపయోగించి రూపొందించిన AI ఫోటో అని, ఆ సంస్థకు చెందిన AI కంటెంట్ డిటెక్షన్ టూల్ నిర్ధారించింది.
జీవశాస్త్రపరంగా మనుషులు, కుక్కలు రెండూ పూర్తిగా వేర్వేరు జాతులకు చెందినవి కావడం వలన, ఒక మహిళ కుక్కలకు జన్మనివ్వడం అసాధ్యం. గతంలో కూడా కొందరు మహిళలు కుక్కపిల్లలకు జన్మనిచ్చారంటూ సోషల్ మీడియాలో కథనాలు రాగా, అవన్నీ పూర్తిగా కల్పితమైన బూటకపు ప్రచారాలని పలు అంతర్జాతీయ మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) నిర్ధారించాయి.
చివరిగా, అమెరికాలో ఒక మహిళ నాలుగు కుక్కపిల్లలకి జన్మనిచ్చిందంటూ జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారం పూర్తిగా అవాస్తవం.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s food regulator, on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) conveyed to the Supreme Court its proposal to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPL) on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.
The regulator sought a four-month period for issuing and finalising the draft regulations under the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSS Act), 2006.
Also Read | Supreme Court questions FSSAI on thresholds for ‘high’ sugar, salt, fat warnings
“In this time period, FSSAI will notify the draft amendment regulations which is mandatorily required to be published for a period of 60 days for inviting comments from stakeholders through domestic consultation and the WTO platform. Comments received will be examined, and, subsequently with the approval of Food Authority, the final notification will be forwarded to the Ministry for publication in the official gazette,” the FSSAI affidavit said.
The affidavit was based on a petition filed by a Kerala-based NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi, seeking directions to the Centre to introduce front-of-pack warning labels.
Also Read | SC seeks clear timeline for FSSAI’s food warning label rollout, calls for nutritional literacy in schools
The affidavit said that there would be a voluntary implementation period of 365 days by food business operators (FBOs). “This time period has been provided in order to avoid any commercial hardships to the food business operators as they have pre-packaged material already printed in bulk,” it explained.
The FSSAI said it was proposing a red hexagon with a white square-shaped background FoPL format, drawing similarity, more or less, with the FoPL format adopted by Canada.
Furthermore, where only one nutrient of concern was present, the corresponding nutrient would be indicated in the hexagon. Where two or three nutrients of concern were present, the applicable two or three nutrients would also be indicated within a single hexagon. The arrangement, it said, would provide clear and specific information to consumers.
Editorial | Front and centre: On the front-of-package labelling issue
It said that any food product, including beverages, containing non-caloric sweeteners would sport a warning statement, ‘CONTAINS NON CALORIC SWEETENER’ on the front of the pack.
The court had pulled up the FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.

SC dismisses BJP MLAs’ plea against KJ George in Karnataka smart meter tender case
The Supreme Court upheld the Karnataka high court’s decision to quash the case against KJ George over alleged irregularities in a ₹4,985-crore smart meter tender.
The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed a plea by three Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) legislators seeking prosecution of Karnataka Energy minister KJ George over alleged irregularities in the allocation of a ₹4,985-crore smart electricity meter tender, upholding a Karnataka high court order that had quashed the case.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran refused to entertain the appeal filed by three BJP legislators — CN Ashwathnarayan, SR Vishwanath and Dheeraj Muniraj — to revive their complaint before a Bengaluru court after the Karnataka high court quashed the case, finding no merit in the allegations in December 2025.
“Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners and having gone through the materials on record, we find no good ground to interfere with the impugned order passed by the high court. The Special Leave Petitions are accordingly dismissed,” the order, passed on Friday and uploaded on Saturday, said.
George was represented in the top court by senior advocate Kapil Sibal along with advocate Vivek Jain, who were not called upon to respond as the bench came to the conclusion after hearing senior advocate Lakshmy Iyenger for the petitioners and going through the case records.
The allegations pertained to 2024, when the petitioners, who are members of the Karnataka legislative assembly, alleged that the energy minister, who is also the chairman of Bangalore Electricity Supply Company Limited (BESCOM), acted in collusion with BESCOM officials to manipulate financial thresholds and circumvent statutory safeguards to award a tender for smart electricity meters to M/s Rajashree Electricals Pvt Ltd.
It was claimed that the tender, having a total project value of about ₹4,985 crore, was artificially projected on an “annual value” to reduce statutory requirements such as earnest money deposit and performance bank guarantee, which resulted in pecuniary advantage to the company that bagged the tender.
The petitioners initially approached the Lokayukta, which refused to direct an investigation, before filing a case before the trial court. In July 2025, the trial judge sought a report from the Lokayukta. Against this order, George and other accused approached the high court seeking quashing of the case.
The high court order of December 2, 2025, said that the allegations did not disclose any criminality and at best gave rise to a civil dispute. The high court further held the entire tender process to be transparent, with participation from multiple bidders and, more significantly, no allegation of any bribe being paid as quid pro quo.
The appeal filed by the three BJP MLAs in the top court said that the complaint pertained to large-scale irregularities, illegality and criminal misconduct in the formulation and execution of a smart meter tender, which could not be dismissed at the threshold without ordering an investigation.
By quashing the complaint at such a nascent stage, the high court foreclosed the possibility of any investigation into serious allegations involving public officials and a high-value public contract, causing grave miscarriage of justice, they added.

While much of society is preoccupied with animal rights, there is a population facing a significant risk of burnout yet which often goes unacknowledged: veterinarians.
Often underestimated as a profession and underfunded as a field, veterinary medicine carries expectations that far exceed what can reasonably be asked of any one individual. Veterinarians are expected to deliver unwavering care, often at the cost of their own.
Like all healthcare professionals, they navigate long hours, emergencies, and loss. But they also have distinct challenges. Their patients cannot speak, forcing vets to rely on instinct as much as expertise. They must master multiple anatomies across species. They absorb not only the suffering of animals, but also the emotional intensity of anxious, grieving pet owners. And uniquely, they carry the burden of deciding when a life should end, often without adequate emotional support for the weight of the decisions made and the grief that comes with executing it.
What they experience is not simply burnout, a condition caused by prolonged stress, but also compassion fatigue (from caring unconditionally) and moral injury (having to make decisions that go against their core moral beliefs)
Over time, all of this takes a toll.
Unlike human medicine, where every organ has its own specialist, veterinary medicine asks one person to be all of them at once. Across a single day, they shift roles constantly: diagnosing, fixing, reassuring, improvising. It’s not just about treating animals, it’s about carrying an entire system of care in one body, adapting to whatever walks (or is carried) through the door.
Alongside their patients, vets take on the emotional aftermath, anger, disappointment, and grief of pet owners. They linger long after the consultation ends.
A euthanasia need not end the day. It is often followed by the next appointment with no space or time in between to process the loss or the weight of the decision.
The rise of alternative medicine which is often cheaper brings another consequence; time lost. If the alternate treatment has not worked, there is delay in diagnosis, treatment and loss of life which falls at the hands of the vet.
Burnout, compassion fatigue, and moral injury show up in both mind and body as insomnia, brain fog, exhaustion, memory lapses and sometimes other physical illnesses.
Their work is not the problem. Most vets still care deeply about healing. It is a system defined by overwork, emotional labour, a variety of pressures, tough decisions, and financial limitations: it is meant to support them but often does the opposite.
Vasini Varadan is a cartoonist and illustrator.

When you think of SeaWorld, you most likely think of orcas, school trips to the aquarium, or eating chicken fingers while contemplating the ethics of marine mammal captivity. But this Halloween, the theme park franchise wants to make SeaWorld synonymous with something else entirely: BookTok smut.
On September 11, SeaWorld Orlando officially opened its annual Howl-O-Scream event, an after-hours Halloween-themed immersive experience featuring various “scare zones” in the park. Scattered between the more expected spooky fare, such as a haunted “Woodrot Hollow” forest and an I Know What You Did Last Summer–themed haunted house is Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-inspired zone featuring the hunky tortured bad boys of romantasy lore.
In videos posted by Orlando-based influencers who got an early look at the park, young men with masks, floppy hair, and painted-on abs gallivant around wearing black denim, loitering next to brick walls, beckoning to park attendees, and gifting them with roses. And on Instagram, influencers posed around a central set piece, an oversized book open to a chapter called “The Cathedral,” emblazoned with the slogan “Good Girls Go for the Bad Boys.”
Some of the TikToks from the scare zone went viral, garnering mixed reactions. “Booktok dark 'romantasy' cancer is RUINING heterosexuality,” wrote one X user, “every little tasteful drop of eros has to be squeezed out of everything so it can be refined into pure concentrated fucking CRINGE.” The fact that the event took place at SeaWorld, an amusement park franchise that is perhaps most closely associated with a harrowing documentary about an orca, also lent to the absurdity.
But I did speak to one content creator present at the scare zone who had an entirely different reaction. “I wouldn’t say it was scary,” said the creator, who declined to provide their name because they did not want to “jeopardize their relationship with SeaWorld.” “But it did leave me with a good feeling—I guess you could say a sexy feeling, in a way.”
According to Jessie Kinsey, the art director at SeaWorld Orlando, that was precisely the point. She came up with the idea for the event last year, after seeing romantasy bestsellers like Lights Out and Haunting Adeline go viral on TikTok. She knew that a dark romance-themed scare zone was not necessarily “something that you would expect from a traditional horror event,” but she had a feeling it would resonate with the BookTok girlies. “I remember texting my production manager, saying, ‘Don't judge me, but I have an idea,’” she tells WIRED.
A fiction writer in her spare time (she actually wrote the text for the oversized book set piece at SeaWorld), Kinsey came up with the narrative for the zone: It would be set in a crumbling Gothic cathedral, built in a town run by a wealthy family called the Blackthorns. “These roses grew up around it, and created this beauty out of destruction,” Kinsey puts it. “Which I thought was kind of fitting for the themes of these books.”
Romantasy, or romance and fantasy, fuses mythology and supernatural figures such as faeries or demons with explicit sex scenes, exemplified by books like Rebecca Yarros’ Onyx Storm and Sarah J. Maas’ A Court of Thorns and Roses series. The genre has exploded in popularity thanks to BookTok, with Bloomberg reporting that romantasy pulled in an estimated $610 million in 2024 alone. The male antiheroes of the genre, such as the “shadow-daddy” Rhysand in Maas’ A Court of Mist and Fury and dragon rider Xaden Riorson from Yarros’ Fourth Wing, are tortured, dangerous, (at best) morally complex, and egregiously hot.
The MMC—“male main character,” in fandom terms—is an amalgam of different romantasy tropes, a mysterious, vaguely threatening masked man represented by the eight scare actors employed in the zone. (In one video, one of them inexplicably wears KneeBlades and skids toward a prostrate guest and jumps over them.) For both narrative and legal reasons, they’re not based on any one specific character.
The infusion of the romance genre with themes of psychological manipulation, violence, or nonconsensual sex has led to criticism of the dark romantasy genre in general, and of the Just One More Chapter scare zone. But “the threatening nature” of the romantasy bad boys is why it works in a horror context, says Kinsey: “It’s a love story, but it's not all sunshine. This is someone who is morally gray, who is potentially violent, who is obsessive, and that part of it is threatening. But that also plays into the appeal of it.”
On social media, some pointed out the potential for fans sexually harassing scare actors, a not-uncommon issue at Halloween theme park events. “Being a scare actor, it does come with risks regardless of what area of the park you're working in, because not everyone reacts the same way to being startled or surprised when alcohol is involved,” Kinsey says. “But our actors’ safety is first and foremost.” She says the actors receive extensive training for how to deal with harassment, and that security and stage managers are always present to intervene if necessary.
So far, however, SeaWorld Orlando says that horny millennial ACOTAR fans haven’t posed too much of a problem—in fact, quite the opposite. Kinsey says the viral attention has translated into an explosion in ticket sales, with Howl-O-Scream enjoying its biggest month in the history of its six-year run. “I knew that it was going to get people talking, and I know that the genre isn't for everyone, so it was going to be a bit controversial,” says Kinsey. “I did not expect the size of the reaction, but it's kind of fun.” It is, dare we call it, a Howl-O-Scream.

- Minecraft Ice Caves introduce a new frozen underground biome with ice crystals and icicles.
- Frozen Zombies can freeze, slow, and attack players with Ice Balls.
- Ice Balls can be used to create Freezing potions in Minecraft.
The Minecraft Live on September 26, 2026, revealed Ice Caves, a brand-new underground biome designed to bring the dangers of Minecraft’s frozen regions beneath the surface. This Minecraft biome is packed with ice crystals, icicles, new threats, and mechanics that can turn even a routine cave expedition into a slippery test of survival.
The Ice Caves in Minecraft are expected to enter testing soon, thereby giving players their first chance to glide into the region with their handy boat.
While it can be pitch dark inside the Ice Caves, the ice crystals and towering formations add a glowing effect to the surroundings. The ice crystals naturally generate across the cave floor, acting as a dim light source block in Minecraft, whereas the icicles hang from the ceilings, adding another layer of visual depth.
Players are warned not to wander around placing Minecraft torches all over the Ice Caves since excessive light can cause the icicles to fall and harm you along the way. The caves also contain patches of stone and deepslate, making it a decent place to mine ores as well.
Minecraft Winter Drop Features Frozen Zombie and Ice Balls for Ice Caves
Well, the Minecraft Ice Caves are not particularly peaceful because of the usual hostile mobs in Minecraft, such as zombies, skeletons, spiders, creepers, and strays lurking in the dark.
And then, there is another new zombie variant exclusive to the Ice Caves: the Frozen Zombie. It can charge at players and inflict a freezing effect that slows movement while dealing additional damage.
Adding to the dangers, some of these mobs can also perform a ranged attack using Ice Balls. Do remember that being close can get quite hurtful at times because the Ice Balls have a distance-based damage-dealing mechanic. But one essential use of the Ice Balls is that they can be used to craft Freezing potions in Minecraft. You can later use them to slow enemies and also deal some damage along the way.
While all of these new features are yet to go live in the upcoming Minecraft snapshots and previews, the specific generation rules have not been revealed yet. Once the testing phase is live, you can grab your pickaxe and torch to explore the new caves. Just don’t forget to pick up your extra torches.

In 1998, the newly incorporated Pine Labs was helping petrol pumps accept payments and manage loyalty programmes. Nearly three decades later, Pine Labs is a listed company that has expanded well beyond payments into online checkout, consumer financing, gift cards, card issuing and banking infrastructure By Q1 FY27, the fintech was serving 11.5 Lakh+ merchants, alongside brands and financial institutions, across India, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. A string of acquisitions helped Pine Labs build out this expanding fintech stack. While Qwikcilver added gift cards, Fave brought consumer rewards, Mosambee strengthened merchant acceptance, and Qfix and Shopflo expanded online payments and checkout. Similarly, Setu added fintech infrastructure, while Credit+ and Saluto brought issuing and enterprise rewards capabilities. However, the breadth came at a cost. Despite raising nearly $1.6 Bn before making its public markets debut, Pine Labs struggled for years to turn expansion into consolidated profits. Payment hardware, employees, processing, cloud infrastructure and overseas operations all needed funding. The next logical step was to get listed. But Pine Labs’ path to the public markets was anything but straightforward. It first deferred a planned US IPO, reportedly targeting $500 Mn in 2022, amid a weak market. It eventually opted for an Indian listing, merging its Singapore holding company with its Indian entity in June 2025. The payoff came in FY26, when Pine Labs reported its first full-year consolidated profit of ₹112.5 Cr, compared with a loss of ₹145.5 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue grew 19% to ₹2,710.6 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA jumped 57% to ₹559 Cr. In its FY26 results, Pine Labs said indirect expenses, excluding ESOP costs, grew just 8% against 19% revenue growth. This operating leverage helped lift its adjusted EBITDA margin from around 16% to 21%, even as its contribution margin dipped from 76% to 75%. Lower depreciation and amortisation, higher other income and a smaller exceptional charge also supported its bottom line. The reconciliation shows other income, excluding provision write-backs, rising from ₹44 Cr to ₹84 Cr, while exceptional charges fell from ₹37 Cr to ₹8 Cr. Therefore, the profit improvement combined operating gains with benefits below the operating line. Profitable segments like the Qwikcilver gift card and prepaid platform also contributed substantially to high-margin income. But Q1 FY27 results show why Pine Labs’ turnaround story still warrants close scrutiny. Revenue rose 20% year on year (YoY) to ₹736.9 Cr and net profit more than quadrupled to ₹19.6 Cr, but adjusted EBITDA margin narrowed to 17.1% from 19.6%. The company attributed the pressure to business mix and additional investment. Decoding Pine Labs’ Revenue Engines Pine Labs still gets most of its revenue from its Digital Infrastructure and Transaction Platform (DITP), which comprises checkout infrastructure, affordability and value-added services, transaction processing and fintech infrastructure. DITP generated ₹1,837 Cr in FY26, up 15% YoY, accounting for about 68% of operating revenue. Meanwhile, Pine Labs is trying to increase revenue from its existing merchant network by selling more services — affordability/EMI, online payments, value-added services, etc. — rather than relying only on payment terminals. Mentioned in RHP as Issuing and Acquiring Platform, it contributed the remaining 32%, or ₹874 Cr in FY26. But the competitive landscape is already crowded. PhonePe has expanded beyond QR codes into soundboxes, card terminals and online payments. Paytm combines payment devices and processing with EMI and merchant lending, and ended FY26 with 1.5 Cr subscription merchants. In September 2026, PhonePe announced plans to deploy more than 50 Lakh additional payment devices and hire over 20,000 frontline sales staff over the following year, with a substantial rural focus. Online-first rivals are converging on the same opportunity. Razorpay commands payment acceptance, disbursals, lending and business banking, with an AI payments push extending its reach. Cashfree is building SME and cross-border offerings beyond its gateway. Pine Labs’ competitive proposition is the combination: merchants can connect multiple acquiring banks, billing software and affordability offers through one platform. That integration gives them a reason to use more of its services, although its RHP cautioned that switching costs may not prevent them from moving transactions to rivals. Earning More Beyond The Payment Device As an offline merchant, Pine Labs’ business revolves around the digital checkout point (DCP), which connects cards, UPI, wallets and loyalty points with banks, payment networks and billing software, while handling acceptance and reconciliation. Its RHP listed DCP subscriptions, hardware sales, installation and removal, automation services and maintenance as sources of in-store revenue. Average monthly revenue per DCP was ₹380.08 in FY25. The network reached 20.3 Lakh DCPs in FY26 and 21.7 Lakh in Q1 FY27. Subscription income, however, does not rise simply because a checkout gets busier. Pine Labs needs either more paying deployments or higher revenue per deployment. Transaction-linked affordability, value-added services and processing fees let it earn more from activity at those counters. Alongside this, Pine Labs is shifting more of the upfront device cost to merchants. Rau explained that getting merchants to buy terminals reduced its depreciation burden, although the device sales themselves earned lower margins. Across the business, company-wide contribution grew 11% to INR 533 Cr in Q1 FY27, slower than revenue’s 20% growth. The shift in business mix and higher connectivity, distribution and operational costs weighed on margins. Online payments take the model a step further. Payment gateways, links and recurring collections generate transaction-value-linked fees without another device at the counter. The Plural launch in 2021 and Qfix acquisition in 2022 helped build this business. Online payment revenue grew 56% in FY26, outpacing the group’s 19%, however its scale remains harder to judge, as the results did not disclose a separate revenue figure. Selling More Through The Same Checkout Beyond accepting payments, Pine Labs helps its customers sell. As Rau put it on the July 2026 call, “we help brands, banks, financial institutions, acquire new customers, convert those customers, engage with those customers.” EMI is a key part of this proposition. For financed purchases, Pine Labs earns technology fees from merchants, brands and financial institutions, largely linked to transaction value. The lender provides the credit and takes on the repayment risk. Affordability revenue grew close to 20% YoY in Q1 FY27, Rau said, despite electronics and mobile-phone price increases and supply disruptions. The share of DCPs generating Flow and affordability volumes reached 30%, up from 24% a year earlier, showing greater use of services across the existing network. Demand shifts with the incentives banks and brands fund. On the Q4 FY26 earnings call, Rau described a large bank reducing offers on a leading smartphone brand as customers became willing to buy with fewer incentives. Banks were also backing newer categories, including electric vehicles. “Our job is to come up with newer sectors, come up with newer touch points,” Rau said. Non-electronics affordability volumes grew over 60% in FY26. Sustaining that expansion means finding purchases customers want to finance and banks and brands will support. Moving Deeper Into Banking Infrastructure Pine Labs’ relationship with financial institutions goes beyond merchant payments. Banks and fintechs also need infrastructure within their own applications. Pine Labs supplies APIs for customer verification, financial-data access, digital agreements and collections, allowing institutions to avoid building every connection themselves. Its acquisition of Setu in 2022, reportedly for $70 Mn to $75 Mn, expanded its capabilities across payments, onboarding, digital signatures and financial-data analysis. Pine Labs now wants to move further up the value chain by helping lenders make sense of the financial data flowing through these systems. “The future of payments is not going to be only in terms of money movement, but also in terms of data movement,” Rau said on the July 2026 (Q1 FY27 earnings) call. Six banks and NBFCs signed up for SignalIQ, which analyses financial data to support lending decisions. This creates another potential source of value beyond payments and data collection. Pine Labs has not separately disclosed SignalIQ revenue or FinTech Infrastructure’s FY26 revenue contribution in the cited results. Cards And Rewards Shift The Revenue Mix While banking infrastructure deepens Pine Labs’ relationships with lenders, cards and rewards are changing the company’s revenue mix. The Issuing and Acquiring Platform’s revenue grew 30% YoY, from ₹671 Cr to ₹874 Cr in FY26, compared with 15% growth for DITP. As a result, DITP’s share of group revenue fell from 72.1% in FY24 to 70.5% in FY25 and about 68% in FY26. Issuing and acquiring, meanwhile, increased its share from roughly 28% in FY24 to 32% in FY26. The segment has two key pillars: Pine Labs Prepaid, which handles gift cards and rewards, and Credit+, which provides card-issuing and payment-processing technology to banks and fintechs. For a retailer, Pine Labs Prepaid activates gift cards, maintains balances and processes redemptions. It also distributes cards to consumers and corporate buyers, including through Woohoo, for uses ranging from employee rewards to customer promotions and dealer incentives. Pine Labs earns from both distribution and processing. Credit+ embeds Pine Labs in a different part of the customer’s operations. It supplies systems for banks to manage credit, debit and forex card accounts and process transactions, as well as infrastructure for institutions supporting merchants that accept cards. The Next Test Is Making Expansion Pay Pine Labs has built multiple ways to monetise its merchant and financial-institution relationships. The next challenge is making that larger platform more efficient. AI is central to that effort, although the spending comes before the gains. In FY26, Pine Labs invested around ₹24 Cr in AI-related initiatives: ₹20 Cr in capabilities, infrastructure and customer-facing automation, and ₹4 Cr in enterprise AI technologies and tools. The company says automation cut software testing cycles by more than 95% and improved developer productivity by 25%. It has not quantified the resulting impact on profits. Servicing the existing network offers a more immediate opportunity. “Today, almost 50% of our terminals are self-healing,” CFO Sameer Kamath said on the Q1 FY27 call. Automated diagnostics and recovery could reduce field-service visits and lower the cost of keeping merchants’ payment systems running. Pine Labs is also experimenting with payments initiated by AI assistants. Its Q1 presentation said P3P, its agentic payments system, was live with Vijay Sales and Gullak, allowing payments within user-set rules. The company has not disclosed P3P revenue separately. Competition is already emerging around AI-enabled payments. Razorpay and NPCI unveiled a Claude-based payments pilot in February 2026, while PhonePe launched an AI integration tool in May to help merchants connect to its gateway. These serve different functions, but raise the same commercial question: will the tools win transactions or lower costs? Expansion also needs people. Rau said Pine Labs added about 500 salespeople over six months, with full productivity typically taking 6 to 12 months. Those hires add costs before new merchant relationships deliver their full revenue potential. That spending weighed on Q1 FY27. Data, cloud and technology costs rose 33% to ₹64 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA grew just 5% to ₹126 Cr, against 20% revenue growth. Management reiterated FY27 revenue growth guidance of 21-23.5% and said it expects contribution margins to improve in the second half as processing and transaction-linked services increased. From petrol pumps to banking systems, Pine Labs has built more ways to earn from a payment. Its first profitable year shows that breadth can support earnings. The next test is whether deeper customer relationships and lower servicing costs can sustain them as competition and expansion spending intensify.

The Instagram accounts of three independent journalists — Bindu Gurjar, Lokbhadra Singh, and Monika Singh — were reportedly suspended earlier this month after they reported extensively on the deaths of tribal children in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, and raised questioned about the discrepancies in the government claims surrounding the death.
While Bindu and Monika’s accounts were initially restored after they appealed to Meta, last week, both the accounts were permanently disabled by Instagram. Lokbhadra’s account remained suspended throughout and he was compelled to open a backup account.
Another independent journalist, Saurabh Bhati, who runs a page on Instagram with Monika called The Unsalted, temporarily deactivated that page as well as his personal account as a precautionary measure, after observing the repeated suspensions faced by the other three journalists. The two accounts were later reactivated.
Speaking to Alt News, all three journalists narrated how they were subjected to surveillance, followed by plainclothes personnel, questioned about their movements and pressured through hotel authorities and local intermediaries, creating an intimidating environment that ultimately forced them to leave Balaghat.
Sudden Suspension, Eventual Deletion
Narrating her ordeal, Bindu said that her account was the first to be targeted — on September 5, a copyright strike was issued against her ground report from the Balaghat district hospital, even though it was entirely her original reporting. The following day, on September 6, she received alerts on her phone indicating attempts to log into her account from three different locations. Her account was eventually suspended around 2:30 pm. She initially tried to verify her identity using her Aadhaar card to regain access to her account but was unsuccessful. On September 7, the option to use the PAN card became available, and using this she managed to restore her account around 10:00 am.
However, 11 days after she regained access, Bindu’s account was permanently disabled by Instagram on September 18. She received a notification that she no longer had access to her account, and all her information had been permanently deleted. “You cannot request another review of this decision,” it stated. The account did not follow community standards on account integrity, the notice said. She has now opened a backup account.
A few hours later on September 6, Monika’s account was also suspended twice, but on each occasion, it was restored following an appeal.
However, the account was also permanently disabled with a similar notice on September 20.
Lokbhadra’s account, which had the highest number of followers among the three, was suspended multiple times. Speaking to Alt News, he said the first suspension came at 5:47 pm on September 6. The handle was restored within 30 minutes after an appeal was filed at 10:30 pm. His account was suspended again on September 7 and 8, and for a fourth time around 11 pm on September 9. He said that he did not appeal anymore as cyber experts advised that this could be the work of hackers who might launch another attack immediately upon an appeal. His account remains suspended as of September 23.
The reasons cited by Meta for suspending these journalists’ accounts were identical. It was stated that the account or the activity associated with it did not follow the platform’s “Community Standards on account integrity”. This includes creating an account that impersonates another person, using another person’s photos to deceive others, or generating content that purports to speak on behalf of another individual.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
In a statement released on September 8, the Press Club of India condemned the suspension of these journalists’ accounts, demanding an impartial investigation and describing the move as an attempt to intimidate or silence them.
What Were These Scribes Reporting?
Reports of children dying from fever, rashes, or other symptoms began emerging from the tribal areas of Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district between June and July. Most of the deceased children belonged to the Baiga community, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG). Additionally, some children were from Gond families residing in villages nestled deep within dense forests, located nearly 150 kilometres away from the district headquarters.
The government initially reported an official death toll of only eight children. However, by August, locals, tribal organisations and the opposition began claiming the figure was much higher, ranging from 24 to 30 child deaths. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi raised the issue. Umang Singhar, the Leader of the Opposition in Madhya Pradesh, wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi citing 30 deaths and attributing them to a lack of water, nutrition, and timely medical treatment. The Madhya Pradesh high court sought a response of the state government to a public interest litigation that claimed that over 30 deaths had occurred and that approximately 400 children were admitted to a 50-bed hospital.
Towards the end of August, these four journalists arrived in Balaghat to report on the deaths of tribal children and uncover the reality. Visiting various villages and meeting affected families, they began investigating the death toll. Their reportage revealed discrepancies between the government’s figure and the rising numbers reported from various villages. The real figures, they reported, were much higher than eight.
Further, they highlighted the poor condition of the local hospital, where multiple children were being treated on a single bed. Subsequently, the reporters alleged that they were pressurised to meet officials and forced to leave their hotel — compelling them to leave Balaghat on the night of September 3.
The Ground Reality
Lokbhadra told Alt News that he arrived in Balaghat from Delhi on August 28. He mentioned that he had already learned through local and social media that while official figures cited only eight deaths, reports from the ground indicated 24 deaths. When he visited the district hospital the same day, the hospital staff informed him: “Over the past 12 days, more than 250 children exhibiting symptoms such as malaria or measles have been admitted.”
The next day, he reached the Bondari area of Birsa block, located about 120 kilometres from Balaghat. This was the area where the highest number of children had been affected. He discovered that the death toll, initially reported as 24, had actually risen to 30. There was no official record of these additional deaths at the time. He gathered separate data on these six children and began publishing on-ground video reports by visiting their families. The video embedded below is from Lokbhadra Singh’s backup account.
On September 1, he learned that the district magistrate (DM) was scheduled to visit the district hospital that evening. Consequently, he arrived at the hospital before the visit to observe the conditions there. “When I had reported on the hospital previously, I found four children sharing almost every bed. Some of them were suffering from malaria, while others exhibited symptoms of measles. As soon as news of the DM’s impending visit spread, cleaning operations began, bedsheets were changed, and new beds were set up.”
Upon the DM’s arrival, Lokbhadra asked him about the death toll discrepancy, to which the DM did not provide a clear answer at first. He further questioned the DM on the hospital’s poor condition. Shifting the blame to the child’s background, the DM answered: “Children from tribal backgrounds often have as many as four siblings, and their parents are also present, which makes it appear crowded.”
Journalists countered by asking how children could be kept in the same bed if one was suffering from malaria and the other from measles. The DM failed to provide a satisfactory answer to this as well. However, in the course of the exchange, the DM admitted on camera, for the first time, to the figure of 24 child deaths. “When further questions were asked, the DM became irritated, swatted the camera away with his hand, and walked off,” Lokbhadra said.
Videos of the incident went viral on social media within hours, and reports began circulating that the Balaghat DM appeared to be dodging questions from the media. These videos, posted on Lokbhadra’s account and others’, are now unavailable as his account no longer accessible.
‘Forced To Leave Balaghat’
“Around 2 am that same night, two individuals, one in police uniform and the other in plainclothes, arrived at my hotel room and asked the manager for documents verifying my identity, even though these had already been submitted at the time of check-in… I asked the manager if there was pressure from the police to keep me under surveillance, which the manager denied. However, when I stepped out of the hotel later that day, I spotted a vehicle bearing a police sticker and three or four plainclothes police personnel standing near the shops. As soon as I took out my camera, they were seen hiding behind posters,” Lokbhadra alleged.
“The same night after I questioned the DM, a local influencer visited my hotel, insisting that I meet the SP. I declined a private meeting at night and instead requested a formal press conference… The next day, while we were out reporting, another journalist staying at the same hotel informed us that some individuals had come to the hotel asking for our names and whereabouts,” he added.
A major district-wide shutdown protest was called by tribal organisations in Balaghat on September 3. On that very day, the hotel owner personally arrived and told the journalist that he had a family event, and the entire hotel needed to be evacuated to accommodate guests. No such information had been conveyed previously, Lokbhadra claimed.
After some discussion, it was decided that they would vacate their rooms in the evening after covering the protest. Throughout the demonstration, the same plainclothes individuals kept following them and recording videos, they alleged. He claimed that the journalists encountered the same police personnel all the way from their hotel during check out to the railway station as they were leaving Balaghat.
“Meanwhile, some local influencers from Balaghat started making videos against me, claiming that I lacked knowledge of media ethics and that my way of questioning the DM was inappropriate,” he alleged. He further claimed that he had received information from a local influencer that the SP had stated in a meeting that these four individuals from Delhi would be “taught a lesson”. Due to this “intimidating atmosphere”, they left Balaghat on the night of September 3rd.
‘Malnutrition, Staff Shortage & Lack of Medical Facilities’
Monika and Saurabh arrived in Balaghat on August 31, before which the former had been tracking the story from Delhi. “Initially, information was available only on the pages of local influencers and city journalists, there were no official records. The official death toll stood at eight, but after speaking with protesters and the families involved, it emerged that their children’s names were missing from the lists. On ground, we discovered that the figure had risen from 24 to 30,” Monika told Alt News.
“The children are suffering from malnutrition, even if no one openly admits it, because acknowledging deaths due to starvation would be seen as a major failure on the part of the administration. Children in these hilly tribal areas have weak immunity, and malaria strikes every year but rarely makes headlines, and while symptoms of measles are clearly visible on their bodies, officials avoid explicitly naming measles and speak only of malaria,” Monika said, adding that the district hospital admitted that the children are malnourished and suffering from both measles and malaria.
Monika also visited the primary health centre (PHC) in Songuda village, which she claimed lacked the facilities to treat even a single patient. “Patients were put directly into an ambulance and sent to the district hospital, around 90 kilometres away. In the long journey, many children, who are already in critical condition, would die on the way,” she alleged. “In some cases, families did not even take the children to the hospital because there is a greater reliance on faith healing in that area. Some children died on the way to the hospital, since doctors did not record the cause of death, their names do not appear on any list. Others were referred from the district hospital to a hospital in Gondia, Maharashtra. The change of state meant these children were excluded from the Madhya Pradesh list.”
She echoed Lokbhadra’s observations for the district hospital, where she claimed there was a severe shortage of beds, and three or four children suffering from conditions ranging from measles, malaria, and malnutrition to ordinary fever, would share a single bed. She visited the hospital both at daytime and at night, and highlighted the severe staff shortage. MP police personnel were performing nursing duties, such as administering medication, while actual nurses were few and far between, and doctors were largely absent, often taking considerable time to arrive when summoned for emergencies, she observed. “Children traveling nearly 100 kilometres for treatment often set out in the evening and did not reach the hospital until 2 or 3 am, leaving no one available at that hour to treat them,” she said.
Monika reiterated Lokbhadra’s claim that the district hospital was given a complete makeover before the DM’s visit on September 1. In the same ward where she had previously reported four children sharing a single bed, the DM found only one child per bed, and the entire area had been cleaned up, she said.
Monika also recounted the same situation faced by Lokbhadra — the constant police surveillance and pressure tactics which ultimately forced the independent journalists out of Balaghat. On September 2, she received a message from another journalist stating that some people had come to the hotel asking about her. On her way back on a bike, she noticed people in plainclothes tailing her almost everywhere.
Bindu Gurjar arrived in Balaghat on August 28. A protest was underway on the main road about a kilometer from the district hospital. Speaking to people there, she came to know that the government was acknowledging only eight deaths.
While preparing her report, she learned that the Baiga community was classified as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), and under various government schemes, Baiga mothers received Rs 1,500 monthly to purchase nutritious food for their children. Yet the situation on the ground was dire, Bindu observed while reporting from the Balaghat district hospital.
She learned that separate wards had been designated for patients from tribal communities. Across those wards, there were over 100 patients, and almost every single bed was occupied by over two patients along with their entire families, she said, adding that the hospital lacked basic amenities such as sanitisers and masks.
‘Last Rites Done Before Parents Arrived’
A family at the hospital told Bindu that the parents of a child named Lavkush who had recently died did not live in Balaghat. They had gone to Bengaluru for work.
“By the time they were informed of the child’s illness, they were already on the way back. However, the child passed before they could arrive. In accordance with the traditions of the tribal belt, the last rites involved burying the child. This process was carried out without the parents’ consent. By the time the parents reached, the last rites had already been performed, sparking a dispute,” she told Alt News.
Bindu met Lavkush’s parents at the same hospital where their three other children were admitted and kept on the same bed. They were suffering from fever, symptoms resembling measles, and swollen eyes.
After speaking with the hospital staff, Bindu further learned that just one or two nurses were attending to over a hundred patients, and more than 250 patients had been admitted in the past 15 days. To address this shortage, personnel from the police lines were assisting at the hospital, an observation made by Monika earlier. The police, she said, worked four shifts per day, with ten people per shift helping to move patients around and support the staff.
In the course of her investigation, she also tracked the case of a girl named Kajal, who had died on August 29. Kajal had been referred to Gondia, where she passed away. Bindu’s team visited her village, Kisangarh, and witnessed her burial. Subsequently, Bindu and Lokbhadra launched an independent survey the same day. They recorded details, such as names, fathers’ names, village, the onset and nature of the illness, and prior medical consultations on printed forms.
On August 29, Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav visited Kisangarh village, where, according to Bindu, over eight children had died. He announced compensation of Rs 2 lakh for the families of the deceased children. However, it turned out that none of the eight children from that village, whose deaths had been reported, were on his list. As Yadav left without addressing the issue of accountability, Bindu said that locals there began raising slogans.
Bindu mentioned that she came under state surveillance after posting regular reports on the matter online. She recounted that on September 2, Dr. Nilay Jain, a surgeon at the hospital, had allegedly remarked, “Some people from Jamia Muslim University have arrived. I have spoken to the SP, and we will have to decide whether or not to allow them entry into the hospital.”
Meanwhile, a video had gone viral of Lokbhadra interviewing the sister of a deceased child, Rooplal, where she claimed that CM Yadav had dismissed her when she tried to talk to him about her brother’s death.
View this post on Instagram
“When I went to speak to the CM, he told me stop talking. He said, ‘don’t say anything right now, you talk too much’, so I came back without saying anything. My brother was the first to lose his life…but his name has not appeared on any list, and no compensation has been given to us so far,” she told Lokbhadra.

Slate Auto Fastback SUV
Tisha Johnson is a rarity in the car world: an automotive design leader who is not a man. Women are sometimes put in charge of the interiors or the materials, but few get to shape the whole look of a vehicle. As head of design at the EV-maker Slate, Johnson does. The pickup truck version of its EV starts at just under $25,000, making it the cheapest pickup on sale in the US, electric or not. Trouble is, cheap products are usually a compromise, and compromises rarely inspire affection. Johnson’s Slate, however, has won design awards, not just praise for its price tag.
“We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” Johnson says, “or look like a beast on the road.” That thinking shows in the truck itself—not just in its modular, add-on-friendly design (pictured here in its Fastback guise), but in the fact the EV was designed to be loved. Strong shoulders and approachable round headlamps were favored over macho arrowed surfacing. “The attraction that draws you to Slate is based on something that is lasting from inside out. It’s a deeper connection,” Johnson says. Some 180,000 reservations and counting for the Slate, along with those awards, seem to more than prove her point.
Away The Carry-On: Aluminum Edition
Away was founded in 2015 by entrepreneurs Jen Rubio and Steph Korey, both with backgrounds at the eyewear maker Warby Parker. In its first year, Away generated $12 million in sales and sold more than 100,000 stylish, reasonably priced suitcases. It has been an impressive rise, and the Softside Carry-on currently tops WIRED’s best buy list. Here however, we’ve chosen the aluminum version of the company’s handsome roll-aboard that’s built tough but perfectly sized for the overhead bin. It has a 32-liter capacity, dual TSA locks, 360-degree wheels, and an internal compression system. The signature hidden laundry bag remains a brilliant accoutrement.
Jelenew Mont Blanc Ultralight Long Windproof Jacket
Cofounded by six-time cycling world champion Marion Clignet, Jelenew combines female-specific articulated shaping, recycled nylon, mesh ventilation and an adjustable hem in a windproof shell that packs into a 6.3 x 9.8-inch bag. Clignet brought elite racing experience directly into the brand’s development, with the fit shaped around women’s proportions rather than scaled down from men’s clothing. This particular jacket uses 94 percent recycled nylon, a PFAS-free water-repellent treatment, UV protection, and mesh ventilation. Generous waist pockets and adjustable drawstrings add practical detail.
TaylorMade Kalea Gold Driver
Light, easy to launch, and forgiving, Kaela has been designed for women who want more performance than they can get from hacking a set of men’s clubs. Principal product-development engineer Michelle Penney helped lead the development of the range, with input from female TaylorMade employees, players, and and dedicated women’s advisory board. The final design takes into account the key differences in women’s swing profiles. The 460 cc carbon driver is 44 inches long, with 11.5- or 13.5-degree lofts and a lightweight 47-gram shaft intended to help generate speed without making the club harder to control.
Natural Cycles NC° Band
Cofounded by CERN physicist Elina Berglund Scherwitzl, who helped discover the Higgs boson, Natural Cycles makes the world’s first FDA-cleared birth-control app. Its screenless NC° Band syncs its health readings to the app. Wear it on your wrist while you sleep and it tracks your temperature, heart rate, and movement during the night, then automatically syncs all that data to your phone in the morning. Those numbers are fed into the app’s algorithm to give you accurate—Natural Cycles claims an impressive 93 percent accuracy—daily fertility guidance. A recently announced Whoop partnership helps strengthen both brand’s offerings too.
Adafruit Pimoroni Badgeware Badger
Ladyada, aka Limor Fried, became the first female engineer to appear on the cover of WIRED in April 2011, just six years after she founded Adafruit from her MIT dorm room. Her alias was inspired by 19th-century English mathematician and computing pioneer Ada Lovelace, which in turn provided inspiration for the brand’s name. Fried has grown Adafruit into a 100 percent woman-owned force in open-source electronics, making components, tools, and educational kits that lower the barrier to coding and hardware hacking. The company’s range spans beginner-friendly boards, wearable controllers, and touchscreens, alongside quirky maker gear such as the pictured programmable, wearable e-paper name badge.
Raide Women’s TrailTech Cargo Tank
More than just another running top, this multifunctional design combines an unpadded sports bra, a vest, and much of the carrying capacity of a small hydration pack in a single 4.6-ounce layer. Five well-positioned pockets hold up to 30 fluid ounces of water, a phone, your rain shell, and up to six fuel gels, all while keeping the load close to your body to help minimize bounce. Laser-perforated chest panels add ventilation, and the fit is designed around female anatomy rather than adapted from a men’s cut. It is a neat solution for runners who want to go the distance without adding layers on layers.
Vacheron Constantin Overseas Self-Winding
There was a time, not so long ago, when all serious timepieces had two clear traits. They were massive—we’re talking over 48 mm here, which fine if you have Schwarzenegger-sized forearms but useless for those who don’t—and they were aimed just at men. Women’s watches would have comparatively basic mechanical movements, or be quartz powered and covered in jewels.
Thankfully, general watch size trends have swung back the other way, and now small- and mid-size pieces are very much in demand. This means women with a serious eye for horology now have some truly excellent choices. This new Vacheron is a perfect example: Clocking in at 34.5 mm, this Overseas will suit both men and women very well in either stainless steel or pink gold. It’s a nearly exact shrunken version of the 41 mm model, and nothing has been dropped in the downsizing apart from the outer seconds track on the dial. The quick-release bracelet, two extra quick-change straps, 40-hour power reserve, and sapphire caseback are all present.
Dreame Miracle Pro
AI is drying hair now, or more specifically, adjusting temperature, heat, and airflow automatically. Dreame’s dryer also includes a conditioning essence atomizer and red light therapy to take extra care of your scalp. The 1,400-watt dryer monitors temperature 1,000 times per second to keep the airflow ultra consistent. The dryer also comes with four magnetic attachments: nozzles for styling, smoothing, and defrizzing, plus a diffuser. Snap one on, and the Miracle pro senses which one you’ve attached and adjusts the dryer’s power and heat for the best possible results.
Music Man St. Vincent HHH
Annie Clark, aka art-rocker St. Vincent, sketched the original shape for her signature guitar using angles that combine midcentury retro-futurism with the bold triangular tuxedo worn by avant-garde performer Klaus Nomi. She then worked through around 20 prototypes to get the weight, balance, and feel for the design just right. Despite the sharp lines, the body is heavily beveled with an exceptionally narrow waist, and Clark explicitly designed it to sit comfortably against a woman’s torso. Built from lightweight okoume wood, it weighs around 7.5 pounds, with a roasted maple neck that offers easy access to the upper frets (where the shredding happens). The three custom DiMarzio mini-humbuckers are controlled by a five-way selector.
KiwiCo STEM Kits
Chemical engineer and mother-of-three Sandra Oh Lin founded KiwiCo to make hands-on science, engineering and creative projects fun, practical, and easy to tackle at home. It offers kits for babies, kids, teens, and adults, with age-appropriate builds (and yes, we wouldn’t be surprised if the kids’ stuff was more advanced than the adults’) ranging from simple sensory play and mechanical grabbers to animatronics, marble roller coasters, and working desk lamps. Available individually or by subscription, everything that’s needed to build each device arrives in the box, with clear instructions and explanations of the ideas behind each project.
IDA Helia Pro
Informed by biometric data from professional women soccer players, IDA builds high-performance boots around women’s feet, combining specific fit with lightweight materials. Cofounder Laura Youngson started the company after seeing how poorly existing boots served women players. The Helia Pro packs in the tech with a lightweight mesh upper, a highly responsive soleplate made from Pebax thermoplastic, and a soft foam insole. There are also female-specific flex zones throughout the shoe, and shorter, rounded cleat studs laid out in a unique pattern that’s designed for firm ground and artificial grass.
New Balance Fresh Foam Cremorne Toe Safety Shoe
Looking closer to a pair of trail runners than conventional safety footwear, these are proof you don’t need to be clodhopping around in heavy boots to stay protected on the job site. The composite toe guards shield your piggies from impacts without the weight of steel, an anti-perforation layer protects the sole of your foot, and a reinforced heel support adds stability when you’re lifting loads. Its grippy outsole is designed for wet, slick, or oily floors, and offers antistatic protection while also being able to withstand temperatures of at least 572° Fahrenheit for 60 seconds. The shoes borrow foam cushioning and a springy polyurethane insert from New Balance’s athletic footwear to make long shifts easier on your feet.
Circular Smart Ring 3 Slim
We’re not quite at the point where smart rings are indistinguishable from jewelry, but the gap is closing. At just 1.9 grams, and with a noticeably slimmer profile than the second-generation model, Circular’s Ring 3 Slim blends in well, yet still tracks sleep, heart rate, blood oxygen level, skin temperature, daily activities, and heart-rate variability. It now adds NFC for contactless payments and practical vibration alerts and alarms. There’s also a larger Ring 3 Pro, which adds FDA-cleared electrocardiogram sensors for detecting signs of atrial fibrillation. Blood-pressure trends and glucose insights are planned for a later update.
Posedla Joyseat 3.0
Finally, a saddle that actually fits. Posedla sends an at-home imprint kit, then uses sit-bone measurements, riding position, and algorithmic modeling to 3D-print bespoke padding precisely profiled for your posterior. The resulting Joyseat is not merely made in a chosen width. Its shape and stiffness are individually generated too, using a custom TPU lattice rather than stock foam. Width can be specified from 130 to 170 mm in one millimeter increments, and Joyseat will also take into consideration the bike you use and what sorts of riding you do—whether you’re a racer, a weekend tourer, a bike camper, or a long-haul commuter.
Liv EnviLiv Advanced Pro 0-AXS
Bonnie Tu, chair of the company behind Giant bikes, founded Liv after struggling to find bikes that fitted properly. Liv designs from women’s biometric data, giving every frame size its own geometry, then applies its findings to a collection that includes city, gravel, commuter and elite bikes like the EnviLiv Advanced Pro. Its carbon frame, handlebars and stem are shaped using computer modelling and wind-tunnel testing to reduce drag, while 50 mm-deep carbon wheels and SRAM Force AXS wireless electronic gears complete the race-ready build. More importantly, fit is treated as a complete system, with stem length, handlebar width, crank length and saddle choice all selected to suit the rider rather than added later as generic components.

OPINION: Trump's U.N. speech, a stark contrast with past presidents
The world took note when President Trump told the United Nations General Assembly this week that he had asked himself whether to make a deal with Iran - or...
"Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic…
"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
Those words seem especially forbidding from a leader who can command armies to march and missiles to fly.
On August 6, 1945, President Harry Truman told the world the United States had dropped the first atomic bomb, on Hiroshima, Japan. It instantly killed an estimated 70,000 people. Some 40,000 more died days later in Nagasaki, and tens of thousands more from radiation illnesses in the days, weeks, months and years thereafter.
In his speech announcing the nuclear attack on Hiroshima, President Truman called it "a harnessing of the basic power of the universe," and added cautions about "protecting the world from the danger of sudden destruction."
Nuclear weapons have not been used in war since. And Truman's successors have been pointedly measured when they talk about them. As President Ronald Reagan put it, "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."
When President John F. Kennedy ordered US ships to blockade Cuba to prevent the Soviet Union from installing nuclear missiles in 1962, he told Americans, "We will not prematurely or unnecessarily risk the costs of worldwide nuclear war in which even the fruits of victory would be ashes in our mouth."
In 1974, President Gerald Ford told the U.N. General Assembly, "A very stark reality has tempered America's actions for decades and must now temper the actions of all nations. Prevention of full-scale warfare in the nuclear age has become everybody's responsibility. Today's regional conflict must not become tomorrow's world disaster."
And in 2017, President Obama visited the Peace Park that now stands in Hiroshima and said, "Among those nations like my own that hold nuclear stockpiles, we must have the courage to escape the logic of fear and pursue a world without them."
All strong words from presidents sworn to protect the United States. So strong and measured, they might have felt it wasn't necessary to add threats of annihilation, and "no chance of survival…"

Welcome to Edition 9.12 of the Rocket Report! The big story in the global launch industry remains SpaceX’s plans to wind down Falcon 9 operations for commercial launches, possibly within the next two or three years. That has created a scramble among satellite operators and some positioning among up-and-coming launch providers. Notably, in this week’s newsletter, there’s a story about how Firefly expects launch to become more expensive, and that customers got too used to rapid, reliable launch with the Falcon 9. I’m not sure that philosophy will work out long term.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
The best-named rocket in the world is sadly delayed. French launch startup HyPrSpace announced that it has pushed the inaugural flight of its Baguette One suborbital rocket to 2027, European Spaceflight reports. The 10-meter Baguette One rocket is a single-stage vehicle is capable of carrying up to 300 kg. It is powered by the company’s hybrid propulsion system, which combines liquid oxygen with solid polyethylene fuel.
An appetizing launch … Originally the company had been targeting 2026 for the suborbital rocket’s debut. In moving the target to 2027, however, the company revealed that the vehicle’s launch site will be the French Directorate General of Armaments location at Biscarrosse in southwestern France. “Seeing Baguette One lift off from French soil, after years of development and testing, will be a historic moment for HyPrSpace and its teams,” said HyPrSpace CEO Nicolas Billecocq.
Astra targeting “early” 2027 for return to flight. In a lengthy interview with The Debrief, Astra chief executive Chris Kemp said the company is targeting early 2027 for the launch of the Rocket 4.0 vehicle. The rocket, 18.9 meters tall, aims to eventually deliver up to 1 metric ton to low-Earth orbit. Kemp said Astra is aiming to make hundreds of rockets per year.
New rocket, same Kemp … “We chose not to do what a lot of other companies are doing,” Kemp said. “We’re not making a reusable rocket. We’re not making a very expensive engine cycle where the engines are very, very expensive. We’re trying to build a soda can.” And how good will Rocket 4.0 be? “I think this is going to be the most reliable, most affordable rocket ever produced in the history of the world,” Kemp said.
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
Down Under launch site may be nixed. A launch site under development in southern Australia, near Adelaide, may not go forward, the Australian Broadcast Corporation reports. The Native Vegetation Council denied variations to the heritage agreement at Whalers Way, where Southern Launch hopes to build a space facility. Southern Launch’s bid to create the Whalers Way Orbital Launch Complex has been met with ongoing opposition from conservation groups, including the local Eyre Peninsula Environmental Protection Alliance.
Endangered species … One reason for this is that the proposed site is a recognized conservation area for native vegetation and fauna. Rebecca Boulton from Birdlife Australia welcomed the upholding of the heritage agreement in place at the site since 1987, a habitat she said was home to two endangered bird species. “A couple of species down there at Whalers Way are part of our recovery team, so the mallee whipbird is one of the species that we work with, and the Eyre Peninsula is the stronghold for that species,” she said. (submitted by SubWoofer2)
Serious concerns about space debris. Over the last decade, the European Space Agency has produced an annual report that provides a transparent overview of global space activities and assesses the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight. In its most recently released Space Environment Report, published earlier this month, there are some striking—and concerning—changes. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations, Ars reports.
Sustainability concerns … Based on the growing number of launches, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered. In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers.
Ariane 6 has a turbopump issue. Europe’s Ariane 6 heavy-lift rocket, in the middle of an important ramp in launch rate to its initial target of nine to ten launches per year, will be unable to reach its goal of eight missions this year, according to Space Intel Report. An issue with the rocket’s turbopumps was discovered during ground testing in August, but repairs may be possible on site at the Guiana Space Center.
Not great for Amazon … After the report, the European Space Agency acknowledged the issue, saying it would need to “adjust” this year’s launch manifest. This will delay launches of European spacecraft as well as commercial customers such as the Amazon Leo constellation, which had been counting on Ariane 6 because its other major launch vehicles, New Glenn and Vulcan, are also experiencing technical issues.
Era of cheap launch is over? Several rocket company CEOs, speaking at World Space Business Week in Paris, made some interesting comments in the wake of SpaceX planning to wind down its Falcon 9 program. Most striking were those from Firefly Aerospace Vice President of Strategy Michael Creech. “The customer got comfortable with a high reliability and a low price, that frankly did not support the launch market,” Creech said during a panel discussion, Via Satellite reports.
A new normal … Creech said the industry will “reset” over the next six months to two years. “You’re seeing launchers move away to developing solutions with better revenue. This tells you this subsidized cost-per-kilo model wasn’t supporting launch companies, which led to the current-day crisis of a supply shortage,” he added. “Hopefully the new normal will be a growth environment for launch technologies and not another race to the bottom on price.” Although there is a crunch in launch now, there are enough emerging providers that Ars believes price will definitely be a major factor in launch choice in the coming years.
Beijing-based Chinese startup raises big money. Space Epoch finalized a B++ financing round, bringing its total Series B capital raised over the past six months to more than 2.3 billion yuan ($343 million), Satnews reports. The funding will directly support the qualification and assembly of Space Epoch’s flagship launch vehicle, the medium-lift Yuanxingzhe-1 rocket.
An impressive start … Yuanxingzhe-1 is rated to deliver up to 13.8 metric tons of payload into low Earth orbit in a fully expendable configuration, while supporting propulsive vertical landing recovery operations for the first-stage booster. In May 2025, the company successfully completed a vertical landing during a suborbital test at sea with the Yuanxingzhe-1 vehicle. An orbital test flight of the rocket could come before the end of this year.
How did SpaceX streamline the Raptor engine? The Construction Physics newsletter recently dove into the publicly available material on SpaceX’s Raptor engine to explore how the company simplified the design of the machine from the initial Raptor 1 version to the Raptor 3 version. The result is an excellent read on some of the things SpaceX engineers did in their pursuit of an engine to power the super heavy lift, rapidly reusable Starship rocket. Importantly, the article also notes that the Raptor 3 remains a work in progress.
Simpler, but not simple … “While this streamlining has made the Raptor engine simpler in the sense that various individual parts have been eliminated, it was still an enormously complex task to get it to work, and there’s a huge amount of internal complexity added to the Raptor 3 that these pictures don’t show,” the newsletter states. “And the problems haven’t been completely ironed out: the first launch attempt of Starship’s flight test 13 was aborted automatically by the vehicle’s flight software at T-0 (right before liftoff) this past July when several Raptor 3 engines failed to start.”
Starship stacked for next orbital flight. SpaceX assembled a Starship-Super Heavy rocket on the launch pad at Starbase in South Texas early Wednesday as it awaited approval for the vehicle’s first orbital flight, Spaceflight Now reports. Liftoff of Starship Flight 14 could come as soon as Monday, Sept. 28, but first SpaceX needs to receive regulatory approval from the Federal Aviation Administration.
A dawn launch … The rocket’s Starship upper stage, designated Ship 41 or S41, began its journey from production site about three miles west of the pad at around 7:45 p.m. CDT (0045 UTC) Tuesday night. Nearly 5.5 hours later, the 52-meter-tall (171 feet) ship was lifted by the launch tower’s chopsticks and carefully placed atop Super Heavy booster B21. Assuming approval from the FAA, SpaceX could launch Flight 14 as soon as 7:15 am CDT (1215 UTC) on September 28 on a nearly 10-hour mission that will see the deployment of 26 next-generation Version 3 Starlink satellites.
Next three launches
September 26: Electron | Owlright, Owlright, Owlright | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 00:15 UTC
September 26: Falcon 9 | USSF-385 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. | 11:56 UTC
September 28: Starship | Flight 14 | Starbase, Texas | 12:15 UTC
Eric Berger is the senior space editor at Ars Technica, covering everything from astronomy to private space to NASA policy, and author of two books: Liftoff, about the rise of SpaceX; and Reentry, on the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon. A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

‘World on edge of abyss today, seeing weaponisation of everything’: Jaishankar at UN
Jaishankar emphasized the urgent need for stability and called for accountability against state-sponsored terrorism.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday told the UN General Assembly that the world was witnessing “a weaponisation of everything”. He said finance, market access, supply chains and technology were being used as leverage, and that developing nations were caught in a crisis of food, fuel, fertiliser and finance – with a looming El Nino expected to exacerbate this crisis.
Addressing the general debate of the Assembly’s 81st session in New York, Jaishankar said strengthening stability, security and predictability was imperative for peace, and warned that the world was “living on the edge of an abyss” under continuous threats and pressures. “All it takes is one more step to push us over,” he said. After eight decades of the UN, strengthening them “should have become our second nature”, he said. “Instead, what we are actually seeing is a weaponisation of everything...”
Resources and connectivity had become “particularly subject to leveraging”, pushing nations to focus on de-risking and diversifying, he said, without naming any country. “While this may secure their interest to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill.”
Deep Dive
The predicament of the Global South was “particularly acute”, Jaishankar said, describing a “4F crisis” of food, fuel, fertiliser and finance. “The combined impact of a super El Niño, compounding fertiliser shortages and now impediments to grain movements, all these are cause for alarm,” he said, adding that progress on the Sustainable Development Goals was under increasing pressure.

“The Global South’s right to industrialise is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial.” The World Meteorological Organization forecast on September 3 that El Niño would intensify to “very strong” through February 2027. The Brics New Delhi Declaration adopted under India’s chairship on September 12 had also voiced serious concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures.
The minister reserved his sharpest words for Pakistan, without naming it. A “serial practitioner of terrorism” had “misrepresented facts” before the Assembly the previous day, he said, invoking arguments “to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences”. “That will not stand. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised,” Jaishankar said. “Friendship and goodwill cannot coexist with terrorism. And understandings premised on that will naturally be called into question. It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways,” he said. State-sponsored, cross-border terrorism was “a direct affront to the global order”, he said, calling for governments indulging in it to be held accountable and for terror financing to be exposed and countered.
On the conflict in the Gulf, which he said was “exacerbating an already difficult situation”, Jaishankar called the targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in international waterways “simply unacceptable”. He urged all parties to exercise restraint, de-escalate, and ensure the protection of civilians and the uninterrupted flow of energy and commerce. Attacks on shipping had spread “from the Red Sea to the Black Sea”, he said, and Indian seafarers had lost their lives along with those of other nations. India, he said, had joined Liberia and 23 other partners in an initiative to rally global public opinion against such targeting. At least 15 Indian seafarers have been killed in West Asia and the Black Sea this year, according to government figures.
On the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, Jaishankar said: “As Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated, endless war must give way now to an end to war. India supports ongoing initiatives to bring peace. Even as this is underway, there is an urgent need to address the security of seafarers and supply of food grains and energy. India is prepared to do everything possible to ameliorate this situation, especially with regard to food and energy security.” US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz acknowledged India’s efforts to secure energy and food supplies during a UN Security Council debate on Ukraine earlier in the week.

Jaishankar reiterated India’s support for a two-state solution as the route to durable peace in West Asia, and said India was contributing to humanitarian relief for the Palestinian people.
He said the misuse of artificial intelligence was “sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect”. Pointing to the AI Impact Summit India hosted in February, he argued for “the right of each nation to shape its ecosystem with the development of its own models and deployment strategies consistent with its national goals and priorities”, and said AI would be part of India’s partnership agenda with the Global South. Setting out India’s own contribution, Jaishankar cited 600 major development projects in 78 nations, spanning infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture, IT and capacity building. He also cited the progress of the International Solar Alliance, the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure and the Global Biofuels Alliance, and India’s role as a first responder after disasters, including the recent flash floods in Nepal.
“The post-1945 order is giving way to new realities,” he said, adding that much of the present turbulence stemmed from the difficulty of adjusting to a multipolar world, and that “the case for reformed multilateralism only gets stronger day after day”. Economic rebalancing was well under way and political rebalancing visible, he said, and cultural rebalancing “must now be taken forward”.

“In the lawns outside this building are recorded the powerful words of Mahatma Gandhi, and that should serve as an inspiration for these times. And those words are that there is no way to peace. Peace is the way,” Jaishankar said.
