UP woman murdered, buried in garden in Jaipur; search on for live-in partner: Cops
The motive behind the murder and other circumstances of the case are under investigation, police said.
A 32-year-old woman was allegedly murdered by her live-in partner, who buried her body in the garden of their rented house here before fleeing, police said on Sunday.
The matter came to light when the landlord, who came to inspect the rented premises at Prestige Colony in the Bindayaka area, found the house locked and noticed a woman's hand protruding from freshly dug soil in the garden.
Bindayaka Station House Officer Anil Kumar said the house was taken on rent about two months ago by Pravesh (22), who introduced the woman, Kiran, as his wife. Both hailed from Uttar Pradesh.
According to preliminary police assessment, Pravesh allegedly killed the woman two to three days ago, dug a pit in the garden at night and buried her body. He then locked the house and fled, the SHO said.
On Sunday morning, when the landlord arrived to check the property, he found it locked.
After making inquiries with neighbours, he checked the premises and noticed that soil in the garden had been freshly dug. On examining the spot, he saw a woman's hand protruding from the ground and immediately alerted the police.
Police exhumed the body with the help of a forensics team and sent it for post-mortem at Kanwatia Hospital.
They said Pravesh worked at a factory in Bindayaka. Teams have been formed to trace him, and police are also trying to contact the woman's family in Uttar Pradesh.
The motive behind the murder and other circumstances of the case are under investigation, police said.

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.
“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.
The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.
Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.
In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.
“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.
Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.
“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.
“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”
He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.
“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”
Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.
Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”
She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.
“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
- Published
Warning: This story contains distressing details
The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.
The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion.
Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.
Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.
"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.
"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."
She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.
Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

It’s no exaggeration to say there is a manga for almost anything in Japan.
Eighteen-year-old Kosei Kani had begged his parents to drive him from Kasugai city to Nagoya’s Tokai Gymnasium on Saturday evening. He was a fan of Shakunetsu Kabaddi, the manga written by Hajime Musashino that was also adapted into an anime series. It follows a former football player who is drawn into the world of full-contact kabaddi. What begins as a sport he dismisses as a joke gradually reveals itself to be something closer to martial arts.
Kosei had become curious about the real thing.
“I want to see what it really was,” he told Sportstar.
As introductions to a sport go, watching an India-Iran men’s gold-medal match at the Asian Games is a fairly spectacular one. It would be like deciding to learn about basketball by watching the USA’s Olympic Dream Team in a final, or trying to understand football by starting with Barcelona against Real Madrid.
Kosei was not disappointed.
ALSO READ | India medal tally - September 26: Kabaddi teams wins gold; Sawan, Tajinderpal win silver
The final was everything Shakunetsu Kabaddi had promised him: tangled bodies, double-handed takedowns, backheel kicks, glaring, showmanship and the kind of physical confrontation that makes the line between kabaddi and martial arts seem rather thin.
India won 40-34.
But there was much more to the match than the score.
In global kabaddi, there is no bigger prize than the Asian Games gold medal. And there is no more important rivalry than India against Iran.
“This was our game when we had nothing else at the Asian Games,” said Indian coach BC Ramesh. “In the 1990 Asian Games, we had just one gold medal and that came in kabaddi. This is our game. It matters very much how we do in it.”
For much of the sport’s history, India’s dominance was difficult to challenge. But over the past decade and a half, Iran has emerged as the one country capable of making India genuinely uncomfortable.
Over the last four Asian Games editions, the final has become an India-Iran affair. Iran won once, while the Iranians felt they had been hard done by in the previous encounter in Hangzhou.
“There’s only one country in the world that can challenge India, that can even think of beating India, and that is Iran,” said Indian raider Aslam Inamdar.
So this was never going to be just another final.
If the location had been determined purely by the magnitude of the occasion, the final probably deserved a different venue.
Tokai Gymnasium will revert to being a basketball court for a working-class neighbourhood in Nagoya once the Asian Games are over. The spectator seating is only six rows deep.
It is a world away from kabaddi in India.
The Pro Kabaddi League attracts millions of viewers and is second only to cricket’s Indian Premier League in popularity. Its biggest players can become fabulously wealthy. Yet, the very best players in the league still clamour to play at the Asian Games, just as the very best American basketball players once fought to be part of the Dream Team.
Here, all of that ultra-elite, high-stakes sport was squeezed into a small-town gym hall, against a soundtrack of Punjabi pop.
A stadium emcee tried his best to explain to the Japanese spectators what was happening in the middle. He was not always successful.
ALSO READ | The runner no one expected wins India’s first Asian Games marathon medal in 44 years
He didn’t need to be.
“I still don’t understand what is happening, but I’m appreciating the atmosphere,” said Hiramatsu Hisamoto, who was watching his first kabaddi match.
Indeed, you did not need to understand everything happening on the mat to know that it was exciting.
The spectators were a microcosm of Asia — and of the many different ways people had arrived at this strange little corner of the Asian Games. A couple of girls in headscarves screamed their support for Iran. There were Pakistanis cheering for Iran, while a few Nepalis completed the “Bharat Mata Ki…” chant with a loud “Jai!”
On the mat, there was plenty of glaring, showmanship, slapping of thighs, and pointing towards the opposition bench. After the first half, it was Iran who led 18-17.
But just when it seemed like Iran held the edge, India fought back. The Iranian defence cracked. Their raiders seemed to get caught with every raid. As India emerged on top, the taunting began.
On Iran’s final raid, made by Mohammadreza Shadloui, who competes for Gujarat Giants in the PKL, India captain Sunil stood in front with a grin on his face, knowing India had sealed the win, gesturing with his hands as if to say, “You’re talking too much.”
“When Iran travelled to Pakistan before the Asian Games to prepare, Shadloui said the gold medal would be theirs. I just wanted to remind him that they were playing India and the gold medal is India’s,” Sunil said after the final.
When the final whistle blew, players from both nations embraced. Somewhere in the stands was Kosei, watching the sport he had first discovered on the pages of a manga. “I think I’d like to play this game myself,” he said.

In September 2026, a claim circulated alleging Pope Leo XIV and U.S. Vice President JD Vance had a back-and-forth of verbal jabs criticizing each other on the subject of compassion.
For example, Sept. 23, a Facebook user named Dee Wallace after the "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" actor, shared (archived) an image with photos of Vance and Leo.
(@DeeWallaceOfficialFB via Facebook)
According to the post's caption, Vance responded to one of Leo's messages, with Vance calling compassion a form of weakness. Leo then supposedly responded with a "fiery" retort:
BREAKING: J.D. Vance attacks Pope Leo XIV — and gets a FIERY response he won't soon forget
J.D. Vance thought he could score political points by criticizing Pope Leo XIV's message of compassion and inclusion. Instead, the pontiff delivered a response that left the room stunned.
"You say compassion is weakness," Pope Leo XIV began. "Then when did caring for the sick become weakness? When did helping the poor become weakness? When did loving our neighbors become weakness?"
The audience fell silent.
Then came the line that hit hardest:
"Can we imagine hatred in heaven? Can we imagine cruelty in heaven? Then why do we tolerate these things on earth?"
What started as a political attack quickly turned into a powerful moral challenge — and a message that is now spreading far beyond that room.
Please like and share Pope Leo XIV's inspiring words!
Other Facebook users shared the claim. A Snopes reader also asked of the rumor, "Is this a true story?"
Searches of DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo failed to locate any news media outlets reporting about the alleged discussion, including the purported direct quotes. If the story truly occurred, journalists with reputable outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it. That was not the case.
In sum, we found the rumor was fictional and was created with the help of artificial intelligence.
Some of Vance's authentic past remarks about Leo possibly served as the inspiration for the fabricated story and fake quotes. In April, Vance, speaking at a rally for the conservative Turning Point USA organization, said he likes when the pope comments on immigration, abortion and matters of war and peace, even when there's disagreement. He also said he believed the pope should "be careful" when opining about theology.
Regarding the Facebook account named for Wallace, no evidence credibly confirmed the actor shared the post. The Facebook account displayed the word "official" in the handle — @DeeWallaceOfficialFB — as well as a verification badge supposedly designating authenticity. However, upon selecting the word "Copywriter" near the top of the profile, then clicking "Transparency and privacy policy," we found an older page name previously defined its purpose as a fan page, as well as that six accounts based in Vietnam served as its only managers. The page's recent posts all featured some forms of AI and fiction, as well.
We contacted a representative for Wallace to ask about this matter and will update this article if we receive further details. We were unable to contact the Facebook page via Messenger.
Researching the AI slop rumor
This claim about Leo and Vance resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." Creators of such content capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
One of the aforementioned search engine queries found articles from June telling a longer version of the same story. A generic-looking, advertisement-filled WordPress blog that hosted the stories — named only "News And Tips" — included some Vietnamese-language characters and lacked standard signals of authenticity, for example including standard legal documentation including a terms of service and privacy policy, as well as information about a website's founding.
One of the blog articles included some text appearing to guide users on how to publish monetized, emotionally charged content. A scan of the story's text with the artificial intelligence detection tool Pangram displayed the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," as well as, "100% of this text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
For further reading, we previously reported about a rumor alleging Leo used AI to write parts of his first encyclical.

In mid-August, along the Bengaluru-Mysuru expressway, an agricultural labourer in C.K. Tandya village in South Bengaluru district (formerly known as Ramanagara) noticed something unusual on a strip of farmland: a heap of medical waste.
This wasn’t the first time that the villagers in South Bengaluru had noticed suspicious objects or activity around the area which contained a farmhouse, say the police. They had seen men frequently moving in and out of it on a scooter without a number plate. They had also seen courier and e-commerce delivery vehicles making regular trips to the secluded location.
Spanning nearly eight acres and fenced by a compound wall, the farmland is situated on the outskirts of the village. According to the police, the owners, who live in Bengaluru, seldom visited the place.
The villagers would whisper among themselves about what they suspected — until the day the labourer decided to report the dumped medical waste to the local beat police.
The officers at Taverekere police station put the farmhouse and the movements around it under surveillance, while also making inquiries about the property and its occupants. The people they spoke to did not seem to know anything substantial.
According to an officer, the police learned that the farmhouse had been rented about a year earlier. But what was happening inside the compound remained unclear.
Days later, the police and Karnataka’s health department, in a joint operation, decided to enter the premises. What they saw there — labels, medicine boxes, drugs, and other items associated with the preparation and packaging of medicines — changed the nature of the investigation. They alerted senior officers, who joined hands with officers from the State Drugs Control Department and conducted a raid on August 18.
The police took four people into custody. They discovered that the secluded farmhouse was being used as a counterfeit drug repackaging and re-labelling facility. What began as a local’s suspicion had opened the door to a much larger pharmaceutical investigation.
According to investigators, the operation involved the procurement of low-cost, substandard, or expired pharmaceutical formulations from other States, which were then transferred into fresh vials and given counterfeit labels and packaging. “The aim was to make the medicines appear as genuine products of established pharmaceutical companies and introduce them into the pharmaceutical supply chain,” says a police official familiar with the investigation.
During the seizure, the police recovered more than 5,600 vials of counterfeit antibiotic injections used in treating serious bacterial infections. The total seizure was estimated at ₹4.91 crore.
They also seized ledgers, invoices, mobile phones, and other records, which provided them with details of the supply chain.
From a farmhouse to the big city
The police then moved their investigation beyond C.K. Tandya. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted.
The trail led to Bengaluru and to Krupa Healthcare, a wholesale pharmaceutical distributor located on a busy commercial street in the city. According to the police, the operators in the farmhouse supplied medicines to Krupa Healthcare, which distributed them.
The police found that the counterfeit medicines were not limited to antibiotics, but also included critical-care injections and cancer medicines. They say some of the medicines were offered to hospitals at “discounts of up to 50%”.
Krupa Healthcare owner Veeresh Kumar Jain, who was arrested by the SIT, allegedly employed more than 15 medical representatives to promote the medicines and offered commissions to push the discounted stocks to private hospitals and medical centres.
The police then found that the alleged racket was not confined to Karnataka. A joint force subsequently carried out simultaneous searches across Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Telangana. The police are currently on the hunt for Bengaluru resident R. Prashant, who they believe is a key figure in the network. He is currently in Azerbaijan, and is Jain’s partner, say the police.
Unanswered questions
The families of patients are shocked and angry at these revelations. On his WhatsApp profile picture, Maheshprasad Upadhya, 30, poses with his mother. A cervical cancer patient, she passed away in 2024. After hearing the news, Upadhya, a native of Odisha, cannot help second-guessing the events before his mother’s death.
She was diagnosed with cancer in 2022, he says. For a year, she underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy in Mumbai. The doctors then suggested immunotherapy. As treatment in Mumbai was expensive and there were also logistical difficulties in travelling to the city, the family decided to shift treatment to Bhubaneswar.
“The doctor we consulted referred a Bengaluru-based pharmaceutical distributor to us. I bought a medicine from them. It cost ₹1,65,990 per vial. My mother needed two vials. The distributor said if we purchase one, we would get another free,” recalls Upadhya.
He searched online and found that the manufacturer did offer such a programme. He decided to go ahead with it.
Upadhya spent about ₹20 lakh on the overall treatment. “But we saw no improvement in her condition,” he says. “When she was diagnosed with cancer, the doctor had said she would live up to five years. My mother passed away in one and a half years.”
Upadhya sounds calm, but he admits within him a tumult of emotions — anger, suspicion, and helplessness. “One person who had got his father treated at the Bhubaneswar hospital had advised us against buying this medicine from this particular distributor,” he says. “But we didn’t listen since the doctor himself had advised it. After my mother passed away, I started suspecting something, perhaps a nexus, but I was in no state of mind to think about it. Now I’m questioning everything.”
He confesses that there are times when he considers migrating abroad “after seeing how the corrupt try to profit from the desperation of the most vulnerable.”
Parth Sharma, a resident of Gurugram, returned to India in 2017 to care for his ageing parents and mother-in-law, after spending 37 years abroad. “The people I came here for are no more,” he says.
In October 2020, Sharma’s mother was diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome, a condition where the bone marrow doesn’t make enough healthy blood cells. The doctors informed the family that the disease was not curable. Given the patient’s age — she was in her 70s — a bone marrow transplant was also not an option, they said. Nevertheless, treatment, including chemotherapy injections and blood transfusions, was started at a private hospital in December.
Sharma remembers that some of the expensive medicines were not available in India. “The doctor gave us the phone number of a person and said he would help get it imported. When you are desperate, you simply trust everyone. So, we contacted him,” he says.
Sharma’s mother’s condition never improved. With her body too weak to fight the disease, she passed away in May 2021.
“After the report on the counterfeit drug racket came out, I started wondering more deeply about something I had suspected all along: were the medicines even working? We had spent a lot of money and given her the prescribed medicines. At that point, we trusted the system and did not even suspect the possibility of fake medicines,” he says. He still has some of the tablets, which cost him around ₹80,000.
Living in uncertainty
The police say the suspect medicines have so far reached more than 90 hospitals and clinics in Karnataka and other States. While the State government has published a list of antibiotics seized during the Bidadi raid, it has not yet disclosed the names of oncology drugs or the hospitals and clinics that may have received the medicines, or the names and batch numbers of counterfeit medicines reportedly linked to serious illnesses such as cancer. There is pressure on the government to disclose this information.
According to the Karnataka Minister for Health and Family Welfare, U.T. Khader, the full list of spurious and counterfeit drugs has been communicated to the Union government and all State governments. “The SIT has taken charge of the investigation now. Once the report is finalised, we will reveal everything. We have got the list of hospitals. But when the SIT is there, it is not right on my part to disclose anything,” he says.
As the SIT continues with its investigation, Upadhya wonders what patients must be going through with the information they have. “Imagine their state of mind. Would they want to continue or discontinue treatment when they have no way of knowing whether the medicine they are taking is genuine or counterfeit,” he asks.
Dr. B.S Ajaikumar, radiation and medical oncologist and Founder and Chairman at HealthCare Global (HCG) Enterprises, says counterfeit drugs are a major problem in India today.
“I have been sounding the alarm on this for several years,” he says. “Whenever somebody — say insurance companies — wants to bring drugs from outside, I don’t allow it at HCG because I’m concerned it could be spurious. Any drug we purchase should come directly from the manufacturer. The authorities should also lay down stringent guidelines and ensure they are enforced. They should consult major users of oncology drugs like us, collaborate with us to develop a plan, and ensure spurious drugs don’t enter the system.”
Noting that cancer treatment often depends on the right drug, at the right dose, given at the right time, Dr. Nitish Ranjan Acharya, Surgical Oncologist at Manipal Hospital, Bhubaneswar, points out that any compromise in the authenticity or quality of a medicine can directly affect a patient’s treatment.
“If a patient receives a counterfeit, substandard, or expired medicine, the drug may not work as intended. This can delay disease control, allow the cancer to progress and, in some cases, affect the chances of achieving a good treatment response. The impact may be particularly difficult to identify because a lack of response can sometimes be mistaken for the cancer becoming resistant to treatment,” he explains.
Dr. Acharya adds that there are more risks when the contents of the counterfeit drugs are unknown. “A drug could contain an incorrect dose, inactive ingredients, contaminants, or substances that may cause unexpected side effects. These risks can be especially serious for patients already receiving multiple cancer medicines,” he notes. He also stresses the importance of appropriate storage and handling to maintain quality.
The question of accountability
The alleged racket also raises questions about what hospitals should do when patients may have already been exposed to counterfeit medicines. As S.V. Joga Rao, a lawyer who specialises in healthcare law and ethics, says, “Given the circumstances in India, a detailed investigation may take time. By that time, the spurious drugs may have found their way to patients.”
According to him, hospitals need to work with investigating agencies to identify the medicines in question and their batch numbers. “If there is some kind of leeway in terms of information, the hospital has an ethical duty to inform potentially affected patients,” he says.
Noting that regulatory authorities need to be mindful of Section 17B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which defines a spurious drug, and Section 18, which prohibits their manufacture, sale, stocking, distribution and other related activities, Rao also points to the legal duty of hospitals to procure responsibly, verify authenticity, and detect sophisticated counterfeiting. “If there are warning signs, they need to respond to that. The duties of the hospitals and regulators operate concurrently, although they are different in nature. It is a shared responsibility,” he says.
Dr. Gopal Dabade, president of Drug Action Forum, Karnataka, says, “Drug inspectors are the first line of foot soldiers, but they are not adequately equipped. Punishment for wrongdoing is also not stringent enough.” He is a part of the All India Drug Action Network, a group of non-profits working to “increase access and improve the rational use of essential medicines”.
Another reality is the high cost of medicines, particularly cancer drugs, which can create a parallel market for cheaper counterfeit versions. “Better access to good quality and affordable treatment is the crux of the issue,” Dabade says.
Sylvia Karpagam, a public health doctor and researcher, says people must demand an accountable public health system as part of the election mandate. She also points to the responsibility of doctors, and questions the role they play in ensuring accountability within the healthcare system. “Doctors who harp about ‘evidence-based practice’ in allopathy go mum when such incidents occur. Other than for their own pay cheques and to oppose any form of regulation, one barely sees doctors protesting on behalf of patients,” she says.
She also stresses the importance of adequate budgets, trained and sufficient staff, and regular public scrutiny. “Unless the government has an ongoing system to prevent drug rackets, and makes it known to the public through ongoing reports, these kinds of incidents will continue — some get picked up, and many don’t.”
SIT head C. Vamshikrishna says he cannot comment on the case while the investigation is on. Repeated phone calls and messages to reach Srinivas K. Commissioner of the Food Safety and Drug Administration, Karnataka, have not elicited any response.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has insisted investors think of his electric automaker as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company now. He’s targeted a $20 trillion valuation—nearly four times the value of market leader Nvidia—on that premise. But his Tesla team was in Sparks, Nevada, on Thursday to focus on, well, an electric vehicle: the long-awaited Tesla Semi.
The Semi concept first rolled onto a Tesla event stage in late 2017. Nearly a decade later, Tesla officially launched high-volume production at a livestreamed but invite-only event at the company’s factory. It targeted a niche audience: the cost-conscious people who manage large trucking fleets. A handful of them, all men, trooped across the stage to be thanked for their orders to a pulsing techno beat.
“It’s going to be, really, a driver’s truck. It’s like a sports car in truck form.” Musk said in a pre-taped video played during the evening event. (Musk, for years the ringmaster at Tesla’s circus-like events, skipped his second vehicle debut in a row; he was attending a White House China State Dinner featuring President Xi Jinping.)
The long-range version of the Semi will travel an estimated 500 miles per charge, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice president of Vehicle Engineering, confirmed at the event—around the average number of miles traveled by US long-haul truckers each day. The standard version will get an estimated 325 miles per charge. Competitor EVs advertise ranges of 155 to 430 miles.
Electric Dreams
The Tesla Semi has its work cut out for it.
While electrics account for nearly 30 percent of heavy-duty truck sales in China, according to state media, they’ve had a slow start in the US, as manufacturers struggle to make the vehicles competitive with their traditional diesel-burning counterparts. Electric semis can cost two to three times more upfront. Right now, they’re not easy to charge because they require a countrywide network of specialized megawatt chargers that can fill large batteries in hours. Tesla’s website shows two such public chargers operating in the LA area. However, Dan Priestley, who leads Tesla’s Semi program, says the company plans to open 30 by the end of the year.
Plus, the Trump administration and the GOP—the same group Musk spent millions to get into the White House—cut billions in federal support for electric vehicles last year. The administration is also working to lower fuel economy standards for truck engines, which would have required manufacturers to hit aggressive climate goals. Heavy trucks alone account for some 7 percent of US greenhouse gas emissions.
And yet, it’s not a bad time to be an EV-maker. US diesel prices hit record highs this month as the Iran War continues to disrupt oil production and shipping in the Middle East; prices are up nearly double from this time last year. The truck “is going to make a ton of sense economically because the cost of electricity is much less than the cost of diesel, especially in these crazy times,” Musk said in his pre-taped address, nodding to the conflict launched by the administration he once worked for.
This week, an alliance of shippers including Microsoft and PepsiCo placed a record-setting order for 2,500 Tesla Semis, to be delivered starting this year and through the next 18 months. If those trucks reach customers, they would nearly double the number of heavy-duty electric trucks on US roads today.
The group selected Tesla trucks over competitors’ after “assessing price, performance, production capability, and service support,” Meena Bibra, a spokesperson for the nonprofit Smart Freight Centre, which was involved in the deal, told WIRED. If the carriers are accustomed to another truckmaker’s vehicles, or if other electric trucks better meet their needs, they may also choose to purchase electric trucks from Kenworth, Ride, and Volvo.
Pooling demand among many carriers allowed the electric automakers to bring down the prices of the new trucks, the group said.

Enterprise tech startup CodeKarma is in talks to raise $5 Mn to $6 Mn in a fresh funding round, sources told Inc42. The round will be led by existing investors Prosus and Accel, the sources added. The discussions are ongoing, and the contours of the transaction could change. Queries sent to CodeKarma and Accel did not elicit a response until the time of publishing this story. A Prosus spokesperson declined to comment on market speculation. The development comes a little over a year after CodeKarma raised $2.5 Mn in its pre-seed round, co-led by Prosus, Accel, and Xeed Ventures. SenseAI Ventures and Stargazer Ventures also participated in the round. Founded in 2024 by Anantharam Vanchi Prakash and Priyanka Nahata, CodeKarma operates a production intelligence platform that maps the behaviour of software in production directly to its underlying code. Prakash, a former Amazon and Flipkart executive, is the startup’s cofounder and CEO, while Nahata serves as its cofounder and CTO. The Bengaluru-based startup’s platform helps developers and AI agents identify active and dormant code, detect performance issues, understand dependencies between different parts of a software system, and assess the risks associated with changing code. CodeKarma currently offers four products. KarmaLens provides production insights within developers’ integrated development environments, while KarmaDomain maps dependencies across microservices and APIs. KarmaPulse gives engineering leaders an overview of operational issues, and KarmaIQ supplies production context to AI coding agents. During its previous fundraise, CodeKarma said it planned to deploy the capital to strengthen its AI capabilities, enter new enterprise verticals, expand its presence in the US, hire employees, and invest in product development. Prakash had also said that the startup was working towards building autonomous software agents that could go beyond identifying problems in code and act on fixing them. Accel, which is expected to participate in CodeKarma’s proposed round, is also an existing investor in Rocket. Investor interest extends to the wider AI ecosystem. Iran’s supreme leader 
Mojtaba Khamenei
 was reportedly “pulled from the rubble” of a Tehran hospital after US and Israeli strikes hit the medical centre where he had been taken following earlier attacks, the New York Post reported.
Mohsen Heydari, a member of Iran’s Assembly of Experts, made the revelation in an interview with Qatari television network Al Araby on Thursday.
“Even after he had been wounded and taken to the hospital, three hospitals in Tehran were bombed,” Heydari said. Mojtaba Khamenei was in the third hospital and was pulled from the rubble,” he said.
Speculation has continued over Mojtaba Khamenei’s condition following the earlier strikes. US intelligence reports had reportedly indicated that he was badly disfigured in the attacks.
According to the report, Heydari also spoke about the process through which Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as Iran’s new supreme leader on March 8. He said Mojtaba apparently did not know he had been chosen until the announcement was broadcast on Iranian state television.
The Assembly of Experts, which is responsible for selecting Iran’s supreme leader, was itself reportedly targeted in the strikes. 
The New York Post reported that its Qom Secretariat was bombed, killing eight people and destroying reports and recommendations related to the selection of a new supreme leader.
Heydari said members of the Assembly subsequently recorded their votes on paper before being summoned to a secret room for the selection process. He recalled being the first member to propose Mojtaba Khamenei’s name.
“Given the enemy’s position, we will choose and elect no one as leader and supreme guide of the Islamic Republic except Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei,” Heydari said.
“We obtained information that Mojtaba Khamenei was healthy and able to lead, and we determined that he met the requirements of religious qualification, justice and competence to manage the country,” he said.
Heydari also described Mojtaba Khamenei as a “man of the shadows”, saying he had not held any political position within the Iranian state before becoming supreme leader, although he had reportedly served as an adviser to his father.

Tesla’s pivot from making electric cars to humanoid robots is facing challenges because of complex robot hands and disgruntled employees pushing back against training their robotic replacements. The struggle to scale up production comes as Tesla CEO Elon Musk has bet the company’s future on AI and robotics.
As someone who frequently makes claims that fail to materialize, Musk has described the Optimus humanoid robot as potentially “the biggest product ever” during Tesla’s second-quarter 2026 earnings call. But he also acknowledged that making an autonomous humanoid robot capable of handling many different tasks is “one of the hardest things to solve”—and now extensive reporting by The Information has revealed multiple complications that Tesla is trying to tackle while developing general-purpose robots and scaling up for mass production.
Tesla’s Fremont factory in California has already stopped making the Model S sedan and Model X SUV as of May 2026, with the company switching both line workers and engineers over to working on Optimus, according to The Information.
But the newest version of Optimus, called Optimus V3, has proven challenging from a development and manufacturing standpoint. The Information’s reporting describes troubles with getting production line equipment to precisely line up components, along with limitations in running the production line too fast. Tesla has reportedly scaled up production to hundreds of robots per week—but the company is targeting production numbers surpassing 1,000 robots per week by the end of 2026.
The automotive industry and other industries have already been using specialized industrial robots, such as robotic arms, for decades. Tesla and many other automakers and robotics companies are betting that humanoid robots coupled with advances in AI models could eventually unlock general-purpose robots that can handle a diverse array of tasks while fitting more seamlessly into human workplaces.
Hardware and AI challenges
It’s no secret that making robotic hands capable of doing delicate manipulation tasks on par with human hands is a huge engineering challenge. The complexity of such robotic hands has translated into more production headaches for Tesla as human workers must manually assemble Optimus hands and forearms that together have more than 100 small components such as screws.

New York sued Polymarket today, alleging that it runs an “illegal gambling operation” through its prediction market.
“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” Governor Kathy Hochul said in a press release announcing the lawsuit.
Polymarket is “sidestepping its obligation to pay taxes like licensed casinos and mobile sports gambling platforms do,” New York said. “This tax revenue from gambling regulation funds public schools, sports programs for underserved youth, and problem gambling education and treatment.”
Polymarket is “available to users between the ages of 18–20, even though New York law requires a person to be at least 21 years old to participate in mobile sports betting,” exposing young people to gambling’s “damaging effects on their mental and financial well-being,” New York said.
New York previously sued Kalshi, Polymarket’s chief rival. The Trump administration is on the side of the prediction markets, with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) asserting exclusive jurisdiction over the platforms. In August, the CFTC declared a “market emergency” in New York in an attempt to stop the state from applying its gambling laws to Kalshi.
Gambling with a different name
Polymarket and its rival Kalshi offer sports bets in the form of “event contracts” or “swaps,” which state governments and some courts say are just gambling with a different name.
“Our gambling laws exist to protect New Yorkers, prevent the potential harms of problem gambling, and ensure funding for educational and public benefit programs,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said. “By skirting New York’s laws, Polymarket is targeting the most vulnerable and depriving New York families of critical services and support.”
The New York press release said the state government is “seeking a court order stopping Polymarket from operating as an unlicensed gambling business and requiring the company to pay fines, forfeit all illegal gains and pay restitution to users.” The lawsuit was filed today in a New York County court.

Wakefield Trinity hailed after stunning win over Wigan Warriors to reach Super League Grand Final: 'No team would have competed with them'
Wakefield Trinity booked their spot in their first-ever Super League Grand Final with a 33-6 win against Wigan Warriors; the victory will see them face Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final; watch the Super League Grand Final live on Sky Sports Main Event on Saturday
Sunday 27 September 2026 07:23, UK
Jon Wilkin believes some of the best teams in Super League history would not have beaten Wakefield Trinity on Saturday night, as Daryl Powell's side sealed a huge upset victory against Wigan Warriors to book a spot in the Grand Final.
A flurry of second-half tries saw Trinity end Wigan's 16-match winning streak, with the visitors leaving Matt Peet's side stunned by their ferocious pace and power.
Wigan went down to 12 men after 45 minutes, with Adam Keighran being sin-binned for a tip-tackle. Wakefield ruthlessly took advantage, scoring three tries while the Australian five-eighth was off the field.
Wigan did impress in the opening exchanges, matching Wakefield for intensity, with Brad O'Neill breaking the deadlock after a tense first 15 minutes.
But the League Leaders' Shield winners, who had two weeks off coming into this match, stumbled in the second half.
"Wigan were bad, but that was completely induced by what Wakefield threw at them," Wilkin told Sky Sports.
"It was a clinical performance that was full of power, pace, energy, enthusiasm and execution.
"Nobody would have competed with Wakefield today. Not one team in Super League.
"I'd go as far as to say some of the great teams we've had in the history of Super League wouldn't have competed with that 80 minutes that Wakefield have dished up."
After Keighran was sent to the bin, Tom Johnston touched down in the corner with a diving finish, before Jack Sinfield beat Junior Nsemba from close range to score another.
They had a third in seven minutes, with Corey Hall sprinting down the wing before smashing his way over the tryline.
Ky Rodwell wrapped up the 27-point win, thanks to some great hands from Jake Trueman.
After the match, Peet lauded Wakefield, adding his Wigan side were "well prepared" but came up second on the night.
"Wakefield were outstandingly good," the Warriors coach said. "All the credit in the world to them, to Daryl. We were outplayed, outcoached, and beaten all ends up.
"Credit to them, it hurts, but the night belongs to them."
A new name on the Super League trophy is now guaranteed, with Trinity to face Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford next Saturday, which is live on Sky Sports.
Powell lauded as top coach
Powell left his role with Castleford Tigers at the conclusion of the 2021 Super League season, having guided the side to a Challenge Cup final appearance and their maiden Super League Grand Final.
He was appointed head coach at Wakefield in October 2023, and has been instrumental in lifting the club from the Championship to its first Super League Grand Final, after one of their best seasons on record.
"I think the jury was still out after his spell at Castleford," Wilkin said.
"But there is no doubt that Daryl Powell is an exceptional coach, who can get a group of men organised and directed to success.
"That's what he's done, and he's done it with such style and class.
"Wakefield play with risk and they play the game in a beautiful way."
Ellis: I didn't think in my wildest dreams we'd do that
Wakefield owner Matt Ellis heaped praise on his team following the match:
"It's still not sunk in yet. Four-and-a-half thousand fans still singing away. What a performance.
"That was the best performance in my time owning the club. So proud of them. We just nailed it today, didn't we?
"I didn't think in my wildest dreams [we'd be four scores up].
"I had a good feeling all week about it; all the pressure was on them. We came here, we were confident.
"It's a happy group, but it's an even happier group right now.
"There's so many good stories, three years after relegation, and now we're there!"

Telangana to remove eligible private properties from 22-A list
Telangana has removed private properties from the prohibited list for registration, benefiting 1.41 lakh homes and plots, amid political controversy.
The Telangana government on Thursday ordered the removal of all eligible private properties from the prohibited list under Section 22-A of the Registration Act, 1908, paving the way for their registration, people familiar with the matter said. The decision is expected to benefit around 1.41 lakh houses and plots across the state.
The orders issued by principal secretary (revenue) Lokesh Kumar, following a meeting led by deputy chief minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka, will allow registration of eligible houses, plots and flats that have valid layout, building or apartment approvals from competent government authorities.
According to a senior revenue department official, Section 22-A empowers the government to identify categories of properties whose registration should be prohibited. These include government waste lands, assigned lands, properties belonging to municipalities and government institutions, endowment and Wakf properties, surplus lands under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, forest lands, tribal lands covered by Regulation 1 of 1970, and properties under court orders or disputes.
The official said more than 3.72 lakh acres had been inadvertently included in the prohibited list while changes were being made to Dharani, the previous land registration portal, which has now been replaced by Bhu Bharati.
“Thousands of genuine private properties, including decades-old residential layouts, apartments and lands that had previously received clearances from government agencies, were brought under Section 22-A without adequate verification,” the official said.
The issue has triggered a political controversy over the past two months, with opposition parties accusing the government of harassing people by blocking property transactions. Thousands of complaints were received from owners who said the restrictions prevented them from selling or registering their properties.
The issue particularly affected areas in and around Hyderabad, including parts of Medchal-Malkajgiri, Rangareddy, Sangareddy and Hyderabad districts. When it came up in the state legislative assembly on September 16, chief minister A Revanth Reddy assured that the problems would be resolved shortly.
Revenue minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy said properties covered by the 22-A list can be considered for registration if they were developed with valid statutory permissions from competent authorities, including GHMC, HMDA, DTCP, municipal bodies and panchayats.
Owners will have to produce valid approvals and at least one link document relating to a registration carried out after the relevant approval was granted.
The government has also constituted district-level committees headed by collectors to scrutinise individual cases based on revenue records, statutory approvals, title documents and the legal status of the land.
“Eligible cases will be resolved at the earliest,” Reddy said.

US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
- Published
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Heartburn is commonly described as acidity and treated with antacids. But gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is not simply acidity. It occurs when the stomach contents repeatedly move into the oesophagus because the normal anti-reflux barrier does not function effectively.
“GERD is not simply a problem of producing too much acid,” said Vishnu Abishek Raju, senior consultant, medical gastroenterology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. Heartburn, therefore, is a symptom, rather than a diagnosis. Some people living with reflux have visible inflammation of the oesophagus, while others have symptoms without any visible injury.
GERD is common in India. A 2021 analysis of nine Indian studies involving 20,614 people estimated its pooled prevalence at 15.6%.
How reflux occurs
The lower oesophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the oesophagus and stomach. It can undergo brief, inappropriate relaxations, allowing stomach contents to move upwards.
A hiatal hernia can weaken the anti-reflux barrier by allowing part of the stomach to move above the diaphragm. Obesity, particularly excess abdominal fat, increases pressure within the abdomen, while delayed gastric emptying can increase the volume and pressure inside the stomach.
The oesophagus also has protective mechanisms. Saliva helps clear refluxed material, while alkaline mucus helps limit acid-related injury.
“People may have acid reflux within a stipulated period. But if that goes beyond the protective mechanisms of the body, those defensive mechanisms fail and the food pipe can ger damaged, a condition called oesophagitis,” said Arul Prakash, clinical lead and senior consultant in medical gastroenterology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai.
Why symptoms can be misleading
The amount of reflux does not always correspond to the severity of symptoms.
“Some people have increased sensitivity of the oesophagus, so even normal amounts of reflux can produce significant burning or chest discomfort,” Dr. Abishek Raju said. This includes reflux hypersensitivity and functional heartburn. In reflux hypersensitivity, symptoms are linked to reflux events despite normal overall reflux exposure. In functional heartburn, symptoms occur without evidence that reflux is responsible.
“These are people who may feel a burning sensation with almost anything they eat because the nerves in the food pipe are very sensitive,” Dr. Arul Prakash said.
This is one reason why simply increasing acid-suppressing medicines does not necessarily resolve persistent symptoms.
Establishing the diagnosis
A response to a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) can support a diagnosis of GERD, but it does not prove that reflux is the cause.
When symptoms continue despite appropriately used treatment, doctors may need to investigate other causes, including oesophageal motility disorders and disorders of oesophageal sensitivity.
Endoscopy is particularly important when there are alarm symptoms such as difficulty or pain while swallowing, bleeding, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting or anaemia. It can detect oesophagitis, ulcers, strictures and Barrett’s oesophagus.
A normal endoscopy, however, does not exclude reflux. In such cases, 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring can measure reflux episodes, distinguish acid from non-acid reflux and assess whether symptoms occur in association with reflux.
Manometry assesses pressure and movement within the oesophagus and can identify motility disorders. It is also used in selected patients before anti-reflux procedures.
Chest discomfort should not automatically be attributed to GERD because cardiac pain can have a similar presentation. Even discomfort after a heavy meal cannot by itself establish reflux. In people with cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac causes may need to be assessed first.
Lifestyle measures
Weight loss can reduce reflux symptoms in people who are overweight or obese. Avoiding food for about three hours before lying down can help, particularly with night-time symptoms.
Food triggers vary. Rather than eliminating multiple foods routinely, patients should identify those that consistently worsen their symptoms. Coffee, spicy and high-fat foods, chocolate, mint and acidic foods can trigger symptoms in some people.
For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed and, for some people, sleeping on the left side may help.
Complications and treatment
Persistent GERD can cause erosive oesophagitis, ulcers and strictures. It can also lead to Barrett’s oesophagus, in which the lining of the lower oesophagus changes. Barrett’s is associated with an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
New difficulty in swallowing, painful swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or persistent vomiting require medical evaluation.
For patients with objectively confirmed reflux who remain significantly symptomatic, endoscopic or surgical treatment may be considered in selected cases. Laparoscopic fundoplication is one surgical option, while endoscopic anti-reflux procedures are available for some patients.
