Congress legislator from Bandipora constituency, Nizamuddin Bhat, Tuesday alleged that Jammu and Kashmir’s dual power structure has spawned a “devil’s authority”, creating administrative paralysis.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Assembly complex, MLA Bandipora said the civil secretariat stands divided with no hierarchy and no link between authority and subordination.
“There is one elite class which is controlled by the Lok Bhavan and another class of officers which is controlled by the popular government. Naturally, there are two types of decisions,” he said.
“This is the first problem, and the second problem is the lack of power with the elected government,” he added.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Lieutenant Governor earlier held absolute authority before the formation of the popular government.
“He made the law. He broke the law. He could do whatever he wanted to do because there was one single authority. This is the nature of democracy. Now they (elected government) is in power but with limited authority,” he said.
He said authority now stands divided at administrative, political, constitutional and legal levels.
“You have divided the law as well because there is one constitution which is in J&K. We are being attributed to the Reorganisation Act. When there are two laws, there is no need to go to the second law,” he said.
About the Wular Lake, MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the lake was the largest clean water body in the world once, hosting a larger community. “But when human fiddling, population boom and negligence at the administrative or environmental level came, our natural assets suffered,” he said.
He rejected the popular notion that the lake was fed by the Jhelum, Kishan Ganga or their tributaries, calling them merely flowing streams. “Wular’s source is not in Jhelum, not in Kishan Ganga, not his tributaries. Jehlum passes through the middle. When Jehlum has a level, it comes to the level of Wular. When Jehlum weakens, the ground is visible below. So that is not the source,” he said.
The actual source, he said, was a natural, gushing, oozing spring in the Watlab area that cleaned the lake and maintained its water level as well.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Wular project was conceived at Rs 360 crore, with Rs 307 crore allocated in 2011 and Rs 120 crore released, leading to the formation of the Wular Development Authority (WDA).
“Then that Wular Development Authority was also divided. So there too, devil authority was formed again. To save this lake, Rs 360 crore was not enough money to make an authority, create human resources, infrastructure, then add inhabitants of the lake. That cannot be done in Rs 360 crore,” he said.
Asked about the Manasbal and Wular development authorities, both linked to tourism and equipped with monetary and human resources, MLA Bandipora Nizamuddin Bhat said the core question remains unanswered.
“Why has Wular lost its size and the level of the water? Why has that declined?” he asked.
He said the government has not adopted the scientific approach it should have and has failed to stop human fiddling.
“Sand mafia is either growing on Jhelum or is growing on Walur. Look at the banks of Wular; they are so deep. The sound of fish is also gone. The sound of sandals is also gone. The water is also unclean, ugly,” he said.
MLA Bhat said he raised the issue at various forums.

The 52nd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu examines the growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, including its potential applications in drug and vaccine development, medical imaging and clinical decision-making.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Abdul Gaffur, infectious diseases expert, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about the opportunities and limitations of AI in healthcare and the questions its growing use raises for patients and healthcare professionals.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored across healthcare and medical research. The episode discusses how AI could help researchers identify potential drug candidates, analyse large volumes of information and accelerate some stages of medical research.
The conversation also looks at the possible use of AI in vaccine development and other areas of biomedical research. While these applications could support research, the discussion examines the need to consider the limitations of AI-generated outputs and the importance of scientific and clinical validation.
A key focus of the episode is the use of AI for health-related information. AI systems can produce answers that appear confident and authoritative but may contain incorrect information. The episode discusses why patients should be cautious about relying on AI-generated responses for medical advice and why such information needs to be assessed against reliable medical sources and professional advice.
The discussion also examines the use of AI in clinical care. AI-powered clinical intelligence could potentially bring together information from radiology, laboratory investigations, pharmacy records and medical records to support doctors in screening and triaging patients.
The episode looks at how such systems could assist healthcare professionals without replacing clinical assessment. It also considers the importance of understanding the limitations of AI when it is used in decisions that can affect patient care.
Data is another aspect of the discussion, particularly as healthcare AI systems may involve large amounts of medical information. The episode considers questions around the use of health data and the need for appropriate safeguards as AI becomes more integrated into healthcare.
The conversation also touches on the potential misuse of AI in biology and why advances in artificial intelligence need to be considered alongside questions of safety and responsible use.
The discussion focuses on both the potential applications of AI in healthcare and the limitations that need to be considered as these technologies are increasingly used in research, clinical settings and the communication of health information.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

George Russell won the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix for Mercedes, leading from pole position to the checkered flag for the first time in his Formula 1 career. A last-lap crash by Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas forced Russell and Verstappen to slow and the Dutch driver hunted down Russell right after that, closing fast as the finish line approached.
Max Verstappen ultimately finished second for Red Bull Racing, with returning teammate Isack Hadjar completing the podium in third after missing out on three races with a wrist injury sustained in training over the summer break. He had been cleared to race in Baku following simulator work and FIA medical checks.
This is Red Bull’s first double podium since the Saudi Arabia GP in 2024.

Charles Leclerc took fourth for Ferrari, ahead of Russell’s teammate Kimi Antonelli, who started 16th and finished fifth after a qualifying incident. The Italian had a lucky day as he benefited from a string of mistakes from drivers ahead, without being swept up in their incidents.
Lewis Hamilton followed to take sixth for Ferrari, Arvid Lindblad crossed to finish seventh for the Racing Bulls, Esteban Ocon finished eighth for Haas and Oliver Bearman took ninth place to secure a double points finish for Haas. Carlos Sainz rounded of the point scorers by coming in tenth for Williams.
On a miserable day for McLaren, defending champion Lando Norris was taken out in a crash started by Franco Colapinto before Oscar Piastri went off-track defending his initial third place and ended up crossing the finish line out of the points in 14th.

There's a global pandemic treaty that's signed — and in 'limbo.' What's the holdup?
The World Health Organization adopted the pandemic agreement in May 2025, aimed at making the world better prepared for the next global health crisis — but countries were only able to get the votes because they agreed to kick the can on finalizing the most contentious details.
That can kicking has continued for the past year and half. Countries met last week for the eighth round of negotiations in Geneva, but there was little to show for it.
"The pandemic agreement is really in a state of continued limbo," says Suerie Moon, co-director of the global health center at the Geneva Graduate Institute. "The mood is somber, I think a lot of countries know we have to make progress, and yet the path forward is not obvious."
At the center of the debate is access and equity — whether countries should be obligated to share data on new pathogens with the international community quickly, and what obligations countries have to share the vaccines, drugs or tests developed from those data.
"There was staggering inequity during COVID-19, where rich countries had access to vaccines almost immediately, and were able to procure it multiple times over for their population," while lower-income countries got scraps, says Sangeeta Shashikant, a legal adviser for the Third World Network, a nonprofit. "The pandemic agreement is an attempt to bridge that gap."
In principle, countries have agreed to these obligations. And they see them as crucial to having a system in place that allows for rapid response to the next pandemic in a more equitable way.
But countries haven't been able to agree on what that system, known as the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex (PABS), would actually look like.
At the UN General Assembly on Friday, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged countries to come together.
"Although differences remain, I am confident that countries will find common ground, just as they did with the agreement itself," he said. "So today, I leave you with just one request, just one: get [it] done, as soon as possible. Further delays are not just delays in procedure or process. They are delays that cost all countries dearly when the next pandemic arrives."
Global north versus global south
In broad strokes, negotiations are generally between the global north and the global south, or wealthy countries and lower-income countries, says Moon.
"The global north is concerned about setting up a system that would allow for the continued, very rapid development of new products," she says. Such a system would involve a database where countries quickly upload new pathogen data, and scientists around the world can easily use it.
COVID-19 demonstrated why that's valuable.
In early January 2020, Chinese scientists uploaded the SARS-CoV-2 genome to a publicly available database. That early access was part of why scientists were able to develop a vaccine so quickly, says David Reddy, director general of the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations. "It worked incredibly well."
Lower-income countries see it differently. "I think they have very bitter memories of what happened during COVID-19," says Moon. "Countries in the global south want ironclad guarantees that if they share a sample or a data today, tomorrow they will get the drugs or vaccines and diagnostics that are developed with them."
These countries want to tie strings to accessing the database, as a kind of leverage.
Who wants what
Those strings could come in a variety of forms. Some countries are arguing to put all of this pathogen data in a closed database, available only to parties who register and sign contracts with WHO.
Such contracts might require a share of any resulting products to be provided to WHO at reduced cost for distribution to lower-income countries. WHO's pandemic influenza preparedness network works something like this: Countries submit virus samples in exchange for more equitable vaccine access.
Wealthy countries have already agreed that 20% of vaccines produced in a pandemic emergency would go to WHO. Yet they're not in favor of these strings as a condition of being able to use data. They argue it will slow science down at precisely the time it needs to be most nimble.
A researcher may want to study how a new virus enters human cells, for instance, to figure out how to stop it. That would require analyzing the virus's genetic data, but also data on human proteins, says Amber Sholz, head of science policy at the Leibniz Institute.
Putting boxes around some of that data creates "a huge amount of friction that leaves us not super prepared for understanding pathogen biology," she says.
Middle ground
Right now, the two sides still seem far apart in negotiations. But there are some proposals for a middle ground.
One involves attaching strings not to the data itself but to any products generated from the data. James Love, director of Knowledge Ecology International, a nonprofit, has been advocating this idea.
In this framework, scientists and companies would have access to pathogen data and develop a product from it. But to sell that product in a given country, they'd need to sign some kind contract that guarantees a degree of equity, he says. "Our proposal gives you the best on equity and the best on open science."
Not everyone agrees. Shashikant argues if manufacturers haven't agreed to terms and conditions upon the point of accessing data, lower-income countries have lost their bargaining edge. "If you have WHO chasing a company five years later, trying to get a contract, they can just say no," she says.
Negotiations are set to continue up until May of 2027, when WHO member states will come together again for the World Health Assembly.
"It does seem that countries are coming to the table with good faith efforts to try to find a resolution," says Alexandra Phelan, global health law expert at Johns Hopkins University. But she worries that good faith could erode over time. She views next May as a deadline for reaching a deal.
The United States is another wildcard. Since leaving WHO last year, the U.S. hasn't been part of the negotiations. But it is signing bilateral health aid agreements with individual countries outside of this framework — such as deals to exchange pathogen data for health aid, says Moon. She believes that could undermine the pathogen access and benefit sharing system.
"They're like termites in the wood of the house that we're trying to build," says Moon. If those termites keep eating away before negotiators reach a deal, she worries that the house could collapse. "We need a breakthrough if we're going to cross the finish line by next May."

Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala has rejected Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan’s allegation that the United Democratic Front (UDF) government was attempting to undermine the independence of the Kerala Lok Ayukta.
While Mr. Vijayan alleged that the Home Minister chaired a high-level meeting attended by the Lok Ayukta, Upa Lok Ayuktas and senior government officials to bring the institution under executive control, Mr. Chennithala maintained the discussion was convened to address long-pending administrative issues.
The exchange followed a Facebook post by Mr. Vijayan, who claimed the government was setting a dangerous precedent by attempting to bring an independent institution responsible for investigating corruption and abuse of power under its control.
‘Undermines Lok Ayukta Act’
The Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] veteran contended that the meeting violated the constitutional principle of separation of powers and undermined the spirit of the Kerala Lok Ayukta Act, 1999. The Lok Ayukta, he pointed out, is empowered to investigate allegations of corruption, nepotism and abuse of authority against public servants, including the Chief Minister, Ministers, legislators and government officials.
He also questioned the propriety of the Home Minister, who himself falls within the Lok Ayukta’s investigative jurisdiction, chairing a meeting involving the institution’s judicial authorities and senior officials, including the Director General of Prosecution. Such interactions could create public doubts about the institution’s impartiality and independence, he cautioned.
Mr. Vijayan also accused the UDF of adopting contradictory positions on the Lok Ayukta’s autonomy, as he recalled that the coalition leaders had approached the Governor to oppose amendments to the Lok Ayukta Act introduced by the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) government, alleging that they would curtail the institution’s powers. Besides, Mr. Chennithala had moved the Kerala High Court to challenge the amendments as an encroachment on the Lok Ayukta’s adjudicatory powers. However, his petition was subsequently dismissed.
Counters allegations
Countering the allegations, the Home Minister said the meeting was requested by the Lok Ayukta against the background of several unresolved administrative issues, particularly during the last decade when the LDF was in power.
The institution sought the referral of complaints and petitions against government employees to the Kerala Lok Ayukta for investigation under Section 7(3) of the Kerala Lok Ayukta Act, 1999. It also requested that the preparation of rules that govern contempt proceedings relating to the Lok Ayukta be expedited.

Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
- Published
At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues.
From the ceremonial welcoming at a military air base on Wednesday to the honour-guard arrival at the White House this morning, President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet – literally and figuratively – for his Chinese counterpart.
The public remarks from the two leaders have teemed with warm words and diplomatic niceties. In a statement before today's formal meetings, Xi announced a gift of Chinese pandas and unveiled a new student exchange programme.
"Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world," he said.
Trump, for his part, outlined some of the topics the leaders planned to discuss in their meetings, including "pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence" - using his preferred term for artificial intelligence.
"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said.
The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however – at least for Trump.
"This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability."
Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes.
In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" – a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations.
"China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said.
The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more.
On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war.
The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI.
China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to Taiwan, which has been on hold for months.
When it comes to AI, China and the US have two very different goals for any agreement on the race to develop the technology, Robyn Klingler-Vida, a professor of political economy at Kings College London, told the BBC.
"On the US side, it's about existential risk and slowing down AI potentially," she said. "Whereas in China, it's about acceleration, maybe winning the AI tech race and the application of AI to the real economy."
A number of leading American AI executives plan to attend tonight's formal state dinner at the White House, which many view as a means for the US side to tout its current technological advantage.
Muscle-flexing aside, more pageantry – and the promise of stability – may be the end result of Xi's China visit, even with additional face time between the two leaders to come before Xi departs on Friday afternoon.
"What China talks about is metaphysical and abstract. The United States wants to solve specific problems," Miles Yu, who served as principal China policy planner and strategist to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo during Trump's first term, told the BBC.
"These different approaches are not going to lead to any result."

No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains
- Published
It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case.
Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules?
Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome.
However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from City
Does that put an end to it?
Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely.
Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing.
- Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City 
  - Published17 hours ago
"I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal."
It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City.
Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford.
City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right?
Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles.
Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage.
City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.
So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules?
Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City?
Those clubs are:
Premier League
2011-12: Manchester United
2013-14: Liverpool
2017-18: Manchester United
FA Cup
2010-11: Stoke City
EFL Cup
2013-14: Sunderland
2015-16: Liverpool
2017-18: Arsenal
Community Shield
2012-13 Chelsea
Such a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments.
For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018.
Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea?
It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.
And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations?
Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.
Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023.
Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?
For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.
And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.
There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.
There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.
In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.
And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club.
On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won.
"What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added.
"It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day.
"I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."
Others, however, will insist the rewriting of history is the only way of restoring the competition's official record, and rewarding clubs that competed within the rules.
In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles.
A lawyer told me: "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's: Where does the line of people who have a case actually end?
"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals...
"It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."
Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

Back and loving it - Pietersen on his history, Brook & helping win the Ashes
- Published
Kevin Pietersen is asked, after everything that came before, what he would have said if told he would work for the England and Wales Cricket board again one day.
In 2014, he was sacked by the ECB in one of most ugly and acrimonious periods in English cricketing history – a period that brought one of the most exciting but divisive international careers to an end.
"What do you think I'd have said," Pietersen says with a smile.
Bigger stars in English cricket are harder to find.
This is the man who had a brief but high-profile relationship with American celebrity Caprice, married a pop star, Jessica from Liberty X, and once tried to explain cricket to Taylor Swift on The Graham Norton Show.
Back in the dressing room as a mentor, he is speaking to the media at Headingley - the location of his famous "it's tough being me" press conference.
The hair is greyer, but he still carries all of that aura.
"I'm 46, man," he says, asked whether animosity remains.
"That stuff is so long gone. I am a completely different person.
"I live in South Africa. I love doing what I do. I am just here to help Brendon first and foremost, help the players try and become the best versions of themselves."
My preconceptions of England 'completely different' to reality
Pietersen was the most intriguing of appointments to England's dressing room staff because of his own history, but also what he has said before.
While commentating on England's white-ball tour of India last year, he suggested the Brendon McCullum outfit were not training enough.
"Clearly the perceptions I had before being asked to do the job were completely different to what I feel now," he says.
"It is nice to being part of an England team and set-up that is actually really, really driven."
Pietersen answers every question with poise. Almost all are given and lengthy, considered responses.
His only terse response comes when pushed on what exactly those preconceptions were - and how quickly they took to disappear.
"You know what the preconceptions were," he says. "I am not going near it."
I can help these players 'stay away from the ugly'
Despite that, he appears to be loving his return.
Pietersen is "not sitting here wanting to be the coach of England" but wants to help McCullum and the players, many of whom grew up idolising him.
One of those, Tom Banton, said last week he is still in awe of the four-time Ashes-winner, so much so he was struggling to build up the courage to speak to him.
"He wants a YouTube channel," Pietersen laughs. Pietersen, a 50-over great who played in a way ahead of his time, can also help him there.
His official title is "specialist mentor" and he will dip in and out to work with the white-ball teams through to the 50-over World Cup next autumn.
Before the first ODI in Durham, England posted a clip on social media of Pietersen leading a batting session.
Holding court, he had Joe Root and Rehan Ahmed alike involved in a batting drill on how to rotate the strike against spin.
"All I want to be is a great person to these guys," Pietersen says.
"I want to be the best guy in the room, so that they come to me, and they ask me for information, and if I've got stuff for them, I'll give it to them.
"I am lucky to have worn every T-shirt an England cricketer can wear – the good, the bad the ugly.
"I can potentially help them to stay away from the ugly."
'Frightening how good Brook could be'
Pietersen's eyes roll slightly when he is asked about Ben Stokes' recent comments comparing Harry Brook's talents to his.
Pietersen, like Brook, was a maverick – a batter capable of incredible highs. Those highs mean the lows come with a disproportionate level of criticism.
"Where I can help him is playing situations, because there was a lot of method in my madness," Pietersen says.
"Yes, occasionally, I got out to reckless shots and crazy shots in the '80s and '90s but there was a lot of structure to the way that I batted.
"I've still got notes on my phone on how I played in T20 cricket, one-day cricket, Test match cricket, and about hitting straight back at the stumps, and the techniques, and how I did it, and don't play certain shots.
"That all-round structure is something I could potentially help him with because he's so flipping good.
"It's actually frightening how good he is and how good he can be."
And Pietersen says he will not limit himself to working purely on white-ball cricket.
He has already spoken to new Test coach Stephen Fleming about how he can help the Test batters during his time with the white-ball squads.
Though he said he would not have time for a full-time role, he suggested he is open to working with the Test side before next summer's home Ashes series.
"I have got a pretty mad schedule," he says. "I wouldn't say no.
"I don't think that necessarily means I need to be in a dressing room.
"There is a lot of time in the lead up to an Ashes series and a tour of South Africa, when I will be with the Test batters.
"There are conversations I can have there."
Who knows how long this will last. England may as well make the most of this second chance.

Fuel price spike squeezes French baguette bakers as heating oil costs soar
Kevin and Sandrine Luce run a bakery in northern France and are struggling with soaring fuel prices
SAINT-JUST-EN-CHAUSSÉE, France -- As the lights of their small bakery flicker on in the early morning darkness, Kevin and Sandrine Luce’s oven is already cranked up to 270 degrees Celsius (518 degrees Fahrenheit) to give their latest batch of baguettes a crunchy crust.
When the couple first fired up the oven in their store in Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, a small town about 90 kilometers (55 miles) north of Paris, in March, they paid 2,230 euros ($2,540) for 2,000 liters (528 gallons) of the heating oil that it burns. Last week, they spent almost the same amount on just 1,200 liters (317 gallons).
Fuel prices that have spiked since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28 are dealing a hard blow to the couple and other small businesses across Europe.
“Originally, it was a good deal, because initially, a fuel-heated oven is more economical than an electric one,” Kevin Luce said. “That is until the price (of fuel) increased by 50%. So, yes, now it’s not a good deal.”
The Luces aren't alone. There are more than 34,000 bakers across France churning out around 6 billion baguettes each year, according to the national federation of bakeries and patisseries, which says that about one quarter of them use oil- or gas-fired ovens.
As customers filed through the bakery for their morning baguettes, croissants and other pastries, Luce told The Associated Press that “all this superfluous expenditure on energy represents a loss of earnings. It’s salary we can’t take, it’s salary increases we can’t give to our employees. It’s investments we can’t make.”
Although inflicting pain globally, the energy crisis is biting particularly hard in the rural expanses and communities of the European Union’s largest country by area. The roughly 21 million people who live in the countryside — about a third of the French population — often rely on cars to get around, because public transportation is limited. Rural areas make up nearly 90% of France’s territory.
The so-called yellow vest protest movement, which rocked French President Emmanuel Macron’s government during his first term in office, put down wide roots in rural towns and villages, with protesters setting up camps on roundabouts.
The demonstrations, some violent, gripped France for months. Fuel prices were one of the triggers of the anger then, a painful memory for Macron’s ministers that hangs over them now, as they wrestle with renewed angst and fury about soaring costs.
The French government responded this week with its latest aid package — worth an estimated 450 million euros (around $512 million) — for people and industries battered by the eye-watering prices at the pumps. It includes subsidies for people who commute at least 15 kilometers (9 miles) to work and support ranging from 48 euros to 277 euros ($54 to $315) to assist 5.8 million families with their winter energy bills.
Martial Realland sold his home to help realize his long-held dream of owning a food truck that he drives from village to village in the l’Oise region of northern France, selling savory ham and cheese pancakes, fries and other snacks. Filling the truck with diesel costs 200 euros (around $228), compared to 120 euros ($136) before the Iran war, he said.
“It really hurts,” he told the AP. “It’s catastrophic.”
And as the fall and winter loom, he’s also bracing for a sky-high heating bill, because the home that he rents is warmed with heating oil.
“I’m scared” of that bill, he said, estimating that filling his 1,500-liter (396-gallon) tank could cost 2,500 euros ($2,847). “Last year, it cost 1,600 euros.”
With that in mind, he may not fill the tank at all this year.
Realland said he is already turning down work that requires a long drive, because the diesel that his truck burns wouldn’t make it worthwhile financially.
Christine Loir, a lawmaker from the National Rally party of far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen, said that more than 10% of homes in L’Eure, the Normandy region she represents in the National Assembly, use heating oil. The prices for the fuel are soaring, and Loir said that many can't afford to install other heating systems or better insulate their homes.
She is lobbying the government to lower taxes on heating oil, which is more commonly used in rural areas, both in homes but also by enterprises, including in some bakers’ ovens. She said some constituents have told her that this winter they’ll have to choose between heating and food.
“People are extremely worried,” Loir told the AP. “People say that if fuel prices don’t come down, they’ll stop going to work, they can't cope.”
There is at least one crumb of comfort for customers of the Luces’ bakery in Saint-Just-en-Chaussée who come not just for bread and cakes but often for a chat, too.
Their prices: 1 euro (about $1.14) for a basic baguette and 1.10 euros ($1.25) for a “traditional” baguette, which takes longer to make, aren't rising in line with fuel prices.
“I won’t change my price,” he said. “It wouldn’t be of any help. It wouldn’t soak up the lost revenue and it would be counterproductive, because our customers would feel betrayed. They shouldn’t have to pay more. They’re already paying enough at home.”

OpenAI Codex can help beginners build Android apps with Expo and TypeScript using simple prompts. You can generate the app, preview it on your phone with Expo Go, fix errors, build an APK with EAS, and even add optional cloud sync using Supabase.
We recently shared a detailed guide on how to build Android apps using Google Antigravity. That approach is best for someone who wants an affordable way to build AI apps that work.
Current Google models in Antigravity offer way better rate limits than models from ChatGPT or Claude. However, Gemini isn’t the best for building advanced AI apps or if you want to include any other advanced features in your app.
For advanced apps, using Claude or ChatGPT Codex is the most reliable option. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using Codex. OpenAI’s ChatGPT models in Codex are not free; you need a minimum ChatGPT Plus subscription to access top models. Also, the rate limits are very poor, which you can easily exhaust if you play with them for some time.
However, these models are way more powerful and currently among the leading frontier models. Also, thanks to the different connections, plugins, and MCP servers, the process of building Android apps using Codex is more convenient and takes fewer steps compared to Google Antigravity. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To build an Android app in Codex, you need:
- ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription (which you can get from here)
- An Android app with Expo Go installed – Download the Expo Go app
- An Android phone
- A free account on supabase.com – Sign up here
- A free account on expo.dev
Once done, you can follow the process below to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Set Up Codex
Step 1: First, download and install the ChatGPT app on your Mac or Windows. It is also available for Linux.
Step 2: Once installed, sign up with your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription account.
Step 3: Once done, switch to Codex.
Step 4: Now tap on New chat, and from here, tap on Choose Folder.
Step 5: Now, you can create a new folder or use the existing folder, which stores all your app files.
Create Your App
Step 1: Now, enter the following prompt. You can edit the prompt to include your own prompt. For this guide, I am building a simple Pomodoro app.
Build a simple Pomodoro timer app using Expo and TypeScript.
The app should let users start, pause, resume, reset, and skip Pomodoro sessions. Include focus, short break, and long break modes. Show the remaining time clearly, track completed focus sessions, and save the timer settings and session history locally using SQLite.
Create a clean, polished mobile UI that works well on Android. Do not create an Android build yet. First, implement the app, check for errors, and explain how I can preview it using Expo Go.
Step 2: Now, in the model selector, select GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-6 Astra.
In this guide, we are building a simple Pomodoro timer application that keeps track of your focus and how much time you have been distracted.
The latest Codex GPT-6 Astra model is very good at frontend development. Even if you haven’t included reference images of the app UI, since it is a simple app, it can generate a very reliable UI based on the prompt.
However, if you want something unique that is personalized to yourself, I highly recommend submitting UI references. It will generate exactly what you are looking for, including the font options that you used while designing the app. You can use Google Stitch to generate UI.
Design the UI With Google Stitch (Optional)
You can use Google Stitch for designing the UI. It is very similar to Figma, but more AI-focused: it lets you generate UI through AI prompts and also lets you customize with basic tools.
We created a detailed course on how you can create UI designs using Google Stitch, with 12+ videos guiding you through all the core features of Google Stitch.
If you want to quickly create UI designs using Google Stitch, you can go to stitch.withgoogle.com and follow these steps:

Step 5: To upload the references to the Codex file in the entry box, after entering the prompt, you can click on the plus icon and select Files and folders. From here, you can attach the UI reference images (Remember you need to extract the folder).

Step 1: Wait for Codex to generate the full design in the Expo app, and then you can enter the prompt so that it can show you a preview of the app. You can install the Expo Go app on your Android phone. Open the app and scan the QR code generated by Codex after following these steps.
Step 2: Carefully review everything and ensure that everything works.
Step 3: Once finished, enter this prompt to preview the app on your mobile. If it asks you to run the terminal code, you can ask GPT to run the code for you.
GPT models are often known for lying: even though something isn’t finished, it confidently mentions that it has finished or fixed the issue. I highly recommend you verify each and every output.

Once everything is ready, you can build the Android app. Since we are using Expo, the free version only allows you a limited number of builds, and afterward, you need to wait for a set time to build it into an Android app.
Step 1: Once everything is ready, enter the following prompt:
Step 2: Now, once you have created your Expo account (if you haven’t, you can go to expo.dev and create one), open the terminal in this app folder and run the following command:

Step 3: Now sign in to your account using your username and password. This is a one-time process. Every time you want to build an Android app, you can just ask Codex to use this account to build it.

Step 5: Once you have entered the prompt, Expo.dev will begin creating your app. You can see the progress from your account, or you can directly click on the link provided by your Codex platform. Once it’s done, you can see the status.

For Supabase, you can directly install the Supabase extension or use an MCP server. To do that:

Step 2: Create a new project.
Step 3: Copy the project URL ID and the shareable URL. You can watch the video below.

Connect the official Supabase MCP server to my existing Supabase project.

Add optional cloud sync to this Expo Pomodoro app using my connected Supabase project.
Keep the existing local SQLite functionality as an offline fallback. Create a reviewed database migration for user profiles, timer settings, and completed focus sessions. Enable Row Level Security and ensure each user can only access their own data.
Use only the Supabase project URL and publishable key in the Expo app. Never use or expose a service role key in the mobile app. Show me the migration and security policy plan before applying any database changes.

This is how you can easily create Android apps using Expo with Codex. Your app is just one idea away, or perhaps even one Codex subscription away, and you can get any app you want. It could be a video editing app, or the app you have wanted all the time but no developer has built yet.

Mobile retailers to observe No UPI Day on October 2 over 0.4% transaction fee
Mobile phone retailers across India will observe October 2 as No UPI Day to protest the proposed 0.4 per cent MDR on eligible UPI merchant transactions. AIMRA says the charge will hurt small retailers and wants merchant UPI payments to remain under a zero-MDR structure.
Mobile phone retailers across India will observe October 2 as “No UPI Day” to protest the proposed 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on eligible merchant UPI transactions, the All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) said.
The protest will be held on Gandhi Jayanti, with retailers planning to symbolically cover their UPI QR codes with black cloth and refrain from accepting UPI payments for the day.
AIMRA Vice President and Delhi-NCR President Tarvinder Singh said the move was aimed at highlighting concerns among mobile retailers over the financial burden of the proposed MDR.
The government has introduced a 0.4 per cent fee on UPI transfers above Rs 2,000 to merchants from October 15. Person-to-person transactions and small payments will remain exempt from the charges.
In a representation to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, AIMRA said the MDR would result in an immediate net monthly loss of Rs 2,000 to Rs 12,000 for small retailers processing between Rs 5 lakh and Rs 30 lakh through UPI every month.
The association said the additional cost could wipe out a substantial portion of small retailers’ net income.
AIMRA estimates that the 0.4 per cent MDR could impose a financial burden of around Rs 40 crore per month, or nearly Rs 500 crore annually, on small mobile retailers across India.
Singh said the protest was not against UPI or digital payments but against the additional cost for merchants.
“If we want Digital India, UPI must remain zero MDR,” Singh said, adding that digital payments should remain affordable for the entire retail ecosystem.
AIMRA’s demand is that UPI merchant payments continue under a zero-MDR structure.

The Jammu and Kashmir government has approved the diversion of 51.501 hectares of forest land for 33 projects in Uri over the 2024-25 to 2026-27 financial years, with 20.9352 hectares allocated for the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri Road, the Legislative Assembly was informed Tuesday.
The figures were disclosed by the Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Department, Javed Ahmad Rana in response to an unstarred question by Uri National Conference MLA Sajjad Shafi, who sought details of forest and agricultural land affected by government and private construction in the constituency.
The Ministry said the projects were cleared under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Abhiniyam and related rules.
These projects include work by the Jal Shakti Department, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) and the Uri-II Stage-II hydroelectric project.
The government said the diversions were in the public interest and subject to “statutory environmental safeguards, conditions and compensatory measures” to minimise and mitigate their impact.
“Under the applicable provisions, user agencies must provide equivalent non-forest or State forest land for compensatory afforestation,” it said.
If such land is unavailable, the government said afforestation is carried out over twice the diverted area on degraded forest land.
Approved plans provide for 1,000 plants per hectare and 10 years of maintenance.
Depending on the project, agencies must also fund slope stabilisation, muck disposal, wildlife mitigation, Catchment Area Treatment and biodiversity management measures.
The Ministry said compensatory, mitigation and strip plantations have been undertaken near developmental and hydropower projects in Uri through CAPEX and CAMPA schemes, wherever feasible.
The response also lists the Uri-I Stage-II hydropower project and several water-supply schemes in Boniyar and Uri among the projects involving forest-land diversion.
Plantation and compensatory afforestation sites have been identified under approved plans, and the respective user agencies or companies are required to bear the costs, the Ministry said.

An event organized by the team of Ramayana yesterday, September 26, was attended not only by the film’s actors and makers but also by global YouTube sensation MrBeast. With more than 517 million subscribers, his main channel is the most subscribed channel on YouTube. However, what was meant to be a high-profile promotional event ended up leaving several members of the media frustrated, with a number of prominent journalists even walking out in anger.
SHOCKING: MrBeast’s Ramayana event leaves media FURIOUS; several journalists WALK OUT after 3½-hour delay
The confusion began even before the event. The invite was sent to members of the media on Friday, September 25, a day before the event. What raised eyebrows was that revised invites followed within a span of barely two hours, each mentioning a different timing. The first invite stated that the event would tentatively begin at 12:30 pm. Soon after, the media was informed that it would start at 12:00 pm. The call time was then changed to 1:00 pm, with the revised invite assuring journalists that the event would begin sharp at 1:30 pm. Accordingly, journalists, photographers, cameramen and paparazzi made their way to Film City, located far from the city’s central media hubs, and reached the venue around the prescribed time.
A journalist who attended the event told Bollywood Hungama, “The event didn’t begin at 1:30 pm, but we assumed that it would start by 2:00 pm or, at the most, 2:30 pm. The publicity team was unable to give us a proper answer regarding the reason for the delay or when the event would finally begin. It was only after 3:00 pm that we were informed that MrBeast’s flight from Bengaluru had been delayed and that was causing the hold-up.”
According to a report by India Today, when journalists questioned the lack of communication, members of the publicity team reportedly told the media that they were free to leave if they did not wish to wait. This reportedly angered several journalists, many of whom decided to stage a walkout.
The India Today report further stated that when Ranbir Kapoor was informed about journalists leaving, he remarked, “Aap logon ko jana hai toh chale jao.” However, the journalist who spoke to Bollywood Hungama stressed that Ranbir’s comment was not made arrogantly. He explained, “Ranbir didn’t mean it in an arrogant manner. When the journalists apprised him of the situation, he told them that if they felt like leaving, they could do so. Even Ranbir was irritated by the delay as he had arrived before the media. Sai Pallavi, too, had been present since morning and she also made her displeasure over the delay clear to the team.”
The journalist further claimed, “The PR team was kept in the dark by MrBeast’s team, which largely comprised foreigners. They were not giving proper and timely information about when he would land and reach the venue.”
A brief event after a very long wait
The event finally commenced at around 5:00 pm, that is, three-and-a-half hours after the promised 1:30 pm start. The media’s frustration might perhaps have subsided had the event turned out to be an elaborate or announcement-heavy affair. Instead, it concluded in barely 20 minutes, with no major new announcement being made. Moreover, except Ravie Dubey, no one from the team apologized for making the media wait endlessly.
Ranbir Kapoor, Namit Malhotra and Ravie Dubey were seen lifting the ‘Shiv Dhanush’, while MrBeast enthusiastically chanted “Jai Shri Ram”. The moments certainly made for striking photographs and social-media videos, but several journalists felt that making the media wait for hours for such a brief event was unreasonable.
The journalist remarked, “The event was held at Film City, which is around 5 kms away from the railway station and nearly 4 kms away from the nearest Metro station. If the makers knew that they had such a short event planned, they could easily have organized it in Juhu or Andheri. MrBeast could also have reached such a venue much faster from the airport.”
He continued, “By the end of it, everyone was exhausted. Many journalists had expected to be free by 2:00 or 2:30 pm, but the event wrapped up only around 5:20 pm. And imagine, many of them had left their homes at 11:00 am or 12 noon. For several people, it felt like their entire Saturday had gone to waste.”

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Andy Burnham says he will show he will take 'difficult but real decisions' as Labour's conference starts
Good morning, and welcome to coverage of the Labour party conference. Or the Hope Again conference, as it is being billed here in Liverpool.
As a good Catholic, Andy Burnham (probably) believes in the resurrection and, since he has become prime minister, his party has certainly staged a miraculous recovery. When it met in this city a year ago (at a conference which ended with Burnham’s leadership ambitions becoming the subject of mild mockery from the Starmerites, and much of the media), Labour was about 10 points behind Reform UK and Nigel Farage seemed on course to become prime minister. That is not true any more. On Thursday two MRP polls showed that, with Burnham as Labour leader, Reform UK has suffered a huge setback. More in Common has another out this morning. “More in Common’s latest MRP projects Labour on 250 seats and Reform on 147, a sharp reversal from July’s projection of Reform 293 and Labour 110,” it says.
But what next? That is what the next four days may (or may not) clarify.
Burnham has given an interview to the Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, and he told her that he wants to show the public that he is willing to take “difficult but real decisions”. Burnham said:
I think the public want to see, number one, honesty about things. So not spin or putting things a certain way that’s self-serving. They want honesty, and then they want, I think, difficult but real decisions.
Not difficult decisions and making a fetish out of that, but actually grasping nettles and then moving things forward. I don’t think politics has been prepared to do that enough in recent times.
Burnham said he would show that he was willing to take these decisions.
Always in politics, there are things that you can do. The question is sometimes: Are you prepared to do them? Yeah, I am prepared to do them.
What all those things are, sadly Burnham didn’t tell Pippa. We will find out on Tuesday afternoon, when he delivers his conference speech. But he has an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg coming up soon, and we might learn a bit more from that.
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.30am: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, is interviewed on Sky’s Sunday Morning with Kate McCann.
9am:Andy Burnham is interviewed on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.
12.30pm: Lucy Powell, the Labour deputy leader and education secretary, addresses the conference. The other main speakers are Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, at 2pm, and Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, at 3.15pm.
3.15pm: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, speaks at a New Statesman in conversation fringe event. Other fringe events include Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, speaking on preparing workers for AI at 3.30pm; a LabourList rally where Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, Streeting, and Angela Rayner are due to speak at 4.30pm; and an IPPR in conversation event with Louise Haigh at 4.30pm. You can read the full conference timetable here.
Also, at some point this afternoon Burnham is due to meet his Norwegian counterpart Jonas Gahr Støre.
Burnham says he wants to reform social care in England so it works 'on NHS principles', implying free at delivery point
Q: What are you going to do?
Burnham says for years he has been talking about a national care service.
You have to have a situation where the care system speaks the same language as the health system, because at the moment, social care is charged for, provided, on a very different basis, and the two just don’t connect.
And the worst of all worlds is happening in that the care system is so threadbare it can’t support people in their own homes.
Q: Do you mean free personal care for everyone who needs it in England?
Burnham replies:
I will set out more this week at the conference, and I will set out a timetable as to how we make this reform happen. But I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles.
Burnham says he is determined to 'grasp the nettle' on social care
Kuenssberg is introducing Burnham.
Q: In July you said you would sort out social care quickly. Where have you got to?
Burnham says the government is making “really good progress”.
The death of his father, who had Alzheimer’s, has pushed him on, he says.
I’m going to grasp the nettle. On social care, when I was in parliament first time round, in fact when I was a new MP, my gran was going through the care system and as health secretary, I remember saying we shouldn’t let what happened to my grandparents’ generation …
Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that, and I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].
Labour has already made three policy announcements at this conference, before the main proceedings have already started. They are:
1) A revived version of “help-to-buy”, called “Your First Home”. (See 8.39am.) In a note explaining the policy, Labour says:
A new equity loan scheme to help first-time buyers to purchase new build homes will be set out by the chancellor at the budget next month, with pre-registration open by the end of 2026.
Support will be targeted to help those without access to the ‘bank of mum and dad’ to get on the housing ladder to buy a modest new build home.
The ‘Your First Home’ equity loan scheme will be open to first-time buyers with just a 2.5% deposit.
It will provide a 20% equity loan to help first-time buyers buy a new build home, with an initial interest-free period to ensure housing costs are affordable.
The scheme will be funded by reprioritising existing government budgets.
Developers will also contribute to the running costs of the scheme, which will give industry confidence to bring forward much-needed, high-quality new homes across the country.
2) Guaranteed jobs for out-of-work young people with disabilities and health conditions. This was announced yesterday, as an extension of the existing jobs guarantee programme. Labour said:
Under the scheme, eligible young people on health benefits will be offered a guaranteed job on a voluntary basis just three months after their work capability assessment.
They will receive mentoring and tailored support with their mental health, finances and housing to prepare them for work from partner organisations, while employers will be supported with onboarding costs.
The government will also cover 100% of wage costs for up to 25 hours a week for six months.
The move marks a significant expansion of the jobs guarantee, a government scheme launched earlier this year for long-term unemployed young people aged 18-24 who have been claiming universal credit for 18 months.
The expansion to young people on health benefits after just 13 weeks, will start from April 2027.
3) Giving councils in England stronger powers to take over empty homes. Announcing this move this morning, Labour said:
Empty Dwelling Management Orders (EDMOs) allow councils to take over the management of long-term empty homes and bring them back into occupation for an initial period of 12 months, up to a total of 8 years, but no applications have been made since 2021.
In the English devolution white paper, the government committed to strengthen local authority powers to take over management of empty properties.
Ministers are today announcing that they will reverse damaging changes made in 2012 by the Tories during the coalition government by:
-reducing the period a property must be empty before it becomes eligible for an EDMO from two years to six months, to prevent homes from falling into serious disrepair and accelerating their return to use.
-removing the evidential requirements for local authorities to provide the residential property tribunal, simplifying the process and empowering local authority empty homes officers to act more decisively and with greater speed.
-exploring further changes to protect local authorities from absorbing the costs they face managing homes subject to EDMOs.

On Thursday, the Senate health committee met with Heidi Overton, nominee for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. When asked about her views on mifepristone, a key abortion medication, Overton danced around the issue.
As the CEO of Reproductive Futures, a legal organization advocating for reproductive rights, I am deeply concerned. Overton’s anti-abortion views are crystal clear. As FDA commissioner, she would have a chance to implement them and do serious harm.
When her nomination was first announced, anti-abortion groups cheered it as an opportunity to remove access to mifepristone. The head of Americans United for Life said he had spoken with Overton five or six times and predicted that she would “expose this drug.”
With this latest appointment, mifepristone has a new boss but an old problem. Few medications have been sued, petitioned against, and unnecessarily hauled before Congress as often as this one has. For the past two decades the U.S. has probed, cross-examined, and disparaged mifepristone, despite the medication’s well-documented safety. Even under this unprecedented scrutiny, mifepristone’s impressive safety and efficacy record stands strong in the U.S. and globally.
As a human rights lawyer, I spent more than a decade working with women in Ireland to challenge the country’s complete ban on abortion. Back then, those who needed an abortion made “the Irish Journey,” traveling by ferry or flight to England, sometimes using borrowed money, often in isolation and always with unnecessary hardship. That work inspired me to launch Reproductive Futures, an organization that brings legal firepower to the fight for patients to have the option to access abortion through telemedicine and avoid “the American journey.”
The vast majority of all abortion now relies on mifepristone and patients should not have to travel to a clinic to receive the same safe, effective medications they could receive at home.
So you can see why mifepristone makes abortion opponents lose their minds.
Paired with a second drug, misoprostol, mifepristone is standard care around the world. An estimated 7.5 million Americans have used it. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends it for early pregnancy loss too. Yet the FDA has never added miscarriage management to mifepristone’s label. Patients experiencing miscarriage get tangled in the same medically unnecessary red tape — and today’s hearing indicated that birth control is next.
The red tape wrapped around mifepristone is thick. FDA regulations require clinicians to be specially certified to prescribe mifepristone. Because pharmacies must join a unique registration system in order to dispense mifepristone, very few do even in abortion-friendly states. Patients must sign a special agreement form that creates another layer of exposure and bureaucracy for them.
All this unneeded rigamarole for a safe drug, with a comparatively very low rate of reported deaths across its decades of use in the U.S., none of which the FDA can attribute to the drug with certainty. Meanwhile acetaminophen, sold next to the gum at the local gas station, is far less safe and directly linked to an estimated 458 deaths a year. Birth control pills went over the counter in 2023. Emergency contraception has safely sat on drugstore shelves for years. Mifepristone still needs a permission slip.
None of that caution is driven by the data. Abortion opponents see red when they see mifepristone because it makes abortion simple and safe, affordable and accessible. Opponents are willing to undermine the FDA’s reputation and the drug approval process itself just to take mifepristone away from women. They repeatedly have challenged mifepristone in courts. In 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously threw out a nationwide challenge to the FDA’s approval and regulation of mifepristone in FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, because the doctors who sued lacked standing.
Louisiana then filed its own suit to stop remote prescribing of mifepristone and end telemedicine nationwide. This spring, a 5th Circuit order briefly reinstated in-person dispensing nationwide, but thankfully the Supreme Court stepped in to pause that order and preserve access while the case continues.
But just weeks ago, Louisiana was back at the 5th Circuit seeking the same restrictions again, and the FDA’s own review of mifepristone has been conveniently scheduled to finish after the midterms. Overton acknowledged that the FDA’s internal research safety study of mifepristone would “immediately be on [her] desk,” and said she is eager to get to work to respond to Louisiana’s anti-mifepristone litigation — presumably to support it.
In response to that case, a biotech CEO recently warned in these pages that letting courts and politicians second-guess the FDA’s scientific judgment endangers the whole drug pipeline. Overton inherits an agency that has fired more than 3,000 staff in the past year, whose last commissioner resigned after clashing with the White House. During Thursday’s Senate hearing, she continuously sidestepped questions about renouncing or correcting the White House’s misinformation about vaccines schedules, food safety, and tobacco use, frustrating both Republican and Democratic Senators alike.
Her inability to prioritize science over the White House’s political agenda was so obvious that Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) outright asked Overton to name one thing she thought the president had ever been wrong about, but she received no answer. Overton will now be the fox guarding the hen house.
Public trust in the FDA approval process took decades to earn. It will not survive a commissioner who treats settled scientific evidence as negotiable to appease the Trump administration.
For more than 30 years, abortion opponents have harassed patients outside clinics, threatened providers, and attacked facilities with arson and bombings. Clinics were targets because they were visible. Telemedicine took that target away. With mifepristone, a patient can consult a clinician by video, receive pills by mail, and end a first trimester pregnancy at home. No hassle or expense of a journey across state lines and past protesters needed. About 30% of U.S. abortion patients now choose to receive care via telehealth, many prescribed by clinicians working from states where telemedicine shield laws offer them protections from anti-abortion elected officials.
That is what truly alarms abortion opponents: safe, affordable abortion on a patient’s own terms. During Overton’s hearing, anti-abortion Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) noted his distress that telemedicine has allowed greater access to abortion despite the overturn of Roe v. Wade, and reiterated his desire to halt it in its tracks.
But make no mistake: The horse has left the stable. Messing with mifepristone will not make abortion disappear. Care will continue, including through clinicians who prescribe misoprostol alone, an effective regimen with more side effects or new medications being developed. And some patients will access pills through other channels, without the guidance of a licensed medical professional.
While they can’t eliminate access to abortion medications, what we all stand to lose is abortion care from doctors in the US offering the best possible care, a government that respects scientific rigor and a country that embraces reproductive rights as human rights. Let’s stand strong for our rights, and circle up to protect mife, and science.
Julie F. Kay, a human rights attorney, is the founder and CEO of Reproductive Futures and co-author of “Controlling Women: What We Must Do Now to Save Reproductive Freedom.”

For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common with Antarctica and the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats.
But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of a dead rat and called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate.
“If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.”
Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found.
But as global temperatures increase, rat numbers have surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years.
Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all.
“Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide.
It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation.
In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south.
In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats.
The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found; made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents.
Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats.
But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice.
Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”
